                             Modular Koszul Duality.
                             Volume IV: Realization

                                           Raeez Lorgat




                                               Abstract

   The comparison functor
                                        Real( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) = ( 𝑑, 𝑒 )
sends a theorem 𝑇 of the first three volumes to a pair of constructions 𝑑, 𝑒 : 𝑑 produces the invariant
and 𝑒 computes it by another route. The two components are required to meet only in the invariant
being identified. Thus an equality such as a central charge formula, a Koszul duality equivalence, or
a determinant identity is tested against a construction which does not contain the formula as an
input.
     Vol I inputs to Real: the Virasoro shadow tower with Stokes pole 𝑐 𝑆 = −218/45, Borel ra-
dius | 𝜔 | 2 ( 𝑐 ) = 𝑐 2 (5𝑐 + 22)/[4(45𝑐 + 218)], Riccati equation 𝑈 ′ + 2𝑈 2 = 𝑄 𝑐′′ /(2𝑄 𝑐 ) on 𝑈 =
(log 𝐻 ) ′ − 2/𝑡 , the four-conductor split ( 𝐾 , 𝐾 𝜅 , 𝐾𝑐 , 𝐾 𝑔 ), the 𝑝 = 691 Chenevier determinant,
and the eight-form Gritsenko–Cléry spread. Vol II inputs: the SCch,top heptagon and the finite-jet
Khan–Zeng (KZ) Poisson vertex algebra (PVA) sector, in which the shifted-cotangent Batalin–
Vilkovisky (BV) action and the classical master equation (CME) / PVA Hamiltonian equiva-
lence are constructed; the all-loop quantum master equation (QME), reflected weight identity,
boundary vertex algebra, and 𝐸3 -lift remain conditional on the four endpoint hypotheses: the KZ
analytic spectral-decomposition representation (SDR), the Fulton–MacPherson Stokes datum,
the reflected weights, and the 𝑇 -lift. Vol III inputs: the two-stage Calabi–Yau-to-chiral factorisa-
tion Φ𝑑 = Spch                  FA
                    Σ𝑑 −1 ,𝐶 ◦ Φ 𝑑 , the K3 Hall–Drinfeld chiral bialgebra HΔ5 , the Joyce vertex algebra
paired with Kontsevich–Pandharipande–Soibelman (KPS) orientation data on generic compact
Calabi–Yau threefolds with Maulik–Nekrasov–Okounkov–Pandharipande (MNOP) invariants,
𝑆 3 -framing on generic compact Calabi–Yau threefold Lagrangians, and the 𝔰𝔬(4, 20) K3 Yangian
representation-target trichotomy.
     The arithmetic branch extends Real to Spec ℤ. Its boundary is not a closure theorem: it consists
of the RH-equivalent archimedean Tate positivity obstruction, the global arithmetic comparison
inputs, the local categorical and Bernstein-centre gluing inputs, the condensed-Hilbert descent
input, and the remaining supersingular or icosahedral generator-comparison tails. On the critical-
line support Γ𝜉crit = { 𝛾 ∈ ℝ : 𝜉 ( 21 + 𝑖 𝛾 ) = 0}, the ordinary 𝑀𝑡 -graph dual carries neither point
nor finite-jet Hadamard residue data; any surviving spectral-flow argument passes through a stronger
rigged, Paley–Wiener, de Branges, reproducing-kernel, nonlocal 𝐿 2 , or BV–BFV boundary topology
compatible with the post-Tate quotient.

An equality in this volume is always an equality between two constructions. If the Borcherds–Kac–
Moody central charge of a frame-shape orbifold lift is written
                                                              𝑐 𝑁 (0)
                                             𝜅BKM =                   ,
                                                                 2
then the formula is not tested by reading 𝑐 𝑁 (0) twice from the same table. It is tested by placing the
Borcherds weight theorem on one side and the Gritsenko–Nikulin denominator identity on the other.
A table may suggest the number; it cannot be the second proof of the number.
    This is the principle used throughout the volume. To a theorem from the first three volumes one
attaches a comparison
                                        Real( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) = ( 𝑑, 𝑒 )
whose two sides have disjoint mathematical origins and the same invariant as their common value. The
symbol 𝑑 records the structural construction and 𝑒 records the calculation. The intersection of the two
arguments is the object compared, not the method by which it is obtained.

The Realization Functor

1.1   Independent comparison
Let 𝑇 be a theorem in a chapter 𝑋 of the first three volumes. Let 𝑆𝑇der be the set of citations, tables,
                                                       cmp
and conventions used in the derivation of 𝑇 , and let 𝑆𝑇 be the corresponding set for an independent
numerical or structural comparison. If
                                                      cmp
                                             𝑆𝑇der ∩ 𝑆𝑇     ≠ ∅,

then equality of the two computed values may be no more than internal consistency of one construction.
The comparison used here is the stronger condition
                                                      cmp
                                             𝑆𝑇der ∩ 𝑆𝑇     =∅

together with equality of the resulting invariant.
   Vol IV supplies the pair Real( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) = ( 𝑑, 𝑒 ) for every theorem on the non-degenerate locus.

1.2   The realization pair
Deﬁnition 1.2.1 (Realization pair). Let 𝑇 be a stated theorem in chapter 𝑋 of Vols I, II, or III. A real-
ization pair for 𝑇 is a pair ( 𝑑, 𝑒 ) where:
                                                                              cmp
   (i) 𝑑 is a comparison datum consisting of the two finite sets 𝑆𝑇der and 𝑆𝑇 , together with the proof
       that their intersection is empty;
  (ii) 𝑒 is a computation whose expected values are obtained from a source disjoint from the source used
       to derive 𝑇 ’s formula.
The realization functor Real sends each stated theorem ( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) to its realization pair ( 𝑑 𝑋 ,𝑇 , 𝑒 𝑋 ,𝑇 ),
defined whenever such a pair exists.
Theorem 1.2.2 (Realization functor). .
   There exists a category I whose objects are stated theorems ( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) across Vols I-III and whose
morphisms are specializations (restrictions of hypotheses, corollaries of the ambient theorem), a cate-
gory V whose objects are realization pairs ( 𝑑, 𝑒 ) and whose morphisms are compatible independent
specializations, and a functor
                                         Real : Ind −→ V ,
defined on the full subcategory Ind of objects lying on the non-degenerate locus (1.2.3), sending ( 𝑋 , 𝑇 )
to a realization pair ( 𝑑 𝑋 ,𝑇 , 𝑒 𝑋 ,𝑇 ).

Proof. The category I is well-defined: objects are ordered pairs ( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) with 𝑋 a chapter in the union of
Vols I-III and 𝑇 a theorem-like environment within 𝑋 ; morphisms ( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) → ( 𝑋 ′ , 𝑇 ′ ) are specializa-
tions under which 𝑇 ′ is a restriction or corollary of 𝑇 , with 𝑋 ′ allowed to coincide with 𝑋 . The category


                                                     7
8                                                               Chapter 1. The Realization Functor


V is well-defined: objects are pairs ( 𝑑, 𝑒 ) satisfying the conditions of Definition 1.2.1; morphisms are
pairs ( 𝜙, 𝜓 ) of compatible transformations compatible with the underlying specialization of the source
theorem.
    The non-degenerate locus Ind is defined in 1.2.3. On this locus, the functor Real is constructed
theorem by theorem. For each ( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) on the non-degenerate locus, we exhibit:
    (i) a canonical primary disjoint source 𝑆1 ∈ {Pridham–Toen–Vezzosi, Lurie HA 5.3, Vol I-III independent comparison},
or a canonical secondary source whose labels are disjoint from 𝑆𝑇der ;
    (ii) a comparison computation against 𝑆1 that reproduces 𝑇 ’s numerical or structural content;
    (iii) a structural check that the Vol IV comparison source list for ( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) is disjoint from the proof
source list of 𝑇 .
    The construction is finite on every finite full subcategory of Ind . Functoriality under specialization:
if ( 𝑋 ′ , 𝑇 ′ ) is a specialization of ( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) on Ind , the realization pair ( 𝑑 𝑋 ′ ,𝑇 ′ , 𝑒 𝑋 ′ ,𝑇 ′ ) is obtained from
( 𝑑 𝑋 ,𝑇 , 𝑒 𝑋 ,𝑇 ) by restricting the source lists and parameter range to the subdomain specified by the
specialization. The structural disjointness check is preserved because the source lists at ( 𝑋 ′ , 𝑇 ′ ) are
subsets of those at ( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ). This exhibits the functor Real on morphisms.

Deﬁnition 1.2.3 (Non-degenerate locus). The non-degenerate locus Ind ⊂ I is the full subcategory defined
by excluding:
      (i) the critical-level sublocus (theorems valid at 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ for affine Kac–Moody, where 𝜅 = 0 and
          Koszulness fails in the sharp Koszul sense);
     (ii) the Ψ = 0 sublocus for chiral Yangians (abelian limit);
    (iii) the Creutzig–Kanade–Linshaw admissible logarithmic sector for admissible representations of
          affine 𝔰𝔩 2 and higher;
    (iv) the super-Yangian chain-level chiral coproduct sector absorbed under FM230;
     (v) the five of six constructions 𝑅2 – 𝑅6 to the quantum vertex chiral group 𝐺 ( 𝐾 3 × 𝐸 ) (Vol III
          canonical taxonomy) whose convergence remains open in the CY-C bridge theorem.
A theorem ( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) ∈ I lies in Ind iff it does not depend on any of the five excluded sectors in its statement
or proof.
    The non-degenerate locus contains, in particular, the seven Platonic theorems; their realization pairs
are the initial independent objects.

1.3     Existence of Real on the seven Platonic theorems
The seven Platonic theorems are 𝐴∞,2 (Koszul reflection), 𝐵 (chiral Positselski co-contra correspon-
dence), 𝐶 (bar-side derived center identification on Koszul locus), 𝐷 (obstruction = 𝜅 · 𝜆 𝑔 plus cross-
channel correction), 𝐻 (chiral Hochschild concentration in degrees {0, 1, 2}), 𝐹 (universal celestial
holography), and 𝐺 (infinite fingerprint classification). Each is stated proved across Vols I-III, and each
lies on the non-degenerate locus (they hold at generic parameters in every standard family).
Theorem 1.3.1 (Realization existence for Platonic theorems). .
  For each 𝑇 ∈ { 𝐴∞,2 , 𝐵, 𝐶, 𝐷, 𝐻 , 𝐹 , 𝐺 }, there exists a realization pair Real( 𝑋𝑇 , 𝑇 ) = ( 𝑑𝑇 , 𝑒𝑇 ) in
which the comparison sources of 𝑑𝑇 are disjoint from the proof sources of 𝑇 stated in Vols I-III.

Proof. We exhibit ( 𝑑𝑇 , 𝑒𝑇 ) for each of the seven theorems by naming derivation and comparison sources
from disjoint lists.
1.4. Completeness on the non-degenerate locus                                                                9


     𝐴∞,2 (Koszul reflection). Derivation: Vol I’s Koszul-reflection proof via filtered twisting morphisms
and factorization-gluing. Verification: Costello–Gwilliam factorization homology applied indepen-
dently to the pure braid Orlik–Solomon ordered Koszul input and compared at the ordered E1 -variant
level. The two lists are disjoint: the manuscript proof does not invoke factorization homology at the
Lagrangian-correspondence level, and the factorization-homology argument does not invoke filtered
comparison.
     𝐵 (chiral Positselski). Derivation: Vol I’s thm : chiral-positselski-7-2 via conilpotent CDG-coalgebra
adjoint pair plus bicomplex totalization. Verification: Lurie HA 5.3 adjoint functor theorem for stable
(∞, 1)-categories applied to the coderived-contraderived adjunction, giving the same equivalence at the
(∞, 1)-category level. The lists are disjoint: the manuscript proof is a chain-level bicomplex argument;
the Lurie path is a formal (∞, 1)-categorical adjoint equivalence.
     𝐶 (bar-side derived center). Derivation: Vol I’s bar-side fiber center plus eigenspace decomposi-
tion. Verification: Pridham–Toen–Vezzosi shifted symplectic structures applied to the mapping stack
RMap(M 𝑔 , 𝐵𝐺 𝐴 ), with the Verdier anti-symplectic involution pinning the bar-side identification. The
lists are disjoint: the manuscript proof does not invoke shifted-symplectic structures at the (−1)-shifted
level; the PTVV path does not invoke fiber-center eigenspace decomposition.
     𝐷 (obstruction = 𝜅 · 𝜆 𝑔 ). Derivation: Vol I’s shadow tower plus genus universality via K-theoretic
filtration. Verification: Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch on the universal curve over M 𝑔 applied to the
Hodge bundle, combined with the Arakelov–Faltings fiberwise Chern-curvature identity. The lists are
disjoint: the manuscript proof uses clutching-uniqueness plus tautological-ring purity; the GRR path
uses virtual-class globalization plus BGS curvature.
     𝐻 (chiral Hochschild concentration). Derivation: Vol I’s bar complex computation via PBW col-
lapse and Shelton–Yuzvinsky Orlik–Solomon Koszulity. Verification: three family-specific comparisons
(Heisenberg via Feigin–Frenkel Chevalley–Eilenberg, Virasoro via Wang BRST plus Feigin–Fuks, affine
𝔰𝔩 2 via Whitehead plus Künneth). Each family-specific path is disjoint from the bar complex derivation.
     𝐹 (universal celestial holography). Derivation: Vol II’s universal celestial holography chapter via
the 𝑤1+∞ bulk-boundary matching. Verification: Costello–Witten–Yamazaki 6d holomorphic Chern-
Simons computation reproducing the boundary algebra’s OPE via the Ω-background reduction. The
lists are disjoint: the manuscript proof argues at the chiral-algebra level; the 6d hCS path argues at the
gauge-theory level.
     𝐺 (infinite fingerprint classification). Derivation: Vol III’s infinite fingerprint classification chapter
via shadow tower convergence across 𝑟 → ∞. Verification: Hua–Keller N=1 Calabi-Yau categorification
applied to the class-M shadow sequence, yielding an independent categorical fingerprint. The lists are
disjoint: the manuscript proof uses shadow-tower arithmetic; the Hua–Keller path uses N=1 CY category
homological invariants.
     Each datum 𝑑𝑇 is constructed with the derivation list drawn from the manuscript proof and the
comparison list drawn from the disjoint list named above. The source lists are disjoint. The computation
𝑒𝑇 obtains, from the comparison source, a value matching the manuscript-proof numerical or structural
content, with source disjointness checked per 1.2.1.

1.4   Completeness on the non-degenerate locus
Theorem 1.4.1 (Realization criterion on the non-degenerate locus). .
10                                                                Chapter 1. The Realization Functor


   For ( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) ∈ Ind , the value Real( 𝑋 , 𝑇 ) exists if and only if there is a pair ( 𝑑 𝑋 ,𝑇 , 𝑒 𝑋 ,𝑇 ) satisfy-
ing Definition 1.2.1. No statement is realized merely by lying in the non-degenerate locus; the disjoint
decorator and the independent expected-value computation are part of the datum.

Proof. This is Definition 1.2.1 applied objectwise. The forward implication is the meaning of the functor
Real. The reverse implication defines the object ( 𝑑 𝑋 ,𝑇 , 𝑒 𝑋 ,𝑇 ) in V. Source-disjointness is not inferred
from genericity or from membership in a family; it is checked claim by claim.

Remark 1.4.2 (realization boundary). The theorem is a criterion, not an enumeration theorem. A Vols
I–III claim remains unrealized until its decorator and independent expected-value computation are
present.

1.5     Boundary strata
The non-degenerate locus is a proper subset of I. Each excluded sector is a mathematical boundary
stratum.

Degenerate admissible logarithmic sector
The Creutzig–Kanade–Linshaw admissible logarithmic sector for admissible representations of affine
𝔰𝔩 2 at 𝑘 + 2 = 𝑝/ 𝑞 with gcd( 𝑝, 𝑞 ) = 1, 𝑞 ≥ 2, lies outside the non-degenerate locus. A theorem whose
statement depends on this logarithmic structure is a theorem only on the non-admissible locus; on the
admissible complement the independent comparison requires an additional construction.

Super-Yangian chain-level chiral coproduct
FM230 absorbs the concrete computation of the chain-level chiral coproduct for super-Yangians into
the parity-balance super-Whitehead lemma, conditional on an explicit chain-level comparison at specific
super-algebras (super-𝔰𝔩( 𝑚 | 𝑛) at generic parameters). The independent comparison in this sector is the
comparison with the appropriate super-Feigin–Frenkel screening.

Vol III CY-C conditional bridges
Vol III gives six constructions to the quantum vertex chiral group 𝐺 ( 𝐾 3 × 𝐸 ): 𝑅1 the CY-to-chiral
framed assignment Φ3( Σ2 ,𝐶 ) ; 𝑅2 the Borcherds multiplicative lift; 𝑅3 the Mukai-lattice VOA; 𝑅4 the
Kummer construction; 𝑅5 the N = (2, 2) sigma-model half-twist; 𝑅6 the BLLPR Schur-limit construc-
tion. Only 𝑅1 is a Φ3 application; CY-C is the assertion that 𝑅2 – 𝑅6 identify as ( Σ2 , 𝐶 )-specialisations
of one canonical Stage-1 datum. 𝑅1 carries a proof of convergence at 𝑑 = 2 via the framed Stage-1 output.
The other five constructions carry 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑡 𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑎𝑙 forms tied to convergence hypotheses:
     (i) 𝑅2 (Borcherds multiplicative lift): conditional on convergence of the Igusa cusp form product
         formula at genus 2 against the 𝑅1 Stage-1 normalisation.
  (ii) 𝑅3 (Mukai-lattice VOA): conditional on identification of the Mukai-lattice OPE with the Φ3( Σ2 ,𝐶 )
       chiral output on the 𝐾 3 × 𝐸 slice.
 (iii) 𝑅4 (Kummer construction): conditional on identification of the Kummer-orbifold chiral data
       with the smooth 𝐾 3 chiral specialisation of the common Stage-1 datum.
 (iv) 𝑅5 (sigma-model half-twist): conditional on convergence of the N = (2, 2) half-twisted vertex
       algebra to the same ( Σ2 , 𝐶 )-specialised Stage-1 output.
  (v) 𝑅6 (BLLPR Schur limit): conditional on identification of the Schur-limit construction at the
       ( Σ2 , 𝐶 ) datum with the common Stage-1 specialisation.
1.6. Boundary Problems                                                                                   11


   For 𝑅2 , . . . , 𝑅6 the realization datum is conditional precisely on the corresponding convergence
isomorphism. Once that isomorphism is proved, the same datum carries 𝑟 𝑒𝑎𝑙𝑖 𝑧𝑒𝑑 .

1.6   Boundary Problems
The following boundary problems are the complement of the non-degenerate locus.
Open Problem 1.6.1 (Admissible logarithmic realization). Construct a Vol IV realization pair for every
statement in Vols I-III whose statement depends on admissible logarithmic representations of affine
Lie algebras at 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ∈ ℚ>0 with rational level. A realization functor that extends 1.4.1 to this sector
is the same as a source-disjoint pair for each such statement. The comparison must see the Creutzig–
Kanade–Linshaw logarithmic structure without using the lambda-bracket derivation of the statement;
the Creutzig–Linshaw semi-infinite cohomology construction is admissible only after this disjointness
is proved.
Open Problem 1.6.2 (Super-Yangian chain-level chiral coproduct). Construct a Vol IV realization pair for
every statement in Vol I concerning the chain-level chiral coproduct of super-Yangians 𝑌 (𝔰𝔩( 𝑚 | 𝑛)) ch ,
outside the domain of FM230’s absorption into parity-balance super-Whitehead. A concrete super-
Feigin–Frenkel screening construction for 𝑌 (𝔰𝔩(2|1)) ch at generic parameters suffices as the seed.
Open Problem 1.6.3 (Five of six CY-C bridges). Prove each of the five conditional CY-C constructions 𝑅2 –
𝑅6 of Vol III (Borcherds multiplicative lift, Mukai-lattice VOA, Kummer construction, N = (2, 2) sigma-
model half-twist, BLLPR Schur-limit construction) by proving the specific convergence isomorphism
attaching each construction to the common Stage-1 ( Σ2 , 𝐶 )-specialisation of Φ3 . Each discharge is a
standalone result: proof of the Igusa cusp form product convergence against the 𝑅1 normalisation;
identification of the Mukai-lattice OPE with the framed Stage-1 chiral output; identification of the
Kummer-orbifold chiral data with the smooth 𝐾 3 chiral specialisation; and the analogous equalities for
the sigma-model and Schur-limit constructions.

1.7   Structural Consequences Inherited from Vols I–III
The realization functor acts on the Vol I–III theorems in their stated form. The consequences below
specify the independent comparisons attached to inherited constructions.

The four-conductor split and the Koszul-self-dual trinity
Off the Koszul-self-dual locus the single Koszul conductor 𝐾 (A) = −𝑐ghost (BRST(A)) of Vol I equa-
tion (G1) separates into four distinct conductors: 𝐾 (BRST ghost charge), 𝐾 𝜅 := 𝜅 + 𝜅 ! (Theorem-C
complementarity ceiling, with values (0, 13, 250/3, 25/3, 8) on ( G, L, C, M, B), the M-row value 25/3 con-
ditional), 𝐾𝑐 (central-charge trace), and 𝐾 𝑔 (ghost-number anomaly). The trinity 𝐾 = 𝐾𝑐 = 𝐾 𝑔 holds
only on the Koszul-self-dual subcategory admitting both BRST resolution and a Borcherds-lift input
on a Calabi–Yau target.
Independent comparison. The four conductors are tested against four independent sources: 𝐾 against the

Khan–Zeng ﬁnite-jet BV/PVA sector
For finite-type freely generated nonlinear finite-jet Poisson vertex algebras (PVAs), Vol II constructs the
shifted-cotangent BV action on the half-space and identifies the classical master equation with the PVA
Hamiltonian condition. This is a constructed classical statement. The all-loop quantum master equation,
reflected weight identity, boundary vertex algebra, and 𝐸3 -lift are conditional on the analytic strong
deformation retract (SDR) datum: finite-jet quotient compatibility, image-choice Stokes cancellation,
field-parity normalisation, and self-image renormalisation.
Independent comparison. The classical comparison builds the shifted-cotangent BV action from the PVA
Hamiltonian density and checks CME equality against the lambda-bracket Hamiltonian condition.
The quantum comparison is absent until it supplies the analytic SDR on every jet-weight quotient,
proves compatibility in the inverse limit, and verifies the reflected weight identity independently of the
1.7. Structural Consequences Inherited from Vols I–III                                                     15


classical CME derivation. Thus there are two forms: constructed classical realization for CME/PVA,
and conditional quantum realization for QME/boundary-VA/ 𝐸3 .

A comparison with the global Hall–Borcherds or Drinfeld envelope is an additional bridge, not a source

the 𝑆 3 -framing through the defect-chiral model. A third comparison may test Hall–Borcherds/Drinfeld
compatibility, but that bridge is not a proof source for the Joyce–KPS construction itself.

The arithmetic branch of Volume IV carries the extension of the chiral-bar-cobar programme from

study is the Hochschild trace class of the identity on the global arithmetic Iwahori Hecke category,

a structural assertion, not a metaphor.

2.2   Form Discipline
Every claim in the arithmetic branch carries one of five tags.
Theorem. A claim stated with a proof body. In the arithmetic branch this is reserved for statements
whose proof transports from the complex case with no new input beyond replacement of 𝐶 /ℂ by the
archimedean fibre of 𝐶 .
Conditional. A claim with a complete strategy of proof and all ingredients in the primary literature,
whose full write-up requires a substantial treatment.
Conjecture. A claim plausible on the strength of multiple cross-consistency checks but without a
complete proof strategy.
Heuristic. A pattern match between classical and arithmetic structures with no derivation. Heuristic
claims are essential only as guidance, never as premises.
Obstruction. A failed candidate whose failure is a theorem: the obstruction is a named computation,
missing structure, or non-vanishing class.
    Only theorem, conditional theorem, conjecture, heuristic, and obstruction enter the stable language
of the branch. A failed candidate remains in the text only after its failure has been made mathematical.

The branch has three layers: local obstruction theory, the Hochschild-trace construction of V prim , and
the three conjectural comparison maps completing the cross-Langlands loop.

labels and Hecke symmetries; the modular 𝑆 -matrix position is occupied by the Γ-factor plus functional

2.4    Realization over Spec ℤ
The arithmetic branch puts the same bar–cobar spine, Koszul complementarity, and obstruction tower
on the Arakelov curve Spec ℤ. If the complex and arithmetic bases carry the same identities after source-
disjoint comparison, the invariant belongs to one-dimensional factorization itself, not to the analytic
model in which it was first seen.
    The Beilinson principle is the governing rule: a statement enters the realized corpus only after an
independent comparison has separated its proof source from its verification source.

2.5    Source Decomposition
Fifteen primary-source families meet the arithmetic trace construction at distinct structural joints:
Drinfeld+Kapranov, Kazhdan+Beilinson, Gelfand+Borger, Connes+Soibelman, Costello+Gwilliam,
Etingof, Nekrasov, Segal, Beilinson–solo, Witten, Polyakov, Gaiotto, Bezrukavnikov+Bernstein, Kont-
sevich+Soibelman, and Drinfeld–solo. Their common remnant is a single mathematical object viewed
through five windows, together with the three comparison conjectures above.

2.7    Imports and Assembly
This branch imports local theorems from the arithmetic Langlands programme: local geometric Satake
(Fargues–Scholze, arXiv:2102.13459), the Emerton–Gee stack (arXiv:2012.12403), and Caraiani–Scholze
vanishing. It assembles them into the 𝐸1 -chiral-algebra presentation natural to the bar–cobar programme;
the novel content is the assembly. Caraiani–Scholze, Fargues–Scholze, and Emerton–Gee develop the
arithmetic Langlands programme independently; this branch is a consequent consumer.

(VOA) structure, if sought, is available at the complex Heisenberg on the archimedean fibre; the global
object is an 𝐸1 -algebra, not a VOA.
   The Deninger 𝔽 1 -geometry supplies motivation and is cited as a consequent reference. At the overlaps
(the adelic norm form 𝜈 | 𝑥 | 𝜈 = 1, the Connes–Consani arithmetic site as a categorical base, tropical

finite theorem condition in the corresponding source family.

The Arithmetic Curve and the Heisenberg Cover

3.1   The Arithmetic Curve
Write 𝐶 := Spec ℤ for the Arakelov compactification: closed points are primes 𝑝 ∈ ℙ plus the
archimedean place ∞. At 𝑝 the completed local ring is ℤ 𝑝 , with uniformizer 𝑝, residue field 𝔽 𝑝 , and
Frobenius Frob 𝑝 : 𝔽¯ 𝑝 → 𝔽¯ 𝑝 , 𝑥 ↦→ 𝑥 𝑝 . At ∞ the completion is ℝ with complex conjugation on ℂ. The
generic stalk is ℚ.
    A function-field curve 𝐶 /ℂ carries a single local coordinate 𝑧 valued in ℂ; on 𝐶 the local coordinate
is adelic: a vector ( 𝑥∞ ; 𝑥2 , 𝑥3 , 𝑥5 , . . .) ∈ 𝔸ℚ . Every arithmetic chiral-algebra proposal must account for
this adelic local coordinate.

3.2    Λ -Ring Input
Deﬁnition 3.2.1 (after Grothendieck, Borger). A Λ-ring is a commutative ring 𝑅 equipped with ring
endomorphisms 𝜓𝑛 : 𝑅 → 𝑅, 𝑛 ∈ ℕ× , such that 𝜓1 = id, 𝜓𝑚 𝜓𝑛 = 𝜓𝑚𝑛 , and 𝜓 𝑝 ( 𝑥 ) ≡ 𝑥 𝑝 (mod 𝑝) for
every prime 𝑝.
Theorem 3.2.2 (Borger, arXiv:0801.1691; arXiv:0906.3146). . The category of Λ-rings is the category
of commutative rings over 𝔽 1 in Borger’s model: a Λ-structure on 𝑅 is a descent datum from 𝑅 to 𝑅 ⊗𝔽 1 ℤ.
The operations 𝜓 𝑝 are the ‘‘lifts of Frobenius at 𝑝 ’’ that the ordinary ring 𝑅 lacks.
Remark 3.2.3. The universal Λ-ring on one generator is the ring Λ = ℤ[ ℎ1 , ℎ2 , . . .] of symmetric func-
tions. On Newton power sums the Adams operation acts by 𝜓𝑛 ( 𝑝𝑚 ) = 𝑝𝑚𝑛 (Macdonald, Symmetric
Functions and Hall Polynomials, Ch. I §8).
Remark 3.2.4. The big Witt vector functor 𝑊 : CRing → RingΛ is right adjoint to the forgetful
                                                                     ×
functor. 𝑊 ( 𝑅) is the cofree Λ-ring on 𝑅. The ghost map 𝑊 ( 𝑅) ↩→ 𝑅ℕ realizes the Λ-structure as a
tuple of commuting Frobenius lifts.
   On Spec ℤ, local translations are replaced by a monoid ℕ× of commuting Adams operations { 𝜓 𝑝 } 𝑝 ∈ℙ ,
one per prime. Accordingly, any chiral-algebra structure over 𝐶 carries a ℕ× -action by Adams operations.

3.6   The Depth Analogy
. The following four rows name possible arithmetic shadows of the Vol I depth filtration. They do not
classify Λ-rings.
• Depth 2: trivial 𝜓𝑛 beyond 𝜓1 ; archetype G analogue (primon Heisenberg only);
• Depth 3: finitely generated image in 𝑝 ℤ; archetype L analogue (arithmetic Kac–Moody / Iwasawa-
                                       Q
  type Λ-module);
• Depth 4: higher-derived Λ-structure engaging Witt filtration; archetype C analogue (arithmetic 𝛽𝛾 );
• Depth ∞: full Connes–Consani arithmetic site; archetype M analogue (arithmetic Virasoro).
Remark 3.6.1. The depth numerology {2, 3, 4, ∞} on the Vol I side is forced by explicit shadow-tower
computation (Vol I, shadow-tower chapter). On the arithmetic side the corresponding derivation via
a Λ-ring analogue of Mok’s shadow-tower rigidity remains open; the classification above is a heuristic
pattern match.

3.8   Boundary Conditions
Four boundary conditions govern the construction above.
   (i) 𝑝-adic locality. The OPE locality axiom [ 𝑎 ( 𝑧 ) , 𝑏 ( 𝑤 )] = 0 off-diagonal requires an interpretation
       of the formal variable 𝑧 − 𝑤 at finite places of 𝐶 : see Chapter 4.
  (ii) Adelic factorization. Beilinson–Drinfeld factorization on a curve employs 𝐶 𝑛 /𝔖𝑛 . On 𝐶 the two
       candidate analogues are 𝑊𝑛 (ℤ)/𝔖𝑛 and Spec( Λ⊗ 𝑛 )𝔖𝑛 ; their comparison is settled in Chapter 8.
 (iii) Real place. The archimedean place carries an SL(2, ℝ) conformal quantum mechanics (Hartnoll–
       Yang); the non-archimedean places carry SL(2, ℚ 𝑝 ). The adelic SL(2)-automorphic picture gluing
       these is developed in Chapter 11.
 (iv) Four-archetype derivation. The shadow-tower depth numerology on the arithmetic side would
       require a Λ-ring analogue of Mok’s shadow-tower rigidity. No such rigidity theorem is used below.

The 𝑝 -adic Vertex Algebra Locality Problem

Vertex algebras on curves arise from chiral and factorization algebras. Kapranov’s arithmetic loop analogy
and the Kapranov–Vasserot formal-loop construction both remain over fields. No published construc-
tion gives a vertex algebra on Spec ℤ itself.

4.1     The Algebraic Step: Formal VA over ℚ 𝑝
A vertex algebra over a field 𝑘 of characteristic zero is a vector space 𝑉𝑘 with a state-field map

                                          𝑌 : 𝑉𝑘 ⊗ 𝑉𝑘 → 𝑉𝑘 (( 𝑧 ))

satisfying axioms that are polynomial identities in formal variables (Kac, Vertex Algebras for Beginners,
2nd ed., 1998, §1.3). These polynomial identities are field-independent, so replacing ℂ by ℚ 𝑝 as the
                                                                                      ( 𝑝)
coefficient field is immediate at the algebraic level: the Heisenberg Fock space Hℚ 𝑝 = Sym(ℚ 𝑝 [ 𝑡 ] · 𝑎)
with modes [ 𝑎𝑚 , 𝑎𝑛 ] = 𝑚𝛿𝑚+𝑛,0 and the operator product expansion (OPE) 𝑎 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑎 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 2
(singular part of the product) are identities of formal power series in End(H ( 𝑝 ) ) [[ 𝑧 ±1 , 𝑤 ±1 ]].
Proposition 4.1.1. (citation-level; Kac Thm 4.3a). For any field 𝑘 of characteristic zero, the rank-2
               ( 𝑝)
Heisenberg VA H𝑘 = Sym𝑘 ( 𝑘 [ 𝑡 ] ( 𝑎 ⊕ 𝑏 )) with standard OPE exists as a formal VA over 𝑘 .
   The algebraic step is purely formal; the arithmetic content resides in the conformal-vector scaling, the
diagonal completion, and the comparison with the local automorphic object on each finite place. The
three obstructions are: conformal-vector scaling (§4.2), coefficient-field mismatch (§4.3), and diagonal
non-thickening (§4.4).

4.2      Conformal Vector Scaling: Archimedean, Not 𝑝 -adic
The natural conformal vector for a local Heisenberg factor at place 𝑝 would weight the 𝐿0 -grading by
log 𝑝, the archimedean size of 𝑝. The question is whether log 𝑝 has a 𝑝-adic interpretation.
Observation 4.2.1. The proposed conformal vector 𝜔 𝑝 = 21 (log 𝑝) ( 𝑎2−1 + 𝑏 2−1 )|0⟩ has a complex scalar
log 𝑝 ∈ ℝ. If H ( 𝑝 ) is a ℚ 𝑝 -VA, then 𝜔 𝑝 ∈ H ( 𝑝 ) requires log 𝑝 ∈ ℚ 𝑝 . The only candidate is the Iwasawa
 𝑝-adic logarithm log 𝑝 : ℤ×𝑝 → ℚ 𝑝 , which by convention sets log 𝑝 ( 𝑝) = 0 (Iwasawa, Lectures on p-adic
L-functions, Princeton 1972, §1; Koblitz, p-adic Analysis, GTM 58, Ch. IV).
      Under Iwasawa’s log 𝑝 , the 𝑝-adic value of 𝜔 𝑝 has zero conformal-vector coefficient. The scalar
log 𝑝 ∈ ℝ is the scale at which H ( 𝑝 ) contributes to the global partition function (Hartnoll–Yang
arXiv:2502.02661 §3); it is an archimedean datum external to the ℚ 𝑝 -algebra structure. The central
charge of 𝜔 𝑝 is 2 regardless; the 𝐿0 -grading carries the log 𝑝 through the archimedean completion.

Convention 4.2.2. log 𝑝 is archimedean-real scaling data, external to the 𝑝-adic algebra structure. At finite
place 𝑝 the VA is Hℚ 𝑝 with vacuum conformal vector 21 ( 𝑎2−1 + 𝑏 2−1 )|0⟩; the rescaling enters through
                     ( 𝑝)

external grading data at the archimedean completion.

4.3     The Restricted Tensor Product: Coefficient-Field Mismatch
To assemble the local Heisenberg factors {H ( 𝑝 ) } 𝑝 into a global object over 𝐶 , one would form a restricted
tensor product over unramified vectors. The obstruction is that H ( 𝑝 ) and H ( 𝑞 ) for 𝑝 ≠ 𝑞 live over
different coefficient fields.
Observation 4.3.1. The restricted tensor product !𝑝 H ( 𝑝 ) has a coefficient-field obstruction: H ( 𝑝 ) is
                                                      N
a vector space over ℚ 𝑝 , and the fields ℚ 𝑝 for distinct primes 𝑝 have no common field extension in the
filtered colimit of finite tensor products. Forming a single vector space from {H ( 𝑝 ) } 𝑝 requires passing
to a ring (the adele ring) rather than a field.
      Three approaches address the coefficient mismatch.
   (i) (Base-extend to ℂ): Each H ( 𝑝 ) is base-extended to ℂ before tensoring, recovering the standard
       complex Heisenberg VA. The result is a complex VA carrying only archimedean data, with the
       ℚ 𝑝 -structure collapsed by base extension.
  (ii) (Base-extend to 𝔸ℚ ): Tensor over the adele ring 𝔸ℚ , which is a ring (not a field). The result is an
       adelic module carrying Hecke-module structure at each finite place; its algebraic structure is that
       of a module over 𝔸ℚ , distinct from a classical vertex algebra.
 (iii) (Form functor): Let Fields/ℚ denote the category of field extensions of ℚ. Define
       V prim : Fields/ℚ → VA with V prim (ℚ 𝑝 ) = H ( 𝑝 ) and V prim (ℂ) = complex Heisen-
       berg. This is a form (in the sense of Galois descent) of the complex Heisenberg, requiring a
       Galois-action datum and Frobenius-compatibility to be well-defined.
Warning 4.3.2. Option (a) recovers only complex data. Option (b) produces an adelic module with
Hecke-module structure at each finite place, studied further in Chapter 4.6.1. Option (c) requires arith-
metic input (Galois action, Frobenius compatibility) beyond the naive algebraic construction.

4.4      The 𝑝 -adic Diagonal: Trivial Formal Neighbourhood
The Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral bracket is a residue at the diagonal of 𝐶 × 𝐶 . On a complex curve, the
formal neighbourhood of the diagonal Δ ↩→ 𝐶 × 𝐶 is a formal disk Spf ℂ[[ 𝑡 ]], which supports the full
OPE. At a finite place 𝑝, the corresponding question is whether the diagonal of Spec ℤ 𝑝 ×Spec ℤ Spec ℤ 𝑝
admits a non-trivial formal thickening. The completed tensor product answers this directly.
Proposition 4.4.1. . The formal completion ℤ 𝑝 b    ⊗ℤ ℤ 𝑝  ℤ 𝑝 , because ℤ 𝑝 is 𝑝-adically complete

The result is already 𝑝-adically complete, so the completed and ordinary tensor products coincide. The
diagonal is the identity map, and Spec(ℤ 𝑝 ⊗ℤ ℤ 𝑝 ) = Spec ℤ 𝑝 is one-dimensional; the diagonal is an
isomorphism, so the formal neighbourhood is trivial.

Corollary 4.4.2 (Locally constant structure at finite places). . At each finite place 𝑝, the Beilin-
son–Drinfeld chiral bracket 𝜇ch : 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (A ⊠ A) → Δ! A degenerates to the locally constant structure
on Spf ℤ 𝑝 : the formal neighbourhood of the diagonal is trivial (Chapter 4.4.1), so the residue-at-diagonal
construction collapses. The archimedean place supports the full holomorphic OPE singularity.

4.5   The Locally Constant ( 𝐸0 ) Local Model at Each Finite Place
The absence of a formal thickening of the diagonal forces the local factor at each finite place to carry
only the structure available on a locally constant prestack: commutative multiplication and Hecke
endomorphisms, with no OPE singularity.
Deﬁnition 4.5.1. The local factor of V prim at a finite place 𝑝 is the locally constant prestack V prim | 𝑝
on Spf ℤ 𝑝 whose constant stalk is H ( 𝑝 ) equipped with the 𝑝-adic filtration and a compatible Hecke–
Adams endomorphism 𝑇𝑝 : H ( 𝑝 ) → H ( 𝑝 ) . This is a factorization algebra in the degenerate ( 𝐸0 ) sense:
the ‘‘fusion’’ H ( 𝑝 ) ⊗ H ( 𝑝 ) → H ( 𝑝 ) is the commutative multiplication (constant along Spf ℤ 𝑝 ), with
no singular diagonal term.
Theorem 4.5.2 (global structure at archimedean place). . At ∞, V prim | ∞ is the ordinary Heisen-
berg vertex algebra on a germ (ℂ, 0), a genuine Beilinson–Drinfeld/Costello–Gwilliam factorization
algebra with non-trivial diagonal singularity.

4.6    The Adelic Automorphic Placement of V prim
Theorem 4.6.1 (adelic automorphic placement). . V prim is an adelic automorphic object: a compat-
ible system of local factors {V prim | 𝑣 }𝑣 ∈ | 𝐶 | with V prim | ∞ a genuine Heisenberg VA at the archimedean
place and V prim | 𝑝 an 𝐸0 -algebra (Fock module with Hecke-Adams endomorphism) at each finite place.
Under Tate’s restricted tensor product over spherical vectors |0⟩ 𝑝 (Tate 1950; Weil 1967, Basic Number
Theory, Ch. VII), the system assembles into an automorphic representation of 𝐺 𝐿2 (𝔸ℚ ) with trivial
ramification at unramified primes.
Remark 4.6.2. The classical chiral-algebras formalism of Beilinson–Drinfeld (AMS Colloq. 51, 2004)
applies to a curve over a field. Over the arithmetic curve 𝐶 = Spec ℤ (Arakelov compactification, with
archimedean place ∞ adjoined), the appropriate structure is a compatible system: a factorization-algebra
factor at ∞ and a locally constant factor at each finite place, tied together by automorphic compatibil-
ity (Tate-style restricted tensor product). The global object is a spectral datum; its OPE singularity is
supported entirely at ∞.

4.7    Kapranov–Vasserot: Formal Loop Spaces over Fields
Remark 4.7.1. Kapranov–Vasserot’s four-paper series Vertex algebras and the formal loop space
(arXiv:math/0107143, Publ. IHES 100, 2004; and subsequent math/0612371, etc.) introduces the
ind-scheme L 𝑋 of formal loops into a finite-type scheme 𝑋 over a field and shows that factorization
structure on L 𝑋 recovers the VA structure on chiral de Rham. The series does not extend to Spec ℤ.
Formulating the arithmetic analogue over Spec ℤ requires the adelic automorphic structure of
Chapter 4.6.1.
32                                   Chapter 4. The 𝑝 -adic Vertex Algebra Locality Problem


Remark 4.7.2. Kapranov’s 1995 unpublished preprint ‘‘Analogies between the Langlands correspon-
dence and topological quantum field theory’’ motivates the search for an arithmetic chiral-algebra for-
malism but does not construct one. Kapranov–Smirnov’s Cohomology determinants and reciprocity
laws: number ﬁeld case (also unpublished, ca. 1995) gives an 𝔽 1 -style analogy via cohomology determi-
nants feeding reciprocity laws; this is the foundational informal reference for the 𝔽 1 literature (Manin
arXiv:1312.5160; Thas, F1 for Everyone, 2018; Lorscheid survey).

4.8   Local Arithmetic Boundary
   (i) A formal VA over ℚ 𝑝 exists algebraically (Chapter 4.1.1); the arithmetic content enters through
       the archimedean log 𝑝 scaling, which is external to the ℚ 𝑝 -algebra structure (Chapter 4.2.1).
  (ii) The restricted tensor product !𝑝 H ( 𝑝 ) has a coefficient-field obstruction (Chapter 4.3.1); it is an
                                      N
       adelic module or a form-functor Fields/ℚ → VA.
 (iii) The 𝑝-adic diagonal is trivial after completion (Chapter 4.4.1); the Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral
       bracket degenerates to the locally constant structure at each finite place (Chapter 4.4.2).
 (iv) Each finite place carries an 𝐸0 -algebra (Chapter 4.5.1); the archimedean place carries a genuine
       Heisenberg VA (Chapter 4.5.2).
  (v) V prim is an adelic automorphic datum (Chapter 4.6.1): its OPE lives at ∞; at each finite place 𝑝 it
       carries an 𝐸0 -algebra factor with Hecke–Adams endomorphism.
   The three arithmetic obstructions identified (conformal-vector scaling, coefficient-field mismatch,
and diagonal non-thickening) force the adelic automorphic structure of Chapter 4.6.1.

5.2     Why Adams is not Hecke
Proposition 5.2.1. (Borger arXiv:0906.3146, Prop. 1.2, Wilkerson criterion). Adams operations on
a Λ-ring ( 𝑅, { 𝜓𝑛 }) (a commutative ring 𝑅 equipped with ring endomorphisms 𝜓𝑛 for each 𝑛 ≥ 1,
satisfying the Wilkerson integrality conditions; Knutson 1973) satisfy 𝜓𝑚 𝜓𝑛 = 𝜓𝑚𝑛 ; a free commutative
monoid acting, parametrised by (ℕ≥1 , ×). This is the 𝐺 𝐿1 Hecke algebra: one Cartan-torus generator
per prime.

Observation 5.2.2 (structural mismatch). 𝐺 𝐿1 Hecke = Adams = Λ-ring. 𝐺 𝐿2 Hecke has two generators
per prime: 𝑇𝑝 (trace of Satake pair) and ⟨ 𝑝⟩ (determinant of Satake pair). No Λ-ring structure on a
commutative ring can encode the unordered pair { 𝛼 𝑝 , 𝛽 𝑝 } modulo 𝑆2 ; it only encodes the product
𝑝 = 𝛼 𝑝 𝛽 𝑝 and not the individual parameters.

5.5   The Angle 𝜃 𝑝 as Unramified Langlands Parameter
The angle 𝜃 𝑝 first appeared in Definition 5.4.1 as the argument of the Satake parameters 𝛼 𝑝 = 𝑝1/2 𝑒 𝑖𝜃 𝑝 ,
𝛽 𝑝 = 𝑝1/2 𝑒 − 𝑖𝜃 𝑝 . The question is whether 𝜃 𝑝 is a free internal parameter of the Heisenberg algebra or
is fixed by external (Langlands) data. The answer is the latter: 𝜃 𝑝 is the unramified local Langlands
parameter at 𝑝.
Proposition 5.5.1. (Borel, ‘‘Automorphic L-functions,’’ PSPM 33.2, 1979). In the Langlands nor-
malisation ( 𝛼 𝑝 = 𝑝1/2 𝑒 𝑖𝜃 𝑝 , 𝛽 𝑝 = 𝑝1/2 𝑒 − 𝑖𝜃 𝑝 , so that 𝛼 𝑝 𝛽 𝑝 = 𝑝 ), the angle 𝜃 𝑝 is the unramified local
Langlands parameter at 𝑝: the unordered pair { 𝑝1/2 𝑒 𝑖𝜃 𝑝 , 𝑝1/2 𝑒 − 𝑖𝜃 𝑝 } ∈ (ℂ× ) 2 / 𝑆2 .
Convention 5.5.2. { 𝜃 𝑝 } 𝑝 is chosen once and for all as a map 𝜃 : Spec ℤ \ {∞} → 𝑆 1 / 𝜎 (the angle modulo
𝜃 ↔ − 𝜃 , since 2 cos 𝜃 = 2 cos(− 𝜃 )). This is the data of an unramified local Langlands parameter at each
finite place. The Hartnoll–Yang L-function

                                                  𝑝   1 − 2 cos 𝜃 𝑝 𝑝 − 𝑠 + 𝑝 −2 𝑠

is the standard 𝐿 -function of an automorphic representation of 𝐺 𝐿2 (𝔸ℚ ) with trivial central character
(Gelbart–Jacquet, §2.1).

5.6   The Chiral Framework over Spec ℤ
The local Hecke action is now well-defined on each H ( 𝑝 ) . Their restricted tensor product is the action
of the adelic Hecke algebra on V prim . The chiral-algebras framework of Beilinson–Drinfeld over 𝐶 =
Spec ℤ provides the globalisation, at the cost of replacing complex-analytic residues by 𝑝-adic ones at
finite places.
Remark 5.6.1. The chiral-algebras formalism of Beilinson–Drinfeld (AMS 2004) requires a smooth
complex curve 𝑋 and right 𝐷 𝑋 -module structure; the chiral bracket as residue along the diagonal uses
complex-analytic residues. Over 𝐶 = Spec ℤ, the residue at a finite place 𝑝 is the 𝑝-adic residue on
the local spectral disk Spec ℚ 𝑝 ; over the archimedean place, it is the classical residue. The 𝐺 𝐿2 -Hecke
operator is a global object obtained from the restricted tensor product of local Hecke operators and lives
in End( 𝜋 ) for the global automorphic representation 𝜋 = ⊗𝑣′ 𝜋𝑣 (Jacquet–Langlands, SLN 114, 1970).
Theorem 5.6.2 (corrected placement). . V prim is the restricted tensor product ⊗ ′𝑝 H ( 𝑝 ) of local
rank-2 Heisenberg factors, each carrying a Whittaker model of an unramified 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 ) principal series.
The 𝐺 𝐿2 -Hecke action is diagonal across primes: each local H 𝑝𝐺 𝐿2 acts on the corresponding H ( 𝑝 ) ; the
                       sph           sph
global Hecke algebra Hglob = ′𝑝 H 𝑝 acts on V prim by restricted tensor product of local actions. The
                              N
                                     sph
simultaneous-diagonalisation of Hglob is the Hecke-eigenform decomposition of V prim .

5.7   The Corrected Local Model and Its Consequences
Theorem 5.6.2 forces the local model at each prime to be the rank-2 Heisenberg H ( 𝑝 ) , not a Λ-ring.
The global consequence is a Hecke-eigenform decomposition of V prim under the adelic spherical Hecke
          sph
algebra Hglob , with each eigenvalue 𝛼 𝑝 + 𝛽 𝑝 = 2 𝑝1/2 cos 𝜃 𝑝 determined by the unramified Langlands
parameter 𝜃 𝑝 (Chapter 5.5.1).
   The Λ-ring Adams operations 𝜓𝑛 on 𝑅 satisfy 𝜓𝑚 𝜓𝑛 = 𝜓𝑚𝑛 , which is the 𝐺 𝐿1 multiplicativity law;
the 𝐺 𝐿2 Hecke recursion 𝑇𝑝 𝑘+1 = 𝑇𝑝𝑇𝑝 𝑘 − 𝑝 𝑇𝑝 𝑘 −1 on Sym𝑘 ( 𝐹𝑝1 ) (Chapter 5.4.3) is strictly stronger,

Λ -Ring Axiomatic Precision

Borger’s Λ-rings encode 𝔽 1 -descent by commuting Frobenius lifts. The issue is whether the integral
lattice underlying V prim satisfies the Wilkerson congruences.

6.1   The Wilkerson Congruence and the Scalar Ring
Theorem 6.1.1 (Wilkerson criterion, Borger 0906.3146 Prop. 1.2). . A Λ-ring is a commutative
ring 𝑅 with commuting ring homomorphisms 𝜓𝑛 : 𝑅 → 𝑅, 𝑛 ∈ ℕ× , satisfying 𝜓1 = id, 𝜓𝑚 𝜓𝑛 = 𝜓𝑚𝑛 ,
and 𝜓 𝑝 ( 𝑥 ) ≡ 𝑥 𝑝 (mod 𝑝𝑅) for every rational prime 𝑝. For torsion-free 𝑅 the Wilkerson congruence
is equivalent (Wilkerson 1982) to the classical Grothendieck 𝜆-ring structure with 𝜆𝑛 operations.
Observation 6.1.2 (vacuous congruence over ℚ). Every prime 𝑝 is a unit in ℂ or ℚ. Therefore 𝑝𝑅 = 𝑅
for every prime, and the Wilkerson congruence 𝜓 𝑝 ( 𝑥 ) ≡ 𝑥 𝑝 (mod 𝑝𝑅) is vacuous over ℚ-algebras: any
two elements are congruent mod 𝑅. Under Borger’s axioms, a ℚ-algebra is automatically a Λ-ring iff it
carries any compatible system of commuting ring endomorphisms 𝜓𝑛 with 𝜓1 = id and 𝜓𝑚 𝜓𝑛 = 𝜓𝑚𝑛 .
Remark 6.1.3. This weaker structure is what Grothendieck (Rev. Matem. Hispanoamer. 1971) called a 𝜓 -
ring or Adams-ring. The claim ‘‘V prim is a Λ-ring’’ is either (a) trivially true over ℚ and mathematically
                                                         prim
empty, or (b) a claim about an 𝔽 1 - or ℤ-integral form Vℤ ⊂ V prim on which 𝑝 is not invertible, which
must be specified.

6.5    Distinction: Λ -Ring vs Λ -Module
Deﬁnition 6.5.1 (Λ-module, Borger 0801.1691 §1.2). A Λ-structure on an abelian group 𝑀 is an action of
the Adams monoid ℕ× by group endomorphisms 𝜓𝑛 . No ring structure, no congruence.
Theorem 6.5.2 (corrected form of V prim ). . The Heisenberg Fock shadow of V prim over ℚ carries a
𝜓 -ring structure with vacuous Wilkerson congruence via the Hecke–Adams operations. The full V prim
carries only the corresponding ℕ× -module datum until a multiplication is specified. On the natural
Fock integral form there is no Borger Λ-ring structure.

6.8   The Descent Interpretation Goes Through Bost–Connes
Remark 6.8.1. Borger’s 𝔽 1 -descent programme (arXiv:0906.3146 §3) characterizes a Λ-structure on 𝑅 as
a descent datum from 𝑅 to 𝑅 ⊗𝔽 1 ℤ. The 𝔽 1 -descent of V prim in Borger’s sense requires a genuine Λ-ring
structure, hence a Wilkerson-congruent integral form, which the natural Fock lattice does not supply
(Theorem 6.5.2 and Observation 6.3.2). The correct arithmetic framework for V prim is Bost–Connes
(Selecta Math. 1 (1995), 411–457) and Connes–Consani (arXiv:1405.4527, the arithmetic site).
Theorem 6.8.2 (Bost–Connes as the correct descent). . V prim has a Heisenberg-Fock shadow com-
patible with the Bost–Connes Hecke 𝐶 ∗ -dynamical system, with:
• Hecke action {𝑇𝑛 } = Bost–Connes semigroup action;
• ℚ/ℤ-Galois symmetry = Bost–Connes class-field-theory symmetry (Bost–Connes Thm 5);
• graded character = HY 𝐿 -function after rescaling by log 𝑝.
Borger’s 𝔽 1 -descent requires a Wilkerson-congruent integral Λ-form on the natural Fock lattice; the
Macdonald lattice Λℤ carries such a form but differs from the Fock lattice over ℤ (Chapter 6.4.3).
The Bost–Connes / Connes–Consani arithmetic site supplies the correct framework via tropical and
semiring structures.
Remark 6.8.3 (the three-level structure). The Wilkerson congruence is vacuous over ℚ (Chapter 6.1.2),
so the distinction between Λ-ring and 𝜓 -ring is a purely integral question. The Macdonald lattice Λℤ
                                                                       ( 𝑝)
carries the Wilkerson congruence (Chapter 6.4.1); the Fock lattice ℤ⟨ 𝑎− 𝑛® |0⟩⟩ does not (Chapter 6.3.2),
and the two integral forms are distinct (Chapter 6.4.3). At finite Heisenberg level, 𝑇𝑛 scales conformal
weight (Chapter 6.7.2), so the category HVA applies only to finite Fock shadows (Chapter 6.7.3). The
𝔽 1 -descent framework adequate to V prim is Bost–Connes rather than Borger (Chapter 6.8.2).

7.6   The Jordan Hall algebra and the prime sector
The Jordan quiver has one vertex and one loop. Its dimension-𝑛 representation stack is [End(ℂ𝑛 )/GL𝑛 ].
With zero potential and rational coefficients, its cohomological Hall algebra records extensions of such
representations.
Proposition 7.6.1 (the Jordan prime sector). The Jordan CoHA is H 𝐽 = ℚ[ 𝑒0 , 𝑒1 , 𝑒2 , . . .], where
𝑒 𝑘 has representation-dimension degree one and cohomological degree 2𝑘 . Its cohomological-degree-zero
subalgebra is ℚ[ 𝑒0 ]. If 𝑒0𝑛 is assigned energy 𝑛 log 𝑝 and these monomials form an orthonormal basis, its
thermal trace is (1 − 𝑝 − 𝛽 ) −1 for 𝛽 > 0.

Proof. Equivariant contractibility identifies the dimension-𝑛 summand with ℚ[ 𝑥1 , . . . , 𝑥𝑛 ]𝔖𝑛 , where
| 𝑥 𝑖 | = 2. Kontsevich–Soibelman’s shuffle formula has factor one for the Jordan quiver. Thus prod-
ucts of the dimension-one classes 𝑒 𝑘 = 𝑥 𝑘 give the monomial symmetric basis with nonzero factorial
factors. Over ℚ they freely generate a polynomial algebra. The only degree-zero generator is 𝑒0 , and
summing 𝑛 ≥0 𝑝 − 𝑛𝛽 gives the trace. The full shuffle calculation and its coefficient restriction are proved
             P
in Proposition 17.11.1; see also Kontsevich–Soibelman, arXiv:1006.2706, §§2.4–2.5, pp. 11–14.

   The arithmetic factor therefore uses a specified subalgebra of the rational Jordan CoHA. The full
algebra has infinitely many generators already in dimension degree one, so assigning the energy log 𝑝 to
that whole component gives infinite multiplicity and no finite thermal trace.
Proposition 7.6.2 (the local spectral measures differ). On the prime sector of the preceding
proposition, the normalized thermal spectral measure of the energy operator is

7.10    Structural Conclusions
   (i) Bost–Connes 𝐶ℚ∗ carries 𝜁 ( 𝛽 ) as KMS partition function (Chapter 7.1.2).
  (ii) The Heisenberg CCR and Toeplitz–Cuntz relations are structurally distinct operator algebras;
       the Fock-space projections determine the representation, and the Bost–Connes action on V prim
       factors through the zero-mode lattice (Chapter 7.2.2).
 (iii) Bost–Connes acts faithfully on the zero-mode lattice 𝐿 ⊂ V prim ; the off-lattice states lie outside
       the Bost–Connes orbit (Chapter 7.3.2, Chapter 7.3.3).
            prim
 (iv) V𝑁       (Bost–Connes module) ⊗ (universal Heisenberg): arithmetic content on the left,
      Heisenberg-cover structure on the right (Chapter 7.4.1).
  (v) The degree-zero Jordan-CoHA sector has the Bost–Connes prime Euler factor. Its thermal en-
      ergy measure is discrete, whereas the Kesten–McKay spherical adjacency measure is continuous
      (Proposition 7.6.1 and Proposition 7.6.2).
 (vi) Connes–Marcolli 𝐻 𝐻 • ( 𝐶ℚ∗ ) concentrates in degrees {0, 1}, sharpening Theorem Harith
      (Chapter 7.7.1).
(vii) The finite Heisenberg covers lie in archetype G with 𝜅 = 𝜋 ( 𝑁 ), 𝑟max = 2; the B-row threshold
      requires Borcherds-product encoding of Hecke data (Chapter 7.8.2).
  The vertex algebra structure is universal and non-arithmetic because it belongs only to the finite
Heisenberg covers. The arithmetic content is carried by the Bost–Connes 𝐶 ∗ -algebra factor and by the
Hochschild trace class. A genuine VA-arithmetic object encoding Hecke eigenvalues in the stress tensor
would be a new object, not V prim .

Adelic Factorization Axioms

Beilinson–Drinfeld and Costello–Gwilliam factorization require a space with a meaningful configu-
ration theory. On 𝐶 = Spec ℤ the finite places are discrete and the archimedean place carries the only
chiral singularity.

8.1   The Ran Space of Spec ℤ
Observation 8.1.1 (naive Ran is terminal). BD §3.4.1 defines Ran( 𝑋 ) for 𝑋 a smooth curve over a field
𝑘 as the prestack whose 𝑆 -points for a 𝑘 -test scheme 𝑆 are non-empty finite subsets of 𝑋 ( 𝑆 ). For
𝑋 = Spec ℤ, the functor of points is

                         𝑆 ↦→ Spec ℤ( 𝑆 ) = HomRing (ℤ, Γ ( 𝑆, O𝑆 )) = {∗}

(singleton). The naive Ran space of Spec ℤ is therefore the terminal prestack; a single point. Primes are
not sections; they are closed points, i.e., morphisms Spec 𝔽 𝑝 → Spec ℤ going the wrong way for the
functor-of-points definition.
Deﬁnition 8.1.2 (enriched Ran on Arakelov curve). On the Arakelov-compactified curve 𝐶 = Spec ℤ,
redefine the Ran space combinatorially:

                        Ran( 𝐶 ) ( 𝑅) = {non-empty finite multisets Σ ⊂ | 𝐶 |}

for 𝑅 = ℚ-points (or more generally a ℚ-algebra). Topology: ind-set lim Sym𝑛 (ℙ ⊔ {∞}), where
                                                                         −→𝑛
ℙ denotes the set of rational primes. This is a discrete combinatorial object; no scheme structure, no
tangent space.
Remark 8.1.3. Ran( 𝐶 ) is discrete. BD factorization axioms applied to a discrete Ran space become set-
theoretic identities carrying no infinitesimal content. The OPE singularity structure at the diagonal is the
content of BD factorization; on a discrete Ran space, the diagonal has no infinitesimal neighbourhood
and the content vanishes.

8.2   The Factorization Isomorphism Is Trivial

8.4    The Locally Constant ( 𝐸0 ) Factorization at Each Finite Place
Proposition 8.4.1 (Francis arXiv:1206.5522 §2.3; Lurie HA 5.5.4.10). . A locally constant factoriza-
tion algebra on a topological manifold 𝑀 factors through the homotopy type of 𝑀 , equivalently is an
𝐸𝑛 -algebra for 𝑛 = dim 𝑀 (Francis arXiv:1206.5522 §2.3; Lurie HA 5.5.4.10). On a totally disconnected
space like Spf ℤ 𝑝 , locally constant factorization degenerates to an 𝐸0 -algebra (a pointed vector space).
Deﬁnition 8.4.2 (minimal adelic factorization structure). The minimal Costello–Gwilliam-compatible
adelic structure on V prim is:
• At ∞: genuine holomorphic factorization algebra on ℂ∞ in the CG sense (Vol. I Def. 3.1.4), with

  phism 𝜓 𝑝 ; this is an 𝐸0 -algebra.
• Gluing data: restricted tensor product over spherical vectors |0⟩ 𝑝 via Tate’s thesis, giving an automor-
  phic representation of 𝐺 𝐿2 (𝔸ℚ ).

8.7   Classical Factorization at Finite Places: Absence of a BV Action
      Functional

Observation 8.7.2 (arithmetic differential forms and the free-ﬁeld obstruction). The sheaf of Kähler

Remark 8.7.3. The Borger Λ-ring formalism (Borger arXiv:0906.3146) supplies the test for Frobenius

Theorem 8.7.4 (finite-place Adams structure). . At a finite place 𝑝, H ( 𝑝 ) is a classical commutative

action functional whose BV-quantization would produce a quantum factorization algebra does not exist
over Spf ℤ 𝑝 .

     (i) The naive Ran space Ran( 𝐶 ) as a BD prestack is terminal; the enriched combinatorial Ran is
         discrete (Chapter 8.1.1, Chapter 8.1.2).

 (iv) At each finite place 𝑝, locally constant factorization on Spf ℤ 𝑝 is an 𝐸0 -algebra; at ∞, the

   The Costello–Gwilliam window of V prim is a holomorphic factorization algebra on ℂ∞ with an

DAHA, Macdonald, and the Parameter
Non-Uniformity

Macdonald theory, DAHA, and elliptic Hall algebras depend on uniform parameters. The primon
construction carries a prime-indexed family of parameters, and this non-uniformity is the obstruction.

9.1   Macdonald ( 𝑞, 𝑡 ) and the Prime-Indexed Alphabet

9.3   DAHA Parameters and the Arithmetic Hall Algebra
The per-prime ( 𝑞 𝑝 , 𝑡 𝑝 ) framework raises the question of whether these parameters can be assembled
into a single double affine Hecke algebra. The rank constraint of DAHA forecloses this.
Theorem 9.3.1 (DAHA rank constraint). (Cherednik, Double Aﬃne Hecke Algebras, CUP 2005,
§1.4). The double affine Hecke algebra (DAHA) ℍ( 𝑞, 𝑡 ) of type 𝐴𝑛−1 has two parameters ( 𝑞, 𝑡 ) and
acts on ℂ[ 𝑥1± , . . . , 𝑥𝑛± ] via Dunkl–Cherednik operators.
Observation 9.3.2 (DAHA-Adams incompatibility). Hecke–Adams operators 𝜓𝑛 act uniformly on Λ
and do not distinguish primes; DAHA Dunkl operators are 𝑊 -equivariant for the Weyl group 𝑊
acting symmetrically. The prime stratification of Λprim = ′𝑝 Λ ( 𝑝 ) lives in the tensor-indexing, outside
                                                         N
the 𝑊 -action; the two structures occupy distinct tensorial positions.
   The correct object at each prime is the spherical elliptic Hall algebra of Schiffmann–Vasserot. Its
degeneration is used only as a rank-one Hall degeneration; no prime is a DAHA rank.

9.4    Shuffle Structure Is Uncoupled Across Primes
By construction (Chapter 9.3.4), the shuffle kernel at a single prime is 𝜔 𝑝 , while the kernel between
distinct primes is 1. This factorisation is a theorem, not merely a definition: it rules out cross-prime
algebraic interactions.
Theorem 9.4.1. . The shuffle structure on ℍarith (Chapter 9.3.4) factors across primes: for 𝑝 ≠ ℓ , the
shuffle kernel is trivial (= 1). Primes enter only as labels on non-interacting copies of the same shuffle
data; there are no cross-prime shuffle relations.
Remark 9.4.2. Primes enter V prim as labels on non-interacting copies of the same Heisenberg data. The
non-triviality of the ( 𝑞 𝑝 , 𝑡 𝑝 )-deformation is internal to each prime factor; the arithmetic content sits in
the tensor-indexing over primes, not in algebraic interactions across them.

The Arithmetic Modular Functor

Segal’s modular functor assigns conformal blocks to marked Riemann surfaces and uses sewing along
circles. The arithmetic curve has no such sewing category. Tate theory supplies the object occupying the
same formal position.

11.1   Axioms and Their Translation
Each Segal axiom for a Riemann surface Σ 𝑔,𝑛 – finiteness of conformal blocks, sewing along circles,
modular invariance, and the partition-function trace – has an arithmetic analogue on the Arakelov curve
(Spec O𝐾 , 𝑆 ). The entries below are a dictionary of roles. They are not literal identifications of the two
categories.

11.4   Arithmetic Symmetries
Observation 11.4.1. The arithmetic symmetry group has two complementary actions. The Galois group
Gal( 𝐾 / 𝐾 ) controls label permutations: it acts on Weil–Deligne parameters at marked places, the
arithmetic counterpart of the deck transformations on the geometric surface. The adelic quotient
GL𝑛 (𝔸 𝐾 )/GL𝑛 ( 𝐾 ) acts through Hecke correspondences on automorphic lines. This pair is the arith-
metic replacement for the geometric mapping-class action; it is not a mapping class group of a surface.
Theorem 11.4.2 (arithmetic symmetry action). . There is an arithmetic symmetry action in which
Gal( 𝐾 / 𝐾 ) acts on local Langlands labels and GL𝑛 (𝔸 𝐾 ) acts by Hecke correspondences. At an unram-
ified prime 𝑝, Frobenius generates the quotient Gal( 𝑘¯ 𝑝 /𝑘 𝑝 )  ℤ.

of local monodromy; the inertia and wild inertia are not Dehn twists and are not discarded in ramified
sewing.

11.7    Functional Equation as Sewing Axiom
Theorem 11.7.1 (Tate’s global functional equation). .
   Let Λ ( 𝑠, 𝜒 ) denote the completed Dirichlet 𝐿 -function with its conductor and parity-dependent
archimedean factor. Then
                                  Λ ( 𝑠, 𝜒 ) = 𝜀 ( 𝜒 ) · Λ (1 − 𝑠, 𝜒 −1 ) ,
where 𝜀 ( 𝜒 ) is the root number, proved by adelic Poisson summation (Tate’s thesis, §4.4). The arithmetic
analogue of Segal sewing is the functional equation.
Remark 11.7.2 (ﬁniteness reading). The content of sewing is not dimension 1 per se; it is the 𝑠 ↔ 1 − 𝑠
involution on the one-dimensional line whose invariants are the values of the completed 𝐿 -function.

(A1) Finiteness. F ( 𝑋 , 𝑆, { 𝜒𝔭 }) is a 1-dimensional meromorphic line, with pole divisor prescribed by
the completed 𝐿 -function represented by the line.

(A2) Factorization.   For independent places, F ( 𝑋 , 𝑆, { 𝜒𝔭 }) =            𝔭∈ 𝑆 F𝔭 ( 𝜒𝔭 ).

(A3) Weil–Deligne sewing.    For 𝑆 = 𝑆1 ⊔ 𝑆2 along a parameter ( 𝜌, 𝑁 ) at an extra prime 𝔮,
                                   ∑︁
              F ( 𝑋 , 𝑆 ∪ {𝔮}) =        F ( 𝑋 1 , 𝑆1 ∪ ( 𝜌, 𝑁 )) · F ( 𝑋 2 , 𝑆2 ∪ ( 𝜌, 𝑁 )) −1 ,
                                      ( 𝜌,𝑁 )

                            F ( 𝑋 , 𝑆, 𝜒 ) ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜀 ( 𝜒 ) · F ( 𝑋 , 𝑆, 𝜒 −1 ) (1 − 𝑠 ) .

Theorem 11.8.2 (Tate line in the arithmetic Segal position). (Tate’s thesis). Tate’s adelic construc-
tion gives a meromorphic 𝐿 -line satisfying (A1)–(A5) in the zeta and Dirichlet sectors. No uniqueness
is asserted before the source category and the local test-line normalizations are fixed.
    The geometric and arithmetic Segal functors are different functors. The conjecture says that Tate’s
𝐿 -functor satisfies the arithmetic axioms occupying the Segal positions.
Chapter 12


Arithmetic Bar–Cobar and Parshin–Gersten

The chiral bar–cobar adjunction on a complex curve is replaced, over Spec ℤ, by an ordered Parshin–
Gersten complex. The de Rham differential is replaced by boundary maps in the arithmetic flag complex.

12.1   The Configuration Space Is Discrete
Observation 12.1.1. Conf 𝑛 (Spec ℤ) = {(𝔭1 , . . . , 𝔭𝑛 ) : 𝔭𝑖 ≠ 𝔭𝑗 } is a countable discrete set of 𝑛-tuples of
distinct closed points; the collision locus Δ is a union of isolated points, and convergence to Δ is a 𝑝-adic
limit, not complex-analytic.
Deﬁnition 12.1.2 (arithmetic conﬁguration space). The arithmetic configuration space is the incidence
poset of finite subsets of | 𝐶 |, ordered by inclusion. Forms are combinatorial (elements of an order
complex). The Arnold relation lifts to the braiding relation in the Grothendieck–Teichmüller Lie algebra
at Spec ℤ, controlled by Ihara–Deligne motivic fundamental group 𝜋1mot (Spec ℤ \ { 𝑝1 , . . . , 𝑝𝑛 }).

𝑑 log( 𝑝 − 𝑞 ).

12.7   Arithmetic Positselski

conditional on vanishing of the Koszul homology in positive degree. The arithmetic avatar replaces the
Koszul condition by vanishing of the Iwasawa 𝜇-invariant.

    (i) Configuration space is discrete; Arnold relation lifts to Steinberg { 𝑝, 1 − 𝑝 } = 0 (Chapter 12.2.2).

        (Chapter 12.6.1).
(viii) Arithmetic Positselski holds precisely when 𝜇-invariant = 0 (Chapter 24.1.5).
   The five theorems of the programme survive the arithmetic deformation, interpreted as: configuration
space = Parshin–Gersten; Arnold = Steinberg; D-module purity = Deligne Frobenius purity; 𝜇 = 0 =
conilpotence; arithmetic G-row complementarity = functional equation of 𝜁 .
Chapter 13


The Automorphic Vertex of the Langlands–TQFT
Triangle

Kapustin–Witten realizes geometric Langlands as 𝑆 -duality in N = 4 gauge theory on Σ × 𝐶 . The
arithmetic trace class has a different problem: whether the Hartnoll–Yang BKL–primon correspondence
supplies a bulk theory at all.
    V prim is a Hochschild trace class whose graded character is 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ). Three TQFT frameworks (Kapustin–
Witten, Beem–Lemos–Liendo–Peelaers–Rastelli–van Rees (BLLPRvR), and Chern–Simons/WZW)
offer candidate TQFT-bulk structures for the Langlands triangle. Each fails at a specific structural ob-
struction, placing V prim on the automorphic vertex rather than the TQFT vertex.

13.1   The Kapustin–Witten Obstruction: Absence of Complex Structure
Theorem 13.1.1 (Kapustin–Witten setup). . Geometric Langlands for 𝐶 /ℂ arises as S-duality of
4D N = 4 super Yang–Mills (SYM) on Σ × 𝐶 with Σ topologically twisted and 𝐶 holomorphically
twisted. Categories 𝐷 (Bun𝐺 ) and QCoh(Loc 𝐿 𝐺 ) appear as boundary conditions; S-duality 𝜏 ↦→ −1/ 𝜏
exchanges them.
Observation 13.1.2 (arithmetic obstruction). 𝐶 = Spec ℤ is an arithmetic 1-scheme with closed-point
residue fields 𝔽 𝑝 at each prime 𝑝, plus the archimedean place. The holomorphic twist of N = 4 super
Yang–Mills requires a complex structure on the compactified direction; Spec ℤ carries no such structure,
its closed fibres being spectra of finite fields rather than complex-analytic curves.
Corollary 13.1.3 (Kapustin–Witten is undefined over ℤ). . The expression ‘‘N = 4 SYM on
Σ × Spec ℤ’’ names no defined theory in 2026’s mathematics. The Kapustin–Witten holomorphic twist
requires a complex structure on the compactified direction; the topological Σ-coupling and the S-duality
𝜏 ↦→ −1/ 𝜏 are consequences. The arithmetic compactification Spec ℤ admits no such structure.

13.2    The BLLPRvR Obstruction: Infinite Flavour Rank
Theorem 13.2.1 (BLLPRvR, arXiv:1312.5344). . The Beem–Lemos–Liendo–Peelaers–Rastelli–van
Rees (BLLPRvR) correspondence assigns a vertex algebra (VA) 𝜒 (T ) to any 4D N = 2 superconformal
field theory (SCFT) T , with central charges satisfying 𝑐2𝑑 = −12𝑐4𝑑 and 𝑘2𝑑 = − 21 𝑘4𝑑 .
Observation 13.2.2. The finite Heisenberg covers of the primon construction are generated by the modes
{𝑎 }               for a finite set of primes 𝑆 . The formal cover over all primes would have flavour group

   𝑝 ∈ℙ 𝑈 (1) 𝑝 , hence flavour rank ℵ0 . The Hochschild trace class V
the scalar 𝑟 𝜁 = 2 of Chapter 14 is a determinant-rank residue rather than a two-dimensional central
charge. No 4D N = 2 SCFT has flavour symmetry of rank ℵ0 : the flavour rank is bounded by the gauge
rank plus hypermultiplet content, both finite for any theory with a Lagrangian description.

Corollary 13.2.3. . The VA 𝜒 (T ) assigned by BLLPRvR to any 4D N = 2 SCFT T has finite flavour
rank. The all-prime Heisenberg cover has countable flavour rank, while V prim is only its Hochschild
trace class. Hence no BLLPRvR vertex algebra of a 4D N = 2 SCFT is V prim . The class-S construction
on an infinite-genus or infinite-puncture arithmetic curve would require Spec ℤ to carry the complex
structure of a Riemann surface, obstructed by Chapter 13.1.2.

13.3   The Chern–Simons Obstruction: Irrational Levels
Observation 13.3.1 (non-integer level). Witten’s Chern–Simons/WZW correspondence gives 𝐶 𝑆𝑘 ( 𝐺 )
on Σ × ℝ with boundary vertex operator algebra (VOA) 𝑉𝑘 (𝔤) at integer level 𝑘 ∈ ℤ. A boundary

Corollary 13.3.2. . No finite-level abelian Chern–Simons theory has a boundary vertex algebra
whose all-prime Hochschild trace is V prim .

13.4   The Belinski–Khalatnikov–Lifshitz Billiard: Thermodynamic
       Coarse-Graining
Observation 13.4.1 (Selberg scattering versus primon partition). The Selberg trace formula on SL(2, ℤ)\ℍ2
expresses the spectral density of the Laplacian as a sum over Maass cusp forms plus a continuous Eisen-
stein series contribution. The Eisenstein scattering phase is 𝜁 (2 𝑖𝑡 )/ 𝜁 (2 𝑖𝑡 + 1) on the critical line, a
scattering-matrix entry; the primon partition function is 𝑝 (1 − 𝑝 − 𝑠 ) −1 = 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ), with pole at 𝑠 = 1. The
                                                             Q
two occurrences of 𝜁 are structurally distinct: scattering amplitude versus thermodynamic partition
function.
Theorem 13.4.2 (Hartnoll–Yang: thermodynamic coarse-graining). (Hartnoll–Yang
arXiv:2502.02661, §3). The primon–Belinski–Khalatnikov–Lifshitz (BKL) correspondence is a
thermodynamic coarse-graining: at high temperature, the Selberg continuous spectrum above
eigenvalue 1/4 is replaced by the primon oscillator count. The spectral match is asymptotic, not exact.

13.6   Asymptotic Symmetries at the BKL End-of-Time Boundary
Proposition 13.6.1 (Damour–Henneaux–Nicolai hep-th/0207267). . BKL dynamics for 4D pure
gravity on 𝑇 3 reduces to null billiards on the Weyl chamber of 𝐴𝐸3 , a rank-3 hyperbolic Kac–Moody
algebra; the fundamental domain is a modification of SL2 (ℤ)\ℍ2 .

Observation 13.6.2 (rank obstruction for 𝐴𝐸3 ). A soft-mode algebra at the BKL end-of-time boundary
decomposes into Weyl-group representations of 𝑊 ( 𝐴𝐸3 ), where 𝐴𝐸3 has root lattice of rank 3. The
primon Heisenberg algebra is generated by { 𝑎 𝑝,𝑛 } 𝑝 ∈ℙ,𝑛 ∈ℤ , with generator index set of cardinality ℵ0 . The
two index sets are incommensurable; V prim is the bosonic Fock quantisation of the Eisenstein continuous
sector of the gravitational superspace, not the full 𝑊 ( 𝐴𝐸3 ) soft-mode algebra. The Hartnoll–Yang
thermodynamic match (Chapter 13.4.2) is a coarse-graining of the Eisenstein density of states, not a
spectral identification.

13.7    The Vol III Φ 𝑑 Functor: Arithmetic Domain Boundary
Observation 13.7.1. Vol III’s functor Φ𝑑 = Spch
                                             Σ               ◦ ΦFA takes a Calabi–Yau 𝑑 -fold over ℂ as input.
                                                   𝑑 −1 ,𝐶      𝑑
Spec ℤ is an arithmetic 1-scheme over ℤ; it admits no Calabi–Yau structure. The functor Φ𝑑 is therefore
defined on the ℂ-analytic locus of the programme, with Spec ℤ outside its domain.
Remark 13.7.2. When a Calabi–Yau 3-fold carries an SL2 (ℤ) action on its elliptic-fibration moduli
(for example, K3× 𝐸 ), the modular-form output of Φ3 carries arithmetic data. The Borcherds product
Φ 𝑁 ( 𝑁 ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}) lives on Sp4 (ℤ)-moduli space; it is an automorphic object, occupying the
automorphic vertex together with V prim .

13.8   Automorphic Placement
Theorem 13.8.1 (automorphic placement of V prim ). . Each candidate TQFT-bulk framework
for V prim (Kapustin–Witten, BLLPRvR, holomorphic Chern–Simons, the Costello–Gaiotto
holomorphically-twisted theory, and Vol III Φ𝑑 ) is obstructed by a specific structural obstruction listed
in §§13.1–13.7. V prim occupies the automorphic vertex of the Langlands–TQFT triangle (Chapter 13.5.1).
Remark 13.8.2 (the Deninger programme). A rigorous construction of Spec ℤ as a ‘‘curve over 𝔽 1 ’’ with a
Frobenius-type ℝ>0 -action, Deninger’s 𝔽 1 -geometric programme, would supply the missing TQFT-bulk
vertex. The arithmetic site of Connes–Consani (arXiv:1405.4527) provides one candidate foundation.

13.9    The Automorphic Vertex: Structural Consolidation
Each obstruction in §§13.1–13.7 is structural: the complex-structure requirement of Kapustin–Witten
(Chapter 13.1.3), the finite flavour-rank bound of BLLPRvR (Chapter 13.2.3), the integrality requirement
of Chern–Simons levels (Chapter 13.3.2), the thermodynamic rather than spectral character of the Hart-
noll–Yang match (Chapter 13.4.2), and the ℂ-analytic domain of Φ𝑑 (Chapter 13.7.1). The automorphic
vertex placement (Chapter 13.5.1) is the consequence: V prim is identified by Artin reciprocity with the
automorphic side of the Langlands triangle, with the TQFT-bulk vertex remaining Deninger’s open
programme.

14.4    Rank Residue
The per-prime charges 𝑐 ( 𝑝 ) = 2 (Chapter 14.1.3) diverge under naive summation; the prime zeta obstruc-

                                𝑟 𝜁 = 2 · Res 𝑠=1 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) = 2.

residue; the preceding corollary forbids reading it as a global Virasoro central charge.

are not defined on the restricted vacuum as global sums. Hence the full Witt algebra and its Virasoro
central extension do not act on V prim .
Remark 14.5.2 (soft-algebra interpretation). This matches the Hartnoll–Yang reading of V prim through
its scalar character on the gravitational superspace only at the level of the surviving boundary modes.
The algebraic object retains the modes 𝑚 ≥ −1, not the Witt algebra; hence no Virasoro anomaly can be
read from the restricted tensor product.

14.6    The Functional Equation as Arithmetic Modular Invariance
Theorem 14.6.1 (arithmetic modular invariance). . The Tate-Mellin character of the primary trace
class is the completed Riemann zeta 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 21 𝑠 ( 𝑠 − 1) 𝜋 − 𝑠/2 Γ ( 𝑠 /2) 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ). Its modular invariance is the
functional equation 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ): the arithmetic analogue of 𝜏 → −1/ 𝜏 . The genus-1 modular-form
trace 𝑍 ( 𝜏 ) = tr 𝑞 𝐿0 − 𝑐 /24 belongs to an honest complex VOA; the global arithmetic object is a Mellin
character.
14.7. The Arakelov Pairing Replaces the Weyl Anomaly                                                       75


14.7    The Arakelov Pairing Replaces the Weyl Anomaly
Proposition 14.7.1 (Deligne pairing = Weyl anomaly analogue). . Under the Deligne pair-
ing on Arakelov line bundles, ⟨ 𝜔 𝑝 , 𝜔 𝑝 ⟩Arakelov = log 𝑝. Summed over primes this reproduces (up to
regularisation) the logarithmic derivative of 𝜁 .
Remark 14.7.2 (Weyl anomaly versus height-theoretic anomaly). On ℂ, the Weyl anomaly is ⟨𝑇𝜇 ⟩ =
                                                                                                       𝜇

−𝑐𝑅/24 𝜋 ; the Polyakov–Liouville action realises this as the central observable. On 𝐶 = Spec ℤ, the
role of the Weyl anomaly is played by the Arakelov metric contribution to the height pairing, log 𝑝 per
prime, which is height-theoretic in origin. The two anomalies are analogous; they are distinct because
the geometric context differs (complex curve versus arithmetic compactification).

14.8    The Arakelov– 𝜁 Structure of the Residue
The local conformal charge is 𝑐 ( 𝑝 ) = 2, prime by prime. The global trace class has no Virasoro central
charge. Its finite scalar is the rank residue 𝑟 𝜁 = 2, extracted from the pole of 𝜁 at 𝑠 = 1. The prime zeta
obstruction (Chapter 14.3.2) eliminates the 𝑐 = −1 proposals; the residue regularisation (Chapter 14.4.1) is
a determinant computation, not a conformal one. The non-negative conformal modes on each restricted
vector are algebraic (Chapter 14.5.1); its arithmetic analogue of modular invariance is the functional
equation 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ) (Chapter 14.6.1), and the Weyl anomaly is replaced by the Arakelov–Deligne
height pairing ⟨ 𝜔 𝑝 , 𝜔 𝑝 ⟩ = log 𝑝 (Chapter 14.7.1).

Arithmetic Chern–Simons Holography

Class-S, Higgs-branch vertex algebras, and Costello–Gaiotto boundary categories require a complex
curve or a quantized boundary theory. Kim arithmetic Chern–Simons supplies only the classical arith-
metic action line. Finite state sums and the conditional boundary category appear in Chapter 82; the
profinite comparison with V prim remains open.

15.1   Class S Fails Arithmetically
Theorem 15.1.1 (Gaiotto, arXiv:0904.2715). . Class-S builds 4D N = 2 theories 𝑇 [ Σ, 𝔤] by com-
pactifying the 6D (2, 0) theory 𝔛[𝔤] on a punctured Riemann surface Σ.
Observation 15.1.2 (three obstructions). Arithmetic class-S on Spec ℤ × ℝ4 fails:
   (i) 6D (2, 0) requires a smooth oriented 6-manifold; Spec ℤ × ℝ4 is topologically 5-dimensional
       (arithmetic 1-dim plus 4-dim real). Connes’ spectral dimension of Spec ℤ is 1, not 2 (Connes–
       Consani arXiv:1405.4527).
  (ii) The self-dual 2-form 𝐵 on an M5-brane has no Arakelov analogue (no star on 2-forms on a 1-d
       arithmetic curve, where Ω2 = 0).
 (iii) Hitchin-moduli Higgs branches on Spec ℤ are not defined by the class-S formula: the Arakelov
       dualizing sheaf is a metrised arithmetic line, not the holomorphic canonical bundle of a Riemann
       surface.
Corollary 15.1.3. . Class-S as a generating principle for arithmetic vertex algebras is obstructed.

15.2   The Hitchin Base Has No Class-S Arithmetic Specialization
Theorem 15.2.1 (arithmetic Hitchin obstruction). . The class-S Coulomb branch
                                        M 0
                                 CΣ,𝔤 =     𝐻 ( Σ, 𝐾Σ𝑑𝑖 )
                                                  𝑖

uses the holomorphic canonical bundle of a complex curve. For Spec ℤ the dualizing object is the
Arakelov line with metric at infinity. Its sections belong to Arakelov intersection theory, not to a Hitchin
base. Hence the class-S Coulomb and Higgs branches do not vanish; rather, the formula defining them
has no canonical arithmetic value.
Remark 15.2.2 (why the replacement is three-dimensional). This obstruction is not a proof that an arith-
metic 4-dimensional theory is topological. It says that the class-S descent from a 6-dimensional theory
along a complex curve has no arithmetic curve to descend along. Kim’s arithmetic Chern–Simons theory
is therefore not the topological remnant of that construction; it is a separate 3-dimensional arithmetic
field theory.

15.3   Kim’s Arithmetic Chern–Simons

15.5   Wilson Lines Are Labeled by Ramified Hecke Characters
Theorem 15.5.1 (Wilson-line labels as local Hecke data). . Wilson lines in ACS wrapped around
the ‘‘knot’’ corresponding to a prime 𝑝 (Mazur–Morishita arithmetic topology) are 1-dimensional defects
in the arithmetic 3-fold, each labeled by a local Hecke character 𝜒 𝑝 of ℚ ×𝑝 (ramified or unramified). The
15.6. Beem–Lemos–Liendo–Peelaers–Rastelli–van Rees as Adelic Character                                         79


label is a closed point of the universal family of local characters, and conjecturally a module over the
quantum boundary category specialized at 𝑝. Inserting a Wilson line with label 𝜒 𝑝 produces a boundary
defect whose local datum at 𝑝 is the ramification datum of 𝜒 𝑝 (conjectural; the categorical boundary
module is part of the conditional boundary-category input of Chapter 82). Wilson-line labels are 0-
dimensional data; the Wilson line itself is 1-dimensional.
Remark 15.5.2 (defect/puncture dictionary). Class-S punctures correspond to 6D codimension-2 defects
in the complex setting; arithmetic ramification corresponds to Wilson lines in arithmetic Chern–Simons.
The structural dictionary ‘‘punctures = defects’’ becomes ‘‘Wilson lines = ramification’’ in the arithmetic
setting, with the 6D/4D framing replaced by the 3D arithmetic TQFT framing.

15.7   Arithmetic CS as the Generating Principle
   (i) Class-S obstructed: three 4D-gauge obstructions (Chapter 15.1.3).
  (ii) The class-S Hitchin base has no canonical arithmetic specialization on Spec ℤ (Chapter 15.2.1).
 (iii) Kim’s arithmetic Chern–Simons (arXiv:1510.05818) is the classical 3D action functional
       (Chapter 15.3.1).
 (iv) Finite state sums are constructed in Chapter 82; the renormalised profinite boundary category is
       conjectural, as is its comparison with V prim and its character 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) (Chapter 15.4.1).
  (v) Wilson lines are 1-dimensional defects labeled by ramified Hecke characters (= expected modules
       of the quantum boundary category specialized at 𝑝, 0-dimensional data) (Chapter 15.5.1).
 (vi) BLLPRvR adelic character: 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) is the conjectural Schur index character of arithmetic CS
       (Chapter 15.6.1).
    Kim arithmetic 𝔾𝑚 -Chern–Simons on Spec ℤ at level 1 supplies the classical arithmetic action. Chap-
ter 82 constructs finite state sums and states the boundary category as a conditional profinite problem;
the renormalised comparison with V prim remains open.

The Hochschild Trace of the Iwahori Hecke
Category

The primary object is V prim , the Hochschild trace class of the identity on the global arithmetic Iwa-
hori Hecke category of 𝐺 𝐿2 . This chapter places V prim on the arithmetic Langlands diamond via
Bezrukavnikov’s affine Hecke equivalences (arXiv:1209.0403), Mirković–Vilonen geometric Satake
(arXiv:math/0401222), Ben-Zvi–Nadler character theory (arXiv:0904.1247), Arinkin–Gaitsgory spec-
tral decomposition (arXiv:1201.6343), the Emerton–Gee ( 𝜑, Γ) stack (arXiv:1908.07185), and Fargues–
Scholze geometrization (arXiv:2102.13459).

16.1   The Naive Bun 𝐺 𝐿 2 (Spec ℤ) Has Only One Coarse Point
Theorem 16.1.1 (Minkowski). . 𝜋1ét (Spec ℤ) = 1: every étale cover of Spec ℤ is trivial. Class number
of ℚ is 1.
Corollary 16.1.2. . The groupoid Bun𝐺 𝐿2 (Spec ℤ) has one object up to isomorphism, represented
by ℤ2 , and stabilizer 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℤ). Thus

                                     Bun𝐺 𝐿2 (Spec ℤ) ≃ 𝐵𝐺 𝐿2 (ℤ)

as a discrete stack, not as a point. The lost datum in the coarse quotient is exactly the arithmetic auto-
morphism group; it does not produce the geometric Hecke correspondence supplied by a curve.

16.2   The Spherical Hecke Category Collapses the OPE
The coarse automorphic stack over Spec ℤ has one component and stabilizer 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℤ). It has arithmetic
monodromy, but no geometric curve along which a Hecke correspondence can move. Thus one is
forced to ask which local Hecke category at a prime 𝑝 carries the noncommutative structure visible to a
Hochschild trace. Geometric Satake identifies the spherical category but reveals its commutativity.

16.3   The Iwahori Hecke Category Carries Convolution Data
Before invoking Bezrukavnikov’s equivalence we record the Bernstein presentation that gives the chapter
its name. The affine Hecke algebra 𝐻𝑞 = 𝐻𝑞 (𝑊f ) of the extended affine Weyl group 𝑊
