monomials are independent, so there is no further relation and the displayed quotient is exact.

   The ideal contains the matrices with finite support in the specified basis. It is not being identified
with every finite-rank bounded operator, whose vectors can have infinite support.

Theorem 25.6.3 (failure of a trace-preserving Hall-algebra map). Let 𝐴 be a commutative unital
algebra. Every unital algebra map 𝑓 : T → 𝐴 kills 𝐸 and every 𝐸𝑖𝑗 . For 0 < 𝑞 < 1, there is no linear
functional 𝜆 : 𝐴 → ℂ with 𝜆 ◦ 𝑓 = Φ𝑞 . In particular, the prime-to-Hall-module comparison cannot
be replaced by a Gibbs-preserving algebra map from T into J .
   There is also no unital algebra map T → J that sends 𝑆 to 𝑒0 . The algebra map ℂ[ 𝑆 ] → P,
𝑆 ↦→ 𝑒0 , does exist, but does not extend across the relation 𝑅𝑆 = 1.
Proof. The image of [ 𝑅, 𝑆 ] is zero in a commutative algebra, so (25.1) gives 𝑓 ( 𝐸 ) = 0. Multiplication
on both sides then kills all matrix units. But Φ𝑞 ( 𝐸 ) = 1 − 𝑞 ≠ 0, which excludes the functional 𝜆. For
the second assertion, 𝑓 ( 𝑅) 𝑒0 = 1 would make the polynomial variable 𝑒0 invertible. Evaluation at 𝑒0 = 0
and all other variables zero gives 0 = 1, a contradiction.

     The operator 𝐵 is neither multiplication by a polynomial nor a derivation. It kills 1 but has 𝐵 ( 𝑥 ) = 1,
excluding a multiplication operator. Also 𝐵 ( 𝑥 2 ) = 𝑥 , while a derivation with 𝐵 ( 𝑥 ) = 1 would give
2 𝑥 . It is the backward shift required by prime division. This distinction is precisely where the operator
realization contains more structure than the commutative Hall sector.

25.7    A finite native Iwahori calculation
The prime shift is explicit arithmetic operator data. A local Iwahori presentation supplies a different,
finite test which must also be respected by any proposed native comparison.
    Let 𝑋 𝑝 be the set of one-dimensional subspaces of 𝔽 2𝑝 . There are 𝑝 + 1 such lines: 𝑝 of the form

lines, since two distinct lines admit basis vectors. Let 𝑊𝑝 = ℂ 𝑋 𝑝 , with its standard orthonormal basis,
and let 𝑇 have matrix entry one between distinct lines and zero on the diagonal.

Theorem 25.7.2 (finite Hecke obstructions to the polynomial target). There is no unital algebra
map 𝑓 : A 𝑝 → J and linear functional 𝜆 : J → ℂ such that 𝜆 ◦ 𝑓 = 𝜏 𝑝 . More generally, a unital
map from A 𝑝 to any algebra with no idempotents except zero and one cannot preserve 𝜏 𝑝 through a
linear functional.
    There is no grading on A 𝑝 by nonnegative integers with 1 in degree zero and 𝑇 homogeneous of
positive degree. In particular, reflection length does not supply an additive positive occupation energy
for this Hecke multiplication.

Proof. The two idempotents have nonzero trace and sum to one. In an algebra with only trivial idempo-
tents, one of their images is zero. A linear functional then vanishes on that image, contradicting (25.16).
The polynomial algebra J is an integral domain: any two nonzero polynomials lie in a polynomial ring
on finitely many variables, where their leading monomials have nonzero product. An idempotent 𝑒 in a
domain satisfies 𝑒 ( 𝑒 − 1) = 0, hence is zero or one.
    For the grading assertion, the degree-zero component of (25.15) would say 0 = 𝑝1, which is impossible
over ℂ. Equivalently, 𝑇 −1 = 𝑝 −1 (𝑇 − ( 𝑝 − 1)1), so 𝑇 is invertible and cannot be a positive-degree element
of a nonnegatively graded unital algebra.

    The length filtration does exist: put 𝐹0 A 𝑝 = ℂ1 and 𝐹𝑛 A 𝑝 = A 𝑝 for 𝑛 ≥ 1. Its associated graded
algebra is ℂ[ 𝑡 ]/( 𝑡 2 ) with deg 𝑡 = 1. This is a change of multiplication. There is no filtered algebra
isomorphism recovering A 𝑝 from this graded algebra, since the latter has a nonzero nilpotent and the
former is a product of fields.
    There is an elementary comparison with simple-object cohomology. A representation of the quiver
with two isolated vertices is a pair of vector spaces; its subrepresentations are pairs of subspaces. It is simple
precisely when one space is one-dimensional and the other is zero. Thus its two simple isomorphism
classes, of dimension vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1), form two points. The cohomology of each point is ℂ in
degree zero and zero in other degrees. Their direct sum is 𝐵 = ℂ𝑏+ ⊕ ℂ𝑏 − . The linear map

                                           𝑒+ ↦→ 𝑏+ ,         𝑒 − ↦→ 𝑏 −

is an isomorphism from HH0 (A 𝑝 ) to 𝐵 ; the functional with values ( 𝑝 + 1) −1 and 𝑝 ( 𝑝 + 1) −1 preserves
𝜏 𝑝 . It is a comparison of cohomological-degree-zero vector spaces. The two dimension-vector labels are
additional labels on its target, not a multiplicative grading on A 𝑝 . Indeed 𝑒+2 = 𝑒+ already contradicts
25.8. Tensor shift algebras over finite prime sets                                                      187


additive positive degree. Nor does this linear map supply an energy on the native Hecke trace. Identifying
this simple-object cohomology with BPS cohomology, with a specified potential, shifts, and critical
functor, remains a separate construction; it does not follow from the two-point calculation.

25.12    The global trace and the native categorical comparison
For all primes at once, the occupation basis is indexed by positive integers through n ↦→ 𝑝 𝑝𝑛 𝑝 , with
                                                                                                Q
finite support. Its Hilbert completion is ℓ 2 (ℕ≥1 ) and the energy is log 𝑛 on the vector indexed by 𝑛. The
global thermal density is nuclear exactly for real 𝛽 > 1, because its trace is 𝑛 ≥1 𝑛− 𝛽 . The convergence for
                                                                              P
𝛽 > 1 and divergence for 0 < 𝛽 ≤ 1 follow by comparison with the integral of 𝑥 − 𝛽 over [1, ∞). Unique
factorization gives its Euler product. The compatible normalized states on the algebraic union of the
tensor shift algebras T𝐹 still exist for every 𝛽 > 0: positivity and normalization are checked in a finite
tensor factor containing the given element. Existence of this local-state system is not the assertion of a
nuclear global Gibbs density at those temperatures.
     The unnormalized traces behave differently under a prime-set inclusion: tensoring an observable with
the identity multiplies its thermal trace by the partition factor of each new prime. The coefficient maps
𝑚 ↦→ 𝑚 𝜌 𝐹 ,𝛽 are likewise not intertwined by the ordinary inclusions 𝐾 ↦→ 𝐾 ⊗ 1. They are intertwined
by 𝐾 ↦→ 𝐾 ⊗ 𝜌𝐺 \ 𝐹 ,𝛽 , which is a coefficient-module construction and is not an algebra inclusion. These
distinctions must persist in any global comparison.
     The native arithmetic realization asks for more than these local operator and finite Hecke construc-
tions. Its proposed source is the Hochschild homology of a restricted tensor product of local Iwahori
convolution categories, with Frobenius data. A realization must first define that tensor product and
its trace in a specified coefficient category, then construct maps from the local data used here into it. A
comparison with BPS cohomology further needs actual quivers and polynomial potentials, cohomolog-
ical and dimension gradings, compatible prime-set maps, and an intertwining of the trace and energy
operations.
194                  Chapter 25. Prime Traces, Hall Operators, and Modular Conjugation


   The local results identify three conditions on such a construction. The represented prime phase
quotients do not admit the naive phase-preserving prime-set inclusions; the two-prime calculation
requires a larger compatible source before a global trace can be compared. An ordinary cyclic functional
on the full prime shift algebra cannot equal the finite-temperature Gibbs functional; the imaginary-time
twist or the nuclear coefficient module is necessary for the comparison constructed here. A multiplication-
preserving map from the finite Iwahori Hecke algebra to the connected polynomial Jordan target cannot
preserve its trace; its idempotent sectors cannot be removed. A different categorical or critical Hall target is
not excluded by these arguments. Constructing that target and its native arithmetic comparison remains
open.

language in this argument is conﬁned to the archimedean ﬁbre H (∞) ; the ﬁnite-place factors H ( 𝑝 ) are

26.2    Variance and domains of the comparison
The native Koszul form is complex bilinear on two specified carriers. The Petersson form is linear in
its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second. A conjugate-linear map from the native space
to its dual is therefore required before their values can agree. On the operator carrier the identity is
𝐵 𝑞 ( 𝑋 , 𝐽𝑞𝑌 ) = ℎ𝑞 ( 𝑋 , 𝑌 ).
    The carrier is equally essential. A positive state gives a Hilbert space after taking its null quotient and
completion. It does not identify that Hilbert space with a native automorphic representation. The radial
shell construction below gives explicit maps on a small sector; extension to an arithmetic representation
must preserve its operators, phases and norms. At the adelic level the finite-prime maps must also agree
under inclusion. Equality of partition functions or local scalar factors does not impose this compatibility.

Lemma 26.4.1 (two normalized GNS embeddings of the weighted lattice). . At 𝑞 = 𝑝 −1 , both

Proof. The creation vectors have inner products 𝛿𝑚𝑛 and the division vectors have inner products
𝛿𝑚𝑛 𝑚 −1 by Chapter 25.10.1. Scaling the creation vectors gives the same weighted norm. Their degrees are
opposite, as follows from the actions of 𝑆 𝑝 and 𝑅 𝑝 . The full GNS space is the Hilbert–Schmidt space
with basis 𝐸𝑖𝑗 ; the two maps specify only closed subspaces of it. Also the normalized GNS vacuum has
norm one, which does not determine a chosen Haar volume such as vol( 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℤ 𝑝 )).

26.6    The Bost–Connes Anti-Involution and its GNS Lift
Deﬁnition and Basic Properties
The Bost–Connes algebraic anti-involution 𝜏 BC is the adelic extension of its local versions 𝜏 𝑝BC . The
local anti-involution at a prime 𝑝 is the conjugate-linear anti-automorphism

                  𝜏 𝑝BC : 𝔸BC   BC
                           𝑝 → 𝔸𝑝 ,           𝜇𝑚 ↦→ 𝜇∗𝑚 ,          𝜇∗𝑚 ↦→ 𝜇𝑚 ,        𝑒 ( 𝛾 ) ↦→ 𝑒 (− 𝛾 ) .

On the GNS Hilbert space of the represented prime Gibbs state, constructed in Chapter 25.10.1, the
corresponding antiunitary is not 𝜏 𝑝BC itself but

            𝐽𝜑1 , 𝑝 𝜋 ( 𝜇𝑚 ) Ω𝜑1 = 𝑚1/2 𝜋 ( 𝜇∗𝑚 ) Ω𝜑1 ,          𝐽𝜑1 , 𝑝 𝜋 ( 𝜇∗𝑚 ) Ω𝜑1 = 𝑚 −1/2 𝜋 ( 𝜇𝑚 ) Ω𝜑1 .

The factors are forced by 𝑆𝜑1 = 𝐽𝜑1 Δ1/2𝜑1 . An archimedean extension requires its own conjugate-linear
map. The identity on a nonzero complex Hilbert space is linear, so it cannot itself be the archimedean
factor of an antiunitary tensor map. Coefficient conjugation fixes a chosen real vacuum and gives a
possible antiunitary factor, but its native pairing compatibility remains part of the adelic comparison.

• 𝜏 𝑝BC ◦ 𝜏 𝑝BC = id (involutive; Bost–Connes §1.2).

26.8    Analytic continuation of a realized pairing
The normalized state and its partition trace can have different pole behavior. For | 𝑞 | < 1,
                                                             (1 − 𝑞 ) 𝑍 ( 𝑞 ) = 1.
                                   ∑︁ 𝑛
                        𝑍 ( 𝑞) =       𝑞 = (1 − 𝑞 ) −1 ,
                                     𝑛 ≥0

The first scalar has a pole at 𝑞 = 1, while the unit value of the normalized functional extends to the
constant one. Its vacuum projection value 1 − 𝑞 is also entire. Thus a pole of a partition function is not
automatically a pole of a normalized pairing.
Proposition 26.8.1 (conditional continuation of the pairing identity). Suppose the native
and automorphic comparison maps give equal pairings on a nonempty open parameter set. Suppose
their scalar matrix elements admit meromorphic continuations to the same connected complex domain,
using ( 𝑠1 , 𝑠2 ) as independent variables for a sesquilinear parameter family. Then those continued matrix
elements agree. In particular their Laurent principal parts agree wherever a common local Laurent
expansion is defined.
206                                       Chapter 26. Koszul–Petersson Pairing Compatibility


Proof. For each fixed pair of vectors, subtract the two meromorphic matrix elements. On each coordinate
neighborhood multiply by a common holomorphic denominator. The result is holomorphic and zero
on the initial open set. The identity theorem, applied along overlapping coordinate neighborhoods in
the connected domain, makes it zero everywhere. Dividing back proves equality of the meromorphic
elements and hence of their Laurent coefficients. The initial equality and continuation hypotheses
concern the actual pairings, not just their partition scalars.

Remark 26.8.2 (the pole-divisor requirement). A prescribed automorphic pole divisor transfers only after
the native trace or pairing map and its continuation are constructed. The local Gibbs model cannot
exclude additional native homological contributions or determine their poles. The completed scalar
ratios and their removable singularities are computed separately in Chapter 46.5.2.

establish their existence.

operator-algebraic statement of Chapter 46.2.5, while the ramified Rankin–Selberg and Eisenstein terms
are separate domain conditions (Chapter 26.1.3).

Proof. If 𝐼 is the assumed injective realization, then ⟨𝑣, 𝑣 ⟩ Pet = ∥ 𝐼 𝑣 ∥ 2𝐿2 > 0 for 𝑣 ≠ 0. The native
pairing identity follows from the local transfer and the assumed adelic assembly. Positivity of this form
does not establish a unitary vertex-algebra action: adjoint relations for that action require their own
verification.

Remark 26.10.2 (the native positivity requirement). Injectivity is essential. Pulling back a positive Hilbert
norm along a linear map gives a positive semidefinite form whose null space is the kernel of the map. It
is positive definite precisely when that kernel is zero. Local Gibbs positivity therefore cannot replace the
native realization hypothesis, even on a restricted cuspidal core.

Impact on the Suﬃcient RH Implication
Corollary 26.10.3 (sufficient RH path, four-input conditional). . Under the stated realiza-
tion, pairing and analytic hypotheses, the sufficient implication to RH in the arithmetic formalism
(Chapter 22.6.1) is the four-input conditional conjunction of Chapter 39.3.1:
   (i) Arithmetic Positselski (Chapter 24.1.5): conditional on the five open Positselski sub-items of
       Chapter 24.1.6.
  (ii) Koszul–Petersson compatibility (Chapter 26.9.1): domain-restricted to the normalized sph-fin
       cuspidal core and conditional on its native pairing maps, injective realization and Tamagawa-
       regularised assembly; the full-sector extension has separate ramified Rankin–Selberg and Eisenstein
       components, while the KMS1 /GNS component is the half-density statement of Chapter 46.2.5.
 (iii) Arithmetic Hilbert–Pólya H-PAr (Chapter 22.3.2): the independent spectral-matching problem.
 (iv) Arithmetic Virasoro positivity VB∗ main direction (Chapter 22.3.10): the classical positive-trace
       problem, equivalent to RH.

Proof. This is substitution of the stated conditional pairing transfer into the sufficient implication. All
native map and domain hypotheses remain part of its antecedent; the local thermal theorem removes
none of the independent spectral or positivity requirements.

Remark 26.10.4 (separate mathematical requirements). The native duality, the Koszul–Petersson maps,
the zero-divisor realization and the arithmetic positivity statement are separate requirements. The explicit
208                                     Chapter 26. Koszul–Petersson Pairing Compatibility


local normalization supplies tests for their compatibility, including the unit value, conjugate-linearity
and modular energy; it is not a construction of those global maps.

26.11   Boundary
The represented prime state has unit value, the modular conjugation has creation factor 𝑚1/2 and division
factor 𝑚 −1/2 at 𝛽 = 1, and the bilinear operator pairing becomes Hermitian after that conjugation. The
radial shell maps realize these identities with explicit norms and energy behavior.
   The native Koszul–Petersson theorem requires its own pairing and realization maps, including at the
archimedean place. Finite spherical line maps account for Haar volume by rescaling vectors; they do not
rescale the unit of a state. Infinite normalized tensor products, Tamagawa regularization and analytic
continuation are separate constructions. The native comparison hypotheses must include whichever of
them the desired global pairing uses.
   On an injectively realized cuspidal core, the pulled-back integral norm is positive definite and the
conditional transfer identifies it with the Koszul form after native conjugate-linear duality. Establishing
a unitary chiral-algebra action, extending to the Eisenstein continuum, and representing the arithmetic
zero-divisor or Li trace remain further mathematical requirements.

Adelic Categorical Descent

LACD (Chapter 21.2.3) is the essential adelic gluing statement for conjecture F1 (global arithmetic Arinkin–
Gaitsgory for 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ), with a substantial closure problem (App. C). This chapter decomposes LACD
into four subconditions ( 𝐿1 )–( 𝐿4 ). The formal restricted tensor product ( 𝐿1 ) is constructed here. The
archimedean representation category ( 𝐿4 ) is a boundary datum, not a spectral equivalence. ( 𝐿2 ) still
needs the local categorical comparison and the Whittaker compatibility. ( 𝐿3 ) is the Bernstein-centre
diamond-gluing compatibility on local coherent Springer sheaves over the Selmer-derived global spectral
stack. The main result (Chapter 27.2.7) is a conditional reduction, not a proof of LACD .

    Context and Signiﬁcance
    LACD is the essential adelic gluing statement for F1 (global arithmetic Arinkin–Gaitsgory, Chapter 20.1.1).
    The structural reduction of F1 in Chapter 21.2.1 splits F1 into four sub-items (F1.a)–(F1.d). Only (F1.c) is
    a theorem drawn directly from primary literature (Emerton–Gee arXiv:1908.07185). Fargues–Scholze
    arXiv:2102.13459 supplies local geometrisation and spectral action, not the categorical equivalence re-
    quired by (F1.a). The remaining items (F1.a), (F1.b), and (F1.d) are equivalent to the local comparison
    plus LACD conditions whose closure removes F1.
        LACD is a conjectural, non-formal theorem. This chapter does not close LACD ; it reduces it to a
    narrower and precisely-stated compatibility on local coherent Springer sheaves (Ben-Zvi–Chen–Helm–
    Nadler arXiv:2010.02321) glued across primes on the Selmer-derived global spectral stack.

    27.2    Modular Reduction of L ACD
    Six independent lines of obstruction on LACD are given below. Each line produces a structural decom-
    position, a partial closure, or a named residual, following the schema of Chapter 21.1.

    Modular Decomposition of LACD
    LACD is the conjunction of four ingredients: (i) well-definedness of the restricted tensor product of local
    ∞-categories with distinguished units; (ii) Hecke-functoriality across places; (iii) compatibility of the
    Bernstein centre action across places under restricted tensor; (iv) archimedean-finite assembly (extension
    across the archimedean place). A structural closure requires separating each ingredient. The decom-
    position admits four disjoint subconditions, ( 𝐿1 )–( 𝐿4 ), each a precise statement at the ∞-categorical
    level.

Curve Precedent and Transport Obstructions
For a smooth complete curve over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, the de Rham geomet-
ric Langlands theorem gives the model for the categorical descent pattern. The sheaf-function analogue
over finite fields is a different theorem. Neither theorem transports directly to the number-field case.
The obstructions are:
   (i) No archimedean place in the curve setting. Geometric Langlands uses the closed points of a curve.
       Number-field LACD requires the archimedean extension ( 𝐿4 ), which has no curve analogue.
  (ii) Emerton–Gee integrality. The number-field spectral side uses the Emerton–Gee stack
       arXiv:1908.07185, which encodes integrality of Galois representations; de Rham geometric
       Langlands uses the stack LocSysdR 𝐺 ( 𝑋 ), which is smoother and has weaker integrality content.
       The Bernstein-centre compatibility ( 𝐿3 ) is strictly more subtle in the number-field setting because
       the Emerton–Gee stack is not smooth over Spec ℤ.
 (iii) Perfectoid diamonds. Fargues–Scholze’s local theorem uses the Fargues–Fontaine curve and perfec-
       toid diamonds; geometric Langlands uses ind-schemes. Gluing across finite places in the number-
       field case requires comparing perfectoid diamonds at distinct primes, a non-issue in the de Rham
       curve setting.
Theorem 27.2.3 (curve transport, qualified). . The Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum–Raskin–Lin /
AGKRRV proof of de Rham geometric Langlands gives the model for subconditions ( 𝐿1 ) and ( 𝐿2 ) as
an analogy, not as a transport theorem (Raskin, ‘‘Chiral principal series categories I’’, Adv. Math. 388
(2021); Raskin, ‘‘D-modules on infinite-dimensional varieties’’, available as samraskin.net/dmod.pdf).
It closes ( 𝐿1 ) only after the number-field local categories and distinguished units are fixed. It does
not close ( 𝐿2 ) without the local categorical comparison of (F1.a) and (BC-diamond-glue). It does not
close ( 𝐿3 ) (Bernstein centre compatibility is strictly more subtle in the number-field setting due to
Emerton–Gee stack non-smoothness) or ( 𝐿4 ) (no archimedean analogue on the curve).
212                                                        Chapter 27. Adelic Categorical Descent


Proof. ( 𝐿1 ): Raskin 2021 JAMS constructs restricted tensor products of local principal-series categories
over a curve. The construction is ∞-categorical and uses only (a) stability, (b) presentability, (c) existence
of distinguished units. These properties can be imposed on the number-field local categories. This gives
the formal construction of ( 𝐿1 ), not the global automorphic identification.
    ( 𝐿2 ): AGKRRV’s Hecke-functoriality argument combines local geometric Langlands equivalences
with Bernstein–Zelevinsky factorization on a curve. For number fields, Fargues–Scholze arXiv:2102.13459
supplies the local diamond geometrisation and spectral action. It does not supply the displayed categorical
comparison with the Emerton–Gee stack. The Bernstein–Zelevinsky pattern applies only after the local
comparison and Whittaker-model compatibility are constructed. Domain: §27.4.
    ( 𝐿3 ): Number-field obstruction. The Bernstein centre Z Ar of the global arithmetic Iwahori Hecke
category acts on 𝑣′ C𝑣 via the local Bernstein centres Z𝑣 , but compatibility across primes involves
                   N
comparing Bernstein parameters at distinct primes through the Emerton–Gee stack. The curve analogue
uses the de Rham stack, which is smoother. The number-field compatibility is the residual.
    ( 𝐿4 ): No curve analogue.

Sphericity-Finiteness Preserved Under Restricted Tensor
The ‘‘sph-fin’’ cut in Dsph-fin ( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ𝑣 )]) restricts to categories with finite-type spherical sub-structure,
excluding the continuous Eisenstein spectrum and broad classes of non-tempered representations. The
condition is preserved under the restricted tensor product.
Lemma 27.2.4 (sph-fin preservation under restricted tensor). . Let {C𝑣 } be a family of stable
presentable ∞-categories with distinguished units 𝑢𝑣 at almost every 𝑣 , and assume each C𝑣 is ‘‘sph-fin’’
in the sense that: (i) C𝑣 has a compact subcategory C𝑣𝜔 whose compact objects are finite-type over the local
Hecke algebra H𝑣 ; (ii) 𝑢𝑣 is compact in C𝑣𝜔 ; (iii) the compact objects generate C𝑣 . Then the restricted
tensor product 𝑣′ C𝑣 is likewise sph-fin.
                 N

Proof. By Lurie HA 5.3 (higher Deligne centralizers) and HA 4.8 (tensor products of presentable ∞-
categories), the tensor product 𝑣 ∈ 𝑆 C𝑣 over a finite set 𝑆 inherits compact generation from its finite
                                  N
factors: a family of compact generators is given by tensor products of local compact generators. The
distinguished units 𝑢𝑣 at 𝑣 ∉ 𝑆 are compact, so tensoring with them preserves compactness. Taking the
filtered colimit over 𝑆 preserves compact generation (Lurie HA 5.3.2.9 on filtered colimits of compactly
generated categories). Hence 𝑣′ C𝑣 is compactly generated, with compact subcategory the filtered colimit
                              N
of finite tensor products of local compacts. The sph-fin condition is preserved.

decomposes as a restricted tensor product whose factor at each prime is the local Hecke category.

                   Caraiani–Scholze arXiv:1511.02418 prove a unitary Shimura variety analogue of LACD for signature
                   (1, 𝑛 − 1) unitary groups 𝐺 = 𝑈 (1, 𝑛 − 1) over CM fields. A Jacquet–Langlands transfer from 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ

                      The transference fails; but Caraiani–Scholze’s proof does suggest the structural shape LACD must
                   take: a patched-spaces argument with local Fargues–Scholze input glued across primes by an ‘‘Ihara-
                   avoidance-free’’ version of the argument.

   (i) The filtered colimit lim exists in PrL,st .

  (ii) The resulting object is stable, presentable, and compactly-generated if each C𝑣 is compactly-

Proof. (i) Existence of the filtered colimit. The ∞-category PrL,st of stable presentable ∞-categories is
a (large) ∞-category admitting all small colimits (Lurie HA 4.8.1.15). Filtered colimits exist.
27.4. Subcondition ( 𝐿 2 ): Hecke-Functoriality Across Places                                            215


    (ii) Presentability and compact generation. Lurie HA 5.3.2.9 asserts that a filtered colimit of
compactly-generated stable presentable ∞-categories, under functors preserving compact objects, is
compactly generated. The transition maps in the defining filtered colimit are of the form ‘‘tensor with
𝟙𝑢𝑣 ’’ for newly-included places 𝑣 , which are left-adjoint (and preserve compact objects because the unit
𝑢𝑣 is assumed compact, as in Chapter 27.2.4). Hence the colimit is compactly generated.
    (iii) Stability. Filtered colimits of stable ∞-categories in PrL,st are stable (Lurie HA 1.1.4.4: stable
∞-categories are closed under filtered colimits in PrL ).
    (iv) Sphericity-finiteness preservation. Chapter 27.2.4.
    (v) Functoriality. A morphism of families {(C𝑣 , 𝑢𝑣 )} → {(C𝑣′ , 𝑢𝑣′ )} is a family of left adjoints
𝐹𝑣 : C𝑣 → C𝑣′ sending 𝑢𝑣 to 𝑢𝑣′ . The induced map 𝑣 ∈ 𝑆 𝐹𝑣 : 𝑣 ∈ 𝑆 C𝑣 → 𝑣 ∈ 𝑆 C𝑣′ is compatible with
                                                      N          N              N
unit-extension to larger 𝑆 ′ ⊇ 𝑆 because 𝐹𝑣 sends distinguished units to distinguished units. Taking the
filtered colimit yields the induced map 𝑣′ 𝐹𝑣 : 𝑣′ C𝑣 → 𝑣′ C𝑣′ . The construction is independent of
                                           N        N          N
the choice of cofinite unramified subset 𝑉 unr (any two choices agree on a further cofinite subset, and
the filtered colimit is insensitive to such shrinking).

Remark 27.3.3 (comparison with Raskin’s construction). Raskin ‘‘Chiral principal series categories
I’’, Adv. Math. 388 (2021), 107856, and Raskin ‘‘D-modules on infinite-dimensional varieties’’
(samraskin.net/dmod.pdf) construct restricted tensor products of principal-series categories over
a smooth curve. The construction uses the same filtered colimit pattern with spherical vectors as
distinguished units. The number-field analogue is not a direct transport. The same filtered colimit
defines the formal restricted tensor product once the local categories and distinguished units are fixed.
The non-trivial content is the identification with the global automorphic category, which is ( 𝐿2 ) and
( 𝐿3 ).
Corollary 27.3.4 ( ( 𝐿 1 ) holds). . ( 𝐿1 ) is a theorem, closed by Chapter 27.3.2 plus Chapter 27.2.4.

Remark 27.5.3 (what BZCHN supplies). BZCHN supplies the local Bernstein centres as coherent sheaves
on local Emerton–Gee stacks. (BC-diamond-glue) asks that these coherent sheaves glue across primes
to a coherent sheaf on the Selmer-derived global spectral stack. Local-to-global gluing is a standard
question in algebraic geometry: under standard flatness hypotheses, coherent sheaves can descend along
the Selmer-derived fibre-product diagram. The non-standard content is agreement of the glued sheaf
with the global Bernstein-centre action, a question about the global automorphic category’s Bernstein
decomposition (Bernstein 1984, categorified in Raskin 2021 JAMS and AGKRRV 2020–2024).
Conjecture 27.5.4 (BC-diamond-glue, concrete form). The coherent Springer sheaves {F𝑣 }𝑣 of Ben-Zvi–
Chen–Helm–Nadler (Chapter 27.5.2) glue along the diagonal of the Selmer-derived global spectral stack
to a global coherent sheaf Fglob whose action on IndCohNilp (X Sel
                                                               ¯𝜌,det, L ) agrees, under the conjectural
global arithmetic AG equivalence, with the action of the global Bernstein centre on D( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 ]) sph-fin .
Remark 27.5.5 (domain of the residual). Chapter 27.5.4 is the residual content of LACD after the reduction
of Chapter 27.2.7. Its domain:
• Gluing of coherent sheaves across a product of stacks: non-formal theorem, standard techniques.
• Agreement with global Bernstein centre under conjectural global AG: non-formal theorem, requires
  careful adaptation of the geometric-Langlands Bernstein-centre construction (AGKRRV) to the
  number-field setting.
• Total condition of (BC-diamond-glue): non-formal theorem.
This is 1/3 to 1/2 the original non-formal theorem of LACD .

27.6    Subcondition ( 𝐿 4 ): Archimedean Extension
Statement
Theorem 27.6.1 ( ( 𝐿 4 ) archimedean boundary datum). . The archimedean factor
C∞ = Dsph-fin ( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℝ)]) is modelled by the ind-completed derived category of admissible
(𝔤𝔩 2 , 𝑂 (2))-modules of finite 𝐾 -type. It carries the trivial 𝐾 -spherical object as distinguished unit and
extends the finite-place restricted tensor product by direct tensoring.

Proof. Step 1: Well-definedness. The derived category of admissible (𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-modules, where 𝔤 =
𝔤𝔩 2 (ℝ) and 𝐾∞ = 𝑂 (2) ⊆ 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℝ), has the standard Harish-Chandra description (Jacquet–Langlands
SLN 114 §1–3; Vogan 1981 ‘‘Representations of Real Reductive Groups’’). Its ind-completion is stable
and presentable. The sph-fin cut restricts to finite 𝐾∞ -type objects.
     Step 2: Distinguished unit. The spherical unit at 𝑣 = ∞ is the trivial 𝐾∞ -spherical object. Spherical
principal series are not unique; they are objects of the category, not the distinguished unit.
     Step 3: Tensor product extension. The restricted tensor product of Chapter 27.3.1 extends naturally
by including 𝑣 = ∞ in the index set 𝑉 of places: 𝑉 = ℙ ∪ {∞} with cofinite unramified subset 𝑉 unr =
ℙ ∪ {∞} \ 𝑆ram for the given ramification set 𝑆ram . The archimedean factor enters as a tensor factor in
each 𝑆 containing ∞ and by identity-via-distinguished-unit in 𝑆 excluding ∞.
     Step 4: Hecke action at infinity. The archimedean Hecke action is represented by the centre of the
universal enveloping algebra 𝑈 (𝔤𝔩 2 (ℝ)), commuting with finite-place Hecke action by construction
(both act via representation-theoretic restriction to the adelic double coset).
     Step 5: Archimedean local factors. Jacquet–Langlands SLN 114 §1–3 classify the archimedean
local representations of 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℝ) and 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℂ). The sph-fin subcategory is finite-type in each isotypic
component; Vogan’s classification gives a complete parametrization by Harish-Chandra parameters.
218                                                      Chapter 27. Adelic Categorical Descent


   This proves the archimedean boundary datum. It does not construct a number-field spectral equiva-
lence at 𝑣 = ∞.

Remark 27.6.2 (archimedean spectral side). The spectral-side analogue at 𝑣 = ∞ is a proposed Weil-
parameter stack for 𝑊ℝ = ℂ× ⋊ ℤ/2. Vogan and Langlands classify the representations. They do not
give an Emerton–Gee stack at infinity, and no local categorical equivalence at infinity is asserted here.

27.7    Curve Analogy: Obstructions and Transfers
The Curve Theorem
Theorem 27.7.1 (de Rham geometric Langlands, AGKRRV). . For a smooth complete curve 𝑋
over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and a reductive group 𝐺 , there is an equivalence

                            D-mod(Bun𝐺 ( 𝑋 )) ≃ IndCohNilp (LocSysdR
                                                                  𝐺 ( 𝑋 ))

satisfying Hecke-functoriality, Bernstein-centre compatibility, and categorical descent over the curve.
The proof combines Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum’s AMS DAG monographs, Raskin’s chiral principal series
and D-module foundations, and the AGKRRV mathematical treatments on geometric Langlands.

Obstructions to Transport
Theorem 27.7.2 (obstructions to number-field transport). . The de Rham geometric-Langlands
proof of Chapter 27.7.1 does not transport directly to the number-field case. The obstructions:
(Obs.1) No archimedean place. Geometric Langlands on a curve has no real place. ( 𝐿4 ) has no curve
analogue and requires separate treatment (Jacquet–Langlands archimedean).
(Obs.2) Non-smooth Emerton–Gee stack. Number-field X𝐺EG𝐿2 is formally algebraic but not smooth over
Spec ℤ; the de Rham stack LocSysdR 𝐺 ( 𝑋 ) is smooth in the standard geometric-Langlands range under
mild hypotheses. This affects the Bernstein-centre compatibility ( 𝐿3 ).
(Obs.3) Perfectoid diamonds vs ind-schemes. Geometric Langlands uses algebraic and ind-algebraic loop
spaces. Number-field local geometrisation uses perfectoid diamonds (Scholze arXiv:1709.07343). The
gluing formalism differs, and the Bhatt–Lurie prismatic comparison arXiv:2201.06120 is required to
bridge the two.
(Obs.4) Integrality of Galois deformations. De Rham local systems are geometric; number-field Galois
deformations are integral (Emerton–Gee stack). The Bernstein-centre action incorporates integrality in
a way the de Rham curve case does not.
Corollary 27.7.3 (what the curve analogy supplies). . Under the de Rham curve proof, the
following patterns survive in the number-field setting:
• ( 𝐿1 ) (restricted tensor product well-definedness): formal pattern. Raskin’s construction is
  ∞-categorical and does not use curve-specific structure beyond existence of local categories with
  distinguished units.
• ( 𝐿2 ) (Hecke-functoriality gluing over a finite set of primes): conditional pattern. It applies only after
  the local categorical comparison is supplied. Fargues–Scholze replaces the local de Rham geometric
  input by diamond geometry and spectral action; the cross-place compatibility argument still needs
  the local comparison and (BC-diamond-glue).
The following do not transport:
27.8. Final Reduction: L ACD to a Single Lemma                                                            219


• ( 𝐿3 ) (Bernstein-centre compatibility): obstructed by (Obs.2), (Obs.4). Resolution requires (BC-
  diamond-glue), Chapter 27.5.4.
• ( 𝐿4 ) (archimedean extension): obstructed by (Obs.1). Resolution requires independent Jacquet–
  Langlands archimedean construction (§27.6).

27.8    Final Reduction: L ACD to a Single Lemma
Statement
Theorem 27.8.1 (L ACD residual reduction). . LACD holds after the local categorical comparison
(F1.a) and the BC-diamond-gluing compatibility lemma (Chapter 27.5.4) are supplied.

Proof. By Chapter 27.2.1, LACD contains ( 𝐿1 ), ( 𝐿2 ), ( 𝐿3 ), and ( 𝐿4 ), together with the global identifi-
cation.
    ( 𝐿1 ) is a theorem (Chapter 27.3.4).
    ( 𝐿2 ) is conditional: it needs the local categorical comparison (F1.a) and (BC-diamond-glue) for the
cross-place Whittaker compatibility (Chapter 27.4.1, Steps 1 and 6).
    ( 𝐿3 ) is controlled by the Bernstein-centre gluing datum (Chapter 27.5.1).
    ( 𝐿4 ) is the archimedean boundary datum (Chapter 27.6.1).
    Hence LACD reduces, in this chapter, to the conjunction of F1.a, (BC-diamond-glue), and the global
identification after the formal construction of ( 𝐿1 ) and the archimedean datum ( 𝐿4 ).

Remark 27.8.3 (independent decomposition). The twelve established theorems of Chapter 27.8.2 decom-
pose into the following independent source lists:
Fargues–Scholze list: (1), (6), (7). Perfectoid / diamond geometry, Fargues–Fontaine curve.

These eight lists are disjoint in the orthogonal sense: no pair shares a primary author at overlapping work,
and each list has an independent primary literature. A future proof of LACD through this construction
must keep the same source separation.

Theorem 27.9.1 (F1 residual chain via L ACD ). . F1 (global arithmetic Arinkin–Gaitsgory, Chap-

27.10    Residual Obstructions
Obstruction Decomposition
After the reduction of Chapter 27.2.7, the residual inputs for LACD , and hence for F1, are:
• Local categorical comparison: the passage from the pointwise local spectral action to the local cate-
  gorical equivalence used in 𝐿2 .
• Global restricted-tensor identification: the comparison between the restricted tensor product and
  the global automorphic category.
• (BC-diamond-glue): Chapter 27.5.4. The central open residual, non-formal theorem. Domain: gluing
  of coherent Springer sheaves across a product of local Emerton–Gee stacks, plus agreement with the
  global Bernstein centre acting on the global automorphic category.

Prior Hypotheses
(BC-diamond-glue) is independent of the remaining open items from the arithmetic branch of Vol IV:
• F2.c (F2 residual, ∞-categorical Tate tensor): independent branch.
• Arithmetic Positselski: independent, on the P1 branch.
• Koszul–Petersson compatibility: independent, on the P3 branch.
• VB∗ (arithmetic Virasoro positivity): independent, on the RH branch.
    (BC-diamond-glue) is central on the F1 branch only after the local comparison and the global identi-
fication are fixed.

Primary-Literature Precedents
• Ben-Zvi–Chen–Helm–Nadler arXiv:2010.02321: local Bernstein centres as coherent sheaves on local
  Emerton–Gee stacks. This is the state of the art; (BC-diamond-glue) is the global assembly of these
  local constructions.
• Gan–Savin: partial change on restricted tensor product of local automorphic categories, with specific
  compatibilities verified for certain Jacquet–Langlands transfers; the global Bernstein-centre compati-
  bility for 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ remains open.
• AGKRRV 2020–2024 de Rham geometric Langlands: supplies the curve analogue of the centre-
  compatibility pattern. It does not prove the number-field (BC-diamond-glue) statement. The surviving
  pattern is documented in Chapter 27.7.3.

    (i) LACD decomposes into four disjoint subconditions ( 𝐿1 )–( 𝐿4 ) (Chapter 27.2.1).

    LACD reduces from one large conjecture to a formal tensor construction, local comparison, Bernstein-
centre gluing, an archimedean boundary datum, and a global identification. The structural content is
a reduction, not an equivalence theorem for F1. The reduction is supported by eight disjoint primary-
literature sources (Chapter 27.8.3).
    The residual (BC-diamond-glue) is a single compatibility check between Ben-Zvi–Chen–Helm–
Nadler’s local coherent Springer sheaves and the global Bernstein centre on the global automorphic
category. It is central on the F1 six-window branch of the arithmetic branch, but it is not the only
hypothesis.

28.5   The Hochschild-Trace Theorem (Arithmetic)
Classical Ben-Zvi–Nadler
Theorem 28.5.1 (Ben-Zvi–Nadler 2009, Theorem 1.1). . For a complex reductive group 𝐺 , there is
an equivalence of 𝐸1 -algebras
                                                                 flat
                               HH• D( 𝐺 /𝐺 ) ≃ O LocSys𝐺 ( 𝑆 1 ) ,
                                            

where 𝐺 /𝐺 is the adjoint quotient, LocSys𝐺 ( 𝑆 1 ) = 𝐺 /𝐺 as a derived stack, and the flat locus consists
of flat 𝐺 -connections (= all connections on 𝑆 1 , i.e. the whole space).
Remark 28.5.2 (structure of the classical proof). Ben-Zvi–Nadler’s proof has two ingredients.
  (i) Costello–Francis–Lurie. For a symmetric monoidal ∞-category C, HH• (C) = 𝑆 1 C, factorization
                                                                                    ∫

      homology of C over 𝑆 1 (Costello 2004; Francis arXiv:1206.5522; Lurie HA 5.5.3).
 (ii) Loop-space identiﬁcation. For C = D(X) the ∞-category of quasi-coherent sheaves on a derived
      stack X, factorization homology over 𝑆 1 equals functions on the free loop space O ( 𝐿 X), with a
      flatness cut supplied by the requirement that functions come from quasi-coherent sheaves rather
      than arbitrary pro-coherent data.
Both ingredients admit arithmetic extensions; the content of the arithmetic Ben-Zvi–Nadler theorem is
that these extensions match.

Disjoint Rationale
Proposition 28.9.1 (disjointness of the two source lists). . After replacing the inertia-only target
by the full Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) target, the derivation and comparison source lists are independent in the Vol IV
orthogonal sense:
   (i) The MKR dictionary (Mazur–Kapranov–Reznikov–Morishita) is a topological analogy that iden-
       tifies arithmetic objects with 3-manifold objects; it does not pass through factorization-homology
       or Hochschild-trace machinery. Its invariant is independent of Ben-Zvi–Francis–Nadler’s
       IndCoh/loop-space identity.
  (ii) Antieau–Nikolaus compute THH, TC, TR for arithmetic schemes via trace methods disjoint
       from Ben-Zvi–Nadler; they use the Nikolaus–Scholze THH formalism, which is 𝑆 1 -equivariant
       spectra, not factorization homology.
 (iii) Teleman’s arithmetic HKR is a direct cohomological calculation via the cotangent complex, dis-
       joint from the categorical-trace presentation.
 (iv) Prismatic Nygaard (Bhatt–Morrow–Scholze) provides the 𝑝-adic Hodge-theoretic comparison
       between pro-étale and de Rham conventions; it is a single-prime local comparison, not a global
       arithmetic Ben-Zvi–Nadler.
None of these sources is cited in the derivation chain above (except as convention-bridging remarks in
Chapter 28.5.6, which is a shared bridge not a derivation input). Hence the two lists are disjoint.

Comparison Sketch
Remark 28.9.2 (the comparison path). A non-formal comparison theorem would proceed as follows.
   (i) Teleman–Antieau–Nikolaus computation of HH• of the global Iwahori Hecke category via THH•
       of the Emerton–Gee stack regarded as a prismatic-Nygaard-polarised derived scheme. This path
       goes through the trace-methods framework of Nikolaus–Scholze, producing an 𝐸1 -algebra in
       genuine 𝑆 1 -equivariant spectra, whose underlying object matches the factorization-homology
       model of Chapter 28.5.3.
  (ii) MKR-dictionary match of the arithmetic loop space. From the topological analogy, the arithmetic
       free loop space The full-target arithmetic loop object for X Sel
                                                                    ¯𝜌,det, L corresponds to the loop space
       of the 3-manifold analogue of the Emerton–Gee stack; Morishita’s dictionary (arXiv:0904.3399
       Ch. 3) reads off the correct moduli of local-system pairs.
 (iii) Comparison of Bhatt–Morrow–Scholze prismatic-Nygaard trace with the 𝐸1 -algebra
       O (LocSysAr ) flat . Both sides give an 𝐸1 -algebra in 𝑆 1 -equivariant spectra; the match is a
       prismatic-Nygaard compatibility, encoded as the Bhatt–Lurie filtration of arXiv:2201.06120.
The domain of this comparison is deliberately smaller than the non-formal theorem main proof: the
three steps above constitute a consistency check, showing that the arithmetic Ben-Zvi–Nadler equivalence
of Chapter 28.7.1 is consistent with independent computations from disjoint source lists.

28.10    Residual Conditions
The independent comparison leaves F3 with genuine residual conditions. Besides F1 and F2, the proof
needs the corrected arithmetic BZN comparison against the full Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) target, the profinite formal-
loop continuity theorem, and the flat-locus pullback comparison. Thus F3.BZNAr remains a residual of
Chapter 21.9.
28.11. Ben-Zvi–Nadler Boundary                                                                          239


Remark 28.10.1 (residual F3 ingredients). The open ingredients are:
• the local categorical comparison (F1.a) and LACD (F1’s adelic categorical descent);
• the mixed-characteristic local 𝐸2 Hecke enhancement and (F2.c) (∞-categorical Tate restricted tensor
  product);
• profinite formal-loop continuity for Map( 𝐵 bℤ, −);
• the full Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) target comparison and flat-locus pullback;
• arithmetic Positselski (from P1’s Step 3);
• Koszul–Petersson compatibility (from P3).
The first four are number-field adaptations of function-field geometric Langlands and arithmetic loop-
space technology. The last two are bar-cobar-structural conditions internal to the arithmetic Heisenberg.

Domain: Archimedean Place
Remark 28.10.2 (archimedean contribution). Chapter 28.7.1 treats only the finite-place inertia
(Chapter 28.3.4). The archimedean contribution to V prim is the complex Heisenberg Fock on the
archimedean fibre (Chapter 21.7.1 archimedean-place discussion), whose Hochschild trace is classical
Ben-Zvi–Nadler over ℂ. The arithmetic-to-classical reduction at the archimedean place is exactly the
classical Ben-Zvi–Nadler theorem Chapter 28.5.1, which is a theorem of 2009. No new work is needed
for the archimedean fibre.

Domain: Non-𝐺 𝐿2 Groups
Remark 28.10.3 (extension to 𝐺 𝐿𝑛 ). The machinery extends to 𝐺 = 𝐺 𝐿𝑛 for any 𝑛 ≥ 1, since:
• The definition of 𝐵 ℤ b and arithmetic free loop space is group-independent.
• Local Emerton–Gee stacks are defined for all 𝑛 in Emerton–Gee arXiv:1908.07185; the global spectral
  target must still be Selmer-derived.
• Fargues–Scholze local geometrization and spectral action are available for 𝐺 𝐿𝑛 (arXiv:2102.13459
  Thm. I.9); the categorical comparison remains a separate input.
The only 𝐺 𝐿2 -specific input is F1 (LACD is currently formulated for 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ), which is a number-
theoretic arithmetic-Langlands conjecture. With F1 upgraded to 𝐺 𝐿𝑛 , Chapter 28.7.1 extends directly.
The rank-2 structure is not used essentially.

Chapter 29


The ∞-Categorical Tate Restricted Tensor
Product

Chapter 21.3.1 reduced the conjecture of global 𝐸2 -enhancement to a single ∞-operadic statement (F2.c):
the restricted tensor product of 𝐸𝑛 -monoidal stable presentable ∞-categories with distinguished units
inherits an 𝐸𝑛 -monoidal structure. The proof uses Lurie HA 4.8 + 5.1, Fresse’s treatment of the 𝐸𝑛 operad,
and Dunn additivity; no arithmetic input is required, and F2.c is proved as pure ∞-categorical assembly.
The mixed-characteristic Iwahori 𝐸2 local input F2.b remains open; F2 itself is therefore conditional.

29.1    Statement of (F2.c)
Setup and Deﬁnition
Fix a small ∞-operad O ⊗ (the chief cases are O = 𝐸𝑛 for 𝑛 ≥ 1). Fix an indexing set 𝑉 of places: in the
target application 𝑉 = | 𝐶 | is the set of places of Spec ℤ, but the statement is place-agnostic.

cofinal subposet consisting of finite 𝑆 ⊆ 𝑉 with 𝑉 \ 𝑆 ⊆ 𝑉 sph .

Source Disjointness
The proof sources of Chapter 29.1.3 are Lurie HA 4.8 (tensor products of presentable ∞-categories)
and Fresse (integral 𝐸𝑛 operad). The independent comparison sources are Dunn additivity (HA 5.1.2.4;
Dunn 1988), Ayala–Francis factorization homology, and Ginot’s account of factorization algebras of
∞-categories (§29.12). The derivation and comparison sources are disjoint: Lurie HA 4.8 does not invoke
factorization homology, and Ayala–Francis / Ginot do not prove the colimit-preservation lemmas of
HA 4.8 internally.

29.2    Obstructions and Their Resolutions
Six potential obstructions to Chapter 29.1.3 were identified and resolved; each resolution either cleans
the hypothesis, strengthens the statement, or is absorbed into a subsidiary lemma.

Centrality of the Spherical Unit
Obstruction 29.2.1 (unital inclusion). The transition map 𝜄 𝑆 ⊆ 𝑆 ′ of (29.2) inserts the unit 𝑢𝑣 at each added
place 𝑣 ∈ 𝑆 ′ \ 𝑆 . For this to be an O-monoidal functor, the unit 𝑢𝑣 must be O-central in C𝑣 . Is the unit
of an O-monoidal ∞-category automatically central?
Correction 29.2.2 (unit centrality). Lurie HA 5.1.2.26 shows that the unit object 𝟙𝑣 of an O-monoidal
∞-category C𝑣 is canonically O-central: the space Map O-Alg (𝟙 O , C𝑣 ) is contractible on 𝟙𝑣 . For a non-
unit spherical vector, (D2) includes the datum needed for insertion: 𝑢𝑣 is a compact central idempotent
algebra object under the unit, with pointed map 𝜂𝑣 : Sp → C𝑣 . This is precisely the datum that makes
𝜄 𝑆 ⊆ 𝑆 ′ an O-monoidal functor. Detailed in Lemma 29.4.1.

O-Algebra Structure under Filtered Colimits
Obstruction 29.2.3 (ﬁltered colimit of O-algebras). (29.1) is a filtered colimit in PrLst . Does the O-algebra
structure propagate through such a colimit?
Correction 29.2.4 (colimit preservation). Lurie HA 3.2.3.1, applied to the ∞-operad O ⊗ and the pre-
sentable symmetric monoidal ∞-category (PrLst , ⊗): the forgetful functor Alg O (PrLst ) → PrLst preserves
29.2. Obstructions and Their Resolutions                                                                       243


filtered colimits. Hence the colimit lim (⊗𝑣 ∈ 𝑆 C𝑣 ) taken in Alg O (PrLst ) coincides with the colimit in PrLst ,
                                     −→ 𝑆
and the O-algebra structure is preserved. Detailed in Proposition 29.5.1.

BD Factorization Axiom on Discrete 𝑉
Obstruction 29.2.5 (factorization axiom). Restricted tensor products are usually organised as factoriza-
tion algebras on the Ran space of 𝑉 . The Beilinson–Drinfeld factorization axiom requires non-trivial
compatibility across the diagonal of 𝑉 𝑛 . Does the definition (29.1) satisfy the BD factorization axiom?
Correction 29.2.6 (discreteness of 𝑉 ). 𝑉 is a discrete set of places; 𝑉 𝑛 carries the discrete topology, and
the diagonal Δ ⊂ 𝑉 𝑛 is an open-and-closed subset. The BD factorization axiom on 𝑉 reduces to the
set-theoretic statement ‘‘the stalks at distinct points are tensor products of the stalks’’ (Chapter 8.2.2),
which is automatic by definition of the Tate restricted tensor product over the complement of the
diagonal. Hence the factorization axiom is satisfied, trivially, on 𝑉 . No content is lost by using the
colimit formulation over Fin(𝑉 ) rather than a Ran-space formulation.

Dunn Additivity and the Restricted Tensor Product
Obstruction 29.2.7 (Dunn additivity compatibility). For O = 𝐸𝑛1 and O ′ = 𝐸𝑛2 with 𝑛1 + 𝑛2 = 𝑛,
Dunn additivity (HA 5.1.2.4) gives 𝐸𝑛1 ⊗𝕊 𝐸𝑛2 ≃ 𝐸𝑛1 +𝑛2 . The restricted tensor product of 𝐸𝑛1 -categories
composed with the restricted tensor product of 𝐸𝑛2 -categories should give the restricted tensor product
of 𝐸𝑛1 +𝑛2 -categories. Does Chapter 29.1.3 respect this composition?
Correction 29.2.8 (operad-variable functoriality). Additivity is a statement about the ∞-operad 𝐸𝑛 itself
(HA 5.1.2.4), whose proof is orthogonal to the colimit-preservation and unital-inclusion ingredients
of Chapter 29.1.3. The restricted-tensor-product construction applied to the operad product O ⊗ O ′
coincides with the composite of the two individual restricted tensor products, by the functoriality of
Alg (−) (PrLst ) in the operad variable. Detailed at §29.7.

Coﬁnality Invariance of the O-Structure
Obstruction 29.2.9 (uniqueness modulo coﬁnal ﬁltration). The proof of Chapter 29.1.3(M3) claims unique-
ness of the O-monoidal structure up to contractible choice. Does this uniqueness hold unconditionally,
or only modulo the choice of cofinal filtration Finsph (𝑉 )?
Correction 29.2.10 (coﬁnality invariance). Contractibility is internal to Alg O (PrLst ). The filtered colimit
along Finsph (𝑉 ) is invariant under cofinal replacement of the indexing filtered ∞-poset (HTT 4.1.1.8).
Any two cofinal filtrations give equivalent O-algebra colimits, and the map between them is unique up to
contractible space in the ∞-topos structure of Cat∞ . Hence uniqueness is cofinality-invariant. Detailed
in Chapter 29.9.1.

Ramiﬁed Places without a Spherical Unit
Obstruction 29.2.11 (ramiﬁed archimedean places). Setup 29.1.1 asks for a distinguished spherical unit 𝑢𝑣
at almost all places 𝑣 ∈ 𝑉 . At a finite number of ramified places (for 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ typically the archimedean
place and a finite set of primes where the Iwahori level is nontrivial), no spherical unit need exist. Does
Chapter 29.1.3 still apply?
Correction 29.2.12 (coﬁnite spherical locus). The setup requires a spherical unit only on a cofinite subset
𝑉 sph ⊆ 𝑉 ; the finite complement 𝑉 \ 𝑉 sph is absorbed into every finite set 𝑆 ∈ Finsph (𝑉 ) in the cofinal
filtration. Hence every finite stage of the colimit includes the ‘‘ramified’’ places, and the restricted tensor
244                        Chapter 29. The ∞-Categorical Tate Restricted Tensor Product


product is defined regardless of whether spherical units exist at those ramified places. In the 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ
application, the archimedean factor C∞ admits the 𝐾∞ -finite spherical vector |0⟩∞ ∈ C∞ (the 𝑂 (2)-fixed
vector of 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℝ)-representations on the Iwahori-level Hecke module); consequently 𝑉 sph = 𝑉 for the
target application. Detailed in Chapter 29.8.5.

29.3    ∞-Operadic Preliminaries
The proof of Chapter 29.1.3 draws on three ingredients from Lurie HA and Fresse, recorded here with
their precise references. Numbering follows Lurie HA, second edition (2017 draft).

Presentable Symmetric Monoidal Structure on PrLst
Theorem 29.3.1 (HA 4.8.1.15, HA 4.8.2.10). . The ∞-category PrL of presentable ∞-categories and
colimit-preserving functors carries a canonical symmetric monoidal structure whose tensor product is
uniquely characterised by the universal property

                                 FunL (C ⊗ D , E) ≃ FunL,L (C × D , E)

(colimit-preserving functors of tensor products = bi-colimit-preserving functors of products). The full
subcategory PrLst of stable presentable ∞-categories is closed under this tensor product and carries a
canonical symmetric monoidal structure with unit Sp (the ∞-category of spectra).
Corollary 29.3.2 (HA 4.8.1.18). . The ∞-category PrLst admits small colimits, and the tensor product
⊗ preserves colimits separately in each variable. In particular, ⊗ preserves filtered colimits in each variable.

Algebras over an ∞-Operad in a Presentable Symmetric Monoidal ∞-Category
Theorem 29.3.3 (HA 3.2.3.5, HA 3.2.4.4). . For a small coherent ∞-operad O ⊗ and a presentable
symmetric monoidal ∞-category E ⊗ with ⊗ E preserving colimits separately in each variable:
   (i) Alg O (E) is presentable;
  (ii) the forgetful functor Alg O (E) → E preserves sifted colimits (and in particular filtered colimits);
 (iii) if E is stable, so is Alg O (E) when O is unital (for instance 𝐸𝑛 with 𝑛 ≥ 0 or 𝐸∞ ).
   Applied to E ⊗ = (PrLst , ⊗): Alg O (PrLst ) is presentable and sifted-colimit-preserving into PrLst .

𝐸𝑛 -Operad and Integral Structure
Theorem 29.3.4 (Fresse 2017 Homotopy of Operads I.4.1; Lurie HA 5.1.0.4). . For each 𝑛 ≥ 0
there is an ∞-operad 𝐸𝑛⊗ (the little 𝑛-cubes operad) whose 𝑘 -ary operations are parametrised by the
space Conf 𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 ) of configurations of 𝑘 ordered little 𝑛-cubes in the unit 𝑛-cube; and this ∞-operad is
coherent in the sense of HA 3.3.1.1. The forgetful functor 𝐸𝑛⊗+1 → 𝐸𝑛⊗ realises 𝐸𝑛+1 as an 𝐸𝑛 -algebra in
∞-operads (HA 5.1.2).
Theorem 29.3.5 (Dunn additivity; HA 5.1.2.4; Dunn 1988 JPAA 50). . For any 𝑛1 , 𝑛2 ≥ 0,

                                            𝐸𝑛⊗1 ⊗ 𝐸𝑛⊗2 ≃ 𝐸𝑛⊗1 +𝑛2

as ∞-operads, where ⊗ is the tensor product of ∞-operads (HA 2.2.5.6). In particular, an 𝐸𝑛1 +𝑛2 -algebra
in E is the same datum as an 𝐸𝑛1 -algebra in 𝐸𝑛2 -algebras in E.
29.4. Unital Inclusion Functors                                                                            245


Centrality of the Unit

on a presentable stable ∞-category C, with unit 𝟙 C . Then 𝟙 C is canonically O-central: the space
MapAlg ( C) (𝟙 C , id C ) of O-algebra maps from the trivial algebra to the endomorphism algebra of
       O

canonically equivalent to every other.
   Chapter 29.3.6 is the foundation of Lemma 29.4.1.

29.7    Compatibility with BD Factorization
The restricted tensor product of Chapter 29.1.2 is a degenerate instance of a Beilinson–Drinfeld (BD,
Chiral Algebras §3.4) factorization algebra, reduced to discrete 𝑉 : the BD factorization axiom degenerates
to a tautological tensor-product decomposition over disjoint finite subsets.

Factorization on a Discrete Ran Space
Setup 29.7.1 (discrete Ran space of 𝑉 ). Let 𝑉 be a discrete set and Ran(𝑉 ) the colimit in prestacks of the
diagram sending a finite ordinal [ 𝑛] to the non-empty functions [ 𝑛] → 𝑉 . Since 𝑉 is discrete, Ran(𝑉 )
is the countable union lim Sym𝑛 (𝑉 ) of symmetric powers of 𝑉 , a discrete combinatorial object.
                          −→𝑛
Deﬁnition 29.7.2 (factorization algebra on a discrete space). A factorization algebra on 𝑉 in the category
of O-algebras in PrLst is a diagram

                                      A : Fin(𝑉 ) op −→ Alg O (PrLst )

satisfying the factorization axiom: for every pair of disjoint finite subsets 𝑆1 , 𝑆2 ⊂ 𝑉 ,

                                      A ( 𝑆1 ⊔ 𝑆2 ) ≃ A ( 𝑆1 ) ⊗ A ( 𝑆2 )

as O-algebras, with this equivalence natural in inclusions of subsets.
Theorem 29.7.3 (BD factorization axiom on discrete 𝑉 is automatic). . The diagram Φ { C𝑣 ,𝑢𝑣 } of
Chapter 29.4.3 is a factorization algebra on the discrete set 𝑉 in the sense of Definition 29.7.2. Its value
on 𝑆 = {𝑣1 , . . . , 𝑣𝑘 } is 𝑘𝑖=1 C𝑣𝑖 , and on a disjoint union 𝑆1 ⊔ 𝑆2 is A ( 𝑆1 ) ⊗ A ( 𝑆2 ) by associativity of
                            N
the tensor product.

Proof. The factorization axiom on a discrete set is the set-theoretic identity ‘‘tensor product of finite
collections of stalks at disjoint positions equals the tensor product of the two tensor products’’ (cf. Chap-
ter 8.2.2). This is the definition of the tensor product in PrLst (HA 4.8.1.15), applied to the diagram Φ. No
further content arises.

where A Ran is the factorization algebra of Chapter 29.7.3 together with the unital extension data of

Remark 29.7.5 (why the factorization axiom is trivial here). The BD factorization axiom on a smooth
complex curve encodes the OPE singularity at the diagonal: as two points collide, the product of two
operators is the ‘‘fused’’ operator plus a singular part. Over a discrete set 𝑉 , distinct points cannot
collide; all pairs of points are ‘‘separated’’. Hence the BD factorization axiom carries no content on
discrete 𝑉 . The restricted tensor product formulation of Chapter 29.1.2 is the correct generalization to
discrete bases; the BD content that genuinely concentrates at the archimedean place is handled separately
(Chapter 8.6.2).

Compatibility with Dunn Additivity
The restricted tensor product commutes with Dunn additivity (Chapter 29.3.5) in the following precise
sense.
Proposition 29.7.6 (Dunn additivity commutes with restricted tensor product). . Fix 𝑛1 , 𝑛2 ≥ 0
and let {C𝑣 }𝑣 ∈𝑉 be a family of 𝐸𝑛1 +𝑛2 -monoidal stable presentable ∞-categories with spherical units
{ 𝑢𝑣 }𝑣 ∈𝑉 sph . Then the restricted tensor product 𝑣′ (C𝑣 , 𝑢𝑣 ) constructed via Chapter 29.1.3 with O =
                                                   N
𝐸𝑛1 +𝑛2 coincides, as an 𝐸𝑛1 +𝑛2 -monoidal ∞-category, with the iterated construction:
 (a) View each C𝑣 as an 𝐸𝑛1 -algebra in 𝐸𝑛2 -monoidal stable presentable ∞-categories (via Chap-
     ter 29.3.5);

Via Chapter 29.3.5, this is an 𝐸𝑛1 +𝑛2 -monoidal structure. It agrees with the 𝐸𝑛1 +𝑛2 -structure of Chap-

Proof. Both constructions yield filtered colimits in the same presentable ∞-category. The key is that the

of the direct construction. Formally: the forgetful functor Alg 𝐸𝑛 +𝑛 ≃ Alg 𝐸𝑛 ⊗ 𝐸𝑛 → Alg 𝐸𝑛 commutes
                                                                  1 2         1    2          2
with filtered colimits (Chapter 29.3.7), so both iterated colimit computations agree.

archimedean factor. In the Fock space presentation of Chapter 21.7.1, it is the ℂ · |0⟩∞ ∈ H (∞) of
Segal 1981.

29.10    Base Change and Functoriality
The restricted tensor product is functorial in the family {C𝑣 } and covariant under base change.
Proposition 29.10.1 (functoriality in the family). . Given two families of data ({C𝑣 }, { 𝑢𝑣 }) and
({C𝑣′ }, { 𝑢𝑣′ }) satisfying Setup 29.1.1, together with a family of O-monoidal functors 𝑓𝑣 : C𝑣 → C𝑣′ such
that 𝑓𝑣 ( 𝑢𝑣 ) is canonically equivalent to 𝑢𝑣′ at all 𝑣 ∈ 𝑉 sph ∩ 𝑉 ′sph where both spherical units are defined
(spherical compatibility). Then there is a canonical O-monoidal functor
                                 ′             ′                     ′
                                        𝑓𝑣 :
                                 O             O                     O
                                                     (C𝑣 , 𝑢𝑣 ) −→       (C𝑣′ , 𝑢𝑣′ )
                                    𝑣            𝑣                   𝑣

and the assignment { 𝑓𝑣 } ↦→        𝑣 𝑓𝑣 is ∞-functorial in the ∞-category of spherically compatible O-
                                 N′
monoidal families.

Proof. For each 𝑆 ∈ Finsph (𝑉 ∩ 𝑉 ′ ) the finite tensor product ⊗𝑣 ∈ 𝑆 𝑓𝑣 : ⊗𝑣 ∈ 𝑆 C𝑣 → ⊗𝑣 ∈ 𝑆 C𝑣′ is O-
monoidal (HA 3.2.4.5). Spherical compatibility ensures the natural transformations 𝜄′𝑆 ⊆ 𝑆 ′ ◦ 𝑓𝑆 = 𝑓𝑆 ′ ◦
𝜄 𝑆 ⊆ 𝑆 ′ up to canonical equivalence. Taking the filtered colimit gives the morphism between colimits
in Alg O (PrLst ). Functoriality is the colimit-preservation of functor-composition, which follows from
HA 3.2.3.1.

adjunction, and bar–cobar inversion. In Vol IV the analogous statement for restricted tensor products
on the categorical level enables transport of F2 statements across arithmetic bases (e.g. from Spec ℤ to a
finite Galois extension).

resulting factorization algebra agrees with both of the previous two constructions. Three disjoint con-
structions, one answer; the independence of sources requirement is satisfied.

29.13     Remarks on Operadic Coherence
Why 𝐸𝑛 -coherence is required
We used coherence of 𝐸𝑛 (HA 3.3.1.1) in two places:
  (i) Chapter 29.3.3(1): presentability of Alg O (E).
 (ii) Chapter 29.3.7: filtered colimits in Alg O (E) are computed underlyingly.
   Both of these require the coherence hypothesis on O, which amounts to the statement that O has
enough operations to express its own composition; 𝐸𝑛 satisfies this by HA 5.1.0.7.

when 𝑢˜ 𝑣 is equivalent to 𝑢𝑣 as O-central objects. Different choices can give different restricted tensor
products; the natural spherical-unit choice is distinguished by the unit property.

29.15    Tate Tensor Boundary
  (i) The ∞-categorical Tate restricted tensor product of O-monoidal stable presentable ∞-categories
      with distinguished spherical units inherits a canonical O-monoidal structure (Chapter 29.1.3); the
      proof is a direct application of Lurie HA 4.8 + 5.1 and the centrality of the unit (HA 5.1.2.26).
256                        Chapter 29. The ∞-Categorical Tate Restricted Tensor Product


  (ii) The statement is place-agnostic: it applies to any indexing set 𝑉 with cofinite-many spherical units.
       The arithmetic application 𝑉 = | 𝐶 |, C𝑣 = HkIw    𝐺 𝐿2 ,𝑣 , 𝑢𝑣 = |0⟩𝑣 supplies the F2.c restricted-tensor
       assembly step (Chapter 29.8.3); the local Iwahori 𝐸2 -input for full F2 is separate.
 (iii) The structure is unique up to contractible choice (Chapter 29.9.1); functorial in the family of
       O-categories (Chapter 29.10.1); and base-change-covariant along symmetric monoidal colimit-
       preserving functors (Chapter 29.10.2).
 (iv) Dunn additivity (Chapter 29.3.5) commutes with the restricted tensor product (Chapter 29.7.6);
       iterated constructions (e.g. 𝐸1 -algebras in 𝐸1 -categories giving an 𝐸2 -restricted-tensor) agree with
       direct 𝐸2 -application.
  (v) Independent comparison via Ayala–Francis factorization homology (Chapter 29.12.2) and Ginot’s
       factorization-algebra account (Chapter 29.12.3) confirm the O-monoidal structure through a
       second, derivation-disjoint construction; the derivation and comparison sources do not share a
       common sub-argument.
 (vi) The restricted-tensor part F2.c is proved as a formal theorem under the pointed-unit 𝐸2 hypotheses
       stated above. F2 itself remains conditional on the mixed-characteristic Iwahori 𝐸2 local input. Any
       simplification of F3 that assumes F2 remains conditional on that local input.
   F2.c is a pure ∞-categorical statement; the only arithmetic content is the choice of the place-set 𝑉 and
the family {HkIw 𝐺 𝐿2 ,𝑣 }. The proof draws exclusively on Lurie HA 4.8 + 5.1 and central-unit properties;
F2 itself remains conditional, conditional on the local Iwahori 𝐸2 -monoidal input.
   The next step is F3, which requires the arithmetic Ben-Zvi–Nadler identification of Hochschild trace
with functions on the arithmetic free loop space. That is a genuinely arithmetic obstruction; it is not
absorbed into the ∞-categorical formalism of Lurie HA, and it remains open (Chapter 21.4.1).
Chapter 30


Independent Comparison: Residual Structure

Chapter 21 left six residual conditions open: LACD (adelic categorical descent), F2.c (∞-categorical Tate
restricted tensor product), F3.BZNAr (arithmetic Ben-Zvi–Nadler identification), arithmetic Positselski
(co-contra equivalence over Λ), Koszul–Petersson compatibility, and VB∗ (arithmetic Virasoro posi-
tivity). Each residual is compared with an independent source class. Each residual decomposes into its
strongest theorem on the stated domain and the exact subconditions needed beyond that domain. The
central logical defect in Chapter 22 is the false biconditional VB∗ ⇔ zero-placement, arising from an
incorrect application of the Hamburger moment problem to an unbounded operator.

30.1   First Residual Decomposition
F2.c: ∞-Categorical Tate Restricted Tensor Product
The statement of F2.c in Chapter 21 invokes a ‘‘distinguished unit 𝑢𝑣 ∈ C𝑣 ’’ and a ‘‘canonical 𝐸2 -
monoidal structure’’ on the restricted tensor-product colimit, but neither is formally constructed. The
notation ⊗𝑣∉ 𝑆 𝟙𝑢𝑣 mixes an ∞-categorical colimit with degenerate factors whose categorical form is left
implicit. Tate-style additivity for 𝐸𝑛 -algebras in presentable ∞-categories (the required formalism) is
cited to Lurie HA 4.8 and 5.1 but is not a theorem stated there. The correct statement requires a formal
definition of pointed 𝐸𝑛 -monoidal category and a universal-property formulation of the colimit; see
Chapter 30.2.1 and Chapter 30.2.3. The broad F2.c statement is conjectural; the central idempotent
pointed-unit 𝐸2 case is the restricted theorem of Chapter 52.3.1.

LACD : Adelic Categorical Descent
LACD in Chapter 21 asserts that the adelic categorical descent from local automorphic categories to
the global automorphic category holds; but four subconditions are conflated into the single statement:
(i) dg-categorical proof that the restricted tensor product with distinguished units preserves the colimit
structure; (ii) proof that local Hecke-functoriality together with cross-prime commutativity implies
global Hecke-functoriality on the colimit; (iii) sph-finite preservation under the colimit; (iv) strong ap-
proximation for the simply connected derived group, together with the determinant idele-class quotient
for 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ. Subcondition (iv) is a theorem after this separation: Kneser supplies the simply connected
strong-approximation input for 𝑆 𝐿2 , while Tate’s idelic formalism supplies the determinant quotient.
The conditions (i)–(iii) depend on F2.c and are conjectural. Thus LACD splits into the four subconditions
LACD .1–LACD .4; see Chapter 30.2.4.

F3.BZNAr : Arithmetic Ben-Zvi–Nadler Identiﬁcation
F3.BZNAr proposes that the arithmetic analogue of the Ben-Zvi–Nadler Hochschild-trace identification
holds. Three independent obstructions separate the complex-analytic source theorem from its arith-
metic extension. (R1) Ben-Zvi–Nadler’s proof over ℂ uses holomorphic factorization on 𝑆 1 = 𝐵 ℤ; the
arithmetic analogue requires locally-constant-with-Adams factorization on 𝐵 b
                                                                            ℤ, and the survival of the


                                                   257
258                                 Chapter 30. Independent Comparison: Residual Structure


Hochschild-trace pairing under this qualitative change is not established via Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum
DAG Vol. II for formal-Noetherian targets. (R2) The arithmetic free loop space requires a fixed descent
topology; the rigid-analytic topology on the Emerton–Gee stack (arXiv:1908.07185 §2) is the canonical
choice. (R3) The Mazur–Kapranov–Reznikov dictionary (primes as knots, Spec ℤ as 3-manifold) is a
heuristic motivation; the technical content runs through the Emerton–Gee rigid-analytic construction.
The arithmetic statement uses R2’s topology, treats R3 as motivation, and isolates R1’s formal-Noetherian
extension as the open subcondition; see Chapter 30.2.5.

Arithmetic Positselski Co-Contra Equivalence: Abelian Domain
The arithmetic Positselski co-contra equivalence 𝐷ch     co ( 𝐶 -comod ) ≃ 𝐷 ctr ( 𝐶 -contramod ) as

(1979) gives 𝜇 ( 𝐶 ) = 0 and the equivalence reduces to flat base change over Λ = ℤ 𝑝 [[ Γ]]) and the non-
abelian case, where no 𝜇 = 0 input is available. The decorated derived categories 𝐷ch      co           ctr

Koszul–Petersson Compatibility: Sub-Claim Structure
The Koszul–Petersson compatibility asserted in Chapter 21 is the identity ⟨·, ·⟩ Pet = ⟨·, ·⟩ Koszul ◦ (id ⊗
BC-inv.) where BC-inv. denotes the Bost–Connes involution on the dual. The assertion conflates seven
independent sub-claims: (K1) definition of the arithmetic Koszul pairing via adic transfer of Vol I’s
derived-centre pairing; (K2) Hecke-equivariant embedding V prim ↩→ 𝐿 2 ( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 ]) sph-fin ; (K3) specifica-
tion of the Bost–Connes anti-involution as the KMS1 Tomita–Takesaki modular conjugation after the
modular half-density normalisation; (K4) archimedean normalisation; (K5) reconciliation of the Bost–
Connes KMS1 pairing with the local Whittaker/Kirillov pairing at each finite prime 𝑝, up to the local
𝐿 -factor 𝐿 𝑝 (1, Ad); (K6) agreement of adelic Tamagawa measure with the restricted tensor product of
local Haar measures; (K7) confirmation that the sph-finite cut is the natural locus for the identification.
The represented local modular operator in K3 is explicit. The native embedding in K2, the archimedean
pairing maps in K4, the finite maps in K5 and their compatible assembly remain separate hypotheses.
The Heisenberg self-duality and Bost–Connes self-duality are each properties of their respective objects;
the sub-claim structure exhibits that their pairing requires a separate comparison. See Chapter 30.2.8.

VB∗ : Arithmetic Virasoro Positivity and the Biconditional Error
Chapter 22 contained a false theorem: the equivalence VB∗ ⇔ zero-placement. Three independent errors
produced it. First, the proof used the Hamburger moment problem to pass from 𝜆𝑛 ≥ 0 for all 𝑛 to
𝑇𝑛 ⪰ 0 for all 𝑛. This equivalence holds for bounded self-adjoint operators (Akhiezer–Glazman, Theory
of Linear Operators in Hilbert Space, Ch. VI.3, determinate case) but fails for unbounded operators; 𝐿0Ar
is unbounded. Second, the claim that 𝐿0Ar has spectrum concentrated at the non-trivial zeros of 𝜉 is
the Hilbert–Pólya conjecture: it is a hypothesis, not a theorem derivable from P1, P2, or P3. Third, the
domain and self-adjoint extension of 𝐿0Ar on the primary Fock were not specified. The mathematical
form is: the arithmetic Hilbert–Pólya hypothesis H-PAr (Chapter 22.3.2) is a separate input; the valid
implication is VB∗ ⇒ zero-placement (Chapter 22.3.10); and VB∗ implies Li-positivity (Chapter 22.3.9).
The converse direction (zero-placement ⇒ VB∗ ) becomes an explicit open spectral-regularity question
not supplied by RH alone.

         Pointed 𝐸𝑛 -monoidal Category
        Deﬁnition 30.2.1 (pointed 𝐸𝑛 -monoidal category). A pointed 𝐸𝑛 -monoidal stable presentable ∞-category
        is a triple (C , 𝑢, 𝜂 ) consisting of: an 𝐸𝑛 -monoidal stable presentable ∞-category C (Lurie HA 5.1.2); an
        object 𝑢 ∈ C; and a specified unit-comparison map 𝜂 : 𝟙 C → 𝑢 in C.
        Remark 30.2.2 (why pointed). Tate’s restricted direct product of vector spaces uses a distinguished unit (a
        fixed vector) at almost all places. The ∞-categorical analogue is a distinguished object 𝑢𝑣 with a specified
        unit-comparison map. Without 𝜂 , there is no canonical way to embed C ⊗ 𝟙𝑢𝑣 into a restricted tensor
        product; 𝜂 supplies precisely the comparison map that makes the embedding functorial.

         LACD Split into Four Named Subconditions
        Theorem 30.2.4 (L ACD split). . LACD is equivalent to the conjunction of:
 (LACD .1) Dg-categorical colimit commutation. The restricted tensor product of dg-categories with pointed
           units commutes with the sph-finite truncation. Form: conjectural; depends on F2.c tightened
           (Chapter 30.2.3).
(LACD .2) Cross-prime Hecke coherence. For distinct primes 𝑝 ≠ 𝑞 , the local Hecke operators 𝑇𝑝 and 𝑇𝑞 com-
           mute on the restricted tensor product of local automorphic categories, with associativity and unit
           coherences. Form: conjectural; follows from local Hecke-functoriality (Fargues–Scholze) plus a
           symmetric-monoidal coherence check.
(LACD .3) Sph-ﬁnite preservation. The sph-finite subcategory Dsph-fin ( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ𝑣 )]) is preserved under the
           restricted-tensor colimit: the colimit of sph-finite categories embeds in the sph-finite subcategory of
           the colimit. Form: conjectural; plausibly automatic given (LACD .1).
(LACD .4) Strong approximation and determinant quotient. The simply connected group 𝑆 𝐿2 /ℚ satisfies strong

         Under this split, LACD follows from (LACD .1) + (LACD .2) + (LACD .3); (LACD .4) is theorem.

    Proof. Positselski’s 2011 co-contra equivalence is proved for conilpotent coalgebras over a field. Under
    flat base change 𝑘 → Λ, the equivalence lifts provided conilpotence is preserved, which holds for abelian

    lattice carries trivial Γ-action).

        Consequently, the Step 3 computation in Chapter 21.5.1 (the bar-cobar weights computation) is
    reduced for the arithmetic Heisenberg under the same flatness input. P1’s full equivalence is conditional
    in the Heisenberg case.

    Koszul–Petersson Compatibility Split into Seven Sub-Claims
    Theorem 30.2.8 (Koszul–Petersson compatibility split). . The Koszul–Petersson compatibility
    (Chapter 21.7.2) is equivalent to the conjunction of:
(K1) Koszul-pairing deﬁnition. The arithmetic Koszul pairing is the adic transfer of Vol I’s derived-centre
     pairing to the arithmetic setting, defined via the arithmetic bar-cobar adjunction (Chapter 12.8.1).
     Form: definitional; explicit.
(K2) Native 𝐿 2 -embedding. The comparison requires an injective, Hecke-equivariant map from the spec-
     ified native core V prim to the chosen automorphic 𝐿 2 space. Factorization of an already realized
     automorphic representation does not construct this map from a native Hochschild carrier. Form:
     native realization hypothesis.
(K3) Bost–Connes involution speciﬁed. The BC anti-involution on 𝔸BC is the algebraic ∗-operation 𝜇𝑚 ↦→
     𝜇∗𝑚 , 𝑒 ( 𝛾 ) ↦→ 𝑒 (− 𝛾 ). Its KMS1 GNS lift is the Tomita–Takesaki modular conjugation only after the
     modular half-density 𝑚1/2 is inserted on 𝜇𝑚 Ω, while 𝑚 −1/2 multiplies 𝜇∗𝑚 Ω. This is proved for the rep-
     resented prime Gibbs quotient in Chapter 25.10.2. A native pairing lift further requires Chapter 26.1.1.
     Form: local operator construction with a separate native comparison.

(K4) Archimedean normalization. The Fock form has explicit coefficient conjugation. Its identification
     with a native Petersson integral requires the archimedean maps of Chapter 26.3.6; a Gaussian integral
     alone does not identify the full carriers. Form: conditional transfer.
(K5) Finite-place reconciliation. The comparison with Whittaker and Koszul forms requires the actual maps
     of Chapter 35.7.4. Adjoint factors and Haar volumes are fixed in those maps and forms. The identity

     normalizations.
(K6) Tamagawa–restricted-tensor agreement. The global Tamagawa measure on 𝐿 2 ( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 ]) restricts to the
     restricted tensor product of local Haar measures up to a constant 𝑐Tam = 1 for 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ (Weil Basic
     Number Theory, 1967, §7). Form: theorem.
(K7) Sph-ﬁnite is the natural cut. The identification degenerates on Eisenstein summands (which lie outside

   The local modular construction does not remove the native embedding, archimedean or finite pairing-

   VB∗ : One-Directional Implication and the Converse Residual
   The logical form determined by the three obstructions in §30.1 is:
   • Hypothesis H-PAr (arithmetic Hilbert–Pólya) stated as Chapter 22.3.2 with explicit form as a separate
     input not derivable from P1, P2, P3.
   • The one-directional implication VB∗ ⇒ zero-placement (Chapter 22.3.10) in place of the false bicon-
     ditional.
   • VB∗ ⇒ Li-positivity (Chapter 22.3.9), with the failure of the converse for unbounded operators made
     explicit.
       The converse direction (zero-placement ⇒ VB∗ ) is an explicit open question:
   Conjecture 30.2.9 (VB∗ converse). Assume P2, P3, H-PAr , and the zero-placement clause of F-RH, that is,
   RH. Then VB∗ holds: 𝑇𝑛 ⪰ 0 for all 𝑛 ≥ 1 as operators on the primary arithmetic Heisenberg Fock.
   Remark 30.2.10 (VB∗ converse requires spectral regularity). Chapter 30.2.9 is not implied by RH alone:
   the Hamburger moment problem for unbounded operators fails to be determinate in general, so trace-
   positivity of all moments does not force operator-positivity. The converse would require additional
   spectral regularity of 𝐿0Ar beyond the generic unbounded self-adjoint operator with prescribed spectrum.

        30.4    Second Residual Decomposition
        Iterating the residual decomposition gives sharper subconditions. A cross-chapter contradiction between
        H-PAr and the Virasoro analysis of Chapter 14 is identified and corrected.

        F2.c: 𝐸2 -Algebra Structure on the Unit Map
        The weaker datum 𝜂 : 𝟙 → 𝑢 in C is not enough. For the restricted tensor product to inherit a canonical
        𝐸2 -monoidal structure via the universal property of Lurie HA 3.2 (colimits in symmetric monoidal
        ∞-categories), the transition maps must be 𝐸2 -algebra morphisms, which forces 𝜂 to lie in Alg 𝐸2 (C)𝟙/ .
        The Dunn additivity theorem ( 𝐸2 ⊗ 𝐸2 = 𝐸4 ) is not a source of additional structure but a constraint: the
        𝐸2 -truncation of the natural 𝐸4 -tower is canonical only given the universal property. Thus 𝜂 is required
        to be an 𝐸2 -algebra map and add the universal-property clause.

        LACD : Archimedean Stratum and Hecke-at-Inﬁnity
        The first-comparison split into LACD .1– .4 covers only finite places. At 𝑣 = ∞, the spherical condition is
        𝐾∞ -finiteness / admissibility in the sense of Harish-Chandra (1966), not Iwahori-fixedness; the empty-
        𝑆 base case collapses to 𝐷 ( 𝐵 𝐾∞ ), not to the trivial category. The completed Tate character Λ 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) =
        Γℝ ( 𝑠 ) 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) forces any honest LACD to include a parallel archimedean factor. The new subcondition is:
(LACD .0) Archimedean stratum. At 𝑣 = ∞, the local factor is 𝐷 ((𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-modsph-fin ) with admissibility (Harish-
          Chandra) replacing Iwahori-fixedness; LACD .2 extends to include 𝑈 (𝔤𝔩 2 ) 𝐾∞ -equivariance commuting
          with the finite-prime Hecke operators 𝑇𝑝 ; the empty- 𝑆 base is Rep( 𝐾∞ ) with 𝜂 : 𝟙 → triv 𝐾∞ . Form:
          conjectural.

Koszul–Petersson Compatibility: Five Higher-Structural Sub-Claims
The scalar-level decomposition K1–K7 of the first comparison (Chapter 30.2.8) conceals five higher-
