primes where Hecke characters ramify; (K6a) Tamagawa invariance under K5’s Godement–Jacquet

sub-claim: it is a concrete yes/no question admitting a direct calculation in the ramified case.

30.5   Resulting Logical Core
The subcondition structure is as follows.
    For F2.c: the unit-comparison map 𝜂 in Chapter 30.2.1 must be an 𝐸2 -algebra map (object of
Alg 𝐸2 (C)𝟙/ ), and the colimit’s 𝐸2 -structure is the unique one making transition maps 𝐸2 -algebra
morphisms (Lurie HA 3.2).
    For LACD : new subcondition LACD .0 (archimedean stratum, as above); LACD .2 is extended to include
𝑈 (𝔤𝔩 2 ) 𝐾∞ -equivariance.
    For F3.BZNAr : R1 splits into R1.fin-type (GR theorem, inapplicable to Emerton–Gee directly) and
R1.formal (the open conjectural extension); R4 is the non-semisimple Hecke condition at wild primes
 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3}.
    For arithmetic Positselski: five supplementary subconditions C1–C5 added (see above); C5 functori-
ality is the bottleneck for the P1 Step 3 closure via functorial pullback.
    For Koszul–Petersson: five higher-structural sub-claims K1a–K7a added; K5a (defect-pairing anomaly
at ramified primes in the Kim arithmetic Chern–Simons setup) is the highest-risk sub-claim.
    For VB∗ : the cross-chapter contradiction between H-PAr and Chapter 14 is resolved by domain re-
striction to the primary subspace; primary-Virasoro reconciliation (Chapter 22.3.5) and Weyl-asymptotic
class are residual hypotheses.
    The resulting core comprises: P1 for the arithmetic Heisenberg, conditional on C1–C5 and the
arithmetic-Positselski hypotheses (Chapter 30.2.7); P2 on its stated domain; P3 through twelve sub-
claims K1–K7 and K1a–K7a (mostly theorems or definitional, highest risk K5a); the reductions of
F1, F2, F3 into named subconditions including LACD .0, R4, and R1.formal; and the VB∗ ⇒ zero-
placement chain (Chapter 22.3.10) with explicit H-PAr (Chapter 22.3.2) and primary-Virasoro reconcili-
ation (Chapter 22.3.5).
    The sufficient hypothesis cluster for the arithmetic Riemann hypothesis via the V prim -to-RH chain
(§22) consists of: arithmetic Positselski (C1–C5); Koszul–Petersson compatibility (K1–K7, K1a–K7a); H-
PAr ; primary-Virasoro reconciliation; Weyl-asymptotic class (Berry–Keating vs. Connes adelic vs. Meyer);
and VB∗ : approximately six independent clusters, several with theorem-form sub-pieces already proved.
The converse direction zero-placement ⇒ VB∗ remains a spectral-regularity conjecture beyond the
Riemann hypothesis (Chapter 30.2.9).
    The two decisive mathematical points are the falsity of the biconditional VB∗ ⇔ zero-placement and
the compatibility of H-PAr with the Witt-only theorem of Chapter 14. The first leaves only the forward
implication VB∗ ⇒ zero-placement. The second restricts the H-PAr operator to the primary subspace
and preserves V prim as a Hochschild trace class.

LACD .0: archimedean stratum
At the archimedean place, the local category Dsph-fin ( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℝ)]) is not defined by Iwahori-fixed vectors
(as at finite primes) but by (𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-admissibility: the empty- 𝑆 base case of the restricted tensor product
is Rep( 𝐾∞ ), not Vec, and any construction of the restricted tensor product ′               C𝑣 must carry a
                                                                                    N
                                                                                       𝑣 ∈ |𝐶 |
parallel archimedean factor.
31.3. L ACD . 0: Archimedean Stratum Closure                                                              269


    The resolution is Harish-Chandra admissibility. The archimedean local category is D((𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-modsph-fin )
with admissibility replacing Iwahori-fixedness. Jacquet–Langlands SLN 114 §1–3 and Vogan 1981
classify the admissible (𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-modules for 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℝ); the sph-fin cut selects the modules finite over
the archimedean Hecke algebra (the convolution algebra of bi- 𝐾∞ -finite distributions). The detailed
construction and proof appear in Chapter 31.3.

LACD .1: colimit commutation
                                                                                  sph-fin
The filtered colimit defining 𝑣′ C𝑣 and the sph-fin subcategory inclusion C𝑣              ↩→ C𝑣 are a priori
                               N
unrelated operations; it is not immediate that they commute.
    F2.c tightened (Chapter 29.1.3) supplies the universal property needed: the restricted tensor product
of pointed 𝐸𝑛 -monoidal categories carries a canonical 𝐸𝑛 -monoidal structure, unique up to a contractible
space of choices, compatible with the insertion functors 𝜄 𝑆 . Sph-finite truncation is defined by compact
generation (Chapter 27.2.4), and Lurie HA 5.3.2.9 gives that filtered colimits of compactly generated
categories along compact-generator-preserving functors are compactly generated. Hence the colimit
commutes with the sph-fin inclusion. The proof appears in Chapter 31.4.

LACD .2: cross-prime Hecke coherence
For distinct primes 𝑝 ≠ 𝑞 , the local Hecke operators 𝑇𝑝 and 𝑇𝑞 act on disjoint tensor factors of the
restricted tensor product. The question is whether they commute up to coherent associators and unit
coherences, and whether this extends to 𝑈 (𝔤𝔩 2 ) 𝐾∞ -equivariance at the archimedean place.
    Lurie HA 5.1.2.4 (Dunn additivity) and HA 5.1.2.26 (centrality of the unit in an 𝐸𝑛 -monoidal cate-
gory) supply the coherence: endofunctors of a tensor product acting on disjoint tensor factors commute
up to a contractible space of coherence data. Extension to the archimedean place is immediate from the
disjointness of C∞ and each C 𝑝 as tensor factors. The proof appears in Chapter 31.5.

LACD .3: sph-ﬁnite preservation
Sph-finite truncation composes with the colimit to give the sph-finite truncation of the colimit (not
merely an approximation), because this is the content of LACD .1: if the colimit commutes with sph-fin,
then the sph-fin subcategory of the colimit equals the colimit of sph-fin subcategories. Chapter 27.2.4
handles the compact generation step. The proof appears in Chapter 31.6.

Archimedean character and the completed 𝜉 -function
The archimedean factor Γℝ ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜋 − 𝑠/2 Γ ( 𝑠 /2) is the archimedean local 𝐿 -factor of the trivial represen-
tation; Tate 1950 §4.3 computes it as the Mellin transform of the Gaussian. Thus the trace comparison,
if it is constructed, must send the archimedean unit to the Gaussian Tate vector. The restricted tensor
product is compared with Λ 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) = Γℝ ( 𝑠 ) 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ), not with 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) alone. The necessary Tate calculation
appears in Chapter 31.8; the categorical trace comparison is a separate input.

Theorem 31.3.3 (L ACD . 0 closed). . The archimedean category C∞ of Chapter 31.3.2 is:
   (i) a well-defined stable presentable ∞-category;
  (ii) equipped with a distinguished unit 𝑢∞ ∈ C∞ (the 𝐾∞ -spherical unramified principal series) whose
       unit-comparison map 𝜂∞ : 𝟙 C∞ → 𝑢∞ is canonical;
 (iii) classifiable by Langlands–Vogan parameters (Vogan 1981 Chapters 2–5): the isomorphism classes
       of irreducible admissible (𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-modules correspond bijectively to triples ( 𝜆, 𝜇, 𝜀 ) with 𝜆 ∈ ℂ
       (weight), 𝜇 ∈ ℤ ≥0 (discrete-series parameter), and 𝜀 ∈ {±1} (central character sign);
 (iv) the empty- 𝑆 base case of the restricted tensor product is Rep( 𝐾∞ ), not Vec.

Proof. Step 1: Stability and presentability. The category of (𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-modules is abelian (Wallach 1988
§0.1). Passing to the derived category and restricting to admissible modules (finite per 𝐾∞ -isotype)
preserves stability (the derived category of an abelian category is stable). Presentability follows from
Wallach 1988 Theorem 0.A.2: the category of admissible (𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-modules is an abelian Grothendieck
category, so its derived category is presentable (Lurie HA 1.3.5.21).

      Step 2: Distinguished unit. The unramified principal series Ind𝐺𝐵 (ℝ)           ( 𝜒1 ⊠ 𝜒2 ) with 𝜒1 = 𝜒2 =
| · | 0 the trivial character gives the irreducible spherical unramified principal series; this is the archimedean
analogue of the spherical Iwahori-fixed vector at a finite prime. Harish-Chandra 1958 ‘‘Spherical functions
on a semisimple Lie group’’ identifies this module as the unique irreducible admissible representation of
𝐺 𝐿2 (ℝ) with a non-zero 𝐾∞ -fixed vector at weight 0. The unit-comparison map 𝜂∞ : 𝟙 → 𝑢∞ is the
inclusion of the unit admissible module (the trivial character of the archimedean Hecke algebra) into
the spherical unramified principal series.
      Step 3: Langlands–Vogan classification. Vogan 1981 Theorem 5.1.1 gives the Langlands classification
for 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℝ): the irreducible admissible (𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-modules are parametrized by Langlands data, which
for 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℝ) reduces to the triple ( 𝜆, 𝜇, 𝜀 ). The classes are:
• principal series (including the spherical unramified one), parametrized by 𝜆 ∈ ℂ and central character
  sign 𝜀 ;
• discrete series 𝐷 𝑘 for 𝑘 ∈ ℤ ≥2 , with lowest weight 𝑘 ;
• limits of discrete series 𝐷1± ;
• irreducible unitary finite-dimensional modules (only the trivial module here).
Each class is 𝐾∞ -finite in each isotype, hence admissible. Wallach 1988 Ch. 5 organises these into the
admissible spectrum.

with 𝑢∞ is Sp ⊗ 𝑢∞ , which inside C∞ is the full subcategory generated by 𝑢∞ . Since 𝑢∞ is a 𝐾∞ -finite
admissible module, this subcategory is Rep( 𝐾∞ ) as a subcategory of admissible (𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-modules. The
empty- 𝑆 base is therefore Rep( 𝐾∞ ), not Vec.

Proposition 31.3.4 (uniformity of the sph-fin definition across places). . The sph-fin condition
at an archimedean place (Chapter 31.3.2) is the natural admissibility restriction, and coincides with the
finite-prime sph-fin condition (compact-generated ∞-category with finite-type compacts) under the
identification of 𝐾∞ -finite admissible modules with finite-type modules over the archimedean Hecke
algebra.

Proof. Wallach 1988 §0.A associates to each admissible (𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-module a module over the archimedean
Hecke algebra H∞ , which is the convolution algebra of bi- 𝐾∞ -finite distributions on 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℝ). This gives
a faithful embedding of admissible (𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-modules into modules over H∞ . Finite-type H∞ -modules
correspond to 𝐾∞ -finite admissible modules (Harish-Chandra 1966 §4). Hence the archimedean sph-
      sph-fin
fin C∞        corresponds to the full subcategory of compactly generated H∞ -modules, matching the
finite-prime definition.

Remark 31.3.6 (archimedean admissibility tightens the ( 𝐿4 ) extension requirement). The subcondition

Bernstein–Zelevinsky Compatibility
Conjecture 31.5.3 (∞-categorical Bernstein lift). . The Bernstein–Zelevinsky decomposition of the abelian
category of smooth 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 )-representations lifts to the stable presentable local Hecke category C 𝑝 ,
with the Bernstein centre acting by orthogonal idempotent projectors and with the spherical finite
subcategory generated by compact objects finite over the spherical Bernstein centre.
Proposition 31.5.4 (Bernstein–Zelevinsky local compatibility). , conditional on Chapter 31.5.3.
At each finite prime 𝑝, the local Hecke category C 𝑝 decomposes along Bernstein–Zelevinsky components
(Bernstein–Zelevinsky 1976 Ann. ENS §2): each Bernstein component corresponds to a cuspidal datum
[ 𝑀 , 𝜎 ] of a Levi 𝑀 ⊆ 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 ) and a cuspidal supercuspidal representation 𝜎 of 𝑀 . The Hecke
operator 𝑇𝑝 preserves each Bernstein component.

Proof. Bernstein–Zelevinsky 1976 proves the decomposition of the category of smooth representations
of 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 ) into Bernstein components. Each component is invariant under the centre of the Hecke
algebra, which includes the spherical Hecke operator 𝑇𝑝 acting on the spherical principal series com-
ponent (the unramified component). The passage from this abelian decomposition to C 𝑝 is exactly
Chapter 31.5.3. Under that datum, the idempotent projectors commute with 𝑇𝑝 , so 𝑇𝑝 preserves every
lifted Bernstein component.

Remark 31.5.5 (role of Bernstein–Zelevinsky). Bernstein–Zelevinsky 1976 supplies the local decomposi-
tion of the smooth representation category. After Chapter 31.5.3, the same idempotents act on the stable
local Hecke category and are compatible with cross-prime Hecke coherence, because Hecke operators at
distinct primes act on disjoint tensor factors. The global statement is therefore conditional on the lift
datum; it is not a consequence of the abelian Bernstein–Zelevinsky theorem alone.

Uniformity of the Sph-Fin Subcategory
Proposition 31.6.3 (uniformity across finite primes). , conditional on Chapter 31.5.3. The sph-fin

component inside the local Hecke category.

Proposition 31.6.4 (uniformity at infinity). . The archimedean sph-fin subcategory
Dsph-fin ((𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-modadm ) is the full subcategory of compact objects generated by the spherical
unramified principal series 𝑢∞ , and the compact generators are 𝐾∞ -finite admissible modules
(equivalently, finite-type over the archimedean Hecke algebra H∞ ).

hence compact generation of the derived category.

The arithmetic Ben-Zvi–Nadler comparison factors through four independent inputs. The ﬁnite-type theo-
rem of Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum applies to smooth ﬁnite-type derived stacks. The Emerton–Gee spectral object
is instead a formal Selmer deformation stack, and the formal comparison requires a categorical Hochschild-
colimit hypothesis, an arithmetic loop-space hypothesis, and a ﬂat-singular-support hypothesis. The inertia
shadow does not contain the full Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) datum, and the primes 2 and 3 carry non-semisimple Hecke
summands.

R2 and R1.formal
The conditions R2 and R1.formal are:
  (i) R2 identifies the global spectral target as the Selmer-derived stack. The local Emerton–Gee stacks
      supply local formal algebraic input; the global object must impose the global Galois relation,
      determinant, residual representation, and local Selmer conditions by derived fibre product. Derived
      Noetherianity of that fibre product is left as an open check for the chosen local conditions, not
      subsumed into a product-colimit theorem.
 (ii) R1.formal follows from three hypotheses (R1.formal.a, b,c). The first is a Hochschild trace theorem
      after the categorical colimit presentation of IndCohNilp is supplied. The second and third are
      respectively the arithmetic loop-space comparison and the flat-singular-support comparison.
   R1.fin-type is external. R3 is not definitional: it is the passage from the procyclic inertia shadow to
the full Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) target. R4 is the non-semisimple wild-prime summand.

Derived Enhancement of the Emerton–Gee Stack
Emerton–Gee arXiv:1908.07185 is written in the language of Noetherian formal algebraic stacks in the
sense of the Stacks Project, with the smoothness and mass-formula structure at the level of ordinary
(non-derived) schemes. Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum DAG requires a derived enhancement: the cotangent
complex must be computed as a perfect complex (or almost-perfect, in the formal case) in the ∞-category
of quasi-coherent sheaves, and the ind-colimit presentation must preserve this structure at every stage.
The translation is not automatic. It asks for cotangent-complex functoriality under the chosen formal
presentation, compatibility with formal thickening, and preservation under the Selmer fibre product.
These are hypotheses on the derived enhancement, not consequences of the underived mass formula
alone.

Finite-Type Hypotheses in the Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum Argument
The Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum proof of HH• (IndCoh(X)) ≃ O ( 𝐿 X) uses three ingredients that each
rest on finite-type smoothness and require new arguments in the formal Noetherian setting:
   (i) Atiyah duality for IndCoh: the self-duality IndCoh(X) ∨ ≃ IndCoh(X) under the Atiyah pairing,
       which requires X smooth finite-type.
  (ii) Smooth-base-change for IndCoh, which also uses finite-type.
 (iii) Loop-space duality: the free loop space 𝐿 X of a finite-type smooth stack is itself smooth (with
       dimension equal to dim X, by the standard calculation).
For formal Noetherian X, each ingredient requires a formal analogue: Atiyah duality must be extended
to the formal setting (conjectural in general), smooth base-change must be replaced by formal-smooth
base-change (subject of ongoing work, e.g., Mok 2025), and the loop space 𝐿 X is in general not smooth
finite-type.
    The formal comparison therefore has the form of a criterion. Given the categorical colimit presen-
tation of IndCohNilp , Hochschild trace commutes with it; the loop and flat-locus comparisons remain
separate geometric hypotheses.

32.2   Logical Form of the Inputs
The input structure is as follows:
32.3. R2: The Emerton–Gee Cotangent Complex                                                           283


R2 cotangent complex. The cotangent complex of the Emerton–Gee stack is computable by Galois
deformation theory. Mazur’s deformation functor framework (Mazur 1989 Deforming Galois Repre-
sentations) computes the tangent complex at each closed 𝔽 𝑝 -point; Lurie DAG X builds this into a
functorial cotangent complex on the pro-representable moduli stack. Emerton–Gee §2.4 provides the
pro-representability and smoothness of the mass formula. (See Chapter 32.3.1.)
R2 global Galois constraint. A global Galois representation is not a product of independent local data:
the restrictions to decomposition groups must come from a single global representation subject to the
chosen Selmer conditions. The global object is the Selmer-derived fibre product

R2 derived enhancement. Emerton–Gee constructs the mass-formula smooth finite-type cover
(arXiv:1908.07185 §2.6, Thm. B.0.1(1)): the stack is smooth and hence quasi-smooth. Quasi-smoothness
in the Lurie DAG sense is preserved under formal completion (Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum DAG Vol. II
Ch. II §3.3, formal-completion smoothness). For the Selmer fibre product one must still verify that
the chosen local deformation conditions preserve formal Noetherianity, quasi-smoothness, and the
nilpotent-support condition. The tangent complex is the Selmer complex; the required finiteness is an
additional geometric input. See Chapter 32.3.5.
R1.formal three inputs. The Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum theorem, ported from finite-type to formal
Noetherian, requires three separate arguments: (i) HH-colim-continuity (whether HH• commutes
with the ind-colimit presentation of the formal stack); (ii) arithmetic loop-space formal computation
(whether 𝐿 Ar X ≃ Map( 𝐵 ℤ     b , X) admits a workable formal description); (iii) flat-locus pullback
(whether the nilpotent-singular-support-flat locus on the loop space matches the Emerton–Gee flat
locus of Chapter 28.4.7). The first is a trace theorem once the categorical colimit exists; the other two
are geometric hypotheses. (See Chapter 32.4.1.)
R1.formal sub-reductions. R1.formal.a is the Hochschild trace statement for a given filtered colimit in
the Morita (∞, 2)-category. R1.formal.b reduces to the existence of a cotangent-complex formal loop-
space identification (a precise statement in Lurie DAG and Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum Vol. II). R1.formal.c
reduces to the compatibility of Arinkin–Gaitsgory nilpotent singular support with the ( 𝜑, Γ)-module
Fargues–Scholze flat locus. (See Chapter 32.4.2 and Chapter 32.4.9.)
Consistency with the initial arithmetic comparison. The arithmetic comparison of Chapter 28.5.5
uses a pro-étale extension of Ben-Zvi–Francis–Nadler integral transforms. In the present notation this
is the R1.formal.b loop-space hypothesis together with the R1.formal.c flat-locus hypothesis.

Corollary 32.3.4 (cotangent complex preserves finite products). . For derived stacks X , Y,

                                            𝕃 X× Y ≃ 𝕃 X ⊞ 𝕃 Y ,

the external direct sum of cotangent complexes pulled back to X × Y.
32.3. R2: The Emerton–Gee Cotangent Complex                                                                  285


Proof. The finite product X × Y in derived stacks is a finite limit; the cotangent complex is a left adjoint
and sends finite limits to finite limits (= direct sums in the ∞-category of perfect complexes, by stability
of the target). Lurie HA 7.3.2.4 computes the cotangent complex of a finite limit as a finite colimit of the
individual cotangent complexes, which under the dual identification of direct sum with external-sum
structure gives 𝕃 X ⊞ 𝕃 Y .
    Alternatively, this follows directly from the universal property of the cotangent complex as classifying
square-zero extensions: a square-zero extension of X × Y is a pair of square-zero extensions of X and
Y.

Source and Convention Comparison for R2
Source independence. The argument for R2 draws on five disjoint source lists: Emerton–Gee
arXiv:1908.07185 (Noetherian formal algebraic structure); Mazur 1989 and Kisin–Mazur 2000 (Galois
deformation theory); Lurie HA / DAG X (formal moduli problems and cotangent complex); Illusie
1971 (classical cotangent complex); Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum DAG Vol. II Ch. II (quasi-smoothness of
derived formal algebraic stacks).

Degree conventions. Lurie HA places the cotangent complex in non-positive degrees for smooth schemes
(tor-amplitude [−1, 0] means concentration in degrees −1, 0, equivalently the tangent complex in degrees
0, 1). The statement above uses the Lurie convention. Emerton–Gee’s tangent-space computation places
𝐻 1 in degree 0 and 𝐻 2 in degree 1, matching after the standard shift. Illusie 1971 places the cotangent
complex in non-positive degrees for smooth schemes, uniform with Lurie.

Ambient category. All objects live in derived algebraic stacks with pro-étale topology (Toën–Vezzosi,
Bhatt–Scholze, Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum). The cotangent complex is a left adjoint on this ∞-category.
The (∞, 2)-category of correspondences in which IndCoh is valued (Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum Vol. I
Ch. V) is the ambient category for both the tangent complex and the loop-space computation.

Hypotheses. Three hypotheses enter the formal Selmer target: Emerton–Gee Noetherian formal al-
gebraic structure, Lurie DAG formal-moduli representability, and Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum formal-
completion smoothness. The derived Selmer fibre product also requires the local deformation conditions
to preserve formal Noetherianity and nilpotent singular support.

Functoriality. The cotangent complex is functorial in pointed morphisms of derived stacks (Lurie
HA 7.3.2, Illusie 1971 Ch. II); the ind-colimit and product structures are preserved (Chapter 32.3.3 and
Chapter 32.3.4).

Source of equivalences. Derived deformation theory gives the displayed target and its tangent complex.
It does not by itself prove the finiteness and singular-support hypotheses required by the formal BZN
comparison.
Remark 32.3.7 (derived enhancement). Emerton–Gee do not explicitly formulate their stack in the Gaits-
gory–Rozenblyum DAG language. The tangent-complex computation comes from Mazur deformation
theory and Lurie formal moduli. The passage to the formal BZN theorem still needs the finiteness and
singular-support hypotheses named in Chapter 32.3.5.

   Theorem 32.4.9 (sufficient criterion for F3.BZN Ar ). . Suppose the structural splitting Chap-
   ter 30.2.5 is imposed. The conjunction
   • R1.fin-type (Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum: theorem on smooth finite-type).
   • R1.formal.a (Hochschild trace along the given categorical colimit).
   • R1.formal.b (arithmetic loop-space formal computation: conjectural).
   • R1.formal.c (flat-locus pullback compatibility: conjectural).
   • R2 (Selmer-derived target, tangent complex, formal Noetherianity, and nilpotent-support compatibil-
     ity).
   • R3 (arithmetic free loop space identification: full-target comparison still required, Chapter 32.3.6).
   • R4 (non-semisimple summand at wild primes 𝑝 = 2, 3: wild Hecke summands included).
   implies F3.BZNAr .

   Proof. Chapter 30.2.5 expresses F3.BZNAr as R1 + R2 + R3 + R4, where R1 further splits into
   R1.fin-type + R1.formal (Chapter 32.1). R1.fin-type is Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum; R1.formal splits into
   R1.formal.a (Chapter 32.4.2, theorem) plus R1.formal.b (Chapter 32.4.4, conjectural) plus R1.formal.c
   (Chapter 32.4.7, conjectural) by Chapter 32.4.1. R2 supplies the Selmer target and tangent complex
   and includes the required finiteness and singular-support hypotheses. R3 supplies the full Weil/( 𝜑, Γ)
   comparison. R4 inserts the wild-prime summands. These inputs are exactly the factors in the structural
   splitting, hence their conjunction implies F3.BZNAr .

Source and Convention Comparison for R1.formal
Source independence. The argument for R1.formal draws on four disjoint source lists: Lurie HA 5.5.3
/ 4.8 / 7.4 (HH, cotangent, colimits); Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum DAG Vol. II Part V Ch. III (HH on
smooth finite-type); Arinkin–Gaitsgory arXiv:1201.6343 (nilpotent singular support); Fargues–Scholze
arXiv:2102.13459 (local Langlands).

HH conventions. Lurie HA places HH on symmetric monoidal stable presentable ∞-categories in spec-
tra; Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum uses a derived-category trace on IndCoh; Toën 2014 uses a direct simplicial-
object computation. All three are equivalent: HH of a stable ∞-category is the colimit over the cyclic
category of the self-tensor-product sequence (McCarthy–Schwede, Blumberg–Mandell).

Ambient category. All objects live in derived pro-étale stacks with the (∞, 2)-category of correspon-
dences for IndCoh-valued functoriality.

Hypotheses. The main hypothesis on X is Noetherianness together with derived-formal-algebraic struc-
ture. For the Selmer target this includes the formal Noetherian and nilpotent-support compatibility
conditions of Chapter 32.3.5.

Functoriality. HH-colim continuity is a functorial statement on the ∞-category of stable presentable
∞-categories; the criterion by three inputs is itself functorial in X.

Source of the implication. The criterion Chapter 32.4.1 is one-way. The finite-type theorem, Hochschild
trace continuity, loop-space compatibility, and flat-locus compatibility imply the formal BZN compari-
son. The converse is not used.

32.5   Conditional Form of F3.BZN Ar
Corollary 32.5.1 (conditional arithmetic BZN comparison). . F3.BZNAr follows from Chap-
ter 32.4.9 and the conjunction of:
• R1.formal.b (arithmetic loop-space formal computation, conjectural).
• R1.formal.c (flat-locus pullback compatibility, conjectural).
• R2 finiteness and nilpotent-support compatibility for the chosen Selmer deformation problem.
• R3 (full-target loop-space identification, including the Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) comparison).
• R4 (the non-semisimple Hecke summands at 𝑝 = 2, 3).
R1.fin-type is the finite-type theorem. R1.formal.a is the trace theorem for a given categorical colimit.
The other entries are geometric hypotheses.

Proof. By Chapter 32.4.9: the conjunction R1.fin-type + R1.formal.a + R1.formal.b + R1.formal.c + R2
+ R3 + R4 implies F3.BZNAr , where R2 includes the finiteness and support hypotheses of Chapter 32.3.5.
The corollary is the same implication with the finite-type theorem and trace theorem separated from the
geometric hypotheses.

Remark 32.5.2 (formal-loop and ﬂat-support inputs). The pro-étale extension used in Chapter 28.5.5
contains two distinct geometries. The first is the commutation of Map( 𝐵 ℤ
                                                                         b , −) with the formal Selmer
32.6. Boundary Conditions                                                                                    291


presentation. The second is the equality between the Arinkin–Gaitsgory flat singular-support locus and
the Fargues–Scholze ( 𝜑, Γ)-flat locus.
Remark 32.5.3 (pro-étale extension). Chapter 28 Remark 28.5.4 notes that Chapter 28.5.3 uses a pro-étale
extension of Ben-Zvi–Francis–Nadler that is formal but not in the literature. In the present notation
that extension is the R1.formal.b hypothesis, together with the R1.formal.c comparison of flat loci.

32.6    Boundary Conditions
Form of the Inputs
The seven inputs have different logical weights. R1.fin-type is the Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum finite-type
theorem. R1.formal.a is a trace theorem after the categorical colimit presentation is known. R2 fixes
the Selmer target and tangent complex, but its use in formal BZN requires formal Noetherianity and
nilpotent-support compatibility for the chosen local conditions. R1.formal.b, R1.formal.c, R3, and R4
are geometric hypotheses.

Logical Consequence
The arithmetic BZN comparison is therefore not a consequence of a product formula for local stacks. It
is a statement about a Selmer derived fibre product, a formal Hochschild trace, a pro-étale loop object, a
flat singular-support locus, and wild Hecke summands. The finite-type theorem and the trace theorem
do not eliminate the loop, flat-locus, full-target, or wild-prime hypotheses.

Open Problems
The reduction of Chapter 32.4.9 poses three precise open problems.
   (i) R1.formal.b. Does Map( 𝐵 ℤ   b , −) commute with ind-colimits under closed immersions in derived
       pro-étale stacks? The relevant tools are Lurie’s ∞-topos formalism (HTT 6, HA 4.4) combined
       with Bhatt–Scholze pro-étale (§7). A positive answer proves R1.formal.b; a counterexample re-
       stricts Chapter 28.5.3 to the cofinal finite-type subclass.
  (ii) R1.formal.c. Does the Arinkin–Gaitsgory nilpotent-singular-support flat locus coincide with
       the ( 𝜑, Γ)-module Fargues–Scholze flat locus on each finite-type piece of the Emerton–Gee
       ind-colimit? The comparison between Fargues–Scholze arXiv:2102.13459 and Arinkin–Gaitsgory
       arXiv:1201.6343 can be checked on unramified crystalline representations with fixed Hodge–Tate
       weight.
 (iii) R4. What are the Ext1 -contributions to HH• (HkIw    𝐺 𝐿2 , 𝑝 ) at wild primes 𝑝 = 2, 3, and do they shift
       the arithmetic BZN identification? The Etingof–Ostrik 2004 finite-tensor-category framework
       applies; a model case is 𝑝 = 2 with tame restriction to the depth-1 local category.

BZN Ar : Loop-Space Convention and Wild-Prime
Summands

The F3.BZNAr reduction of Chapter 28 rests on two unresolved conditions. The first: the arithmetic
free loop space 𝐿 Ar X = Map( 𝐵 ℤ   b , X) admits three candidate definitions on formal Noetherian derived
stacks, differing a priori in the formal-Noetherian setting; no canonical choice was specified. The second:
the Iwahori Hecke category HkIw      𝐺 𝐿2 , 𝑝 is not semisimple at the wild primes 𝑝 = 2, 3 of 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ, so the
Hochschild trace picks up Ext1 -contributions invisible to the Ben-Zvi–Nadler semisimple template. The
derived internal-Hom convention is the convention used below. Agreement with the cofiltered-limit
and ind-construction conventions is a formal-convergence hypothesis on the target, not a theorem of the
definition. The wild-prime condition is modeled by an explicit calculation whose conclusion depends
on unverified coefficient-convention compatibility: the expected Ext1 -summand at 𝑝 = 2 and 𝑝 = 3 is
computed via Etingof–Ostrik 2004 Finite Tensor Categories, Bushnell–Henniart 2006 local Langlands
at the wild primes, and Jantzen 2003 modular-representation Ext-machinery; the coefficient conventions
must be verified against the arithmetic mixed-characteristic setting before the calculation has independent
source support. The additive wild summand required by the proposed F3.BZNAr comparison is recorded.
The global F3.BZNAr statement of Chapter 28 remains conditional until the loop-space convergence,
full Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) target, wild-prime Ext, and 𝑝 ≥ 5 semisimplicity inputs are verified in the arithmetic
coefficient conventions.

Logical Structure
R3 is a convention plus a convergence hypothesis: the internal Hom is the chosen definition, and com-
parison with the other two definitions requires compactness and formal-colimit compatibility. R4 is a
conditional wild-Ext model: the 𝑝 = 2, 3 summands and the 𝑝 ≥ 5 vanishing are hypotheses until the
coefficient conventions and cyclic-trace pairings are verified.

  but also address 𝑘 = 𝔽 ℓ .

33.2   Structure of the Argument
The argument for R3 has three parts; the argument for R4 has three further parts. For R3: the three
candidate definitions are compared with explicit fibre-product formulas (Chapter 33.3.2); the fibre-
product formulas are conditionally identified on formal Noetherian derived algebraic stacks via Gaits-
gory–Rozenblyum and Postnikov-tower convergence (Chapter 33.3.4); the internal-Hom convention is
adopted as canonical and confirmed consistent with Chapter 28 (Chapter 33.3.7, Chapter 33.3.9). For
R4: the Ext1 -contribution to the Hochschild trace at 𝑝 = 2 is isolated via Bushnell–Henniart 2006 and
Jantzen 2003 (Chapter 33.4.5); the computation at 𝑝 = 3 is isolated via Carter 1989 (Chapter 33.4.6);
the wild summand vanishes at 𝑝 ≥ 5 only under the large-prime semisimplicity datum (Chapter 33.4.7).
Each step carries its source and convention hypotheses inline.

33.4    R4: Wild-Prime Non-Semisimple Correction
Semisimplicity at 𝑝 ≥ 5
Theorem 33.4.1 (large-prime semisimplicity datum). . For 𝐺 𝐿2 and primes 𝑝 ≥ 5, in the coef-
ficient convention used here, the arithmetic Iwahori Hecke category HkIw
                                                                      𝐺 𝐿2 , 𝑝 has no positive-degree
Yoneda contribution to Hochschild trace.
Source condition. Bezrukavnikov arXiv:1209.0403 Thm 4 (semisimplicity of the local Iwahori Hecke
category above the Coxeter-plus-one threshold); for 𝐺 𝐿2 the Coxeter number is ℎ ( 𝐺 𝐿2 ) = 2, the ‘‘banal
prime’’ threshold is ℎ + 1 = 3, and the genuinely-banal threshold (ensuring Hochschild-trace vanishing
in positive degrees) is 𝑝 ≥ 5 following Bezrukavnikov–Mirković–Rumynin arXiv:math/0205144 §7.
The cited sources do not by themselves construct this vanishing in the mixed-characteristic coefficient
convention of the arithmetic branch. The datum is conjectural.
Corollary 33.4.2 (large-prime positive-degree vanishing). , conditional on Chapter 33.4.1. At
any prime 𝑝 ≥ 5, the higher Hochschild-trace contributions HH𝑖 (HkIw 𝐺 𝐿2 , 𝑝 ) for 𝑖 ≥ 1 vanish identically,
and the Ben-Zvi–Nadler identification of Chapter 28.5.5 has no large-prime positive-degree summand.
33.4. R4: Wild-Prime Non-Semisimple Correction                                                          299


Proof. Hochschild homology of a semisimple category reduces to its Grothendieck group tensored with
the ground ring in degree zero; higher degrees vanish. Apply Chapter 33.4.1.

Proof. Step 1: classification of simples at 𝑝 = 2. By Jantzen 2003 Representations of Algebraic Groups
(AMS Math. Surveys Monographs 107) Ch. II §8, the simple SL2 -modules at 𝑝 = 2 are parametrised
by the dominant weights 𝑛 ≥ 0 with the Steinberg tensor product decomposition; at the Iwahori level,
restricted to the pro- 𝑝 Iwahori, one recovers the two one-dimensional simples 1triv (trivial character)
and 1sgn (sign character of the Weyl group 𝑆2 ) as the lowest-weight simples, plus infinite families of
higher-weight simples whose Ext-structure is computed below.
Step 2: Ext1 among simples. By the affine-Hecke-algebra computation at 𝑝 = 2 following Lusztig 1980
§3 (simple-types classification) and Bushnell–Henniart 2006 The Local Langlands Conjecture for 𝐺 𝐿 (2),
Grundlehren 335, Springer, §12.3 (wild-ramification types at 𝑝 = 2 for 𝐺 𝐿2 ), the Yoneda Ext1 between
the two lowest-weight simples 1triv and 1sgn is one-dimensional:

                                         Ext1HkIw

                                                             1triv , 1sgn        𝑘.
                                                𝐺 𝐿 2 ,2


This Ext is supported by a unique non-split extension whose underlying two-dimensional module 𝐸 is
the 𝑝 = 2 reduction of the standard representation of the infinite dihedral group ℤ ⋊ {±1}: at 𝑝 = 2,
the sign character of {±1} cannot be separated from the trivial one because {±1} has order 2 = 𝑝, placing
both characters in the same projective indecomposable block.
Step 3: higher Ext and other pairs vanish. For pairs of simples 𝐿 𝑖 , 𝐿𝑗 with at least one of weight
≥ 2, the Steinberg tensor decomposition separates them into distinct blocks (their highest weights lie
in different 2-restricted weight sub-alcoves); hence Ext𝑛 Iw ( 𝐿 𝑖 , 𝐿𝑗 ) = 0 for all 𝑛 ≥ 1 between such
                                                         Hk𝐺 𝐿2 ,2
pairs. For the same two low-weight simples, Ext 𝑛 ≥2 also vanishes because the projective cover of each is
two-step (the dihedral block has Loewy length 2); this follows from Jantzen Ch. II §8 Thm 8.14.
Step 4: Hochschild-trace contribution. By the Etingof–Ostrik spectral sequence (Chapter 33.4.4(4)),
the wild HH1 contribution from the principal block at 𝑝 = 2 is expected to be one-dimensional, matching
the off-diagonal Ext1 (1triv , 1sgn )  𝑘 via the Hochschild pairing on the block algebra. The exact form of
the cyclic-trace pairing for off-diagonal Ext between distinct simples in a non-semisimple block requires
the Calabi-Yau or Frobenius structure of HkIw      𝐺 𝐿2 ,2 ; this structure is not verified here. Equation (33.4.5)
is recorded as a conjectural conclusion conditional on an independent verification of the cyclic-trace
pairing.

Proof. Step 1: classification of simples at 𝑝 = 3. At 𝑝 = 3, the restricted weights of SL2 are {0, 1, 2}
(dominant weights 0 ≤ 𝑛 < 𝑝 = 3). By Jantzen 2003 Ch. II §8, the three restricted simples 𝐿0 , 𝐿1 , 𝐿2
33.4. R4: Wild-Prime Non-Semisimple Correction                                                            301


sit in a single non-semisimple block (the principal block of the affine Hecke algebra at a third root of
unity; this is the 𝐴2 -linear quiver block).
Step 2: the block quiver. By Carter 1989 Finite Groups of Lie Type §7.3 and Lusztig 1980, the principal
block of the affine Hecke algebra of 𝐺 𝐿2 at a third root of unity has the following Ext-quiver:
                                                𝛼01        𝛼12
                                          𝐿0 ←−−− 𝐿1 ←−−− 𝐿2 ,

with Ext1 -generators 𝛼01 ∈ Ext1 ( 𝐿1 , 𝐿0 ) and 𝛼12 ∈ Ext1 ( 𝐿2 , 𝐿1 ), and the only non-trivial relation is
𝛼01 𝛼12 = 0 in Ext2 (i.e., the quiver is radical-square-zero of length 2 at each end, length 3 in the middle).
Hence
                      Ext1 ( 𝐿0 , 𝐿1 ) = Ext1 ( 𝐿1 , 𝐿2 ) = 𝑘,      Ext1 ( 𝐿0 , 𝐿2 ) = 0.

Step 3: higher Ext. In a linear quiver with radical-square-zero relations, Ext𝑖 between simples vanishes
for 𝑖 ≥ 2 (each projective indecomposable has Loewy length 2). This follows from Auslander–Reiten–
Smalø 1995 Representation Theory of Artin Algebras (Cambridge Studies in Adv. Math. 36) Ch. VII §2
applied to the block algebra.
Step 4: Hochschild-trace contribution. By the Etingof–Ostrik spectral sequence (Chapter 33.4.4(4)),
the wild HH1 at 𝑝 = 3 is expected to collect the off-diagonal Ext1 ’s of the principal 𝐴2 -linear quiver
block:
                           wild, 𝑝=3
                      HH1            = Ext1 ( 𝐿0 , 𝐿1 ) ⊕ Ext1 ( 𝐿1 , 𝐿2 ) = 𝑘 ⊕ 𝑘.
The exact derivation of this formula from the cyclic-trace pairing on the block algebra requires the same
Calabi-Yau or Frobenius structure as in Chapter 33.4.5 Step 4. It is a conjectural calculation, not a verified
trace formula.

33.5   Consistency with Chapter 28
R3 Consistency
Chapter 28’s Chapter 28.4.1 reads: for an 𝑛-geometric derived pro-étale stack X, 𝐿 Ar X = Map( 𝐵 ℤ b , X),
the internal mapping stack in the ∞-category of derived pro-étale stacks. Chapter 33.3.7 specialises this
to formal Noetherian derived algebraic stacks and commits to the internal-Hom convention. The two
definitions are identical on the intersection of their domains (formal Noetherian derived algebraic stacks
that are 𝑛-geometric and pro-étale). The Emerton–Gee stack lies in this intersection (Chapter 33.3.6).

R4 Consistency
Chapter 28’s Chapter 28.1.1 asserts an equivalence without a wild-prime summand. The model of Chap-
ter 33.4.8 adds such a summand at 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3} under the stated hypotheses. The argument structure of
Chapter 28 (§28.2) is otherwise unchanged; at 𝑝 ≥ 5 its conclusion holds verbatim.
    In particular:
• The Emerton–Gee morphism 𝜄EG of Chapter 28.4.6 is unchanged; it still factors through the flat locus
  (Chapter 28.4.9).
• The arithmetic factorisation homology of Chapter 28.5.3 is unchanged; it applies to any 𝐸2 -monoidal
  stable presentable ∞-category, including the non-semisimple local Iwahori Hecke categories at 𝑝 ∈
  {2, 3}.
• The arithmetic loop-space identification Chapter 28.5.5 is unchanged on the ind-coherent side; it
  gives the degree-0 part of the Hochschild trace under the loop-space hypotheses. The model of Chap-
  ter 33.4.8 supplies the conjectural degree-1 part at the two wild primes.
Proposition 33.5.1 (wild summand forced by the model). . Under the full-target and formal-loop
hypotheses, any F3.BZNAr comparison extending Chapter 28 and compatible with the wild-prime Ext
model contains the direct summand (33.4.8) on the right-hand side of (28.1.1). Further terms may be
forced by the full comparison.

Proof. Chapter 33.4.8 specifies the modeled summand. At each prime 𝑝 ≥ 5 the wild positive-degree part
vanishes (Chapter 33.4.7), so the original equivalence is unchanged there. At 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3} the additional
term is the finite-dimensional wild summand. The assembly via the restricted tensor product (F2) is
unchanged; the summand enters after assembly.

The internal-Hom convention is fixed. Its comparison with the cofiltered and ind-completed models is
conditional on the three formal-convergence hypotheses in Chapter 33.3.4.

R4 Boundary
R4 leaves the following functoriality conjecture.
Conjecture 33.6.1 (wild-prime summand is Langlands-functorial). The wild-prime summand
HHwild
     •
         , {2,3}
                 of (33.4.8) corresponds, under a suitable refined Langlands correspondence, to the

Explicitly, for 𝑝 = 2 the class corresponds to the unique unramified twist of the tame character at 𝑝 = 2;
for 𝑝 = 3 the two classes correspond to the two non-split extensions of tame characters at 𝑝 = 3.

rendering the Positselski equivalence natural. The Positselski equivalence is a natural transformation of
2-functors CoalgΛ,𝜇=0,ab,op → PrSttri .
    Without C5, the corollary Chapter 30.2.7 (abelian Heisenberg satisfies abelian Positselski) does not
propagate through chained arguments: the P1 Step 3 closure via functorial pullback of the Positselski
pairing under the bar-cobar adjunction requires 𝑓∗ to commute with the Positselski equivalence, which
is exactly the statement of C5. Until C5 is verified, the P1 Step 3 argument must be proved directly rather
than functorial pullback.

Cycle 1 (C1): Factorization-Coalgebra Coherence
The bar complex Chapter 12.8.1 writes 𝐵 ch,Ar as a sum of Λ-tensor powers of 𝑠 −1 V prim tensored with
a Parshin Gersten complex. Costello–Gwilliam Vol. II Ch. 3 requires a factorization-coalgebra presen-
tation: for each disjoint inclusion 𝑈1 ⊔ 𝑈2 ↩→ 𝑉 in Ran( 𝐶 ), a coproduct Δ𝑉𝑈1 ⊔𝑈2 : 𝐵𝑉ch,Ar → 𝐵𝑈ch1 ,Ar ⊗
𝐵𝑈ch2,Ar satisfying coassociativity and locality. Direct lift from CG Vol. I is unavailable: CG Vol. I factor-
ization algebras live on smooth curves over a field; Spec ℤ has a discrete Ran space (Chapter 8.1.1), and
disjoint inclusions reduce to disjoint multiset inclusions, making the coalgebra axiom a set-theoretic
rather than a dg-coherence condition. The correct structure is a relative factorization-coalgebra. At each
place 𝑣 , the local factor 𝐵𝑣ch,Ar is a factorization coalgebra in the CG Vol. II relative sense (CG Vol. II
Ch. 3, Def. 3.1.1 extended to profinite bases): a prestack of coalgebras on Ran( 𝐶 ) ( 𝑣 ) with coproduct Δ
valued in the locally constant / 𝐸0 -sheaves at finite 𝑣 and in the holomorphic factorization coalgebra
at ∞. Adelic restricted product: for finite 𝑆 ⊂ | 𝐶 |, define 𝐵 ch   ,Ar
                                                                         = 𝑣 ∈ 𝑆 𝐵𝑣ch,Ar ⊗Λ 𝑣′ ∉ 𝑆 𝟙𝑣CG using
                                                                          N                  N
                                                                   𝑆
the pointed 𝐸2 -monoidal structure of Chapter 30.2.1. The colimit over 𝑆 is a filtered colimit in pointed
𝐸2 -monoidal factorization coalgebras; by Beilinson’s adelic complex theorem (Beilinson 1980 Residues
and adeles, Funct. Anal. Appl., Prop. 1 + Prop. 2) the colimit inherits a factorization-coalgebra structure
compatible with the global Beilinson–Parshin reciprocity adelic complex.

Cycle 3 (C3): Renormalization / Euler-Product Convergence
The naive infinite tensor product ′𝑝 H ( 𝑝 ) with spherical vectors |0⟩ 𝑝 is a Tate restricted direct product;
                                    N

the bar cohomology partition function 𝑝 (1 − 𝑝 − 𝛽 ) −1 converges only for Re( 𝛽 ) > 1 and diverges at

the naive convergence region. Analytic continuation of 𝜁 is the target, not the input: bar cohomology
dimensions are integers, so their generating function converges precisely where the Dirichlet series does,
i.e., for Re( 𝛽 ) > 1. The resolution is pro-nilpotent BV renormalization (Costello 2011 Renormalization
and Effective Field Theory Ch. 1–2; Costello–Gwilliam Vol. II Ch. 3, §3.3–3.4). The naive ′𝑝 H ( 𝑝 ) is

Cycle 6: Cross-Check on P1 Step 3 Functorial Pullback
The P1 Step 3 argument (Chapter 21.5) computes the Positselski pairing 𝜅GAr + ( 𝜅 ! )GAr = 0 by comparing
                                                                  prim
central characters of the bar coalgebra and cobar algebra for VHeis . The abelian Positselski equivalence

entering P1 Step 3. With C1–C5 as hypotheses, the P1 Step 3 Positselski pairing computation is conditional

Remark 34.4.6 (Gelfand–Manin abstract mechanism). Gelfand–Manin Methods of Homological Alge-
bra 1996 IV.2 develops the general machinery for verifying 𝑑 2 = 0 of a sum of three derivations: when
each diagonal term vanishes and the three mixed anticommutators sum to zero modulo coboundaries,
the sum induces a differential on cohomology. For the chain-level arithmetic bar used in the Platonic
variation, one uses the strict completed model of Chapter 34.4.5.

algebra framework, and its bar construction is a pro-nilpotent dg Λ-coalgebra. The renormalization
of H Ar,ren is an instance of Hinich’s abstract pro-nilpotent machinery with the specific regularization
constant supplied by Bost–Connes KMS1 .

34.6    C4: Archimedean Classical Limit
Witt-Vector Truncation and the Classical Limit
Deﬁnition 34.6.1 (Witt-truncated classical limit). Let 𝑊𝑛 ( 𝐴) denote the length-𝑛 Witt vector ring of
a ring 𝐴 (Witt 1936 J. reine angew. Math. 176, §1; Bourbaki Algèbre Commutative IX §1). The classical
limit of a family of 𝑝-adic objects { 𝑋 𝑝 } 𝑝 with Λ-structure is

                                    𝑋 cl := lim 𝑋 𝑝 ⊗Λ 𝑊1 (𝔽 𝑝 ) ⊗ℤ ℝ
                                                                     
                                             ←−
                                            𝑝→∞

where the limit is taken in the category of classical (i.e., archimedean, field-coefficient) objects. The tensor
with 𝑊1 (𝔽 𝑝 ) = 𝔽 𝑝 truncates the 𝑝-adic structure to length 1; tensoring with ℝ embeds the residue field
into the archimedean place.
Remark 34.6.2 (adelic Pontryagin duality interpretation). The archimedean place 𝑣 = ∞ of the Arakelov-
compactified curve Spec ℤ is related to finite primes by adelic Pontryagin duality: the adeles 𝔸ℚ =
ℝ × ′𝑝 ℚ 𝑝 are self-dual under the Tate character 𝜓𝔸 = 𝜓∞ · 𝑝 𝜓 𝑝 (Tate 1950, Fourier analysis in
     Q                                                           Q
number ﬁelds and Hecke’s zeta-functions, Ph.D. thesis, §1). The classical limit via Witt truncation is the
archimedean side of this duality, under which finite-place 𝑝-adic structure dualizes to archimedean
exponential structure.

34.7    C5: Functoriality under Λ -Coalgebra Morphisms
The Functoriality Statement
Deﬁnition 34.7.1 (morphisms of abelian Λ-coalgebras with 𝜇 = 0). A morphism 𝑓 : 𝐶 → 𝐶 ′ in

on both sides) and the 𝜇 = 0 structure (i.e., pseudo-isomorphism at level of Λ-modules).

Corollary 34.8.2 (arithmetic Heisenberg Koszul biconditional). (conditional as in Chap-
ter 34.8.1). The arithmetic Heisenberg Koszul self-duality 𝜅 + 𝜅 ! = 0 is equivalent to the Riemann
functional equation 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ) conditionally on the C1–C5 domain hypotheses and the five open
Positselski sub-items, for the abelian Heisenberg domain.
Remark 34.8.3 (this corollary does not prove RH). Chapter 34.8.1 and Chapter 34.8.2 identify the implica-
tion 𝜅 + 𝜅 ! = 0 ⇒ 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ) for the arithmetic Heisenberg under the stated hypotheses. They do
not prove the Riemann hypothesis; the functional equation is a classical theorem of Riemann 1859, and
RH is the separate assertion that the non-trivial zeros of 𝜉 lie on the critical line. The conditional arith-
metic Positselski equivalence supplies a derivation of the functional equation from arithmetic Koszul
duality; the full RH construction requires independently the VB∗ Virasoro positivity (Chapter 22.3.10)
plus the arithmetic Hilbert–Pólya hypothesis H-PAr (Chapter 22.3.2), neither supplied by the Positselski
reduction.

34.9    Residual Conditions
The Costello-refined Positselski reduction of C1–C5 addresses the abelian Heisenberg domain. Three
residual items remain outside this domain:
  (i) Non-abelian Iwahori level. The non-commutative Iwasawa Λ𝐺 𝐿2 = ℤ 𝑝 [[ 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℤ 𝑝 )]] Positselski
      is not addressed by this chapter; it requires the non-commutative Iwasawa framework of Fukaya–
      Kato 2006 and Coates–Fukaya–Kato–Sujatha–Venjakob 2005 Publ. IHES (the main conjecture
      for non-commutative Iwasawa theory). Residual form: conjectural (recorded as Chapter 24.7).
34.10. Refinement Boundary                                                                               323


  (ii) Wildly-ramiﬁed primes 𝑝 = 2, 3. The Chevalley–Eilenberg 𝑑 2 = 0 proof (C2) uses the Steinberg
       relation { 𝑝, 1 − 𝑝 } = 0, which is valid in 𝐾2𝑀 (ℚ) for every prime. The obstruction at 𝑝 = 2, 3
       is therefore not the reciprocity law but the representation theory: the mod- 𝑝 Iwahori Hecke
       category at these wild primes is non-semisimple and carries Ext1 -contributions (Paskunas 2013
       Publ. IHES 118), so the factorization-coalgebra coherence and the chain-level 𝑑 2 = 0 require
       correction there (Ben-Zvi–Nadler; see Chapter 30.2.1). Residual form: conjectural.
 (iii) Super Bethe-Hecke chain-level chiral coproduct. The 𝜇 = 0 hypothesis and the abelian domain ex-
       clude the super Bethe-Hecke sector where chain-level chiral coproduct computations are required;
       this sector is outside the abelian Heisenberg domain. Residual form: conjectural.

34.10    Refinement Boundary
   (i) Five Costello-refined subconditions C1–C5 are recorded under their named hypotheses.
       C1 (local-global factorization-coalgebra coherence): recorded by Chapter 34.3.3 via CG Vol. II
       Ch. 3 pro-nilpotent factorization algebras plus Beilinson 1980 adelic complex.
       C2 (Chevalley–Eilenberg 𝑑 2 = 0): recorded by Chapter 34.4.4 via Parshin reciprocity { 𝑝, 1 − 𝑝 } =
       0 in 𝐾2𝑀 (ℚ) (Parshin 1975, Kato 1979).
       C3 (renormalization / Euler-product convergence): recorded by Chapter 34.5.3 via Costello 2011
       pro-nilpotent BV + Bost–Connes KMS1 Tomita–Takesaki.
       C4 (archimedean classical limit): recorded by Chapter 34.6.4 via Witt-vector truncation + Segal
       1981 / Frenkel–Ben-Zvi 2004 classical Heisenberg Fock.
       C5 (functoriality): recorded by Chapter 34.7.4 via naturality of bar–cobar adjunction in Λ-linear
       coalgebra morphisms with corrected naturality diagram (direction reversal of pullback vs pushfor-
       ward).
  (ii) P1 Step 3 functorial pullback is conditional for the arithmetic Heisenberg (Chapter 34.8.1): the
       full biconditional 𝜅GAr + ( 𝜅 ! )GAr = 0 ⇔ 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ) closes as a conditional theorem on the
       C1–C5 domain hypotheses and the five open Positselski sub-items of Chapter 24.1.6, for the abelian
       Heisenberg domain.
 (iii) Three residual items remain outside the Costello-refined reduction: non-abelian Iwahori level,
       wildly-ramified primes 𝑝 = 2, 3, super Bethe-Hecke chain-level chiral coproduct. Each is stated
       explicitly with its residual form in Chapter 34.9.
 (iv) Source disjoint list (per Chapter 34.1): Costello–Gwilliam Vol. II for C1 and C3; Parshin 1975 and
       Kato 1979 for C2; Witt 1936, Borger 2010, Segal 1981, Frenkel–Ben-Zvi 2004 for C4; Positselski
       2011 §6 plus Λ-linearity for C5. Secondary: Gelfand–Manin 1996 (general 𝑑 2 = 0 mechanism);
       Hinich 1997 (dg-operads); Costello 2011 (BV renormalization).
  (v) The Costello-refined reduction does not prove RH; it refines the arithmetic Positselski conditional
       equivalence in the abelian Heisenberg domain, which identifies the forward implication 𝜅 + 𝜅 ! =
       0 ⇒ 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ) conditionally on the five open Positselski sub-items and the C1–C5 domain
       hypotheses. The full RH construction requires independently the VB∗ Virasoro positivity and
       the arithmetic Hilbert–Pólya hypothesis H-PAr (neither supplied here).
   The arithmetic Heisenberg Koszul biconditional remains at Conditional form within the abelian
domain: closed conditionally on the C1–C5 domain hypotheses and the five open Positselski sub-items
of Chapter 24.1.6.

BC-Diamond-Glue Lemma and Godement–Jacquet
Absorption (K5)

Two conditions from Chapter 27.2.7 and Chapter 30.2.8 remain: (i) the compatibility ‘‘(BC-diamond-
glue)’’ reducing LACD to a global Bernstein-centre action on the Selmer-derived spectral stack; (ii) the
Godement–Jacquet absorption convention (K5), on which Chapter 26.9.1 was stated conditionally. The
first condition decomposes into three logically independent subconditions; the irreducible cross-prime
compatibility is ‘‘BC-diamond-glue.core’’. The second comparison requires native pairing maps on the
cuspidal sph-fin locus, specified local scalar normalizations and a compatible adelic assembly. Rescaling
alone does not construct these data.

35.1   The two mathematical comparisons
Two compatibility conditions are inherited from earlier chapters.
    (BC-diamond-glue). Chapter 27.2.7 reduced LACD to the single compatibility ‘‘(BC-diamond-
glue)’’: local Bernstein centres on local Emerton–Gee strata glue across primes to a global Bernstein
centre acting on the global automorphic category. Concretely, Chapter 27.5.4 requires that Ben-Zvi–
Chen–Helm–Nadler’s local coherent Springer sheaves (arXiv:2010.02321) glue to a global coherent
sheaf on the Selmer-derived global spectral stack, and that the glued sheaf acts on IndCohNilp (X Sel
                                                                                                   ¯𝜌,det, L )
consistently with the global Bernstein-centre action. The domain estimate from Chapter 27.2.8 was
non-formal theorem; the irreducible primary-source condition is the cross-prime compatibility of these
local actions.
    (K5). The finite-place comparison seeks linear maps realizing the native Koszul and Whittaker pairings
in the prime GNS carrier, with their conjugate-linear duality. The adjoint factor fixes a possible scalar
normalization of these maps; it does not supply the maps themselves. The precise local equations appear
in Chapter 35.7.4.

Theorem 35.3.2 (decomposition of (BC-diamond-glue)). . (BC-diamond-glue) is equivalent to the
conjunction
                    (BCglue.local) ∧ (BCglue.glue) ∧ (BCglue.core) .
Each conjunct is logically independent of the others: supplying any two does not supply the third.

Proof. Forward. Suppose (BC-diamond-glue), i.e. Chapter 27.5.4, holds. Then the local coherent
                                                                      prism
Springer sheaves {F𝑣 }𝑣 exist (supplying (BCglue.local)), glue to Fglob along the diagonal (supplying
(BCglue.glue)), and the glued sheaf’s action agrees with the global Bernstein centre (supplying
(BCglue.core)).
    Reverse. Suppose (BCglue.local), (BCglue.glue), (BCglue.core) all hold. Then (BCglue.local) gives
the local sheaves; (BCglue.glue) assembles them into a global coherent sheaf; (BCglue.core) gives the
Bernstein-centre compatibility. Together, these are exactly the content of Chapter 27.5.4.
    Logical independence. (BCglue.local) without (BCglue.glue): local sheaves exist but may fail to glue
(e.g., if flatness of transition maps fails). (BCglue.glue) without (BCglue.core): formal gluing succeeds,
but the glued sheaf’s action may differ from the global Bernstein action (e.g., if the arithmetic AG
equivalence itself fails). (BCglue.local) ∧ (BCglue.core) without (BCglue.glue): the three conditions are
separate compatibilities, and knowing agreement at the global level does not force local gluability.

                                               (1 − | 𝑟 |/ 𝑝) (1 − 𝑝 −1 ) (1 − | 𝑟 | −1 / 𝑝)
This follows by applying |1 − 𝑧 | ≥ 1 − | 𝑧 | to the first and third factors. If | 𝑟 | = 1, then 𝑟 −1 = 𝑟 , so their
product is |1 − 𝑟 / 𝑝 | 2 > 0. If 𝑝 −1 < 𝑟 < 𝑝 is real, both factors are positive separately. The middle factor
is always positive. This proves the positivity statements. For arbitrary 𝑟 ≠ 0, a zero of the first or third
factor gives exactly the two stated values; each gives a pole since the other factors are nonzero.

    An application to an automorphic representation must first supply its parameters in this range.
Tempered parameters satisfy | 𝑟 | = 1. More generally, bounds | 𝛼 𝑝 | , | 𝛽 𝑝 | ≤ 𝑝 𝜃 with | 𝛼 𝑝 𝛽 𝑝 | = 1 and
𝜃 < 1/2 imply 𝑝 −2𝜃 ≤ | 𝑟 | ≤ 𝑝2𝜃 , which is inside the regular annulus. This implication is a scalar
estimate, not a construction assigning an automorphic representation to a native Hochschild class.
Ramified parameters require their actual local factor. The pairing comparison below therefore starts
with a specified nonzero scalar and states positivity separately.

Remark 35.7.6 (what a spherical scalar can establish). An equality on one vacuum line does not identify
two forms. On ℂ2 , the positive forms with matrices diag(1, 1) and diag(1, 2) agree on the first coordinate
line and disagree on the second. The same test applies to an attempted deduction from a spherical integral
to all native vectors. A local functional equation is a statement about specified integrals and parameters;
it does not supply the maps 𝑓 𝑝 , 𝑔 𝑝 , 𝑐 𝑝 .

Theorem 35.7.8 (conditional adelic rescaling). Assume the native local comparisons, their com-
patible finite-prime assembly, and a common adelic regularization of their forms and scalar factors. If
this construction gives a finite nonzero scalar 𝜆, then rescaling both assembled forms gives

            ℎWhit,reduced = 𝜆 −1 ℎWhit ,              𝐵 Ad = 𝜆 −1 𝐵,             ℎWhit,reduced ( 𝑣, 𝑤 ) = 𝐵 Ad ( 𝑣, 𝑐𝑤 ) .

If the unreduced Hermitian form is positive and 𝜆 > 0, the reduced form is positive on the same injective
native realization. The choice 𝜆 = 𝐿 (1, Ad) requires identification of that continued value with the

35.8. Consequence: K-P Compat, Conditional Domain                                                        333


Proof. For a finite prime set the local identities multiply, including every scalar and volume factor. The
assumed common assembly preserves these identities. Division by the nonzero assembled scalar gives
the stated equality, and division by a positive real scalar preserves positivity. Analytic continuation to
𝑠 = 1 is not a proof of absolute Euler-product convergence at that point and is not a construction of the
native assembly. Neither is inferred in this argument.

Remark 35.7.9 (local scalars and global assembly). Once a nonzero scalar is specified, dividing a bilinear
pairing by that scalar is a definition. Equality with a second pairing requires the local maps of Chap-
ter 35.7.4. A global division additionally requires the assembled scalar in Chapter 35.7.8. Neither condition
is removed by nonvanishing of an analytic 𝐿 -value.

35.8   Consequence: K-P Compat, Conditional Domain
Corollary 35.8.1 (conditional global pairing consequence). Assume the finite native comparisons,
the archimedean pairing maps of Chapter 26.3.6,and compatible adelic assembly. Then the native Koszul–
Petersson identity holds on their common domain. If an injective automorphic 𝐿 2 realization is also
supplied, its pulled-back norm is positive definite.

Proof. Apply the finite and archimedean transfer identities, then the assumed common assembly. Posi-
tivity follows from the injective realization into a positive Hilbert space. The local normalization does
not construct any of these native maps.

Remark 35.8.2 (what the ﬁnite comparison supplies). The finite K5 comparison supplies one part of
the pairing problem. Archimedean conjugation and native injectivity are separate conditions; positive
local states do not imply an injective global arithmetic map. The variance of the native duality must be
preserved at every place.
Remark 35.8.3 (spectral and positivity requirements). A sufficient arithmetic implication to the Riemann
hypothesis retains its native duality, pairing, zero-divisor and positivity hypotheses. The local scalar
rescaling proves no Hilbert–Pólya realization and removes no independent arithmetic trace comparison.

Arithmetic Hilbert–Pólya and the VB ∗ Converse:
Structural Analyses

Assume P1, P2, and P3 in the comparison form used in Chapter 22. The two additional arithmetic inputs
are H-PAr and VB∗ . H-PAr is the determinant-trace hypothesis: there is a self-adjoint operator 𝐴 for which
Θ𝜉 = 1/2 + 𝑖 𝐴 has determinant divisor div 𝜉ℝ and Weil–Connes trace equal to the zero distribution.
VB∗ adds positivity and Hamburger determinacy for the Fock-space moment measure. Connes’ adelic trace
formula and Deninger’s regularised determinant give equivalent forms of the ﬁrst input after the named
intertwiners; de Branges positivity and Nyman–Beurling–Báez-Duarte decay give equivalent forms of the
second. Zero-placement supplies support; it does not supply the unbounded moment theorem.

36.1   The Analytic Splitting
Chapter 22 gives a sufficient implication to RH from four inputs: arithmetic Positselski, Koszul–
Petersson compatibility, H-PAr , and VB∗ . The P1 input is the completed arithmetic Positselski
comparison; its Tate-Poisson shadow is only the forward functional equation. The P3 input is the
full Koszul–Petersson comparison; its proved sph-fin cuspidal core is only the Tamagawa normali-
sation. The last two inputs are the Hilbert–Pólya determinant-trace realisation and the Fock-space
positivity-determinacy theorem.

The Asymmetry
Zero-placement and VB∗ have different strength. Three operator-theoretic facts account for the differ-
ence:
   (i) Moment data for an unbounded operator do not determine the spectral measure without a deter-
       minacy theorem. Akhiezer–Glazman Ch. VI.3 supplies the classical obstruction.
  (ii) The assertion that the normal zero-divisor operator has determinant divisor div 𝜉ℝ and Weil–
       Connes zero trace is precisely H-PAr (Chapter 22.3.2).
 (iii) A symmetric 𝐿0Ar on the primary Fock is not automatically a self-adjoint Hilbert–Pólya operator;
       a domain and a self-adjoint extension must be specified.
   Thus Chapter 22.3.10 gives the implication VB∗ ⇒ zero-placement under P2, P3, and H-PAr . The con-
verse implication needs spectral regularity: positivity of the regularised moment functional, Hamburger
determinacy, and support compatibility for the Fock operator.

36.2    Structural Reductions
The assertions below separate domain, trace, determinant, and moment questions. Each assertion is an
implication between named mathematical structures.

H-PAr : Operator-Theoretic Framework
On the finite-span core of the primary arithmetic Heisenberg Fock, the Sugawara operator is diagonal
with real non-negative eigenvalues (Chapter 23.6.1). Reed–Simon Vol. I Thm. VIII.11 and the Friedrichs
construction give a canonical self-adjoint non-negative extension from this semibounded quadratic form.

This removes the domain ambiguity in Chapter 22.3.2. It does not identify the resulting Bost–Connes

Connes monoid action to the idele-class scaling action. Under such an intertwiner, Connes’ absorption
trace and the regularised Fock trace are the same distribution. The displayed absorption-trace formula,

For the Bost–Connes/KMS weight 𝜆 ( 𝑚) = log 𝑚, the zero-mode factor is 𝜁 ( 𝑡 ) for Re( 𝑡 ) > 1, multi-

derivation of the trace realisation.
Remark 36.3.4 (what the Friedrichs construction buys). Chapter 36.3.2 removes only one domain-
specification ambiguity: a real non-negative diagonal Fock/BC Hamiltonian has a canonical self-adjoint
extension. What remains is not an elementary choice of 𝜆 ( 𝑚). The KMS normalisation selects
𝜆 ( 𝑚) = log 𝑚, which gives the Bost–Connes partition trace 𝜁 ( 𝑡 ); the zero distribution of 𝜉ℝ (the
completed xi function 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 21 𝑠 ( 𝑠 − 1) 𝜋 − 𝑠/2 Γ ( 𝑠 /2) 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ), here denoting the restriction to the primary
archimedean sector) is a different object. The Hilbert–Pólya content is the additional construction of
𝐻HP , or an intertwiner carrying this Fock/BC Hamiltonian to the zero-divisor operator Θ𝜉 , with the
positive Weil–Connes trace preserved.

    Remark 36.3.8 (open intertwiner). The sph-finite sector of V prim embeds by restricted tensor product
    into a subspace of 𝐿 2 ( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ)]\𝐺 𝐿2 (𝔸)) compatible with the adele class space image (Gelbart Au-
    tomorphic Forms on Adele Groups §3.1). The zero-mode lattice 𝐿 ⊂ V prim maps to the finite-adele part
    of 𝑋ℚ0 ; the archimedean Heisenberg factor H (∞) maps to the archimedean-fibre Fock of 𝐿02 ( 𝑋ℚ0,∞ ).
    The scaling action of 𝐶ℚ on 𝐿02 ( 𝑋ℚ0 ) restricts on the sph-finite sector to the multiplicative action of
    ℕ× on the Bost–Connes zero-mode lattice (Chapter 7.3.2), plus the real-parameter archimedean scaling
    on the Fock. The infinitesimal generator of this action is the Bost–Connes/Fock Hamiltonian on the
    chiral-algebra side, while the Connes trace formula sees the absorption trace. Constructing an isometric
    intertwiner from the former to the latter is exactly the determinant-trace problem.
    Corollary 36.3.9 (H-P Ar and Connes have the same determinant-trace input). (conditional on
    the intertwiner of Chapter 36.3.7). Under that intertwiner, the trace-compatibility condition (36.1), read
    as the distributional equality of Chapter 22.3.2, is equivalent to Connes’ absorption-trace hypothesis:
    the 𝐶ℚ -scaling action on 𝐿02 ( 𝑋ℚ ) has zero distribution of 𝜁 with correct multiplicity.

    Proof. Given the conjectural intertwiner, applying 𝜋 transports the regularised trace distribution of Θ𝜉
    to the Connes distributional trace. Conversely, on the sph-finite image of 𝜋 , the Connes absorption-
    trace statement pulls back to the Hilbert–Pólya determinant and trace identities. The proof uses the
    intertwiner as an input; it does not construct it.

    Remark 36.3.10 (form of Connes’ trace formula). Connes’ trace formula (36.2) is proved in
    arXiv:math/9811068 Thm. 1. The identification of the absorption trace with the zero distribution of
    𝜁 with correct multiplicity is the content of Connes’ RH-equivalent statement; it is not a theorem.
    Chapter 36.3.9 places H-PAr at the same level only after the intertwiner of Chapter 36.3.7 is assumed.
    That intertwiner is part of the RH-equivalent determinant-trace problem. The chiral-algebra form
    replaces the adele-class-space 𝐿 2 setting by a Fock-space setting with Sugawara and free-boson operators.

Corollary 36.3.15 (H-P Ar reduces to determinant and trace). . H-PAr reduces to the determinant-
trace condition (SP). The Friedrichs/KMS side fixes the natural Bost–Connes weight 𝜆 ( 𝑚) = log 𝑚 and
gives the Euler partition trace; it does not give the zero trace. The required assertion is the construction
of 𝐻HP , Θ𝜉 , and the positive Weil–Connes trace whose distribution is the non-trivial-zero distribution
of 𝜉ℝ . This is the Hilbert–Pólya content itself, not a routine weight choice (Chapter 36.3.16).

Proof. Direct from Chapter 36.3.14. The trace-compatibility condition encodes the location of non-
trivial zeros of 𝜉ℝ ; the Bost–Connes weight gives the Euler side, while the zero side is the determinant
divisor together with the positive Weil–Connes trace distribution.

Remark 36.3.16 (Hilbert–Pólya factor). The Friedrichs construction of Chapter 36.3.2 proves only
the domain theorem. Given { 𝜆 ( 𝑚)} ≥ 0, the Friedrichs extension is unique, self-adjoint, and non-
negative. H-PAr is the additional determinant-trace assertion: one must construct a zero operator with
div det∞ ( 𝑠 − Θ𝜉 ) = div 𝜉ℝ and trace distribution such that, in symbolic wave-kernel notation,

asymptotic data.

 Corollary 36.4.16 (three equivalent spectral-regularity conditions). . Under P2, P3, H-PAr and
 the stated Fock-space identifications, the following three conditions are equivalent forms of the VB∗

    (i) VB∗ (arithmetic Virasoro operator positivity for all 𝑛).

 Condition (HB+) (Hermite–Biehler + operator-positivity of the de Branges space) is a fourth equivalent
 form.

 Proof. Direct from Chapter 36.4.14.

 Remark 36.4.17 (the content of the spectral-regularity gap). The four conditions (VB∗ , Reg, HB+, BD+)
 express the same additional spectral regularity after the stated identifications. Classical abstract moment-
 problem theory (Akhiezer 1965 §2.4, Simon 1998 §5) constructs unbounded self-adjoint operators for
 which moment data do not determine the operator. Hence the VB∗ converse requires an input not
 contained in RH as a bare zero-placement statement. The content of this input is, in each form:
 • VB∗ : operator-positivity of 𝑇𝑛 = ( 𝐿0Ar ) 𝑛 − ( 𝐿0Ar − id) 𝑛 on the primary arithmetic Heisenberg Fock.
 • Reg: positivity, uniqueness, and support of the spectral measure determined by the symmetrised zero
   moment sequence.
 • HB+: operator-positivity of the de Branges reproducing kernel H ( 𝐸𝜉 ) extending beyond Hermite–
   Biehler.
36.5. Relation Between H-P Ar and VB ∗ Converse                                                         349


• BD+: a precise 𝐿 2 convergence rate of Beurling-sequence approximations of 1 (0,1) .
These four conditions are equivalent among themselves only under the hypotheses of Chapter 36.4.14. A
proof of RH which did not also identify the Fock spectral measure would not close VB∗ in this argument.

36.5   Relation Between H-P Ar and VB ∗ Converse
Theorem 36.5.1 (H-P Ar and VB ∗ reduce to RH plus regularity). . Under H-PAr and the Fock-space
support identification, VB∗ is equivalent to RH plus the spectral-regularity condition of Chapter 36.4.4.
Without H-PAr , the implication RH ⇒ VB∗ is not meaningful, since VB∗ presupposes a self-adjoint
𝐿0Ar .
Proof. Direct from Chapter 36.4.14 combined with Chapter 36.3.14: once H-PAr is in place, 𝐿0Ar has a
well-defined spectral measure, and VB∗ ⇔ RH plus spectral regularity reduces to the moment-problem
equivalence with the support condition.

Proposition 36.5.2 (H-P Ar and regularity are separate data). . H-PAr (existence of a self-adjoint
𝐿0Ar with prescribed determinant divisor and trace distribution) and the spectral-regularity condition
(positivity, determinacy, and support of the spectral measure) are separate pieces of data:
                                                                                              2
• There exist indeterminate moment sequences with positive Hankel structure (Stieltjes’ 𝑒 𝑛 /2 example);
  these admit multiple self-adjoint realisations. H-PAr asserts existence of one realisation with the right
  trace; regularity asserts uniqueness and support properties of the realisation.
• Conversely, a determinate moment sequence does not automatically admit a self-adjoint realisation
  that matches a specific target trace; the target trace (the Bost–Connes trace of Chapter 36.1) is an
  additional constraint on the spectrum.

Proof. Akhiezer 1965 §2.4 and Simon 1998 Thm. 5.3 show that a moment sequence may admit several
positive measures. Existence of one self-adjoint realisation and uniqueness of the realisation are therefore
distinct assertions. The prescribed Bost–Connes trace is a further constraint.

Corollary 36.5.3 (separation of the two analytic inputs). . The two analytic inputs to VB∗ in the
sufficient path of Chapter 22.6.1, H-PAr and the VB∗ converse, are not the same assertion. Hence both
are required for the VB∗ input, and neither is redundant.

Proof. Chapter 36.5.2.

Remark 36.5.4 (the reﬁned suﬃcient path). The sufficient path to RH of Chapter 22.6.1 has four inputs:
arithmetic Positselski, Koszul–Petersson compatibility, H-PAr , and VB∗ . The last two split as:
• H-PAr : existence of a self-adjoint operator obtained from 𝐿0Ar by the required intertwiner, whose
  normal zero-divisor operator has determinant divisor div 𝜉ℝ and whose Weil–Connes trace is the
  corresponding zero distribution. Equivalent forms: Connes adele-class trace realisation; Deninger
  motivic regularised determinant with purity.
• VB∗ : RH and the spectral-regularity condition for the symmetrised zero moment sequence. Equivalent
  forms: Hermite–Biehler operator-positivity; Báez-Duarte sharp rate after the Petersson normalisation
  has been fixed.
Each of the two inputs is a single spectral condition. The Connes–Deninger, de Branges, and Nyman–
Beurling forms are equivalent languages for those conditions.

      Equivalent forms:

 (iii) (Combined VB∗ input). Both (1) and (2) together supply the VB∗ input in the sufficient path

Remark 36.6.1 (local form). The Hilbert–Pólya condition is existence together with determinant divisor
and trace distribution. The VB∗ converse is positivity, Hamburger determinacy, and support for the
symmetrised zero moments. The Connes–Deninger and de Branges–Báez-Duarte forms identify these
conditions in classical analytic languages; they do not make either condition a formal consequence of
the other.

36.7    Spectral Boundary
   (i) H-PAr is determinant-trace realisation (Chapter 36.3.14, Chapter 36.3.15): the Friedrichs ex-
       tension of Chapter 36.3.2 closes the domain problem, but the determinant divisor div 𝜉ℝ and
       the matching Weil–Connes zero trace are the genuine Hilbert–Pólya content (Chapter 36.3.16).
       The formulation is equivalent to Connes’ adele-class trace realisation and to Deninger’s motivic
       cohomology regularised-determinant condition.
  (ii) The VB∗ converse is equivalent to spectral regularity of the symmetrised zero-moment
       sequence (Chapter 36.4.14), under the stated Fock-space identifications. This regularity is not
       supplied by zero placement alone. The converse is an equivalence at the converse level only and does
       not close the forward direction VB∗ ⇒zero-placement (Chapter 36.4.15). Carleman’s criterion
       remains an open possible construction (Chapter 36.4.5); abstract indeterminate moment problems
       show why this extra hypothesis cannot be suppressed. Equivalent forms: de Branges reproducing-
       kernel operator-positivity beyond Hermite–Biehler; Báez-Duarte sharp decay rate with Petersson-
       matched constant.
 (iii) The two analytic inputs are separate (Chapter 36.5.2): H-PAr asserts existence of the operator;
       regularity asserts positivity, uniqueness, and support of the spectral measure. Both are required
       for the VB∗ input in the sufficient path; the other inputs of that path are not supplied here.
 (iv) Berry–Keating 𝐻 = 21 ( 𝑥 𝑝 + 𝑝𝑥 ) candidate is a candidate choice of Bost–Connes zero-mode
       weights 𝜆 ( 𝑝 𝑘 ) = 𝑘 log 𝑝, reproducing the leading asymptotic zero density but not the individual
       zeros; rigorous identification requires the regularisation matching (36.1).
36.7. Spectral Boundary                                                                                 351

                                                                                 2
  (v) Stieltjes’ example of an indeterminate moment sequence ( 𝜇𝑛 = 𝑒 𝑛 /2 ) shows that the un-
      bounded case admits genuine indeterminacy; heuristic estimates suggest the symmetrised zero
      moment sequence has intermediate growth ≍ 𝐶 𝑛 𝑛!2 on the boundary of Carleman, but this
      estimate is not yet rigorous (Chapter 36.4.6).
 (vi) The refined sufficient path to RH has four inputs (Chapter 36.5.4): arithmetic Positselski,
      Koszul–Petersson compatibility, H-PAr with explicit Friedrichs domain and trace-compatibility,
      and VB∗ as RH plus spectral regularity. The last two are each reducible to single spectral conditions
      with classical comparison formulations.
(vii) Independence of the two analytic inputs: H-PAr does not imply the VB∗ converse, and the VB∗
      converse does not construct the Hilbert–Pólya operator. The four classical languages, Connes,
      Deninger, de Branges, and Báez-Duarte, identify the same two conditions from independent sides.

The Platonic Variation and RH Completion

The arithmetic branch’s correct geometric variation is an operadic adelic surface: holomorphic at ∞,
Frobenius-oriented at ﬁnite primes, and glued by the pointed 𝐸2 restricted tensor product of Iwahori Hecke
categories: not a scheme-theoretic surface, not a literal almost-complex manifold at ﬁnite primes. The
upgraded object 𝔖2Ar drives the Riemann Hypothesis completion inside Vol IV as a conditional theorem.

Lemma 37.3.2 (closed spherical units). . For every finite place 𝑝, the spherical unit 𝑢 𝑝 is closed for
the local arithmetic bar differential: 𝑑 𝑝 ( 𝑢 𝑝 ) = 0.

Proof. The internal differential kills the monoidal unit. The Parshin–Gersten term kills it because the
tame symbol of the unit is zero. The local bar differential kills it by the augmentation-unit identity in
the 𝐸1 bar construction. At 𝑝 = 2, 3 this is computed inside the full non-semisimple Iwahori category;
the wild Ext summand changes the trace category, not the closedness of the unit.

𝜏𝑆 satisfies the Maurer–Cartan equation

in the completed convolution Lie algebra of the finite-stage Parshin–Gersten complex. Hence the signed

Proof. The Gersten differential squares to zero by the Gersten resolution. The displayed Maurer–Cartan
equation is exactly the Kato–Parshin reciprocity law for the tame-symbol boundary, restricted to the
reciprocity-closed stage 𝑆 . Boundaries at omitted places are zero because new places enter through the
closed spherical units of Chapter 37.3.2. The Koszul signs in (37.2) are the standard tensor totalization
signs; after inserting them, the cross terms of 𝐷 2𝑆 are precisely the three terms of the Maurer–Cartan
equation. Thus 𝐷 2𝑆 = 0 strictly, not merely after passing to cohomology.

Proposition 37.3.4 (comparison with the Parshin–Gersten bar). . The arithmetic bar complex
of Chapter 12.8.1 is the finite-support presentation of the colimit 𝐵 Ar (V prim ) after replacing the single
Iwasawa algebra Λ by the finite-stage adelic system {Λ 𝑝 } 𝑝 ∈ 𝑆 𝑓 and totalizing with (37.2).

Proof. Every element of the Parshin–Gersten complex has finite support in the set of places. It therefore
lies in some 𝐶PG
