                  ,𝑆 ( 𝐶 ) with 𝑆 ∈ Finrec (| 𝐶 |). The transition maps insert closed spherical units, so the
finite-support union is the filtered colimit. The Λ-action of Chapter 12.8.1 decomposes on a finite stage as
the completed tensor product of the local Λ 𝑝 -actions. This identifies the presentation of Chapter 12.8.1
with the restricted tensor presentation.

Theorem 37.3.5 (bar differential closure on the primary domain). . On the abelian primary
Heisenberg domain, the differential (37.2) satisfies 𝐷 2𝑆 = 0 at every reciprocity-closed finite stage and
is compatible with the transition maps. Therefore 𝐵 Ar (V prim ) is a well-defined arithmetic-chiral bar
complex on 𝔖2Ar .

Proof. The archimedean summand squares to zero by the Vol I chiral bar construction and the Costello–
Gwilliam comparison of Vol II. At finite places, Chapter 37.3.3 gives the chain-level square-zero statement.
Local-global factorisation compatibility Chapter 34.3.4, pro-nilpotent convergence Chapter 34.5.3, the
archimedean classical-limit check Chapter 34.6.4, and functoriality Chapter 34.7.4 supply the ambi-
ent completed coalgebra and functoriality. Transition maps are chain maps by Chapter 37.3.2. The
comparison with the Parshin–Gersten model of Chapter 12.8.1 is Chapter 37.3.4.

37.4    RH Completion
Deﬁnition 37.4.1 (RH completion hypothesis). . The RH completion hypothesis is the conjunction of:
• the Platonic surface 𝔖2Ar of Chapter 37.1.1;
• the primary arithmetic-chiral bar complex of Chapter 37.3.1;
• the arithmetic Heisenberg Koszul biconditional, conditional on the arithmetic Positselski completion
  input of Chapter 34.8.2;
• the arithmetic Petersson positive-form condition, conditional on the restricted Koszul–Petersson
  compatibility input recorded in Chapter 26.10.1;
• H-PAr in the equivalent determinant-trace form of Chapter 36.3.14;
• the positive Hamburger and sampling conditions: VB∗ on the primary Fock, equivalently the strength-
  ened HB+/BD+ forms of Chapter 36.4.14.
Theorem 37.4.2 (Platonic RH completion, conditional). . Conditional on the RH completion
hypothesis of Chapter 37.4.1, the Riemann Hypothesis holds.
37.4. RH Completion                                                                                     357


Proof. The surface 𝔖2Ar and the bar complex 𝐵 Ar (V prim ) of Chapter 37.3.1 place V prim (a Hochschild
trace class; see Chapter 22.1.2) in the correct arithmetic-chiral bar framework. The conditional Koszul
input gives P1 in the abelian Heisenberg domain (Chapter 34.8.2); P2 is Tate’s functional-equation/Zhu-
modularity input from Chapter 21.6.1; the conditional Petersson condition supplies the positive Hermi-
tian form needed for P3 in the restricted arithmetic branch Chapter 26.10.1. H-PAr supplies the self-adjoint
operator, the zero-divisor determinant, and the required Bost–Connes trace. The positive Hamburger
condition gives VB∗ on the primary Fock; determinacy alone is not the positivity input. Chapter 22.3.10
gives the zero-placement clause of F-RH. By Chapter 22.1.2, this clause is RH.

Corollary 37.4.3 (single determinant-positivity sufficient condition for RH). . Conditional on
P1, P2, and P3 in their stated conditional domains, RH is equivalent to the following single determinant-
positivity statement: the Bost–Connes determinant-trace realisation of Chapter 36.3.14 has a positive
Hamburger zero measure on the primary Fock and is determinate; equivalently, the strengthened HB+
or BD+ condition of Chapter 36.4.14 holds.

Proof. H-PAr supplies the operator and trace. The stated positive Hamburger condition supplies the
operator-positivity by Chapter 36.4.14. The remaining implication is Chapter 37.4.2.

Sharp Hypotheses for the Four-Input RH Form

The arithmetic branch separates the following six assertions into their established domains and their
spectral or categorical hypotheses: the P1 arithmetic-Positselski biconditional for the abelian Heisenberg
archetype, the P3 Koszul–Petersson identity, the K5 Godement–Jacquet normalisation, the Costello
refinements C1–C5, the H-PAr comparison, and the VB∗ implication to zero-placement. Tate’s adelic
Poisson formula gives the forward P1 direction. The finite Godement–Jacquet identity is a theorem on
the cuspidal sph-fin core. The Friedrichs construction gives an operator domain. The remaining content
is precisely the passage from these domains to the full spectral object.

39.2    Local Forms
Zero-Placement
Proposition 39.2.1 (one-sided zero-placement). . Assume P2, full P3, the H-PAr determinant-trace
realisation, and the positive VB∗ trace form. Then Chapter 22.3.10 gives the zero-placement clause of
F-RH. The reverse implication is not a consequence of RH; it asks for spectral regularity of the operator
model.

Proof. The implication used in Chapter 22.3.10 is the positive quadratic form statement on the Bost–
Connes regularised trace. P2 and P3 identify the test vectors and the Petersson form with the arithmetic
trace form. H-PAr identifies the zero divisor and the Weil–Connes trace distribution. Positivity then
forces the ordinates entering the Weil form to be real, hence the zeros lie on the critical line. None of
these steps constructs the converse positive form from zero-placement alone.

Arithmetic Positselski
Proposition 39.2.2 (P1 and the abelian arithmetic Heisenberg). . The equivalence in Chap-
ter 24.1.5 and the P1 propagation in Chapter 24.5.4 hold on the abelian-primary Heisenberg domain after
imposing the following five hypotheses:
   (i) completed continuous duals are compatible with the relevant co-derived and contra-derived cate-
       gories;
  (ii) projective and injective resolutions remain exact after derived Λ-adic completion;
 (iii) the Nakayama lifting used in the Λ-coefficient comparison is faithful;
 (iv) the primitive zeta-character computes the 𝜅 -pairing weight;
  (v) the dual curved coalgebra carries the Koszul-dual Bost–Connes interpretation.
With these hypotheses the P1 biconditional is the arithmetic Positselski theorem. Without them Tate’s
Poisson formula supplies only the forward implication from Koszul self-duality to the functional equa-
tion.

Proof. Tate’s formula identifies the local Fourier transforms and the global idele quotient and gives
𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ) from the abelian Heisenberg self-duality datum. The reverse direction must lift this
equality through the Λ-coefficient bar–cobar adjunction. Each of the five hypotheses is used exactly at
one such lift: topological duality, completion, Nakayama faithfulness, the primitive trace weight, and
the Bost–Connes interpretation of the dual coalgebra. Their conjunction is therefore sufficient, and no
smaller statement follows from Tate’s functional equation alone.

Koszul–Petersson Compatibility
Proposition 39.2.3 (P3 on the normalized sph-fin cuspidal core). . On the normalized sph-fin
cuspidal core of V prim , the archimedean Segal–Petersson identity and the finite Godement–Jacquet
identity assemble to the P3 Koszul–Petersson form.

Proof. The archimedean factor is the Segal Fock realisation of the Petersson pairing. At a finite unramified
place the sph-fin vector has the Godement–Jacquet normalisation, and the local zeta integral gives the
same Euler factor as the finite Bost–Connes trace. The restricted tensor product is taken over the spherical
units, so the product of the local identities is the adelic identity on the cuspidal sph-fin subspace.
39.2. Local Forms                                                                                       367


Remark 39.2.4 (full P3). The extension from the normalized sph-fin cuspidal core to V prim requires
the KMS1 /GNS identification, the Rankin–Selberg extension of the local Petersson computation, and
the treatment of Eisenstein summands. These three conditions are spectral hypotheses, not formal
consequences of the cuspidal calculation.

Costello Reﬁnements C1–C5
Proposition 39.2.5 (Costello refinements). . The refinements C1–C5 imply the P1 arithmetic
Positselski biconditional on their common domain after imposing the following five hypotheses:
   (i) C1: the 𝜂 -algebra is obtained as a pointed colimit in the unit-compatible 𝐸2 category of Chap-
       ter 30.2.3;
  (ii) C2: Parshin reciprocity holds modulo Λ-coboundaries, including the 𝑝 = 2 torsion term;
 (iii) C3: the pro-nilpotent limit at 𝛽 = 1 agrees with the KMS1 Tomita–Takesaki state;
 (iv) C4: the Witt truncation has the stated classical limit and is compatible with the archimedean
       Heisenberg Fock object;
  (v) C5: the morphism class is Λ-linear with trivial Γ-action.

Proof. Each C 𝑖 removes one obstruction in the comparison between the curved algebra and curved
coalgebra sides. C1 supplies the pointed 𝐸2 multiplication, C2 identifies the reciprocity defect with
a Λ-coboundary, C3 controls the limit state, C4 fixes the classical shadow, and C5 gives the allowed
morphisms. Their common domain is still the domain of the arithmetic Positselski theorem, so the five
Positselski hypotheses of §39.2 remain present.

K5 Godement–Jacquet Normalisation
Proposition 39.2.6 (K5 on the cuspidal sph-fin locus). . After the local comparison datum, K5
is established on the cuspidal sph-fin locus. Hoffstein–Lockhart nonvanishing excludes the local zero
obstruction in this domain, and the sph-fin projection removes Eisenstein poles from the calculation.

Proof. The local comparison datum identifies the chosen sph-fin vector with the Godement–Jacquet
test vector. The local zeta integral is then the standard local 𝐿 -factor. On the cuspidal sph-fin locus the
Hoffstein–Lockhart nonvanishing theorem prevents the denominator which enters the absorption nor-
malisation from vanishing. Since the sph-fin projection has already removed the Eisenstein summands,
no continuous-spectrum pole enters the identity.

Remark 39.2.7. The propagation of K5 to full Koszul–Petersson compatibility is therefore the full P3
problem of §39.2.

H-PAr and the VB∗ Converse
Proposition 39.2.8 (Friedrichs domain and determinant divisor). . The Friedrichs construction
of Chapter 36.3.2 gives a self-adjoint operator on its quadratic-form domain. The Hilbert–Pólya input is
the further assertion that the associated normal zero-divisor operator has determinant divisor div 𝜉ℝ and
Weil–Connes trace equal to the zero distribution. This assertion is not a choice of zero-mode weights.

Proof. The Friedrichs theorem starts from a lower-semicontinuous positive form and produces a self-
adjoint operator. It does not determine the regularised determinant or the Weil–Connes trace of the
scaling action. The Connes and Deninger forms have the required Lefschetz shape only when the
368                               Chapter 39. Sharp Hypotheses for the Four-Input RH Form


determinant divisor and the trace distribution are the non-trivial zero divisor and distribution of 𝜉ℝ .
Thus the operator-domain theorem and the determinant-trace theorem are distinct statements.

Proposition 39.2.9 (VB ∗ converse). . The converse statement in Chapter 36.4.14 is a spectral-
regularity comparison after the Fock-space identifications. It does not imply the forward positivity
statement VB∗ ⇒ zero-placement.

Proof. A converse spectral-regularity theorem reconstructs regularity of the operator model from a zero-
placement input and auxiliary spectral identifications. The forward theorem requires positivity of the
Bost–Connes regularised trace before zero-placement is known. The directions therefore have different
hypotheses and different content.

Primary-Source Anchors
Remark 39.2.10. Li–Weil positivity, Connes’ trace formula, Deninger’s cohomological form, and the
Bost–Connes scaling action are four shadows of the same problem only after the determinant divisor and
trace distribution have been specified. The symmetrised zero measure gives the VB∗ converse shadow; the
self-adjoint scaling operator with determinant divisor div 𝜉ℝ gives the H-PAr shadow. Their coincidence
is the Hilbert–Pólya content.

39.3   The Four-Input Conditional Conjunction
Theorem 39.3.1 (the four-input conditional conjunction). . Assume the following four statements.
   (i) PArPos
         1    : arithmetic Positselski for the abelian-primary Heisenberg domain, with the five hypotheses
       of §39.2.
  (ii) PKP
         3 : full-sector Koszul–Petersson compatibility, extending the normalized sph-fin cuspidal iden-
       tity by the three spectral hypotheses of §39.2.
 (iii) HPAr : the H-PAr determinant-trace realisation, including determinant divisor div 𝜉ℝ and the
       Weil–Connes zero trace distribution.
 (iv) VB∗+ : the positive Bost–Connes regularised trace form giving the forward VB∗ ⇒ zero-placement
       implication.
Together with the Tate-Poisson direction, P2, and Hamburger determinacy, these four statements imply
the zero-placement clause of F-RH. Hence the arithmetic branch implies RH under precisely this four-
input conjunction.

Proof. The arithmetic Positselski hypothesis supplies P1, because its forward Tate direction and its reverse
bar–cobar lift give the Koszul-duality biconditional. Full P3 identifies the adelic Petersson form with the
arithmetic trace form on the whole primary space. HPAr supplies the zero divisor and Weil–Connes trace
distribution attached to that trace. The positive VB∗+ form is then the Weil-positive form on the zero
distribution. By the Platonic completion theorem Chapter 37.4.2, P1, P2, P3, HPAr , VB∗+ , and Hamburger
determinacy imply F-RH, hence RH.

Remark 39.3.2 (independence of directions). The theorem is a sufficient implication. It does not as-
sert that RH recovers arithmetic Positselski, full Koszul–Petersson compatibility, the Hilbert–Pólya
determinant-trace realisation, or the positive VB∗ trace form. The H-PAr and VB∗ residuals are separated
by Chapter 36.5.2; the Positselski and Koszul–Petersson residuals are separated by Chapter 24.7 and
Chapter 26.10.4.
39.4. Logical Form of the Essential Biconditional                                                   369


Remark 39.3.3 (hypothesis support). The support of the four-input conjunction is local. The P1 support
is the five arithmetic-Positselski hypotheses. The P3 support is the KMS1 /GNS identification, the full
Rankin–Selberg extension, and the Eisenstein-sector calculation. The HPAr support is the determinant
divisor div 𝜉ℝ and the Weil–Connes trace distribution. The VB∗+ support is positivity of the regularised
Bost–Connes trace.

39.4    Logical Form of the Essential Biconditional
The essential biconditional

                              𝜅GAr + ( 𝜅 ! )GAr = 0 ⇐⇒ 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 )

(Chapter 19.2.1, Chapter 21.5.1) has asymmetric proof-theoretic content. The implication from arithmetic
Koszul self-duality to the functional equation is Tate’s adelic Poisson formula. The reverse implication
must reconstruct the arithmetic Positselski equivalence for the Λ-coefficient abelian Heisenberg object.
It therefore has exactly the five hypotheses of §39.2.

39.5   Consequences
   (i) The Tate direction of P1 is unconditional; the full P1 biconditional is arithmetic Positselski.
  (ii) P3 is established on the normalized sph-fin cuspidal core; full P3 is the corresponding spectral
       extension problem.
 (iii) K5 is established on the cuspidal sph-fin locus after the local comparison datum.
 (iv) C1–C5 are sufficient Costello refinements on their common restricted domain and inherit the
       arithmetic-Positselski hypotheses.
  (v) The Friedrichs theorem gives the operator domain for H-PAr ; the determinant divisor and trace
       distribution are the Hilbert–Pólya content.
 (vi) The VB∗ converse is a spectral-regularity comparison and is logically distinct from the positive
       forward implication to zero-placement.

40.5    Obstruction (b): Extension to 𝑝 = 2 , 3
Why DEG Does Not Extend Directly
At 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3} the obstructions to DEG are multiple:
Proposition 40.5.1 (obstructions to DEG at wild primes). . The DEG construction at fixed central
character does not directly extend from 𝑝 ≥ 5 to 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3} for three reasons:
40.5. Obstruction (b): Extension to 𝑝 = 2 , 3                                                                    377


   (i) Non-semisimplicity of the Iwahori Hecke category. At 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3} the category HkIw    𝐺 𝐿2 , 𝑝 is not
                                                                                1
       semisimple (Chapter 33.4.3); the Paskunas block structure has higher Ext -terms missed by DEG’s
       semisimple gluing argument.
  (ii) Non-generic residual representations. At 𝑝 = 2, 3 the residual 𝜌 : 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 → 𝐺 𝐿2 (𝔽 𝑝 ) may factor
       through a non-split extension of a character by a character whose Ext1 -class is non-trivial but
       realised by wild ramification. Colmez’s ( 𝜑, Γ)-module classification requires modification for
       such 𝜌 (Colmez 2010 §9 gives partial results for 𝑝 = 3 under stringent hypotheses; 𝑝 = 2 is treated
       less completely).
 (iii) Breuil–Mezard cycles split. At 𝑝 = 2, 3 the Breuil–Mezard cycles of Emerton–Gee §5 split into
       multiple components per Hodge type (Breuil–Mezard 2002 §2.2; Gee–Kisin 2014 Local Langlands
       correspondence in families, Ann. Math. 179, §3). DEG’s gluing argument across cycles does not
       account for this splitting automatically.

Proof. Each item is documented in the cited sources: (1) is Chapter 33.4.3; (2) is a direct observation from
Colmez 2010 §7.2 and §9; (3) is Breuil–Mezard 2002 Conj. 2.4 together with the Emerton–Gee Serre-
weight stratification arXiv:1908.07185 §5. These are the three obstructions to DEG at wild primes.

The Wild-EG Enhancement Programme
The reduction is two-step: (i) construct a wild-block DEG functor via Bushnell–Henniart types and
local Langlands normalisations; (ii) pair it with an enhanced Emerton–Gee stack incorporating the wild
inertia data absent from the fixed-character setup.

The DEG extension has five residual inputs:
   (i) Chapter 40.4.5 (R1a/F1.a.1): block exhaustion for DEG at 𝑝 ≥ 5, fixed 𝜒 , every residual 𝜌. Reduces

       𝑝 ∈ {2, 3} with four structural properties.
 (iii) Chapter 40.5.5 (R1b’): existence of the Bushnell–Henniart-compatible per-block fully faithful

 (iv) Chapter 40.5.10 (R1c/F1.a.3): the wild-block analogue of Chapter 40.4.5; essential surjectivity per

  (i) The fixed- 𝜒 , 𝑝 ≥ 5, fully faithful DEG embedding (Chapter 40.7.2): no residual needed. This is

 (ii) The global F1 reduction (Chapter 40.8.3): no residual beyond the explicitly named local, family,
      and LACD inputs.

H-P Ar Determinant-Trace Matching and
Hamburger Determinacy

Chapter 36 reduces the arithmetic Hilbert–Pólya hypothesis H-PAr to a determinant-trace realisation
(SP) equivalent to the Connes adele-class-space absorption-trace conjecture and to the Deninger regularised-
determinant axioms, and reduced the VB∗ converse to a four-way equivalence with Hamburger determinacy
of the symmetrised shifted-zero measure. Chapter 37 uses the conditional RH completion hypothesis and
isolates the positivity/determinacy input. The H-PAr side separates the Bost–Connes zero-mode weight-
selection problem from the trace-matching problem: the logarithmic Berry–Keating weight is the only
survivor among a small canonical test family, and is unique under an explicit KMS/zeta-partition nor-
malisation, but existence of the required trace identity is the H-PAr obstruction. The VB∗ side tests the
Carleman construction: the Bombieri–Lagarias Li-coeﬃcient bounds do not imply the Carleman estimate
for the shifted-zero moments. The suﬃcient analytic residual is (Ranalytic ): a linear upper-growth bound
for 𝜇1/(2
      2𝑛
          𝑛)
             , or equivalently a positive regularised moment measure with Carleman divergence.

41.2   Six Reductions
Four reductions concern weight selection; two concern Hamburger determinacy.

Cycle 1 (A, weight enumeration)
Problem. Does the Berry–Keating ansatz 𝜆 ( 𝑝 𝑘 ) = 𝑘 log 𝑝 (Chapter 36.3.17) constitute the unique
natural Bost–Connes zero-mode weight?

Argument. The Berry–Keating ansatz reproduces the leading asymptotic zero density
𝑁 (𝑇 ) ∼ (𝑇 /2 𝜋 ) log(𝑇 /2 𝜋 ) (Bohr–Sommerfeld quantisation of 𝑥 𝑝 = 𝐸 ) but does not re-
produce the individual spectrum; three independent competitors exist among finite canonical
tests.

Sources. Bost–Connes 1995 §2.2 (Hecke algebra structure); Connes–Marcolli 2008 Ch. 3 (KMS 𝛽
classification); Laca 1998.

Conclusion. Four candidate weight systems are enumerated as Chapter 41.3.1; pairwise P1+P2 com-
patibility is proved as Chapter 41.3.5. The KMS 𝛽=1 state of the Bost–Connes system is unique in the
symmetric normalisation, but that rigidity alone does not classify arbitrary additive prime-weight systems.
Trace-compatibility (36.1) for each candidate is equivalent to H-PAr for that candidate; no combination
gives an unconditional trace identity.

Cycle 2 (A, uniqueness under KMS rigidity)
Problem. Does at most one weight system satisfy simultaneous compatibility with P1, P2, and the
H-PAr trace condition?
390        Chapter 41. H-P Ar Determinant-Trace Matching and Hamburger Determinacy


Argument. Existence is not assumed (it is H-PAr itself); uniqueness holds conditionally on existence,
via Connes–Marcolli rigidity.

Sources. Connes–Marcolli, AMS Colloq. Publ. 55 (2008), Thm 4.15 (uniqueness of symmetric KMS 𝛽=1
state); Connes–Marcolli–Ramachandran arXiv:math/0501424 (explicit form).

Conclusion. The KMS 𝛽=1 state on 𝐶ℚ∗ is unique among symmetric states (invariant under Gal(ℚab /ℚ))
by Connes–Marcolli 2008 Thm 4.15. The compatibility theorem identifying the partition function and
prime-generator expectations with the canonical zeta normalisation forces the logarithmic weight under
that hypothesis; see Chapter 41.3.7. Existence of the weight system with the required zero trace is precisely
the H-PAr assertion.

Cycle 3 (A, consistency with H-PAr )
Problem.    Does the Berry–Keating weight 𝜆 ( 𝑝 𝑘 ) = 𝑘 log 𝑝 reproduce the H-PAr trace identity?

Argument. The Berry–Keating partition function 𝑛 ≥1 𝑒 − 𝑡 log 𝑛 = 𝑛 ≥1 𝑛− 𝑡 = 𝜁 ( 𝑡 ), multiplied by
                                                      P               P
the Dedekind-eta inverse, does not equal the zero wave-kernel distribution; the two sides match only
after the archimedean Euler factor is subtracted and the logarithmic-derivative expansion is inverted.

Sources. Edwards, Riemann’s Zeta Function (Academic Press 1974) §§1.13 and 3.3, Mellin inversion of
𝜉 via the logarithmic derivative.

Conclusion. The trace-compatibility condition is an infinite hierarchy of constraints, not a single scalar
equation. By Mellin inversion, the hierarchy is an equality of distributions for the normal zero operator
Θ𝜉 , equivalently det∞ ( 𝑠 id − Θ𝜉 ) = 𝜉ℝ ( 𝑠 ). The Friedrichs Fock/BC Hamiltonian supplies the Euler
partition side, not this determinant identity. The hierarchy is identified with a regularised Weil/Connes
explicit-formula extension only after the admissibility of the test family is supplied; see Chapter 41.3.10.
No weight system is known to close the trace identity.

(Chapter 36); this is exactly on the Carleman boundary, not strictly inside.

Sources. Akhiezer 1965 §2.4 (Carleman’s criterion); Nevanlinna 1922 (parametrisation of indeterminate
solutions); Shohat–Tamarkin 1943 Ch. III.5; Berg–Christiansen 2002 (exponential-moment refine-

Conclusion. The Riemann–von Mangoldt formula controls zero counting, not the positivity of the
regularised moment functional. A saddle-point heuristic suggests the Carleman-scale growth 𝐶 𝑛 𝑛!2 , but
converting that heuristic into the upper bound 𝜇1/(2

41.3   H-P Ar Spectral Matching: Bost–Connes Zero-Mode Weight
Candidate Weights
The residual splitting candidate weight system stated was the Berry–Keating ansatz 𝜆 ( 𝑝 𝑘 ) = 𝑘 log 𝑝
extended multiplicatively to 𝜆 ( 𝑚) = log 𝑚 (Chapter 36.3.17). We compare it with three nearby weights.
This is not an exhaustive classification of all maps ℕ× → ℝ: additive weights are determined by arbitrary
prime values { 𝜆 ( 𝑝)} 𝑝 . The point is to separate the canonical BC/zeta generator from common false
substitutes.
Deﬁnition 41.3.1 (four canonical zero-mode weight tests). . Let 𝐶ℚ∗ be the Bost–Connes algebra of Chap-
ter 7.1.1. Four canonical weight tests { 𝜆★ ( 𝑚)}𝑚 ∈ℕ× are available, each arising from a distinct structural
interpretation of the Hecke action on the zero-mode lattice:
392        Chapter 41. H-P Ar Determinant-Trace Matching and Hamburger Determinacy


(BK) Berry–Keating / logarithmic: 𝜆BK ( 𝑚) := log 𝑚. Extended multiplicatively: 𝜆BK ( 𝑝 𝑘 ) = 𝑘 log 𝑝.
This is the Euler-product generator; yields the BC KMS 𝛽 partition function 𝜁 ( 𝛽 ) at 𝛽 = 1.
(Li-shift) Li spectral translation: 𝜆Li ( 𝑚) := log 𝑚 as a semigroup weight, with the critical-line transla-
tion 𝑠 ↦→ 𝑠 − 21 applied to the spectral parameter rather than inserted as a constant shift in the semigroup
homomorphism. A literal formula log 𝑚 − 21 is not additive on ℕ× and is therefore not a BC weight.
(vM) von Mangoldt / Weil: 𝜆vM ( 𝑚) := Λ ( 𝑚) log 𝑚 where Λ ( 𝑚) is the von Mangoldt function
(Λ ( 𝑝 𝑘 ) = log 𝑝, zero otherwise). This is logarithmic derivative data, not a multiplicative semigroup
weight.
(FS-quad) quadratic ﬁnite-place weight: 𝜆FS ( 𝑝 𝑘 ) := 𝑘 2 log 𝑝 and 𝜆FS ( 𝑚) := 𝑝 𝑘 𝑝 ∥ 𝑚 𝑘 2𝑝 log 𝑝. This
                                                                                    P

records the quadratic-exponent alternative suggested by finite-place Hecke powers on perfectoid Iwahori
charts (Chapter 37.1.1 finite-place orientation). It agrees with (BK) on squarefree integers and differs on
higher prime powers.
Remark 41.3.2 (domain of the four tests). Under the ℚ-positive-semigroup action of ℕ× on the zero-mode
lattice, a weight system 𝜆 : ℕ× → ℝ is compatible with the Bost–Connes Hecke action 𝜇𝑛 𝜇𝑚 = 𝜇𝑛𝑚
only when 𝜆 ( 𝑛𝑚) = 𝜆 ( 𝑛) + 𝜆 ( 𝑚). The additive case reduces to specifying 𝜆 ( 𝑝) for each prime 𝑝,
hence contains infinitely many choices. The zeta partition normalisation
                                           ∑︁ − 𝛽𝜆 ( 𝑚 )
                                              𝑒          = 𝜁 ( 𝛽)
                                             𝑚 ≥1

for all Re( 𝛽 ) > 1 forces 𝑒 − 𝜆 ( 𝑝 ) = 𝑝 −1 prime-by-prime, and therefore forces (BK). Without that nor-
malisation there is no uniqueness theorem. The four tests above only record the canonical logarithmic,
translated, logarithmic-derivative, and quadratic finite-place possibilities used in the obstruction com-
parison.

Pairwise Compatibility with P1 and P2
Lemma 41.3.3 (P1 compatibility within the four tests). . Within Chapter 41.3.1, the additive Berry–
Keating weight is compatible with the formal 𝑚 ↔ 𝑚 −1 functional-equation involution. The Li-shift
test is the same additive weight together with an external critical-line translation. The von Mangoldt
and quadratic finite-place tests are not multiplicative semigroup weights and therefore do not define BC
zero-mode weights satisfying P1.

Proof. For (BK), 𝜆BK ( 𝑚) + 𝜆BK ( 𝑚 −1 ) = 0 after formal extension of log to ℚ>0 . The Li shift is not the
map log 𝑚 − 21 on ℕ× , since such a map fails 𝜆 ( 𝑛𝑚) = 𝜆 ( 𝑛) + 𝜆 ( 𝑚). It is the same additive weight
with the spectral parameter translated by 1/2. The von Mangoldt test is supported on prime powers
and the FS-quad test satisfies 𝜆FS ( 𝑝 𝑎+𝑏 ) ≠ 𝜆FS ( 𝑝 𝑎 ) + 𝜆FS ( 𝑝𝑏 ) for general 𝑎, 𝑏 . Hence neither is a BC
semigroup weight.

Lemma 41.3.4 (P2 compatibility within the four tests). . Within Chapter 41.3.1, the Berry–Keating
weight is the only additive weight whose partition function is the classical zeta partition function. The
Li shift changes only the external critical-line normalisation. The von Mangoldt and FS-quad tests do
not give the 𝜁 -partition function and hence do not satisfy the P2 completed-zeta character condition.

Theorem 41.3.5 (four-test filter under P1+P2). . Among the four tests of Chapter 41.3.1, simultane-
ous P1+P2 compatibility leaves only the Berry–Keating semigroup weight 𝜆 ( 𝑚) = log 𝑚, with the Li
convention understood as the same weight after external critical-line translation. This is a finite filter,
not a classification of all possible prime-weight systems.

Proof. Chapter 41.3.3 and Chapter 41.3.4 eliminate the von Mangoldt and FS-quad tests as BC semigroup
weights. The Li convention does not produce a new additive weight; it is the Berry–Keating weight with
the spectral parameter centred at 1/2. Thus the only surviving semigroup weight in the four-test family
is (BK).

Remark 41.3.6 (what the ﬁlter proves). Chapter 41.3.5 proves only the finite-filter statement just stated.
Full uniqueness requires the zeta partition normalisation or an equivalent KMS compatibility condition;
without such a condition, arbitrary prime weights { 𝜆 ( 𝑝)} 𝑝 remain possible.

Uniqueness under KMS/Zeta Normalisation
The surviving canonical weight is (BK). Existence with the trace-compatibility condition is the H-PAr
assertion. Uniqueness after the partition function is fixed is unconditional.
Theorem 41.3.7 (uniqueness under zeta partition normalisation). . Suppose 𝜆 : ℕ× → ℝ ≥0 is

the Berry–Keating weight.

Remark 41.3.8 (relation to Connes–Marcolli rigidity). Connes–Marcolli rigidity at 𝛽 = 1 is the concep-
tual source of this normalisation. Identifying an arbitrary weight with the unique symmetric KMS state
requires the prime-generator and partition-function bridge proved in the theorem. The theorem records
the exact conditional uniqueness available on the arithmetic path. H-PAr is the Bost–Connes/Dedekind-
eta trace identity, the unresolved determinant-trace matching problem.

Corollary 41.3.11 (the hierarchy is the Connes absorption-trace bridge). (conditional on the

Connes absorption-trace realisation. The admissibility and trace-identification step is precisely what
H-PAr asserts.

Remark 41.3.12 (weight selection and H-PAr ). Chapter 41.3.7 and Chapter 41.3.11 together state: if H-PAr
holds, the weight is uniquely Berry–Keating under the zeta/KMS normalisation. Whether the Berry–
Keating weight satisfies the trace compatibility is the regularised Connes absorption-trace problem.
The reduction is tight: the canonical weight is determined under explicit normalisation, while the trace
identity is the classical absorption-trace problem.

Remark 41.4.8 (domain of Ranalytic ). (Ranalytic ) is a one-sided upper-growth condition, distinct from a

requires. Standard zero-density theorems count zeros in regions; the residual controls a regularised
moment functional.
Remark 41.4.9 (form of the determinacy residual). (Ranalytic ) is a sufficient condition for the Vol IV
determinacy step. It identifies the exact analytic shape of the positivity theorem required; neither the
classical Weil formula nor the Bombieri–Lagarias bounds supply it.

41.6   Residual Conditions
After the determinacy reductions, the Ch 37 RH implication requires:
   (i) (W) Weight normalisation. The BK weight is forced once the additive zeta partition function
       is fixed prime-by-prime. The remaining assertion is that that the Vol IV Friedrichs construction
       really lands in this KMS/zeta normalisation.
  (ii) (H) H-P trace bridge. The analytic theorem is the admissible regularised extension identifying
       the BC/Dedekind-eta heat trace with the Connes zero trace; the classical Weil explicit formula
       applies to admissible test functions and is a step toward, not a substitute for, this identification.
 (iii) (Ranalytic ) Carleman positivity. The required analytic input is a positive regularised shifted-zero
       moment functional with 𝜇1/(2 2𝑛
                                       𝑛)
                                          = 𝑂 ( 𝑛); this estimate lies beyond the reach of the Bombieri–
       Lagarias Li-coefficient bounds by Chapter 41.4.3.
 (iv) Compatibility with the Ch 37 hypothesis. The RH completion hypothesis of Chapter 37.4.1
       requires P1, P2, P3, H-PAr , and Hamburger determinacy together. P1 is conditional on arith-
       metic Positselski (requires a non-formal theorem); P2 unconditional; P3 conditional on Koszul–
       Petersson compatibility (requires a non-formal theorem); H-PAr (RH-equivalent); determinacy
       reduces to (Ranalytic ).

Remark 41.6.1 (determinacy consequences). H-PAr determinant-trace matching and Hamburger deter-
minacy are RH-equivalent or RH-adjacent analytic problems. The determinacy comparison gives:
   (i) Conditional uniqueness of the weight system: the Berry–Keating 𝜆 ( 𝑚) = log 𝑚 is forced by additive
       zeta/KMS normalisation.
  (ii) Explicit identiﬁcation of the trace-compatibility hierarchy: the infinite sequence of conditions is
       the regularised Weil/Connes trace bridge; the classical Weil formula applies to admissible test
       functions and is a step in the bridge.
 (iii) Independence of Li-coeﬃcient bounds and Carleman moments: the Bombieri–Lagarias bounds do
       not imply the Carleman estimate by Chapter 41.4.3.
 (iv) The single analytic residual (Ranalytic ): Hamburger determinacy reduces to positivity plus linear
       upper growth for the regularised moments.
  (v) Compatibility with Ch 37: the three residuals (W), (H), (Ranalytic ) give the H-P/VB implication
       after the conditional P1/P3 inputs are supplied.

41.7   Determinacy Boundary
   (i) Weight selection is uniquely determined after normalisation (Chapter 41.3.7). Among four
       canonical tests, only the Berry–Keating 𝜆 ( 𝑚) = log 𝑚 survives as a BC semigroup weight with
       zeta partition function (Chapter 41.3.5).
  (ii) The trace-compatibility hierarchy is the regularised Weil/Connes bridge (Chapter 41.3.10,
       Chapter 41.3.11). The H-PAr trace identity needs an admissible extension of the explicit formula to
       the BC heat-trace family.
 (iii) Hamburger determinacy reduces to a single analytic positivity residual (Chapter 41.4.7).
       Under (Ranalytic ), the moments are positive and satisfy 𝜇1/(2
                                                                   2𝑛
                                                                      𝑛)
                                                                          = 𝑂 ( 𝑛), so Carleman’s criterion
       holds.
 (iv) Li-coefficient bounds do not give Carleman moments (Chapter 41.4.3). Li-coefficient bounds
       are oscillatory zero-sum bounds; a separate positivity and domination theorem is required for
       Carleman.
  (v) Three precisely-named residuals (Chapter 41.5.2): weight normalisation (W), H-P trace bridge
       (H), and Carleman positivity (Ranalytic ).
 (vi) Domain of the reduction. H-PAr reduces to the Connes absorption-trace conjecture (RH-
       equivalent); Hamburger determinacy reduces to (Ranalytic ) (RH-adjacent); no new RH-equivalent
       positivity language beyond the the residual splitting list of Det, HB+, BD+ is produced.
(vii) The residual conjunction. The three residuals (W), (H), (Ranalytic ) are each precisely stated; their
       conjunction, together with the conditional P1/P3 inputs, gives the conditional Vol IV implication
       to RH.
   The two analytic problems are the Bost–Connes absorption-trace bridge and positivity with
Carleman-scale upper growth for the regularised shifted-zero moments.

Arithmetic FLE: Source Domain and Logical
Corrections

The critical-level fundamental local equivalence (FLE) and its quantum and small variants are theorems
in the geometric Langlands programme over complex curves. The arithmetic branch of this volume
studies V prim , the Hochschild trace class of the identity on the global arithmetic Iwahori–Hecke category
of 𝐺 𝐿2 , and its conjectural companions F1, F2, F3. This chapter records the domain boundaries of the
geometric FLE sources, explains why F1/F2/F3 require a distinct mixed-characteristic framework, and
corrects the form of claims that previously conflated the two settings. No independent comparison
pair is constructed here; arithmetic-FLE realization remains conditional on the boundary conditions of
Section 42.5.

42.1   Source Theorems
Theorem 42.1.1 (geometric critical-level FLE). . The 2024 geometric-Langlands proof constructs
the critical-level fundamental local equivalence in the geometric setting over a smooth projective curve
in characteristic 0:
                                     KL( 𝐺 )crit ≃ IndCoh∗ Opmf
                                                                   
                                                                 ˇ ,
                                                                  𝐺
with compatibility with Kac–Moody localization. Its source is Arinkin–Beraldo–Campbell–Chen–
Faergeman–Gaitsgory–Lin–Raskin– Rozenblyum, Proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture II: Kac–
Moody localization and the FLE, arXiv:2405.03648.
Theorem 42.1.2 (quantum and small FLE sources). . The quantum and small FLE layer consists
of local geometric and metaplectic/quantum statements over a complex curve. Campbell–Dhillon–
Raskin’s Fundamental local equivalences in quantum geometric Langlands (arXiv:1907.03204) and
Gaitsgory–Lysenko’s small-FLE work (arXiv:1903.02279) establish equivalences whose source categories
are Kazhdan–Lusztig or metaplectic representations and whose target categories are quantum groups
or root-of-unity modules over a formal disk. The arithmetic analogue of these equivalences is an open
problem at each finite prime.
Remark 42.1.3 (domain of the geometric FLE sources). The FLE sources operate within the geometric
Langlands, Kac–Moody, Whittaker, and root-of-unity quantum-group framework over complex curves.
A local categorical 𝑝-adic Langlands equivalence over ℚ 𝑝 , a globalization over Spec ℤ, and an Emer-
ton–Gee full Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) target comparison each require additional technology: Fargues–Scholze’s
geometrization, prismatic or pro-étale methods, and the Emerton–Gee eigenvariety construction.

42.2    Domain Distinction: Geometric FLE vs F1/F2/F3
Proposition 42.2.1 (F1/F2/F3 as a distinct mixed-characteristic programme). . The arithmetic
branch’s F1 (local categorical Langlands comparison for 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ 𝑝 against the Emerton–Gee stack), F2


                                                   401
402                 Chapter 42. Arithmetic FLE: Source Domain and Logical Corrections


(mixed-characteristic 𝐸2 Hecke enhancement and restricted tensor product), and F3 (Ben-Zvi–Nadler
Hochschild-trace comparison against the full Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) target) constitute a mixed-characteristic local-
global Langlands and Hochschild-trace programme whose source and target categories are disjoint from
those of the geometric FLE.
Proof. The geometric FLE (Theorem 42.1.1) pairs critical-level Kac–Moody or Whittaker/factorizable
categories as source with oper or quantum-group categories over a smooth projective complex curve
as target. F1 pairs the spherically-finite automorphic category for 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ as source with ind-coherent
sheaves on the Emerton–Gee stack as target. F2 requires a mixed-characteristic 𝐸2 Hecke enhancement
and restricted tensor product. F3 requires a Ben-Zvi–Nadler Hochschild-trace comparison against the
full Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) arithmetic target. The targets of F1, F2, F3 are Emerton–Gee and Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) stacks;
the inputs at finite primes are adelic Hecke categories, not Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral algebras over a
complex curve.
Remark 42.2.2 (ﬁnite-prime categorical structure). At a finite prime 𝑝, the relevant categorical structure
is the category Coh(Bun𝐺 ) of coherent sheaves on the moduli stack of 𝐺 -bundles on the Fargues–
Fontaine curve, equipped with the Fargues–Scholze spectral action (arXiv:2102.13459), together with
Hecke correspondences, diamonds, and ( 𝜑, Γ)-modules. The archimedean fibre carries classical Kac–
Moody and chiral intuition, providing the motivating analogy; the finite-prime framework is governed
by Fargues–Scholze geometrization and Emerton–Gee eigenvarieties.

42.3    Domain Corrections Across Source Categories
Remark 42.3.1 (local/global type distinction). F1, F2, and F3 are local-global Langlands and Hochschild-
trace conjectures. Their source is the automorphic category for 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ or its local 𝑝-adic analogue; their
target is the Emerton–Gee stack or the full Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) coherent sheaf theory. These source and target
types differ from those of the geometric FLE.
Remark 42.3.2 (ﬁnite-prime chiral structure). At a finite prime, the relevant structure is the Beilinson–
Drinfeld factorization algebra and the Hecke correspondence on Bun𝐺 , governed by Fargues–Scholze
geometrization. The archimedean fibre carries Kac–Moody and chiral intuitions as a motivating analogy.
Remark 42.3.3 (quantum-group and root-of-unity source domain). The root-of-unity and small-FLE
sources (Campbell–Dhillon–Raskin, Gaitsgory–Lysenko) are geometric and quantum: they operate
over a complex curve with a quantum parameter 𝑞 a root of unity or with a metaplectic covering. The
parameter 𝑝 − 𝑠 appearing in local Hecke eigenvalues at a prime 𝑝 is a spectral parameter, distinct from a
root-of-unity quantum-group parameter.
Remark 42.3.4 (function-ﬁeld transport and number-ﬁeld domain). Raskin’s globalization operates over
a function field. The transport to a number field requires: (a) a local categorical comparison F1 at each
prime, and (b) a prismatic or BC-diamond-glue transition across primes. Both remain open.
Remark 42.3.5 (mixed-characteristic substrate). The arithmetic compactification Spec ℤ carries an
archimedean place and mixed-characteristic fibres. A curve in characteristic 0 carries neither. The
arithmetic programme requires mixed-characteristic methods (prismatic cohomology, perfectoid
geometry) at each finite prime and complex-analytic methods at the archimedean place.
Remark 42.3.6 (independent form for arithmetic FLE). Arithmetic FLE has no pair of independent con-
structions in the present arithmetic formalism. An arithmetic FLE theorem requires first the boundary
conditions of Section 42.5.

Remark 42.3.8 (F3/BZN form against full Weil target). F3 asks for a Ben-Zvi–Nadler Hochschild-trace

Remark 42.3.9 (spectral parameter vs quantum-group parameter). The Hecke eigenvalue at a prime 𝑝 is
recorded by the spectral parameter 𝑝 − 𝑠 or equivalently by the Satake image in Rep( 𝐺ˇ ). The quantum-

Remark 42.3.10 (Fargues–Scholze, Emerton–Gee, and Dotto–Emerton–Gee). Fargues–Scholze
(arXiv:2102.13459) provides the spectral action on Coh(Bun𝐺 ) via the Fargues–Fontaine curve.
Emerton–Gee (arXiv:1908.07185) constructs the stack of ( 𝜑, Γ)-modules. Dotto–Emerton–Gee
establishes full faithfulness of a functor to mod- 𝑝 representations; an equivalence of ∞-categories
between the automorphic and the Emerton–Gee coherent side is the content of F1.
Remark 42.3.11 (F1/F2/F3 logical-form correction). F1 carries form Conditional: the local categorical
comparison is supported by Fargues–Scholze (arXiv:2102.13459) and Emerton–Gee (arXiv:1908.07185)
and requires the adelic-descent and BC-diamond-glue steps. F2 carries form Conditional: the mixed-
characteristic 𝐸2 Hecke enhancement and restricted tensor product are formally accessible but unproved.
F3 carries form Conjecture: the full Weil/( 𝜑, Γ) target comparison is beyond current techniques. Chap-
ters previously marking F1, F2, F3 with premature theorem-closure have been sharpened accordingly.
Remark 42.3.12 (local Satake/Yangian normalization). The local Satake isomorphism identifies the
spherical Hecke algebra with the representation ring of 𝐺ˇ . An arithmetic Yangian structure, if it exists,
must be grounded in an independent comparison between the Satake filtration and an explicit Yangian
coproduct; this identification remains open.
Remark 42.3.13 (BC-diamond-glue decomposition). The BC-diamond-glue problem decomposes into
three parts: (a) the local BZCHN/Emerton–Gee comparison at each prime 𝑝, (b) cross-prime prismatic
transition maps, and (c) global Bernstein-centre compatibility. Each part is open.
Remark 42.3.14 (wild-prime correction). At 𝑝 = 2 and 𝑝 = 3, the source for the local comparison carries
ramification and wild inertia data not present in the tame case. A conjectural correction accounts for
this; the precise form depends on the source used for the local comparison.

the datum collapses to a zero-dimensional scheme statement (a restriction of commutative rings). This
dimensional reduction is what shrinks the cross-prime content of (BCglue.core): moving from the
coherent- sheaf level to the pseudocharacter level converts a ten-page coherent-sheaf gluing statement
into a three- to five-page commutative-algebra statement of the type (43.5.2).

R analytic : Form, Difficulty, and the Riemann
Hypothesis

Chapter 41 isolates three inputs for a sufficient argument toward the Riemann hypothesis: weight exis-
tence (W), the Weil explicit formula at Gaussian test functions (H), and the sharp moment asymptotic
Ranalytic , which asserts 𝜇2𝑛 ≍ 𝐶 𝑛 𝑛!2 unconditionally for the symmetrised shifted-zero moment sequence
of 𝜉 . Remark 41.4.9 of Chapter 41 characterises Ranalytic as weaker than RH in the implication direction
and as ‘‘classical-analytic’’. The statement has three independent axes: form, implication direction, and
difficulty. The conclusions are (i) the form is classical-analytic; (ii) this reduction does not derive RH
from Ranalytic alone; (iii) the difficulty is not classical but rather density-of-zeros, a major open problem ad-
jacent to RH in depth. The Bombieri–Lagarias upper bound does not imply Carleman divergence. After
the 1/(2𝑛)-th root and inversion, it yields the convergent Bertrand comparison 1/( 𝑛 (log 𝑛) 2 ). This is
                                                                                          P
why Proposition 41.4.3 records the Bombieri–Lagarias construction as inconclusive for the determinacy
estimate rather than as a divergence proof.

44.1    The Four Assertions
Proposition 44.1.1 (form of R analytic ). Ranalytic is classical-analytic in form: a two-sided moment
asymptotic 𝐶−𝑛 𝑛!2 ≤ 𝜇2𝑛 ≤ 𝐶+𝑛 𝑛!2 on a regularised positive measure associated to the symmetrised
shifted zeros of 𝜉 .
Proposition 44.1.2 (no direct implication to RH). Ranalytic is weaker than RH in the conclusion
it states: an off-line-zero configuration with subleading 2𝑛-th moment contribution is not excluded by
the moment statement alone. Thus this reduction does not prove Ranalytic ⇒ RH. (Chapter 41.4.9.)

Bombieri–Lagarias 1999 (Chapter 23.3.6) bounds the Li coefficient 𝜆𝑛 = 𝜌 [1 − (1 − 1/ 𝜌) 𝑛 ] by 𝜆𝑛 ≤
                                                                              P
𝑛 ( 𝑐0 + log 𝑛)/2. This is a bound on a highly oscillatory unit-modulus phase sum: under RH, |1 − 1/ 𝜌 | = 1
for every non-trivial zero 𝜌, so 𝜆𝑛 grows sub-polynomially via phase cancellation. The moment sum
𝜇2𝑛 = 𝜌 (1/4 + 𝛾 𝜌2 ) 𝑛 is a monotone positive sum whose growth is governed by the density of zeros
        P
high in the critical strip via Riemann–von Mangoldt, with no cancellation. These two quantities are

norm bounds; a direct transfer of the Bombieri–Lagarias bound to 𝜇2𝑛 requires a phase-cancellation-
to-magnitude comparison that is not available. The upper bound on 𝜇2𝑛 in Chapter 41.4.3 comes from

from the Bombieri–Lagarias Li-coefficient bound. Closing the (log 𝑛) 4𝑛 → 1 gap requires density-of-
zeros improvements on the critical line beyond Conrey’s 40%, via the Selberg–Levinson–Conrey–Feng
density theory.

44.4    Position of R analytic in the Equivalence Chain
Chapter 36 (Chapter 36.4.14) establishes the four-way equivalence

                              (VB∗ c) ⇔ (Det) ⇔ (HB+) ⇔ (BD+)

under P2, P3, and H-PAr , where (VB∗ c) is the converse ‘‘zero-placement ⇒ VB∗ ’’, not the main direction
VB∗ ⇒ zero-placement. Determinacy is equivalent to the VB∗ converse. Chapter 36 further records
(Chapter 36.4.17, Chapter 36.4.16) that all four conditions require input beyond RH in this reduction: in
particular, no implication RH ⇒ Det is proved here, and Det ⇒ RH requires H-PAr plus the VB∗ main
direction (Chapter 23.1.3). Under P2, P3, H-PAr , one has Ranalytic ⇒ Det ⇒ (VB∗ c), placing Ranalytic
as an input to the converse direction, not to the main direction and not to RH directly. Chapter 41’s
characterisation of Ranalytic as not RH-equivalent in the implication direction is therefore correct, but
the reason is not that the statement is classical: it is that determinacy requires additional input in the
implication hierarchy, as established by Chapter 36.

Remark 44.6.3 (classical-analytic form, RH-adjacent diﬃculty). Chapter 44.6.2 establishes the key
distinction: the form of Ranalytic is classical-analytic (a moment asymptotic), but its diﬃculty is RH-
adjacent. The gap between BL-Conrey’s polylog-inflated bound and the target 𝐶 𝑛 𝑛!2 bound is precisely
the density-of-zeros hypothesis for 𝜁 , which is a major open problem on the same level as RH. Density-
of-zeros is weaker in conclusion than RH: a density-one statement controls the exceptional set but does
not put every zero on the line. Thus Ranalytic is not an RH proof in this reduction, and it is not known
unconditionally either.

Three Independent Axes: Form, Implication, Diﬃculty
Chapter 44.1.4’s conflation of classical form with classical difficulty is resolved by separating three axes.
Form. The statement of Ranalytic is the moment asymptotic 𝐶−𝑛 𝑛!2 ≤ 𝜇2𝑛 ≤ 𝐶+𝑛 𝑛!2 : an object in classical
analysis, a moment sequence controlled by saddle-point asymptotics.
Implication direction. The present reduction does not prove Ranalytic ⇒ RH: off-line zeros with
subleading 2𝑛-th moment contribution are not excluded by the moment statement alone. The con-
verse RH ⇒ Ranalytic holds partially under regularisation: Riemann–von Mangoldt plus saddle-point
gives 𝜇2𝑛 ≍ (2 𝜋 ) −4𝑛 (2𝑛)! up to logarithmic corrections, which by Stirling is 𝐶 𝑛 𝑛!2 up to the density-
hypothesis refinements required to remove the (log 𝑛) 4𝑛 factor.
Difficulty. The remaining gap (Chapter 44.6.2) is the density-of-zeros hypothesis for 𝜁 , a major open
problem of analytic number theory at the level of the density-1 hypothesis, weaker than RH in its con-
clusion but adjacent to RH in depth.

                          Form                       Implication to RH        Difficulty
              Ranalytic   Classical-analytic         Does not imply RH        RH-adjacent
                          (moment asymptotic)        (weaker than RH in       (density-of-zeros
                                                     one direction)           open problem)

   Chapter 44.1.4 infers from the classical form that the difficulty is classical; this conflates the first and
third axes. The implication axis (Chapter 44.1.2) is correct: Ranalytic is strictly weaker than RH in the
implication direction. The difficulty axis is RH-adjacent.

44.7    Determinacy, VB ∗ , and RH
The two propositions fix the two equivalences in the chain Det ⇔ VB∗ main direction ⇔ RH.
422                     Chapter 44. R analytic : Form, Difficulty, and the Riemann Hypothesis


Step 1: Determinacy ⇔ VB∗ (Which Direction?)
Proposition 44.7.1 (Determinacy is equivalent to the VB ∗ converse). . Chapter 36.4.14 asserts

                             (VB∗ c) ⇔ (Det) ⇔ (HB+) ⇔ (BD+)

under P2, P3, H-PAr , where (VB∗ c) is ‘‘zero-placement ⇒ VB∗ ’’. The main direction VB∗ ⇒ zero-
placement is the content of Chapter 23.1.3, a separate conditional implication not equivalent to determi-
nacy.

Proof. Chapter 36.4.15 records: ‘‘The forward direction VB∗ ⇒ F-RH is the separate content of Chap-
ter 22.3.10, which is a conditional theorem under P2, P3, H-PAr , and a positive Bost–Connes regularised
trace. The four-way equivalence of the converse does not close the forward implication.’’ Determinacy
is equivalent to the converse direction.

Step 2: Determinacy vs RH
Proposition 44.7.2 (Determinacy needs input beyond RH in this reduction). . Chapter 36.4.16
asserts that each of VB∗ -converse, determinacy, and Baéz-Duarte sharp decay carries input beyond RH in
this reduction. The implication Det ⇒ RH is used only with H-PAr (Chapter 36.5.1), and no implication
RH ⇒ Det is proved here.

Proof. Chapter 36.4.17: ‘‘No structural property of the zero distribution of 𝜉 independent of RH is
known to force determinacy. Hence the VB∗ converse requires an additional arithmetic input beyond
RH.’’ Hence this chapter does not derive Det from RH. The reverse implication Det ⇒ RH requires
H-PAr plus the VB∗ main direction (Chapter 23.1.3); the two inputs are kept separate without auxiliary
hypotheses.

The Implication Diagram
Remark 44.7.3 (Position of Ranalytic in the implication hierarchy). Under P2, P3, H-PAr :

                Ranalytic =⇒ (Carleman criterion) =⇒ Det ⇐⇒ (VB∗ converse)

Independently, as a conditional theorem (Chapter 23.1.3):

                                    VB∗ main direction =⇒ RH.

Combined (Chapter 36.5.1):

                H-PAr + Ranalytic + VB∗ main direction =⇒ VB∗ ⇐⇒ RH + Det.

Remark 44.7.4 (Ranalytic controls the converse). In the implication diagram, Ranalytic contributes to the
VB∗ converse direction (RH⇒VB∗ ), by forcing Hamburger determinacy which together with H-PAr
and RH gives VB∗ . Ranalytic does not by itself imply the VB∗ main direction nor RH. The main direction
requires VB∗ proper or some alternative construction to the Li positivity, which is not supplied by
Ranalytic .
44.8. Conclusion                                                                                       423


44.8    Conclusion
Theorem 44.8.1 (four assertions on R analytic ). . The four assertions Chapter 44.1.1–Chapter 44.1.4
have the following mathematical form.
  (1) Form (Chapter 44.1.1): Ranalytic has classical-analytic form, a two-sided moment asymptotic.
 (2) Implication (Chapter 44.1.2): Ranalytic is not an RH proof by itself in this reduction. The converse
      RH ⇒ Ranalytic also requires density-of-zeros refinements beyond RH alone.
 (3) Bombieri–Lagarias scale (Chapter 44.1.3): the Bombieri–Lagarias–Conrey construction gives a
      Carleman sum lower bound 1/( 𝑛 (log 𝑛) 2 ), a Bertrand series that converges, hence the Bombieri–
                                      P
      Lagarias construction is inconclusive, not divergent.
 (4) Diﬃculty (Chapter 44.1.4): ‘‘classical-analytic, not RH-equivalent’’ is correct on the form and im-
      plication axes. Its difficulty is RH-adjacent, because the logarithmic inflation can only be removed
      here by density-of-zeros input.

Proof. (1) is Chapter 44.6: the statement is a moment asymptotic.
   (2) is Chapter 41.4.9 combined with the off-line-zeros robustness argument.
   (3) is Chapter 44.5.2 and Chapter 44.5.3: the Stirling identity (2𝑛)!1/(2𝑛 ) ∼ 2𝑛/𝑒 gives the convergent
Bertrand series 1/( 𝑛 (log 𝑛) 2 ).
                P
   (4) is Chapter 44.6.3 and Chapter 44.6.2: removing the logarithmic gap requires density-of-zeros
improvements which, while weaker than RH in conclusion, constitute a major open problem of analytic
number theory.

Corollary 44.8.2 (R analytic is not an RH proof by itself). . The equivalences in the chain Det ⇔
VB∗ main direction ⇔ RH are:
  (i) Determinacy is equivalent to the VB∗ converse, not the main direction (Chapter 44.7.1).
 (ii) Determinacy needs input beyond RH in this reduction (Chapter 44.7.2).
Hence Ranalytic is not, by itself, an RH proof in the present implication chain.

Proof. Chapter 23.1.3 and Chapter 36.4.14 are unambiguous on both the direction of the equivalence
and the need for determinacy input beyond RH in this reduction.

44.9    The Sharp Reduction of R analytic
Theorem 44.9.1 (Sharp reduction of R analytic ). . The term Ranalytic is the demand for an uncondi-
tional two-sided moment asymptotic 𝜇2𝑛 ≍ 𝐶 𝑛 𝑛!2 . It has the following properties.
   (i) Form: classical-analytic; Ranalytic is a two-sided moment asymptotic.
  (ii) Position in the implication hierarchy: under P2, P3, H-PAr , Ranalytic ⇒ Det ⇔ VB∗ converse; it is
       not an RH proof directly.
 (iii) Implication to RH: the present reduction does not prove Ranalytic ⇒ RH.
 (iv) Diﬃculty: removing the unconditional (log 𝑛) 4𝑛 gap requires density-of-zeros hypotheses for 𝜁 ,
       an open analytic-number-theory problem of RH-adjacent difficulty.
  (v) Unconditional Carleman construction via Bombieri–Lagarias and Conrey: inconclusive; the cor-
       rect Bertrand-series lower bound 1/( 𝑛 (log 𝑛) 2 ) converges (Chapter 44.5.3).
                                            P
424                      Chapter 44. R analytic : Form, Difficulty, and the Riemann Hypothesis


Ranalytic is classical in form, not proved here, insufficient by itself to prove RH in this reduction, and RH-
adjacent in difficulty. The summary of Chapter 41 (‘‘classical-analytic, not RH-equivalent’’) is accurate
on the form and implication axes and inaccurate on the difficulty axis.

Proof. (1) is Chapter 44.6. (2) is Chapter 44.7.3. (3) is Chapter 41.4.9. (4) is Chapter 44.6.2. (5) is
Chapter 44.5.3.

Remark 44.9.2 (precise statement). Ranalytic asks for an unconditional two-sided moment asymptotic
at the 𝑛!2 rate. Its form is classical-analytic. Its implication relative to RH is one-directional in this
reduction. Its difficulty is RH-adjacent: removing the unconditional Bombieri–Lagarias–Conrey gap
requires zero-density-hypothesis-level improvements. Carleman’s criterion via the Bombieri–Lagarias–
Conrey bounds alone is inconclusive; a genuine Carleman divergence requires either density-of-zeros
improvements or the unconditional two-sided asymptotic 𝜇2𝑛 ≍ 𝐶 𝑛 𝑛!2 without logarithmic inflation.
The remaining work is zero-density analytic number theory.
Remark 44.9.3 (domain of the statement). The three terms W + H + Ranalytic of Chapter 41.5.2 remain
independent. The Stirling computation affects only the Carleman-divergence inference. The weight
selection (W) and Weil formula at Gaussian test functions (H) components are unchanged.

44.10    Consequences
   (i) The characterisation of Ranalytic as ‘‘classical-analytic, not RH-equivalent’’ (Chapter 44.8.1) is
       accurate on the form axis and the implication axis. The form is classical-analytic; the implication
       does not by itself prove RH; but the difficulty is RH-adjacent via the density-of-zeros problem.
  (ii) The Bombieri–Lagarias and Conrey estimates give Chapter 44.5.3. The lower bound on the Car-
       leman sum is the Bertrand series 1/( 𝑛 (log 𝑛) 2 ), which converges. The Bombieri–Lagarias con-
                                           P
       struction is inconclusive.
 (iii) The form of the chain Det ⇔ VB∗ main direction ⇔ RH is given by Chapter 44.8.2: determinacy
       is equivalent to the VB∗ converse (Chapter 36.4.14), and determinacy needs input beyond RH in
       this reduction.
 (iv) Chapter 44.9.1 separates three axes: form (classical), implication direction (not an RH proof by
       itself), and difficulty (RH-adjacent via density-of-zeros). Ranalytic is the single analytic input of the
       sufficient path; proving it is a genuine open problem of analytic number theory at the zero-density
       level.
  (v) The three terms W + H + Ranalytic of Chapter 41.5.2 remain the sharp reduction of Chapter 22.
 (vi) Proving Ranalytic requires either (a) a density-of-zeros improvement pushing the Conrey lower
       bound from 40% of zeros on the line to the density-1 hypothesis with sub-logarithmic error, or
       (b) an alternative positivity or measure-regularisation construction producing 𝜇2𝑛 ≍ 𝐶 𝑛 𝑛!2 di-
       rectly. Either construction is a substantive analytic-number-theory theorem. The Vol IV sufficient
       argument for RH rests on three open problems of comparable difficulty (W, H, Ranalytic ).
   The three inputs are genuine open problems of substantive analytic-number-theory difficulty. The
term Ranalytic is specifically a density-of-zeros statement adjacent to RH.

The finite primary towers have an ordinary trace 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) in the half-plane Re 𝑠 > 1. The Gaussian test
function has a Mellin integral Γℝ ( 𝑠 ). Their product gives the completed zeta function, with the two
operations kept distinct. The normalized thermal state on the finite tower is a further functional, with
unit value one. We compute these objects and specify the maps that would transfer their scalar identity
to a native Koszul character.

Koszul-Dual Character
The substitution 𝑠 ↦→ 1 − 𝑠 defines the dual scalar 𝜒 𝑔,𝑃 (1 − 𝑠 ) = Γℝ (1 − 𝑠 ) 𝜁 (1 − 𝑠 ), initially on Re 𝑠 < 0.
Its finite factor is a convergent ordinary trace there. It is a Gibbs partition function only when 1 − 𝑠 is
real and greater than one. Calling it a native Koszul-dual character requires Chapter 45.1.2.

The scalar functional equation
The completed functional equation compares the meromorphic continuations 𝜒 𝑔,𝑃 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜒 𝑔,𝑃 (1 − 𝑠 ).
It does not compare two simultaneous Gibbs states: their displayed absolute-convergence half-planes are
disjoint. Under the native character hypothesis, it transfers to the stated native trace functionals.

product is the identity. Dividing by the partition trace gives both formulas, including 𝜑 𝛽 (1) = 1. All
sums are absolutely convergent for 𝛽 > 1.

   The finite-prime tensor shift algebras have compatible normalized states for every real 𝛽 > 0. Their
genuine arithmetic phase extensions do not assemble through the represented singleton phase quotients:
Chapter 25.9.1 computes the obstruction already at {3} ⊂ {3, 2}. At the same time, no global nuclear
density exists at 𝛽 = 1 in the occupation representation, because 𝑘 ≥1 𝑘 −1 diverges. An adelic phase or
                                                                 P
categorical comparison must therefore be constructed separately from this character computation.

Proposition 45.3.7 (the Gaussian line is not a gamma trace). No fixed linear endomorphism 𝐿
of the one-dimensional Gaussian line has Tr( 𝑒 − 𝑠𝐿 ) = Γℝ ( 𝑠 ) on Re 𝑠 > 0.

Remark 45.3.9 (the archimedean operator requirement). Finite occupation energy is defined on the
algebraic primary tower, and its powers have the usual maximal weighted sequence domains in its Hilbert
completion. A Gaussian test line does not carry a continuous energy spectrum. An archimedean dilation
operator requires an enlarged function space and a specified domain; the Gaussian is not itself a dilation
eigenvector. Consequently a global descendant or Virasoro operator cannot be defined from the mixed
character alone.
Remark 45.3.10 (determinant rank and Virasoro reconciliation with Chapter 22.3.5). On the primary
            prim
subspace VHeis,prim , the finite conformal modes 𝑚 ≥ −1 act on finite-support vectors. The negative
modes 𝑚 ≤ −2 do not form global sums on the restricted vacuum, so a Virasoro action is not produced
by the character theorem. The value proved in Chapter 14.4.1 is the determinant rank residue 𝑟 𝜁 = 2,
obtained from the pole of 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) at 𝑠 = 1. The conjectural primary-Virasoro bracket requires a separate
operator construction whose central charge matches this residue.

45.7    Native character and pairing requirements
The finite thermal representation proves its own trace and state formulas. The Gaussian calculation
proves its Mellin integral. Their product and the functional equation are identities of scalar functions.
The original arithmetic character target additionally requires the native bar and cobar trace sectors and
comparison maps of Chapter 45.1.2.
Corollary 45.7.1 (conditional native character transfer). Under the native character realization
hypothesis, the mixed scalar calculation gives the character part of the arithmetic duality target. It gives
no construction of continuous duals, derived completion, faithful lifting or a multiplicative native
comparison.

Proof. The assumed trace maps identify the computed scalar with the native character by definition of
trace preservation. Their existence and all stronger categorical properties remain separate hypotheses.

Proposition 45.7.2 (conditional functional equation for native characters). Under those trace
maps,
                    char𝐶 ( 𝑠 ) = char 𝐴! ( 𝑠 ) ⇐⇒ Λ 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) = Λ 𝜁 (1 − 𝑠 ) .

Proof. Substitute the two character values identified by the hypothesis. Without those identifications,
the scalar functional equation is not a native Koszul character theorem.

Remark 45.7.3 (trace and algebra comparisons). Even equality of characters does not identify multiplica-
tion, higher operations or the bar–cobar pairing. Continuous duals, derived completion and faithful
lifting must be constructed on their stated coefficient and topological carriers. The character part of a
native duality claim retains its trace-map hypothesis.

The ﬁrst native realization map
The phase obstruction and twisted Hochschild calculation of Chapter 25 give explicit tests for the first
native realization map. The local normalized state does not descend to ordinary Hochschild degree zero,
whereas the density multiplication map gives a chain map with its stated twisted coefficient module.
Whether the native arithmetic trace uses that coefficient module, and how it maps to a Hall or BPS
construction, remains a separate realization problem.
Chapter 46


Prime GNS Normalization and Arithmetic
Pairings

The finite primary character determines a partition trace. A Koszul–Petersson comparison additionally
requires a Hilbert representation of the relevant observables and a map from the native pairing to its state.
We first construct the local GNS representation and its modular conjugation with the normalization of
Chapter 25. We then identify the further comparison data needed for the arithmetic pairing problem.
The operator calculation is valid at every real 𝛽 > 0; 𝛽 = 1 is a regular single-prime temperature.

46.1    The Local Comparison Problem
Three constructions are required by the original arithmetic problem. The first is the state and its GNS
modular involution. The second is a pairing-preserving map from the native local Koszul and Whittaker
data to that representation, including ramified factors. The third is an adelic assembly compatible with
the genuine arithmetic phases and the continuous-spectrum domains. The first construction below does
not supply the other two. Temperedness and a local functional equation alone do not construct a map
from a categorical Hochschild trace to a Hilbert space of arithmetic observables.

46.3    Finite-Place Pairings and Representation Domains
The original finite-place target concerns a native representation factor, its Koszul dual, and a Whittaker
or Kirillov function model. The radial shell comparison of Chapter 26.3.2 constructs those pairing maps
on one explicit function subspace. Extending it to an unramified or ramified principal series, or to a
supercuspidal factor, requires a map on the actual representation domain. The state normalization alone
cannot provide such an extension.
Lemma 46.3.1 (linearity of local integral comparisons). A nonzero local zeta integral 𝑍 ( 𝑠,𝑊 , Φ)
linear in the vector 𝑊 cannot have a formula
                                                     ∫
                              𝑍 ( 𝑠,𝑊 , Φ) = 𝐿 ( 𝑠 )    Φ ( 𝑎)| 2 𝑑𝜇 𝑠 ( 𝑎)
                                                       |b

for every 𝑊 with fixed Φ, unless the right side vanishes. If a pairing is positive Hermitian, multiplying it
by a scalar 𝑐 preserves that property only when 𝑐 is positive real.

Proof. Replacing 𝑊 by 2𝑊 doubles the left side and leaves the right side unchanged. For the pairing
claim, evaluate on any vector of positive squared norm. Its rescaled squared norm is 𝑐 times a positive
real number, so positivity forces 𝑐 > 0. Conversely a positive real multiple preserves positivity.

   Thus a local functional equation must retain its vector and test function dependence. Its complex
root number cannot simply be inserted as a common multiplier of two positive Hermitian norms. Scalar
normalizations act differently on the two kinds of forms: rescaling one input of a bilinear form by 𝑐
multiplies its value by 𝑐 , whereas rescaling a vector map in a Hermitian norm multiplies its squared norm
by | 𝑐 | 2 .

Supercuspidal and non-tempered domains
Corollary 46.3.3 (supercuspidal conditional transfer). . If the native pairing maps are supplied
on a chosen supercuspidal factor, the same local pairing identity holds on that factor.

Proof. The proof of the local transfer uses the displayed maps and pairings, and no principal-series
presentation. It therefore applies to that specified core.

Proposition 46.3.4 (the role of temperedness in a transfer). . Suppose compatible native pairing
maps and their adelic assembly are constructed for every factor in a specified tempered cuspidal domain.
Any theorem placing further automorphic representations in that domain allows the same transfer on
those representations. In particular a Ramanujan-type temperedness hypothesis can enlarge that domain;
it cannot replace the native pairing-map construction.

Proof. Membership in the specified domain permits application of its constructed maps. The conclusion
is their local transfer followed by their assumed adelic assembly. Membership alone contains no map
between the native and GNS carriers.

Remark 46.3.5 (modular spectrum and automorphic bounds). Temperedness does not make the local
modular operator bounded: Δ𝑞 𝐸0𝑗 = 𝑞 −𝑗 𝐸0𝑗 is unbounded for every 0 < 𝑞 < 1. The GNS construc-
tion itself works at every positive real inverse temperature. Bounds on automorphic Satake parameters
control a different representation problem and do not alter this matrix calculation.
Theorem 46.3.6 (conditional tempered cuspidal pairing transfer). . Assume the native pairing
maps of Chapter 26.1.1 on the chosen tempered cuspidal domain, including all its ramified factors and
its convergent or specified regularized adelic assembly. Then

                                         ⟨𝑣, 𝑤 ⟩ Pet = ⟨𝑣, 𝑐𝑤 ⟩ Koszul

on that domain, with 𝑐 the native assembled conjugate-linear map.

Proof. Apply the proved local transfer on every factor. The assumed assembly identifies the two products
of local pairings with their global pairings, so equality persists on elementary tensors and on the specified
completion or regularized domain. No independent identification of genuine arithmetic phases with
the tensor shift algebra is used.

Remark 46.3.7 (native comparison boundary). The explicit local state and the radial shell realization do
not construct the maps for all native tempered cuspidal factors. That extension and the genuine arith-
metic phase assembly remain part of the original Koszul–Petersson problem. The operator normalization
provides a test for such maps, including their variance, norms and energy domains.

pairing carriers. For a Hermitian parameter family the complex variables are ( 𝑠1 , 𝑠2 ); meromorphy in

of parameter-dependent lines a common sesquilinear form ℎ0 , a regularized automorphic pairing ℎ 𝑃 ,

                                                                               
                               ℎ 𝑃 − 𝐵 (·, 𝑐 ·) = 𝑃 ( 𝑠1 , 𝑠2 ) − 𝑅 ( 𝑠1 + 𝑠2 ) ℎ0 .
At a pair where ℎ0 ≠ 0, equality of pairings is equivalent to 𝑃 ( 𝑠1 , 𝑠2 ) = 𝑅 ( 𝑠1 + 𝑠2 ). In particular, if

Proposition 46.5.4 (a deciding scalar test on the critical line). Put 𝑀 ( 𝑠 ) = Λ (2 𝑠 − 1)/Λ (2 𝑠 ).
At every point 𝑠 = 1/2 + 𝑖𝑡 where both factors are finite and nonzero, | 𝑀 ( 𝑠 )| = | 𝑅 (2 𝑠 )| = 1. Conse-
quently the proposed scalar identity

                                           1 + | 𝑀 ( 𝑠 )| 2 = 𝑅 (2 𝑠 )

cannot hold at such a point.

Proof. The real coefficients and completed functional equation give Λ (2 𝑖𝑡 ) = Λ (1 − 2 𝑖𝑡 ) = Λ (1 + 2 𝑖𝑡 ).
Thus 𝑀 ( 𝑠 ) is a quotient of a nonzero complex number’s conjugate by that number and has modulus
one; 𝑅 (2 𝑠 ) = 𝑀 ( 𝑠 ) −1 . The left side of the proposed identity is two and the right side has modulus one.
This refutes the scalar identity, independently of any native pairing realization.

Corollary 46.5.5 (boundary of the continuum comparison). The thermal ratios do not determine
a native Eisenstein pairing, and the displayed scalar test does not decide equality of the actual native
and automorphic pairings. That equality requires the maps, domains, normalizations and regularized
spectral measures used in the conditional comparison theorem.

Proof. The trace ratio is a scalar function on the occupation representation. Its construction includes
no map from an induced representation or its Koszul dual. The conditional theorem uses those maps as
hypotheses; its proof does not produce them. The scalar contradiction therefore excludes the proposed
normalization identity, not an independently constructed pairing with a different derived normalization.


Remark 46.5.6 (wave packets and their domains). Individual Eisenstein parameters generally represent
distributions, whereas their suitably integrated wave packets can represent Hilbert vectors. To compare
pairings on the continuum one must specify the test functions, convergence or truncation, the two
spectral distributions, and their equality on those tests. A meromorphic scalar ratio alone establishes
none of these statements. The conditional discrete-spectrum transfer does not use this continuum
comparison.

46.6    Consequence for P3
Theorem 46.6.1 (positive pairing transfer on a realized core). . Suppose the chosen native cus-
pidal core has an injective square-integrable realization and satisfies the pairing-map and assembly hy-
potheses of Chapter 46.3.6. Then its Petersson form is positive definite and equals ⟨𝑣, 𝑐𝑤 ⟩ Koszul on that
core. This constructs a positive Hermitian form under the specified maps; it asserts no vertex-algebra
structure or full-sector equivalence.
46.7. The Remaining Native Construction                                                                443


Proof. For a nonzero native vector, injectivity gives a nonzero 𝐿 2 function, whose integral squared norm
is positive. Equality of pairings is the conditional transfer already proved. The local GNS positivity does
not remove the hypothesis of a native square-integrable realization.

Remark 46.6.2 (domains of the pairing comparison). The tempered cuspidal transfer requires native
maps on that core. Further automorphic temperedness results do not create those maps. Eisenstein
pairings require separate domains and regularizations. Neither the local KMS theorem nor an abstract
Hilbert-space isomorphism supplies a full-sector extension.

The arithmetic implication
Corollary 46.6.3 (the pairing input remains conditional). The local GNS normalization does
not close the native Koszul–Petersson input in a Hilbert–Pólya or positivity argument. Such an implica-
tion retains the native pairing maps, their actual domain and their assembly as hypotheses.

Proof. The local theorem constructs a represented quotient and its operator Hilbert space. The native
transfer theorem explicitly requires the additional maps before its equations can be composed. Omitting
them removes the first equality connecting native and represented pairings.

46.7    The Remaining Native Construction
The prime-power occupation algebra, its normalized state, Hilbert–Schmidt GNS realization, modular
domains and conjugation are explicit. The radial shell model realizes a bilinear pairing, a Hermitian
pairing and their anti-linear comparison by two separate maps with opposite dual energy degrees. These
give concrete local constructions and decisive tests of normalization.
    The original native problem still requires maps from the arithmetic Hochschild and Koszul factors
to the chosen operator and Whittaker carriers, with their actual Hecke and phase actions. It also requires
a compatible adelic assembly. The represented single-prime phase quotients cannot supply that assembly
by the naive inclusions, and a global occupation density at 𝛽 = 1 is not nuclear. The finite-prime tensor
GNS construction is therefore not an adelic arithmetic equivalence.
    The automorphic and continuous-spectrum questions remain separate. A local functional equation
has to retain its vectors, test functions and complex normalization factors. A Hermitian norm has
positive real normalization. A spectral distribution needs its test space and regularization before it can
be compared with a Hilbert pairing. The GNS calculation neither proves these native comparisons nor
decides positivity for a distinct arithmetic Hilbert–Pólya operator.

F1.a.3: Bushnell–Henniart Block Exhaustion at
Wild Primes

Construction 𝛾 in Chapter 40 reduced F1.a at 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3} to the wild-enhanced Emerton–Gee stack, the
Bushnell–Henniart-compatible wild block functor, and the Bushnell–Henniart version of block exhaustion
at the wild primes. F1.a.3 is a small local residual: non-formal theorem at a ﬁrst substantial estimate,
bounded in diﬃculty by the ﬁnite cardinality of the Bushnell–Kutzko type list and by the precise Ext1 -
structure recorded in Chapter 33. The analysis attacks F1.a.3 directly. It does not close it unconditionally. It
proves it conditional on three disjoint, individually tractable inputs, each shorter than the residual itself: the
BH type-block comparison (Chapter 47.7.1), the Paskunas wild-block Ext1 -compatibility (Chapter 47.7.3),
and the wild-EG compact-generator identiﬁcation (Chapter 47.7.5). Under these three hypotheses the wild
block functor is an equivalence; no essential-surjectivity gap remains beyond them.

  at 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3}, substantial 20–40 pp), the wild block functor datum, and F1.a.3 (a substantial non-formal
  theorem). The smaller size reflects three simplifying features: (i) the BH type list is finite, not varying
  over a deformation space; (ii) the Ext1 -structure is already computed in Chapter 33 and is of explicit
  dimension 1 at 𝑝 = 2 and dimension 2 at 𝑝 = 3; (iii) the block-by-block reduction makes each BH type a
  local computation whose domain is bounded.

Remark 47.7.6 (classical case is known). The classical analogue (no derived enhancement) is a theorem of
Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum (AMS DAG monographs Vol. II, Ch. 8): for a connected formal neighbourhood
of a closed point on a formal algebraic stack, IndCohNilp is compactly generated by the structure sheaf
of the closed point. The derived-enhanced case, needed for the degree-1 wild fibre of Chapter 40.5.2,
is the derived-DAG version of this theorem. Pridham–Toen–Vezzosi DAG VIII §5 give the derived
analogue on smooth derived formal stacks; the wild-enhanced EG stack is not smooth in the classical
sense, but is derived-smooth in degree 1; extending the generation statement to the derived-smooth case
is the conjectural content of (C).

48.1    Selmer-Derived Global Spectral Stack
The arithmetic analogue of Gaitsgory’s fundamental local equivalence (FLE) requires a global spectral
target that imposes local conditions simultaneously. The global Galois group 𝐺ℚ,𝑆 is not a product of its
decomposition groups; the correct global object is the derived fibre product of local Emerton–Gee stacks
over the restriction maps, with local conditions imposed simultaneously. This is the Selmer-derived
construction.

  (v) Commutative Bethe–Hecke algebra. At each finite prime 𝑝, the centre of the spherical Hecke

      This commutative Bethe–Hecke structure is the correct Hecke-algebraic shadow; higher Hopf or
      Yangian structures require separate verification at each prime.
 (vi) Classical Kim arithmetic Chern–Simons. Kim’s arithmetic Chern–Simons theory arXiv:1510.05818
      supplies classical arithmetic CS torsors on the arithmetic curve and action lines in 𝐾2 . The quan-
      tum boundary category 𝜕𝑞 ACS of Conjecture 48.3.6 is a distinct object from V prim ; its construc-
      tion is open.
