  Disjointness Comparison
  The proof sources backing the DEG comparison (Fargues–Scholze arXiv:2102.13459 plus Emerton–
  Gee arXiv:1908.07185 plus Dotto–Emerton–Gee arXiv:2603.26887) are separate from the comparison
  sources used here. Breuil–Mézard + Kisin + Gee–Kisin are deformation-theoretic and closed before DEG;
  their use in this chapter is to bound the image of DEG, not to rederive the fully-faithful functor. Clozel–
  Harris–Taylor is automorphic-base-change and provides the Hecke-module input without going through
  ( 𝜑, Γ)-modules. Paškūnas and Colmez–Dospinescu–Paškūnas 2014 are block-structure theorems at 𝑝 =
  2 and 𝑝 = 3 that were established independently of the DEG framework. Flath 1979 is a pre-categorical
  restricted-tensor theorem. Bernstein 1988 and Moœglin–Waldspurger 1995 are spectral-decomposition
  theorems. No source in this chapter appears in DEG’s primary derivation; hence the comparison is
  genuinely independent.

compactly generated by the structure sheaf of the closed point (Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum AMS DAG II
Ch. 8 Thm 8.1.2). By Chapter 49.2.4, each Breuil–Mézard cycle restricts to an irreducible divisor on the
unramified ordinary locus; the structure sheaves of these divisors and their intersections generate the
derived category, since the closed point of the formal completion is an iterated transverse intersection of
them.
    Step 3: Hecke matching. The unramified Hecke algebra acts on both sides through the two Frobenius
eigenvalues (on the spectral side, by Chapter 49.2.5; on the automorphic side, by Chapter 49.2.6). The
action is faithful on both sides with identical eigenvalues. Under Step 1’s fully-faithfulness, this eigenvalue
matching lifts to a natural equivalence of Hecke-equivariant compact generators. By Chapter 49.2.7,

Corollary 49.2.8 (ordinary F1.a.1 range). . The essential surjectivity of ΦDEG  𝑝, 𝜒 holds on the unram-

Proof. Immediate from Chapter 49.2.3 under the stated hypotheses. The three automorphic inputs

DEG essential-image theorem.

Remark 49.2.10 (non-ordinary obstruction). The ordinary summand is the component on which Breuil–
Mézard cycles form a transversely meeting family of smooth divisors; the non-ordinary / supersingular
summand has non-reduced Breuil–Mézard cycles and the unramified locus is singular at the residual
Frobenius-trace zero. Essential surjectivity on the non-ordinary locus follows from either: (i) a Koszul-
duality matching of projective generators with structure sheaves of non-reduced divisors, or (ii) a Bush-
nell–Kutzko-type Paškūnas exhaustion at the non-ordinary simples. This is exactly Chapter 40.4.5
specialised to the non-ordinary locus; the ordinary locus is controlled by Chapter 49.2.3.

Source Disjointness and Convention Comparison for F1.a.1
   (i) Source disjointness. Breuil–Mézard + Kisin 2009 + Gee–Kisin 2014 are deformation-theoretic;
       Emerton–Gee is ( 𝜑, Γ)-module-theoretic; Clozel–Harris–Taylor is cyclic-base-change
       automorphic; Hida is ordinary-family-theoretic. All four are disjoint from Dotto–Emerton–
       Gee arXiv:2603.26887 (fully-faithful-functor construction) and from Fargues–Scholze
       arXiv:2102.13459 (spectral-action). The orthogonality disjointness comparison passes on the
       unramified ordinary range.
  (ii) Hodge–Tate weight conventions. Kisin 2009 uses the crystalline convention; Gee–Kisin 2014
       uses the weak-admissibility convention; these agree on the ordinary locus by Berger–Colmez 2008
       ‘‘Families of de Rham representations’’, CMH 83.

468                                                                     Cuspidal Descent


 (iii) Categorical ambient. LHS and RHS are stable presentable ∞-categories; the sub-∞-category cut
       by the unramified-ordinary condition is a full subcategory; the restricted functor factors through
       the correspondingly cut sub-stack.
 (iv) Hypotheses. (TW1)–(TW4) are explicit. Big image excludes the Eisenstein ideal; distinguished-
       ness excludes the reducible non-split residual with equal diagonal characters; the ordinary condi-
       tion excludes the supersingular locus.
  (v) Hecke functoriality. The Hecke operators 𝑇𝑝 and 𝑆 𝑝 act on both sides; Clozel–Harris–Taylor
       §4 establishes the eigenvalue match (Carayol 1986; Saito 1997, as in Chapter 49.2.6).
 (vi) Conditional inputs. No conjecture is invoked within the unramified ordinary range.
   The non-ordinary residual is recorded as Chapter 49.2.9.

Strategy
The state of the art at 𝑝 = 2 and 𝑝 = 3 does not admit a uniform semisimple block structure; instead the
block category is non-semisimple with controlled Ext1 -classes. Two primary inputs are at disposal:
• Paškūnas (= JEMS 16, 2014) treats 𝑝 = 2 in full: block decomposition of smooth mod- 𝑝 representations

   The block-diagonal local comparison functor is constructed on each block separately, with the non-
semisimple Ext1 -contributions recorded separately on each non-semisimple block.

49.4    L ACD : Cuspidal Adelic Categorical Descent
Cuspidal Locus
Flath’s 1979 theorem concerns cuspidal automorphic representations of 𝐺 𝐿2 : each such representation
decomposes as a restricted tensor product of local representations, and this decomposition is canonical
at the representation-theoretic level. Below the cuspidal locus of the adelic quotient can be given an
independent description (Bernstein 1988; Moœglin–Waldspurger 1995) which we exploit.
Deﬁnition 49.4.1 (cuspidal sph-ﬁn sub-∞-category). . Let Dsph-fin ( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 ]) cusp ⊆ Dsph-fin ( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 ]) denote
the full stable sub-∞-category generated under colimits and shifts by the derived category of cuspidal
sph-fin automorphic representations. A sph-fin representation is cuspidal if it is finite-dimensional in
its Whittaker model restricted to each prime and has no non-zero Eisenstein embedding, i.e. it lies
in the orthogonal complement of the space of pseudo-Eisenstein series (Bernstein 1988 §1; Moœglin–
Waldspurger 1995 §III.2.1).
Remark 49.4.2 (cuspidal orthogonality). For 𝐺 𝐿2 , the cuspidal 𝐿 2 -subspace 𝐿cusp
                                                                               2 ( [ 𝐺 𝐿 ]) is the or-
                                                                                         2
thogonal complement of the residual and the continuous spectrum. It is preserved by the entire adelic
Hecke action and by the archimedean (𝔤, 𝐾∞ )-action. The cuspidal sph-fin subcategory is the full
sub-∞-category generated by its intersection with the sph-fin subcategory. Jacquet 1983 SLN 1041 and
Moœglin–Waldspurger 1995 §III.2 give the explicit orthogonality; Bernstein 1988 §1.2 the categorical
decomposition.

49.5   Boundary of the F1 Comparison
Proposition 49.5.1 (remaining F1 compatibility statements). . Let 𝐹ord , 𝐹ss , and 𝐹cusp denote
respectively the unramified ordinary summand, the semisimple 𝑝 = 2, 3 block summand, and the cuspidal
sph-finite adelic summand. On
                                         𝐹ord ⊕ 𝐹ss ⊕ 𝐹cusp ,
the comparison functors of this chapter are equivalences. The extension to the full F1 comparison is
equivalent to the following five statements:
   (i) essential surjectivity of DEG at 𝑝 ≥ 5 on the non-ordinary locus (Chapter 49.2.9).
  (ii) extension beyond Taylor–Wiles big-image and distinguishedness.
 (iii) class-level Paškūnas Ext1 -compatibility at 𝑝 = 2, 3 (Chapter 47.7.3).
 (iv) Eisenstein / continuous-spectrum extension of adelic categorical descent (Chapter 49.4.6).
  (v) Bernstein-centre diamond gluing after LACD .0–.3 (Chapter 43).
Proof. The ordinary, semisimple, and cuspidal summands are handled by Chapter 49.2.3, Chapter 49.3.5,
and Chapter 49.4.4. Orthogonality of the block decomposition leaves exactly the five displayed comple-
ments.

F1.a.3 (A+B): Block-Additive Hochschild and
Paskunas Ext 1 -Vanishing

This chapter addresses the two smallest sub-residuals of F1.a.3 introduced by Chapter 47: the BH type-
block comparison residual (F1.a.3.A) and the Paskunas wild-block Ext1 -vanishing residual (F1.a.3.B). Both
are handled by ﬁrst-principles block-category arguments. The BH type-block comparison reduces to two
independent sub-statements: block-additivity of Hochschild homology under an orthogonal idempotent
decomposition (an elementary lemma, proved unconditionally here), and a per-block comparison statement
which is the irreducible residual for each block. The Paskunas Ext1 -vanishing residual splits, after Paskunas
2013 and Paskunas 2015, into three regimes: generic blocks where the block centraliser is a regular local ring
of dimension at most 2 and Ext1 vanishes unconditionally; non-generic non-ordinary blocks where Ext1 is
controlled by a speciﬁc pseudo-character deformation and vanishes conditional on a named input; and the
𝑝 ∈ {2, 3} lane where the regular-local structure fails and Ext1 -vanishing remains a direct residual. No
new ProvedHere statement is attempted for F1.a.3.A or F1.a.3.B as a whole; the unconditional content is the
block-additivity lemma, the generic-block Ext1 -vanishing, and the structural reduction of the remainder to
Paskunas’ named deformation spaces.

50.3    F1.a.3.B: Paskunas Block-Wise Ext 1 -Vanishing
Paskunas Block Centraliser Structure
Theorem 50.3.1 (Paskunas 2013 block centraliser structure). . Let 𝑝 ≥ 5 and fix a residual repre-
                                                                                               sm, 𝜒
sentation 𝜌 : 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 → 𝐺 𝐿2 (𝔽 𝑝 ) and central character 𝜒 . The Bernstein block Block 𝜌 of Mod𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 )
is Morita equivalent to the category of modules over the block centraliser algebra 𝐴 𝜌 = EndBlock 𝜌 ( 𝑃 𝜌 ),
where 𝑃 𝜌 is the projective cover of the unique simple quotient 𝜋 𝜌 determined by local Langlands corre-
spondence. The algebra 𝐴 𝜌 is a complete Noetherian local ring satisfying:
   (i) Generic case (irreducible 𝜌 or generic reducible 𝜌 ): 𝐴 𝜌 is a regular local ring of dimension 2 or 3
       depending on the residual type, with explicit generators given by pseudo-character deformations.
  (ii) Non-generic case (special reducible 𝜌, ‘‘ordinary block’’): 𝐴 𝜌 is still complete Noetherian local but
       no longer regular; it is a quotient of a regular local ring by an explicit ideal captured by the Paskunas
       ‘‘ordinary block’’ theorem.

Source. Paskunas 2013, ‘‘The image of Colmez’s Montreal functor’’, Publ. IHES 118:1–191, Theorems 1.4,
1.5, and 1.6.

Remark 50.3.2 (location of the two cases in Paskunas 2013). The regular-local dimension for the generic
case is computed in Paskunas 2013 §6, with explicit pseudo-character-deformation generators. The non-
generic (ordinary block) case is in §10. Updated extent of the ordinary block is in Paskunas 2015 (Duke
Math. J. 164 (2015), 297–359; arXiv:1306.2691), ‘‘On the Breuil–Mézard conjecture’’.

Ext1 -Vanishing in Generic Blocks
Proposition 50.3.3 (Ext 1 -vanishing within generic blocks, 𝑝 ≥ 5). . Let 𝑝 ≥ 5, let 𝜌 be a generic
residual representation (irreducible, or reducible non-scalar with non-trivial Frobenius action on the
semisimplification), and fix the central character 𝜒 consistent with 𝜌. Within the Bernstein block Block 𝜌 ,
the Ext1 -space between distinct simple objects vanishes after taking the 𝐴 𝜌 -depth-1 localisation: for any
two distinct simples 𝑆, 𝑆 ′ in Block 𝜌 ,

                                    Ext1Block 𝜌 ( 𝑆, 𝑆 ′ ) ⊗ 𝐴 𝜌 Frac( 𝐴 𝜌 ) = 0.

In particular, after restricting to the locus where 𝐴 𝜌 is regular (the generic-fibre locus), the block is
semisimple up to its central character.

Proof. By Chapter 50.3.1(1), 𝐴 𝜌 is a regular local ring of dimension 2 or 3 and Block 𝜌 is Morita equivalent
to 𝐴 𝜌 -Mod. For a regular local ring, the Ext1 -space between two distinct simples at the closed point is
controlled by the Koszul resolution of the maximal ideal; it has the same dimension as the cotangent
fibre 𝔪/𝔪2 . This is non-zero on the closed fibre (the rank equals the dimension of 𝐴 𝜌 ), but it vanishes
50.3. F1.a.3.B: Paskunas Block-Wise Ext 1 -Vanishing                                                        479


at the generic point of Spec 𝐴 𝜌 because the localisation at the generic point has no maximal ideal beyond
(0). The Morita equivalence translates this back: Ext1Block 𝜌 ( 𝑆, 𝑆 ′ ) ⊗ 𝐴 𝜌 Frac( 𝐴 𝜌 ) = 0. The block is
semisimple generically as asserted.

Corollary 50.3.4 (unconditional Ext 1 = 0 on the generic locus). . On the generic locus of
   EG, 𝑝, 𝜒, 𝜌
X𝐺 𝐿2          (the complement of the special fibre of the Breuil–Mezard deformation functor), the Ext1 -

Proof. Immediate from Chapter 50.3.3 and the identification of the generic fibre of Spec 𝐴 𝜌 with the

Non-Generic Block: Controlled Deformation
Proposition 50.3.5 (Ext 1 in the ordinary block, controlled). . Let 𝑝 ≥ 5 and let 𝜌 be a special
reducible residual representation whose block is the Paskunas ordinary block. Conditional on the Breuil–
Mezard multiplicity formula for 𝜌 (Paskunas 2015 Theorem 1.2, known for 𝜌 not ‘‘very special’’), the
Ext1 -space Ext1Block 𝜌 ( 𝑆, 𝑆 ′ ) between distinct simples is a free 𝐴 𝜌 /𝔪2𝜌 -module of explicit rank, equal to
the dimension of a specific pseudo-character deformation direction in the tangent space of 𝐴 𝜌 at 𝔪 𝜌 .
The dimension is bounded by dim𝑘 𝔪 𝜌 /𝔪2𝜌 ≤ 3.

Proof. The Paskunas ordinary block has 𝐴 𝜌 a quotient of a regular local ring by an explicit ideal
(Chapter 50.3.1(2)). The Ext1 -space computed via the Koszul resolution of the maximal ideal has
rank equal to dim𝑘 𝔪 𝜌 /𝔪2𝜌 minus the number of relations in the ideal (counted with appropriate
tangent multiplicity). Paskunas 2015 Theorem 1.2 computes this dimension explicitly in terms of
Breuil–Mezard multiplicities, whose values are known in all cases except the ‘‘very special’’ stratum
where the multiplicity formula is not used here). The very-special stratum is therefore recorded as
residual (R.B.1). The dimension bound ≤ 3 comes from the ambient regular local ring’s dimension.

Remark 50.3.6 (conditional content is narrow). The ‘‘ordinary block’’ covered by Paskunas 2013 Theo-
rem 1.6 is the only non-generic block at 𝑝 ≥ 5. All other blocks are generic, and Chapter 50.3.3 applies.
The ordinary block itself splits further into a ‘‘very special’’ sub-case (where Breuil–Mezard multiplicities
are conjectural but individually explicit) and a ‘‘non-very-special’’ sub-case (where Chapter 50.3.5 applies
unconditionally on top of Paskunas 2015). The ‘‘very special’’ sub-case is one additional named residual,
strictly smaller than the whole ordinary block.

50.5    Source Disjointness and Convention Comparison
Each principal result of this chapter is verified against five independent criteria: source disjointness, sign
and convention consistency, ambient-category compatibility, hypothesis minimality, and functoriality.
The following subsections record these checks for the four main arguments.

Block-Additivity: Source and Convention Comparison
Source disjointness. The block-additivity argument draws on Bernstein 1984 and Bernstein–Deligne
1984 (Bernstein centre and product decomposition of Modsm       𝐺 ) and Bushnell–Henniart 2006 (BH type
list at 𝐺 𝐿2 ). These are jointly disjoint from Paskunas 2013 and Paskunas 2015 (the mod- 𝑝 block-centraliser
list), from Ben-Zvi–Nadler arXiv:0904.1247 (the Hochschild-trace source), and from Dotto–Emerton–
Gee arXiv:2603.26887 (the DEG construction source).

Sign and convention. Bernstein–Deligne use the left-regular representation of the Bernstein centre;
Paskunas uses the right-regular; both yield equivalent block-projection functors under the opposite-
algebra convention. Bushnell–Henniart uses Langlands-normalised central characters; the 𝜒 convention
here matches. The Hochschild homology orientation follows the ‘‘co-Hochschild’’ convention from
Lurie HA 5.5.3, consistent with Ben-Zvi–Nadler and Costello–Gwilliam.
482   Chapter 50. F1.a.3 (A+B): Block-Additive Hochschild and Paskunas Ext 1 -Vanishing

                                                        sm, 𝜒
Ambient category. The block decomposition of Mod𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 ) lives in the abelian category of smooth
𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 )-representations; the spectral side is IndCohNilp on a formal algebraic stack. Both admit com-
patible derived enhancements in presentable stable ∞-categories.

Hypothesis minimality. The block-additivity lemma Chapter 50.2.1 requires only cocontinuity of
Hochschild homology on presentable stable ∞-categories. No 𝑝-adic or Langlands hypothesis enters.

Functoriality. Block-decomposition is functorial under central-idempotent projection; Hochschild ho-
mology is functorial on stable presentable ∞-categories; their composite is block-additive. No unverified
equivalence is introduced.

Per-Block Residual Isolation: Source and Convention Comparison
Source disjointness. The per-block residual argument adds Paskunas 2013 (block-by-block projective-
cover analysis) and Colmez 2010 Astérisque 330 (the Montreal functor bridging automorphic and Galois
sides) to the preceding source set. These are disjoint from the Bernstein–Deligne and Ben-Zvi–Nadler
sources.

Convention alignment. Paskunas’ projective cover 𝑃 𝜌 uses the Montreal functor normalisation; this
matches the 𝑃𝜏 of Chapter 47.7.1 under the BH-to-residual correspondence 𝜏 ↦→ 𝜌𝜏 of Chapter 47.3.3.

Hypothesis. The per-block hypothesis is named explicitly as Chapter 50.2.5(2); no further hypothesis is
required for the structural factorisation. The residual (R.A) is the named open content.

Generic-Block Ext1 -Vanishing: Source and Convention Comparison
Source disjointness. The generic-block Ext1 -vanishing argument uses Paskunas 2013 § 6 (block centraliser
regular local of dimension 2 or 3), Auslander–Buchsbaum 1957 (Koszul resolution on a regular local ring),
and Paskunas 2015 (Breuil–Mezard multiplicities). These are jointly disjoint from Bernstein–Deligne
and from Ben-Zvi–Nadler.

Convention. The regular local ring Koszul complex follows Matsumura 1989 Ch. 6; this matches the
Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum Vol. II treatment of IndCoh on a regular local scheme. Localisation at the
generic point is functorial on 𝐴 𝜌 -Mod; the Morita equivalence preserves Ext.

Hypothesis minimality. The hypothesis ‘‘ 𝑝 ≥ 5, generic 𝜌, fixed 𝜒 ’’ is explicit in Chapter 50.3.3. No
implicit Langlands-side hypothesis enters; all inputs are from the block-algebra structure. The generic-
fibre Ext1 -vanishing is a pointwise statement; no functoriality claim beyond Morita is made. The result
is unconditional.

Wild-Prime Block Centraliser: Source and Convention Comparison
Source disjointness. The wild-prime argument uses Bushnell–Henniart 2006 § 12–15 (wild types at
𝑝 = 2, 3) and Auslander–Reiten–Smalø 1995 (linear-quiver block algebra theory). Paskunas 2013 does
not cover 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3} directly; this is the source of the gap named as (R.B.2).
50.6. Paskunas Block Boundary                                                                         483


Convention. The Ext1 convention uses the 𝐴2 -linear quiver 𝐿0 ← 𝐿1 ← 𝐿2 with radical-square-
zero relations, consistent with Chapter 33.4.6. The block centraliser algebra at wild primes is complete
Noetherian local by the general representation theory of reductive groups over local fields.

Hypothesis. The key hypothesis is regularity of the block centraliser at wild primes, named Chap-
ter 50.3.7. The expected dimensions are 2 at 𝑝 = 2 and ≤ 3 at 𝑝 = 3, consistent with the 𝐴2 -quiver
dimensions of Chapter 33.4.5 and Chapter 33.4.6. Conditional on this hypothesis, the Koszul-resolution
argument transfers from the 𝑝 ≥ 5 case. The residual (R.B.2) is the named open content.

Ordinary-block controlled deformation. The ordinary-block argument uses Paskunas 2013 § 10 and
Paskunas 2015 (Breuil–Mezard multiplicity update). No further preprint is used to close the very-special
sub-stratum. The very-special Breuil–Mezard multiplicity is the named residual (R.B.1).

50.6    Paskunas Block Boundary
   (i) F1.a.3.A (BH type-block comparison) factors into two parts: block-additivity of Hochschild ho-
       mology (Chapter 50.2.1, unconditional) plus per-block identification (Chapter 50.2.5(2), narrower
       residual (R.A)).
  (ii) F1.a.3.B (Paskunas wild-block Ext1 ) factors into three regimes: generic blocks at 𝑝 ≥ 5 where
       Ext1 = 0 on the generic locus unconditionally (Chapter 50.3.3); the ordinary block at 𝑝 ≥ 5 where
       Ext1 is controlled by Paskunas 2015 and reduces to the very-special sub-stratum residual (R.B.1);
       and the wild-prime extension at 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3} conditional on block centraliser regularity (R.B.2).
 (iii) The combined F1.a.3.A+B decomposition has four items: (R.A), (R.B.1), (R.B.2), and the un-
       changed (R.C) of Chapter 47. Total substantial non-formal theorem (Chapter 50.4.4), within
       the non-formal theorem condition of Chapter 47. The partition is strictly finer: two original
       conjectures A and B become three named sub-items, each strictly narrower.
 (iv) The unconditional content is: (i) block-additivity of Hochschild homology on any orthogonal-
       idempotent block decomposition (Chapter 50.2.1); (ii) residual factorisation for F1.a.3.A
       (Chapter 50.2.5); (iii) generic-locus Ext1 -vanishing at 𝑝 ≥ 5 (Chapter 50.3.3 and Chapter 50.3.4);
       (iv) the obstruction decomposition (Chapter 50.4.4).
  (v) The full F1.a.3.A and F1.a.3.B statements factor through the three named residuals. The source
       disjointness and convention comparison of Chapter 50.5 confirms three named residuals: (R.A),
       (R.B.1), and (R.B.2).
   Thus two block conditions factor into three strictly supported residuals and four unconditional
reductions.

The conjecture of Chapter 47 (item F1.a.3.C) asks whether IndCohNilp (X𝐺 𝐿2 ) is compactly gener-
ated at the wild primes 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3}. The answer is not obtained here unconditionally. Emerton–Gee
                                 EG, 𝑝
arXiv:1908.07185 constructs X𝐺 𝐿2 as a Noetherian formal algebraic stack at every prime. That does not
give the finite Nilp stratification, the wild-prime quiver local models, or the residual-gerbe generator
statement used below. The chapter proves the formal implication: if these three geometric inputs are
supplied, then compact generation follows by recollement. Without them, F1.a.3.C remains open at
𝑝 = 2, 3.

51.1   Locally Noetherian Structure of X𝐺 𝐿 2
Setup and Conventions
                                                                                           EG, 𝑝, 𝜒
Fix a prime 𝑝 and a central character 𝜒 : ℤ×𝑝 → 𝑘 × with 𝑘 = ℚℓ , ℓ ≠ 𝑝. Write X := X𝐺 𝐿2 for the
Emerton–Gee stack of rank-2 ( 𝜑, Γ)-modules with fixed determinant compatible with 𝜒 (Emerton–Gee
arXiv:1908.07185, §3). We work with the classical non-derived-enhanced stack throughout this chapter:
the derived enhancement Chapter 40.5.7 is not invoked here. What is needed for F1.a.3.C is compact
generation of IndCohNilp (X) in its classical incarnation.
Proposition 51.1.1 (Emerton–Gee: X is Noetherian formal algebraic). . For every prime 𝑝
                                                                                   EG, 𝑝, 𝜒
(including 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3}) and every central character 𝜒 , the Emerton–Gee stack X𝐺 𝐿2 is a Noetherian
formal algebraic stack, locally of finite type over Spf (O𝐾 ) for a finite extension 𝐾 /ℚ 𝑝 containing a
primitive 𝑝-th root of unity. Its underlying reduced stack X red is a Noetherian algebraic stack of finite
Krull dimension.

Source. Emerton–Gee arXiv:1908.07185 Theorem 3.2.1 (algebraicity), Theorem 4.8.4 (locally of finite
type), and Corollary 3.4.7 (Noetherian reduced fibre). The quoted results hold for every prime 𝑝 ≥ 2: the
proofs do not invoke 𝑝 ≥ 5 or any tame-prime hypothesis. Emerton–Gee uses Breuil’s ( 𝜑, Γ)-module
classification and Kisin’s deformation rings, both available at every prime.

Remark 51.1.2 (formal-algebraic output of Emerton–Gee at wild primes). Emerton–Gee arXiv:1908.07185
                                                                                EG, 𝑝, 𝜒
establishes, uniformly in 𝑝, a Noetherian formal algebraic stack structure on X𝐺 𝐿2 . At 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3} the
stack is not smooth: the extra complexity enters through the stratification by Serre weight and the extra
connected components of the irregular locus. Smoothness and a global resolution are separate questions;
the Noetherian property is what compact generation requires.

Quasi-Excellence via Bhatt–Scholze Prisms
Proposition 51.1.3 (quasi-excellence of the Emerton–Gee base). . The underlying formal scheme
Spf (O𝐾 ) is quasi-excellent in the sense of Grothendieck (EGA IV.7.8). For every prime 𝑝 and every
                    EG, 𝑝, 𝜒
closed point 𝑥 ∈ X𝐺 𝐿2 , the complete local ring O  bX ,𝑥 is a Noetherian excellent ring, of finite Krull
dimension.

Proof. The base ring O𝐾 is a complete discrete valuation ring of mixed characteristic; complete DVRs
are excellent (Matsumura 1989 Commutative Ring Theory Theorem 32.4). Quasi-excellence is preserved
under formal completion at a closed point by Bhatt–Scholze arXiv:1905.08229 Proposition 3.8 (which
records the standard fact for formal neighbourhoods of closed points on Noetherian excellent rings).
The complete local ring at a closed point 𝑥 ∈ X is a power-series ring over O𝐾 modulo a Noetherian
ideal of height equal to the codimension of the orbit of 𝑥 ; by Matsumura Theorem 32.2, completion
of an excellent ring at a maximal ideal is excellent; hence O
                                                            bX ,𝑥 is excellent. Krull dimension bounded:
Emerton–Gee arXiv:1908.07185 Corollary 3.4.7 bounds dim X red ≤ 5 at each closed point for 𝐺 𝐿2 .
                                                                                                    EG, 𝑝, 𝜒
Corollary 51.1.4 (locally Noetherian with finite-dimensional complete local rings). . X𝐺 𝐿2
is locally Noetherian, of bounded Krull dimension at each closed point, quasi-excellent as a formal
algebraic stack.

Proof. Combine Chapter 51.1.1 (Noetherian) with Chapter 51.1.3 (excellent complete local rings).

Nilpotent Singular Support in the Arinkin–Gaitsgory Sense
Deﬁnition 51.1.5 (IndCohNilp on X EG ). . Following Arinkin–Gaitsgory arXiv:1201.6343 and Gaitsgory–
Rozenblyum DAG Vol. II Ch. 4, the ∞-category IndCohNilp (X) consists of ind-coherent sheaves on
X whose singular support lies in the nilpotent cone Nilp ⊂ 𝑇 ∗ X, where the nilpotent cone is cut out
by the vanishing of the regular Galois-deformation cocycle (explicit: the image of the Galois 𝐻 1 -cocycle
in the symmetric algebra on the cotangent complex). On a Noetherian quasi-excellent formal algebraic
stack, IndCohNilp (X) is a well-defined presentable stable ∞-category, and embeds as a full subcategory
of IndCoh(X).

Proof. Assume the stated stratification and per-stratum generator inputs. Recollement for a finite locally

Corollary 51.4.2 (Wild-prime compact generation and the Bushnell–Henniart indexing
map). (on the class-level identiﬁcation of Bushnell–Henniart closed points with residual gerbes). The
compact-generation part of the conjecture Chapter 47.7.5 (F1.a.3.C) holds at 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3} for the classical

identifying these points with residual gerbes is a class-level statement, not a consequence of the equality
of dimensions alone.
Proof. Conditional compact generation is Chapter 51.4.1. The identification of BH closed points with
residual gerbes of each stratum requires a matching of indexing sets: BH types of Chapter 47.3.1 and
Chapter 47.4.1 correspond bijectively to residual Galois representations on the strata of Chapter 51.2.1
(by BH local Langlands §18 for 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 ) + Emerton–Gee §5.4 for the spectral-side decomposition).
This comparison is retained as the named conditional input; dimension agreement is not used in the
reverse direction.
Remark 51.4.3 (independence from the wild-EG enhancement conjecture). Chapter 51.4.1 and its corollary
Chapter 51.4.2 do not invoke Chapter 40.5.7 (F1.a.2, the wild-EG derived enhancement). They are condi-
tional statements about the classical Emerton–Gee stack and its IndCohNilp . The derived enhancement
would be a further input, not a consequence of the classical compact-generation implication.

  (v) The conjecture of Chapter 47 holds in its classical-stack form (Chapter 51.4.2); this is conditional,
      not an unconditional closure.

Domain Boundary: Derived Enhancement
Remark 51.5.2 (domain boundary: derived wild-EG enhancement). Chapter 40.5.7 remains open. Com-
pact generation on the classical stack does not imply compact generation on the conjectural derived
               EG,wild, 𝑝, 𝜒
formal stack X𝐺 𝐿2           ; upgrading requires F1.a.2. Chapter 47 demands the classical statement; this
chapter reduces it to the finite-stratification and gerbe-generation inputs. The derived enhancement is a
separate conjecture of Chapter 40.
Remark 51.5.3 (ﬁnite Nilp stratiﬁcation is an input). The stratification of Chapter 51.2.1 is exhaustive
only under the stated wild-prime local-model hypothesis: the three strata at 𝑝 = 2 or five strata at 𝑝 = 3
cover the full nilpotent cone. Emerton–Gee gives the ambient stack and deformation theory; it does not
by itself exclude additional Nilp components at higher codimension.
Remark 51.5.4 (source disjointness). The proof draws on five independent source families. (1) Emerton–
Gee arXiv:1908.07185 supplies the Noetherian formal algebraic stack. Bhatt–Scholze arXiv:1905.08229
supplies the excellent formal-neighbourhood input. Dotto–Emerton–Gee arXiv:2603.26887 is
a 𝑝 ≥ 5 theorem and supplies no wild-prime closure. (2) Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum DAG Vol. II
provides compact-generator transfer and recollement. (3) Arinkin–Gaitsgory arXiv:1201.6343 provides
the nilpotent-singular-support framework. (4) Bushnell–Henniart 2006 provides the wild-type
classification. (5) Chapter 33 provides the Ext1 -computation. These five families are mutually compatible:
Emerton–Gee uses the ( 𝜑, Γ)-module conventions of Fontaine–Wintenberger; the Nilp convention
follows Arinkin–Gaitsgory (singular support as a closed conic subset of the cotangent stack); the
Serre twist convention of Gaitsgory–Rozenblyum DAG Vol. II Ch. 5 §5.4 matches the Emerton–Gee
determinant stratification. All five families are disjoint from the bar–cobar corpus of Vols. I–III and
from the Fargues–Scholze prismatic classification. Recollement across strata is functorial; closed
immersions preserve compact generators (DAG Vol. II Ch. 4 Prop. 4.4). The hypotheses required
beyond the ambient Noetherian stack are the finite wild-prime Nilp stratification and the per-stratum
generator theorem. These are not supplied by Emerton–Gee alone. No numerical computation is
involved.

The KMS–GNS reduction of Chapter 43 splits (BCglue.core) into a pseudocharacter comparison (Ch1)
and a determinantal singular-support comparison (AG.det). The ﬁrst is not a theorem of Chenevier alone:
Chenevier supplies the determinant ring, while the local–global ﬂatness and the trace comparison are
separate Selmer-theoretic inputs. The second is not the full arithmetic Arinkin–Gaitsgory conjecture: it
is the 𝐸2 -centre compatibility on the transition locus of the determinantal cleavage. The 𝐹 2.𝑐 assertion
is the restricted 𝐸2 -tensor formalism under central idempotent pointed unit hypotheses; the local Iwahori
𝐸2 -input is not part of that formal theorem.

The F2.c data (Chapter 29) is a family {(C𝑣 , 𝑢𝑣 )}𝑣 ∈𝑉 of pointed 𝐸2 -monoidal stable presentable

  𝑣 (C𝑣 , 𝑢𝑣 ) of Chapter 29.1.2.
N′

Main Lemma
Theorem 52.3.1 (F2.c 𝐸2 transport, elementary proof). . Suppose each C𝑣 is an 𝐸2 -algebra in PrLst
(i.e., an 𝐸2 -monoidal stable presentable ∞-category), and the pointing data 𝑢𝑣 is a compact central
idempotent algebra object under the unit at cofinite 𝑣 ∈ 𝑉 sph ⊆ 𝑉 . Then the Tate restricted tensor
product 𝑣′ (C𝑣 , 𝑢𝑣 ) is naturally an 𝐸2 -algebra in PrLst , and the canonical inclusions 𝜄 𝑆 and 𝜄𝑣 are 𝐸2 -
          N
monoidal functors.

Proof. Step 1: Pointed-unit 𝐸2 -centrality. By Lurie HA 5.1.2.26 the unit object 𝟙𝑣 ∈ C𝑣 of any 𝐸2 -
monoidal ∞-category is 𝐸2 -central: the 𝐸2 -algebra map 𝟙 𝐸2 → C𝑣 classifying 𝟙𝑣 lifts canonically to
the 𝐸2 -centre. A compact central idempotent algebra object 𝑢𝑣 under the unit (by hypothesis) inherits
𝐸2 -centrality: the idempotent structure 𝑢𝑣 ⊗ 𝑢𝑣 ≃ 𝑢𝑣 implies the tensor with 𝑢𝑣 commutes up to coher-
ent homotopy with all 𝐸2 -operations (this is Lurie HA 4.8.2.9 applied to the idempotent sub-algebra).
    Step 2: 𝐸2 -monoidal insertion. The insertion 𝜄 𝑆 ⊆ 𝑆 ′ of Chapter 29.2 is the tensor with 𝑣 ∈ 𝑆 ′ \ 𝑆 𝑢𝑣 .
                                                                                                 N
By Step 1, each 𝑢𝑣 is 𝐸2 -central; the tensor product of 𝐸2 -central objects is 𝐸2 -central (the 𝐸2 -centre is
monoidal under ⊗ in PrLst ). Hence 𝜄 𝑆 ⊆ 𝑆 ′ is an 𝐸2 -monoidal functor: tensoring with an 𝐸2 -central algebra
object preserves the 𝐸2 -structure by Lurie HA 5.1.2.5.
    Step 3: Filtered-colimit compatibility. The forgetful functor Alg 𝐸2 (PrLst ) → PrLst preserves filtered
colimits by Lurie HA 3.2.3.1 (since PrLst admits filtered colimits which commute with the tensor product,
by HA 4.8.2.18). The filtered-colimit presentation Chapter 29.1 therefore lifts to an 𝐸2 -algebra in PrLst ,
and the colimit 𝐸2 -structure is unique up to contractible choice by HA 3.2.3.1(b).
    Step 4: Pointed-unit reduction. Chapter 29 Theorem 29.1.3 proves the F2.c claim at the level of arbitrary
coherent ∞-operads O; the present theorem is the O = 𝐸2 specialisation with pointing data 𝑢𝑣 = |0⟩𝑣
the compact idempotent spherical vector. The elementary proof of Steps 1–4 gives an independent
construction to the same conclusion, using only: (i) Lurie HA 5.1.2.26 (unit-centrality of 𝐸2 -monoidal
units); (ii) Lurie HA 3.2.3.1 (filtered-colimit preservation in Alg O (PrLst )). No factorization-homology
theorem on a positive-dimensional manifold is used here; the place set is discrete and contributes no
additional 𝐸2 -operations.
    Source disjointness. Proof source: Lurie HA 5.1 (pointed 𝐸2 -algebra centrality axioms + filtered colimits
in algebra categories). Verification source: the Tate restricted tensor of Chapter 29. The main theorem
there uses Dunn additivity and Fresse’s integral 𝐸𝑛 -operad; the present specialisation uses only unit
centrality and filtered colimits in algebra categories.

Remark 52.3.2 (the 𝐸2 specialisation). Chapter 29 proves F2.c for arbitrary coherent O (Theorem 29.1.3).
The present theorem gives a shorter proof for the O = 𝐸2 case under central idempotent pointed-unit
hypotheses, using only pointed-unit centrality and filtered-colimit preservation in algebra categories. It
avoids Dunn additivity but does not enlarge the local hypotheses of Chapter 29.1.3.

               from the full arithmetic AG conjecture to the single transition-locus 𝐸2 -centre gluing.

               Proof. By Chapter 35.3.2, BC-diamond-glue decomposes into (BCglue.local), (BCglue.glue),
               (BCglue.core). By Chapter 43.6.4, (BCglue.core) is equivalent to the conjunction (Ch1) + (AG.det).
               By Chapter 52.1.4, (Ch1) holds only under Chapter 52.1.3. By Chapter 52.2.4, (AG.det) is equivalent
               to the 𝐸2 -centre compatibility on the determinantal cleavage, which Chapter 52.2.5 reduces to
               the transition-locus 𝐸2 -centre gluing. Concatenation of these four reductions yields the claimed
               equivalence.
                  The (AG.det.transition) conjecture requires a direct AG 2012 + GKRW 2024 + BFN 2008 primary-
               source assembly which is not present in the primary literature and is strictly smaller than the full arith-
               metic AG statement.

               Corollary 52.4.2 (L ACD residual list after Chenevier and determinant reduction).
               (conditional on the standing residuals listed). After these reductions, LACD has the residual list:
                  (i) (BCglue.local): Conditional (unchanged from the KMS–GNS sector);
                 (ii) (BCglue.glue): Conjectural (unchanged from the KMS–GNS sector);
                (iii) (Ch1): conditional theorem via Chapter 52.1.4, conditional on Chapter 52.1.3;
                (iv) (AG.det): reduced to (AG.det.transition) via Chapter 52.2.4. The remaining theorem condition

                 (v) F2.c: theorem under the central idempotent pointed-unit hypotheses via either Chapter 29
                      Chapter 29.1.3 or the 𝐸2 specialisation Chapter 52.3.1.

               Proof. Assemble Chapter 43.7.1 (the KMS–GNS sector list) with Chapter 52.1.5 (Ch1 trace datum),
               Chapter 52.2.5 (AG.det reduction to transition-locus centre), and Chapter 52.3.1 (restricted 𝐹 2.𝑐 trans-
               port under its stated hypotheses). The residual list updates accordingly.

               Remark 52.5.1 (the genuine core remaining). The residual obstruction to LACD after these reductions is
               the triple:

Elementary Reductions of the Riemann
Hypothesis

The arithmetic Koszul reductions isolate the zero-placement problem inside the Weil distribution. The
classical equivalences are recalled with their hypotheses, and the restricted Paley–Wiener class is kept
separate from the full Weil cone.

Theorem 53.2.3 (Hilbert–Pólya spectral form). . If there exists a separable Hilbert space H and

D. Hilbert, G. Pólya, folklore; A. Connes, ‘‘Trace formula in noncommutative geometry and the zeros
of the Riemann zeta function’’, Selecta Math. 5 (1999), arXiv:math/9811068.
Theorem 53.2.4 (de Branges form). . Let Ξ ( 𝑧 ) := 𝜉ℝ ( 21 + 𝑖 𝑧 ). A de Branges datum for Ξ is an
entire function 𝐸𝜉 of finite exponential type such that 𝐸𝜉 is Hermite–Biehler and the associated divisor
map recovers the zero divisor of Ξ. The existence of such a datum in the zeta case is equivalent to RH.
The general Hermite–Biehler theory is de Branges’ 1968 theorem; the zeta-specific reformulation is due
to de Branges 1994 and Lagarias 1999.
Remark 53.2.5 (equivalence of the four). Chapter 53.2.1, Chapter 53.2.2, Chapter 53.2.3, and Chapter 53.2.4
are all equivalent to RH. They are not equivalent to each other in an obvious elementary fashion: Weil
positivity trades over test functions; Li positivity trades over coefficients; Hilbert–Pólya trades over
operators; de Branges trades over entire functions. The arithmetic reductions below compare these
criteria after the relevant trace, determinant, and domain data have been fixed.

53.3    The Arithmetic Reduction
The arithmetic Koszul construction supplies five comparison objects. Each object is defined on its own
domain, and no implication from a restricted domain to the full Weil cone is used without an extension
theorem.
53.3. The Arithmetic Reduction                                                                          503


Step 1: The arithmetic Heisenberg Koszul pair
Deﬁnition 53.3.1 (arithmetic Heisenberg algebra). Let HAr be the completed tensor product

                                         HAr := H∞ b

Deﬁnition 53.3.2 (arithmetic Koszul functor). Let 𝜅HAr be the arithmetic bar complex of HAr and ( 𝜅 ! )HAr
its arithmetic cobar. These are functors from chain complexes of HAr -modules to chain complexes of
( HAr ) ! -comodules and back; their composition is the identity on modules up to quasi-isomorphism
whenever the arithmetic Positselski compatibility holds (Chapter 24.1.5).
Theorem 53.3.3 (P1: functional equation from Koszul self-duality). . The identity 𝜅HAr + ( 𝜅 ! )HAr =
0, interpreted as the cancellation of the bar and cobar differentials on the primary diagonal subspace,
implies 𝜉ℝ ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉ℝ (1 − 𝑠 ). Conversely, the functional equation implies the Koszul identity on the
primary diagonal. This is Chapter 19.2.1.
Remark 53.3.4 (elementary content of P1). The primary diagonal of HAr carries a character 𝜒𝑠 defined
by 𝛼 𝑝 ↦→ 𝑝 − 𝑠 and 𝛼∞ ↦→ 𝑒 𝑖𝜋 𝑠/2 Γ ( 𝑠 /2). The bar complex pairs 𝜒𝑠 with its cobar dual 𝜒𝑠! ; the dual is
𝜒1− 𝑠 by Poisson summation and Tate’s local functional equation at each place. The Koszul cancellation
statement 𝜅 + 𝜅 ! = 0 on this character says 𝜒𝑠 and 𝜒1− 𝑠 are cohomologically identified, equivalent to the
functional-equation identity (53.1).

Remark 53.3.13 (the zero-divisor problem). These operators construct occupation weights. A self-adjoint
operator whose determinant has divisor div 𝜉ℝ requires further arithmetic and trace maps. Literal in-

𝑠 = 1/2, whereas 𝜉ℝ (1/2) ≠ 0 (Chapter 56.4.2). The grading and the proposed zero-divisor operator in
Chapter 56.4.1 are separate data.

tive cuspidal or automorphic interpretation of this holomorphic series requires an additional realization
map. Its Fourier expansion alone does not prove modular transformation laws or native membership.
Hypothesis 53.3.15 (a native Weil–Petersson norm realization). On a specified arithmetic test space E,
                             prim
assume a map Υ : E → Vcusp whose image lies in an injectively realized positive Petersson core, and
assume the actual norm identity

                                     𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) = ⟨Υ ( 𝑓 ) , Υ ( 𝑓 )⟩Pet .

The Fourier series above is a proposed construction to test against this identity; native membership and
the identity are separate requirements.
Theorem 53.3.16 (positivity under a realized norm identity). Under the norm realization hypoth-
esis, 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) ≥ 0 for 𝑓 ∈ E. If a specified Li trace is a finite limit of these nonnegative values along
test functions in E, that trace is also nonnegative. The approximation and trace identity are additional
hypotheses; this statement does not assert them for all Li coefficients.

Proof. The squared Petersson norm is nonnegative on its realized Hilbert core. Substitution in the
assumed identity proves the first assertion. A finite limit of nonnegative real numbers is nonnegative,
proving the second. Neither assertion constructs the native map or the Li trace approximation.

  53.4    The Restricted Test Class
  Theorem 53.4.1 (restricted-class Weil positivity). . Assume the domain-restricted P3
  (Chapter 53.3.9), the Weil–Petersson isometry on the restricted test class (Chapter 53.3.15), and HP–Li
  positivity on the restricted test class (Chapter 53.3.16). Then

                                                 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) ≥ 0

  for every 𝑓 in the restricted test class. No zero-placement conclusion follows until the positivity is
  extended to the full admissible Weil class.

  Proof. The domain-restricted P3 and the Weil–Petersson isometry give

                                        𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) = ⟨Υ ( 𝑓 ) , Υ ( 𝑓 )⟩Pet

  on the restricted domain. The right hand side is non-negative by P3. Weil’s RH criterion applies only
  after this inequality holds for all admissible Weil test functions, so the restricted statement is not a zero-
  placement theorem.

  Remark 53.4.2 (domain boundary). Chapter 53.4.1 is a theorem on a proper test domain. The passage to
  the full Weil cone requires:
  (i) P3 on the non-tempered and Eisenstein sectors (Chapter 55.6.1);
 (ii) extending the Weil–Petersson isometry to an unrestricted test class compatible with all admissible
      Weil test functions (Chapter 57.5);
(iii) handling the Eisenstein continuous-spectrum contribution either by domain restriction or Langlands–
      Shahidi normalization correction (Chapter 55.3).
  These three analytic assertions are independent of positivity on the restricted class.

53.6    The Full Weil Cone
The preceding reductions leave a single full-domain statement.
Theorem 53.6.1 (full-domain Weil positivity). . Assume the restricted-class comparison conditions
of Chapter 53.5 hold. Then RH is equivalent to the unrestricted Weil-positivity statement:

                      𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) ≥ 0 for every admissible Weil test function 𝑓 .

Equivalently, RH is equivalent to the full-domain extension of Chapter 53.3.16 from the restricted test
class to the unrestricted Paley–Wiener class.

Proof. The assumptions give the restricted comparisons on their stated domains. Weil’s theorem, Chap-
ter 53.2.1, says that positivity of the Weil distribution on the full admissible Paley–Wiener class is equiva-
lent to RH. Thus the full-domain extension is neither weaker nor stronger than RH; it is RH in Weil’s
form.

Remark 53.6.2 (domain of the reduction). Chapter 53.6.1 identifies the unrestricted extension with RH.
The restricted construction supplies no theorem forcing this extension; the continuous and Eisenstein
sectors remain part of the full Weil inequality.

53.7   Classical Boundary
  (i) RH classical form (Chapter 53.1.4): zeros of 𝜉ℝ on Re( 𝑠 ) = 1/2.
508                       Chapter 53. Elementary Reductions of the Riemann Hypothesis


  (ii) Four classical equivalents (Chapter 53.2.5): Weil positivity, Li positivity, Hilbert–Pólya, de
       Branges.
 (iii) Five structural ingredients: Heisenberg + Koszul (P1), Hochschild character + functional equa-
       tion (P2), Petersson positivity (P3), Bost–Connes log-modular operator, Mellin–Petersson lift.
 (iv) Restricted-class positivity (Chapter 53.4.1): Weil positivity on the restricted test class.
  (v) Restricted-class comparison (Chapter 53.5): the comparison conditions factor through ten
       named mathematical reductions.
 (vi) Full Weil cone (Chapter 53.6.1): extension of the Weil–Petersson isometry to the unrestricted
       Paley–Wiener class, equivalent to RH.
   Each step in the construction above is independent of Vols I–III and has a stated mathematical
domain. The full-domain statement (Chapter 53.6.1) is the Weil–Petersson isometry extension to the
unrestricted Paley–Wiener class.
Chapter 54


Arithmetic Positselski: Four Residual Sub-Items

Of the five open Positselski sub-items recorded in Chapter 24.1.6, sub-item (4) (primitive zeta-character
theorem) is closed unconditionally in Chapter 45 via Tate 1950 Mellin–theta and Julia 1990 primon
gas. Four remain: (1) completed continuous duals for the Iwasawa algebra Λ 𝑝 = ℤ 𝑝 [[ 𝐺 𝑝 ]], (2) derived
𝑝-adic completion of chain complexes of Λ 𝑝 -modules, (3) faithful lifting of mod- 𝑝 representations
along Λ 𝑝 → 𝔽 𝑝 , and (5) Koszul-dual description of the Bost–Connes system as the enveloping sheaf of
the adele class space. This chapter closes three of the four by first-principles tools and closes the fourth
conditionally: Pontryagin duality on locally compact abelian groups (classical since Weil 1940), Greenlees–
May derived completion (Trans. AMS 340, 1992), Matlis duality on the compact heart (Matlis 1958),
and Bost–Connes 1995 Selecta Math. 1 (1995), 411–457, combined with the stated Consani–Marcolli
adele-class duality. None of the four arguments uses Iwasawa theory proper; each reduces to a classical
compactness or completion argument applied to the correct Pontryagin-dual lattice. Combined with
sub-item (4) of Ch. 45, Chapter 24.1.5 holds on the abelian Heisenberg sector conditional on the Consani–
Marcolli adele-class duality used below. The non-commutative Iwahori extension remains outside the
abelian sector.

54.1   Continuous Duals
Iwasawa Algebra and Pontryagin Dual
Fix a prime 𝑝. Let 𝐺 𝑝 = Gal(ℚab
                              𝑝 /ℚ 𝑝 ) and

                                Λ 𝑝 := ℤ 𝑝 [[ 𝐺 𝑝 ]] = lim ℤ 𝑝 [ 𝐺 𝑝 /𝑈 ] ,
                                                       ←−

the inverse limit over open normal subgroups 𝑈 ⊴ 𝐺 𝑝 of finite index. By local class field theory (Serre
1962, Corps locaux, Ch. XIV §5), 𝐺 𝑝 is a profinite group and Λ 𝑝 is a compact topological ring in the
inverse-limit topology (each ℤ 𝑝 [ 𝐺 𝑝 /𝑈 ] is a finite ℤ 𝑝 -module in the 𝑝-adic topology). The underlying
additive group is a compact topological abelian group; in the notation of Weil 1940 L’intégration Ch. II,
Λ 𝑝 ∈ LCA, the category of locally compact abelian groups.
Deﬁnition 54.1.1 (continuous Pontryagin dual). . For 𝐴 ∈ LCA, the continuous Pontryagin dual is

                                       𝐴∗ := Homcts ( 𝐴, ℝ/ℤ) ,

the group of continuous homomorphisms into the circle, topologised by compact-open convergence. For
𝐴 compact, 𝐴∗ is discrete; for 𝐴 discrete, 𝐴∗ is compact (Pontryagin 1934, Weil 1940 Ch. II §2). For 𝐴 a
𝑝-primary torsion group (a ℤ 𝑝 -module in the sense that 𝑝𝑛 𝐴 → 0), 𝐴∗ takes values in ℚ 𝑝 /ℤ 𝑝 ⊂ ℝ/ℤ
and one writes
                                     𝐴∨ := Homcts ( 𝐴, ℚ 𝑝 /ℤ 𝑝 ) ,
the 𝑝-adic Pontryagin dual.

Theorem 54.1.2 (Pontryagin double duality, LCA version). . The contravariant functor 𝐴 ↦→ 𝐴∗
from LCA to LCA is an anti-equivalence of categories: the double-dual natural transformation 𝐴 →
𝐴∗∗ , 𝑎 ↦→ ev 𝑎 , is an isomorphism of topological groups for every 𝐴 ∈ LCA. Restriction to compact
abelian groups: the anti-equivalence exchanges compact and discrete. Restriction to 𝑝-primary: the
anti-equivalence exchanges compact pro- 𝑝 and discrete 𝑝-primary torsion.
   The proof is Pontryagin 1934 (originally for separable compact abelian groups); the general LCA
formulation is Weil 1940 Ch. II §5 and Folland 1995 A Course in Abstract Harmonic Analysis Ch. 4,
Thm. 4.31 (the latter has the cleanest topological-group-valued statement).

Positselski Duality of Λ 𝑝 -mod and 𝐶 ( 𝐺 𝑝 , ℚ 𝑝 /ℤ 𝑝 )-comod
Theorem 54.1.4 (Positselski duality for continuous duals). . The derived categories
D𝑏 ( Λ 𝑝 −modcts ) of bounded complexes of continuous Λ 𝑝 -modules and D𝑏 ( 𝐶 ( 𝐺 𝑝 , ℚ 𝑝 /ℤ 𝑝 )−comod)
of bounded complexes of comodules over the Pontryagin dual coalgebra are equivalent by Pontryagin
duality:
                                              (−) ∨
                       D𝑏 ( Λ 𝑝 −modcts ) −−−−−→ D𝑏 ( 𝐶 ( 𝐺 𝑝 , ℚ 𝑝 /ℤ 𝑝 )−comod) op ,
with quasi-inverse (−) ∨ . The equivalence is compatible with the classical Positselski correspondence
(Chapter 24.1.1) under base change to the residue field: restriction along Λ 𝑝 → 𝔽 𝑝 recovers Positselski’s
original theorem over 𝔽 𝑝 .

Proof. Three steps.
    Step 1. Abelian equivalence. The abelian categories Λ 𝑝 −modcts (continuous Λ 𝑝 -modules in the
inverse-limit topology) and 𝐶 ( 𝐺 𝑝 , ℚ 𝑝 /ℤ 𝑝 )−comod are Pontryagin-dual: Chapter 54.1.3 gives ( Λ 𝑝 ) ∨ =
𝐶 ( 𝐺 𝑝 , ℚ 𝑝 /ℤ 𝑝 ) as a coalgebra, where the coalgebra structure on the dual is the standard dual of an
augmented algebra (Sweedler 1969 Hopf Algebras Ch. 1 §1.2). The Pontryagin dual functor 𝑀 ↦→ 𝑀 ∨
sends continuous Λ 𝑝 -modules to discrete 𝐶 ( 𝐺 𝑝 , ℚ 𝑝 /ℤ 𝑝 )-comodules and is anti-equivalence of abelian
categories (dualising an exact sequence yields an exact sequence, by exactness of Pontryagin duality on
LCA; Weil 1940 Ch. II §5).
    Step 2. Derived extension. An anti-equivalence of abelian categories extends to the bounded derived
categories by the universal property of D𝑏 as the Verdier quotient of the homotopy category of bounded
complexes by acyclic complexes. The Pontryagin dual sends quasi-isomorphisms to quasi-isomorphisms
(cohomology commutes with exact functors), hence descends to an anti-equivalence D𝑏 ( Λ 𝑝 −modcts ) ≃
D𝑏 ( 𝐶 ( 𝐺 𝑝 , ℚ 𝑝 /ℤ 𝑝 )−comod) op .
    Step 3. Base-change compatibility. Reduce modulo 𝑝 and modulo the augmentation 𝐼𝐺 𝑝 = ker( Λ 𝑝 →
ℤ 𝑝 ): Λ 𝑝 ⊗ℤ 𝑝 𝔽 𝑝 = 𝔽 𝑝 [[ 𝐺 𝑝 ]], with Pontryagin dual 𝐶 ( 𝐺 𝑝 , 𝔽 𝑝 ) ⊗ (ℚ 𝑝 /ℤ 𝑝 ) [ 𝑝] = 𝐶 ( 𝐺 𝑝 , 𝔽 𝑝 ) (the
 𝑝-torsion sector). Over 𝔽 𝑝 , Positselski 2011 arXiv:0905.2621 Thm. 5.2 gives the classical correspondence,
and the square

                                                 (−) ∨
                       D𝑏 ( Λ 𝑝 −modcts )      −−−−−→ D𝑏 ( 𝐶 ( 𝐺 𝑝 , ℚ 𝑝 /ℤ 𝑝 )−comod) op
                            ↓ −⊗𝔽 𝑝                                   ↓ −[ 𝑝]
                                                 (−) ∨
                    D𝑏 (𝔽 𝑝 [[ 𝐺 𝑝 ]]−mod) −−−−−→           D𝑏 ( 𝐶 ( 𝐺 𝑝 , 𝔽 𝑝 )−comod) op

commutes (naturality of Pontryagin duality under base change to the residue field, a consequence of ex-
actness of − ⊗ 𝔽 𝑝 on torsion-free Λ 𝑝 -modules; the torsion sector is handled by the 𝑝-torsion subfunctor
−[ 𝑝]).

Remark 54.1.5 (domain). Chapter 54.1.4 is elementary: the only ingredients are Pontryagin duality on
LCA (Weil 1940) and the inverse-limit presentation of Λ 𝑝 . The sub-item (1) of Chapter 24.1.6 is thereby

Bounded Tor Hypothesis
Deﬁnition 54.2.2 (bounded Tor). . A dg algebra 𝐴 over a Noetherian ring 𝑅 has bounded Tor against
the residue quotient 𝑅/ 𝐼 if Tor𝑖𝑅 ( 𝐴, 𝑅/ 𝐼 ) = 0 for all 𝑖 ≥ 1. Equivalently, the flat dimension of 𝐴 as a
graded 𝑅-module (with its internal dg differential absorbed) against 𝑅/ 𝐼 is zero: the graded pieces of 𝐴
are flat 𝑅-modules relative to 𝑅/ 𝐼 (Stacks Project 0BKE, §066A).

Corollary 54.2.5 (closure of sub-item (2)). . Sub-item (2) of Chapter 24.1.6 (derived completion

derived 𝑝-adic completion on Λ 𝑝 -modules matches ordinary completion under the Heisenberg bar’s
bounded-Tor hypothesis.

54.3    Faithful Lifting
Matlis Duality on the Compact Heart
Let 𝑅 be a complete Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal 𝔪 and residue field 𝑘 = 𝑅/𝔪. The Matlis
dual of an 𝑅-module 𝑀 is
                                   𝑀 M := Hom 𝑅 ( 𝑀 , 𝐸 ( 𝑘 )) ,
where 𝐸 ( 𝑘 ) is the injective hull of 𝑘 as 𝑅-module (Matlis 1958 Pacific J. Math. 8, §3).
Theorem 54.3.1 (Matlis duality). . Let 𝑅 be a complete Noetherian local ring with residue field
𝑘 . The Matlis dual (−) M is a contravariant exact functor 𝑅−mod → 𝑅−mod, and restricts to an
anti-equivalence between the categories of finitely generated (Noetherian) 𝑅-modules and Artinian
𝑅-modules. (−) MM is the identity on both categories: finitely generated modules are reflexive, and
Artinian modules are reflexive, under Matlis dualisation.
  The proof is Matlis 1958 Thm. 4.2 and Thm. 5.2; modern accounts in Bruns–Herzog 1993 Cohen–
Macaulay Rings Ch. 3 §2, and Enochs–Jenda 2000 Relative Homological Algebra Ch. 5.

side.

54.4    Koszul-Dual Bost–Connes
Bost–Connes System
The Bost–Connes system of Bost–Connes 1995 Selecta Math. 1 (Selecta Math. 1 (1995), 411–457) is the
𝐶 ∗ -dynamical system
                               (𝔸BC , 𝜎𝑡 ) := ( 𝐶𝑟∗ (ℚ+∗ ⋊ ℤ̂∗ ) , 𝜎𝑡 ) ,
the reduced 𝐶 ∗ -algebra of the semidirect product of the multiplicative positive rationals with the unit
ideles ℤ̂∗ = 𝑝 ℤ∗𝑝 , equipped with the scaling action 𝜎𝑡 ( 𝜇𝑛 ) = 𝑛𝑖𝑡 𝜇𝑛 on the rational-shift generators.
            Q
Bost–Connes 1995 Thm. 27: the KMS 𝛽 partition function at inverse temperature 𝛽 > 1 is the Riemann
zeta function 𝜁 ( 𝛽 ); there is a symmetry breaking phase transition at 𝛽 = 1 (no KMS state for 𝛽 ∈ (0, 1]
outside the unique 𝛽 = ∞ vacuum state, and an infinite family of extremal KMS states for 𝛽 > 1
parametrised by unit ideles).

Adele Class Space and Enveloping Sheaf
The adele class space of Connes 1999 (Selecta Math. 5, §1.4; Consani–Marcolli 2006 Noncommutative
Geometry, Arithmetic, and Related Topics §2) is

                                            𝑋AC := 𝔸ℚ /ℚ∗ ,
the quotient of the full adèle ring by the diagonal multiplicative action of ℚ∗ . This is a ‘‘bad quotient’’
(not Hausdorff in the classical sense) and is replaced by its non-commutative 𝐶 ∗ -algebra analogue;
Connes’ insight (1996 Selecta Math. 5, Thm. 1) is that the scaling action on the adele class space has an
absorption trace governed by the zero distribution of 𝜁 . This trace formula identifies the Bost–Connes
KMS partition with the 𝜁 Euler product through a Hilbert-space duality after regularisation.
Deﬁnition 54.4.1 (enveloping sheaf on adele class). . The enveloping sheaf of 𝔸BC on 𝑋AC is the sheaf
E BC on 𝑋AC whose sections over an open 𝑈 ⊂ 𝑋AC are the elements of 𝔸BC supported on the adelic
fibre 𝔸𝑈 ⊂ 𝔸ℚ (pullback of the projection 𝔸ℚ → 𝑋AC ); the structure maps are the restriction maps of
sections. Consani–Marcolli 2006 §2.4 show E BC is a sheaf of 𝐶 ∗ -algebras with Γ ( 𝑋AC , E BC ) = 𝔸BC .

Combined Theorem
Theorem 54.5.1 (four-sub-item combined theorem). . The four residual open sub-items (1), (2), (3),
(5) of Chapter 24.1.6 are each closed by the arguments of §§54.1–54.4, with sub-item (5) conditional on
the Consani–Marcolli adele-class duality in the form stated above. Explicitly:
   (i) Continuous duals: Chapter 54.1.4.
  (ii) Derived completion: Chapter 54.2.5.
 (iii) Faithful lifting: Chapter 54.3.3.
  (5) Koszul-dual Bost–Connes: Chapter 54.4.3.
Combined with the closure of sub-item (4) in Ch. 45 (primitive zeta-character theorem, Chapter 45.1.3),
all five open sub-items of Chapter 24.1.6 are closed under this same condition.

Remark 54.5.4 (domain and comparison). The four categorical sub-items reduce to elementary argu-
ments: Pontryagin duality (Weil 1940, Folland 1995), Greenlees–May derived completion (Trans. AMS
340, 1992), Matlis duality on the compact heart (Matlis 1958, Matsumura 1989 via Krull intersection),
Bost–Connes 1995 §1.2 plus the stated Consani–Marcolli adele-class duality. None of these arguments
uses the full force of non-commutative Iwasawa theory; each reduces the sub-item to a classical compact-
ness, completion, or duality theorem applied to the correct Pontryagin-dual lattice. The residual that
remains is the non-abelian Iwahori extension of §24.2, which is explicit out-of-domain. For the abelian
Heisenberg sector needed by the G-row of P1 and the Riemann functional equation, the remaining
named condition is the Consani–Marcolli adele-class duality used above.

Remark 54.6.1 (disjointness of sources). The four arguments draw from four disjoint classical sources:
(1) Pontryagin/Weil harmonic analysis (1934–1940); (2) Greenlees–May derived completion (1992); (3)
Matlis duality (1958); (5) Bost–Connes KMS theory (1995) plus Consani–Marcolli adele-class duality
(2004–2006). None of the four sources feeds into the primitive zeta-character theorem of Ch. 45, which
used Tate 1950 and Julia 1990. The five sub-item reductions proceed by mutually disjoint primary sources,
so the conditional arithmetic Positselski equivalence (Chapter 54.5.2) rests on independent lines of
argument.

Full V prim P3 and the Koszul–Petersson
Compatibility on the Discrete Core

The discrete-core pairing problem requires an injective native realization in square-integrable automor-
phic functions and maps which identify its Koszul pairing with that Hilbert pairing. The local GNS
construction determines the operator normalization, but does not construct these native maps. Tem-
peredness assumptions and the continuous-spectrum normalization are separate inputs. The following
transfers retain the maps explicitly.

55.1   Native Pairing Maps on a Tempered Cuspidal Core
The local construction applies to a native core only after its pairing maps and adelic assembly are supplied.
Theorem 55.1.1 (conditional tempered cuspidal pairing transfer). . Assume the native pairing
maps of Chapter 26.1.1 on the chosen tempered cuspidal core, including its actual ramified factors and
its specified adelic assembly. Then
                                            ⟨𝑣, 𝑤 ⟩ Pet = ⟨𝑣, 𝑐𝑤 ⟩ Koszul .
Here 𝑐 is the assembled native conjugate-linear map. Its identification with GNS modular conjugation
is one of the map conditions, not a consequence of equality of scalar characters.
Proof. The local calculation is 𝐵 𝑝 ( 𝑣, 𝑐 𝑝 𝑤 ) = 𝐵 𝑞 ( 𝑓 𝑝 𝑣, 𝐽𝑞 𝑓 𝑝 𝑤 ) = ℎ𝑞 ( 𝑓 𝑝 𝑣, 𝑓 𝑝 𝑤 ). The assumed native
metric maps and adelic assembly turn these local identities into the displayed global identity. This is
Chapter 46.3.6. The GNS factor used there is Hilbert–Schmidt, with the stated density; it has no inde-
pendent orthogonal phase-coordinate factor.
Remark 55.1.2 (temperedness and modular domains). The modular operator on a represented prime
GNS space is unbounded: Δ𝑞 𝐸0𝑗 = 𝑞 −𝑗 𝐸0𝑗 for 0 < 𝑞 < 1. The GNS Hilbert pairing is nevertheless
defined on its full Hilbert completion, and the modular operator has its explicit self-adjoint domain.
No automorphic temperedness hypothesis is used in that construction. Temperedness restricts a native
representation domain; it does not give a bounded modular operator or supply its native pairing maps.

55.2    Non-Tempered Cuspidal Representations: Deligne and Kim–Shahidi
The Non-Tempered Locus
Cuspidal automorphic representations of 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ decompose as 𝜋 = 𝑣′ 𝜋𝑣 , with archimedean com-

ponent 𝜋∞ of one of three types: a holomorphic discrete series 𝐷 𝑘 of weight 𝑘 ≥ 2; a Maass cusp form
with Laplace eigenvalue 𝜆 = 1/4 + 𝑟 2 ( 𝑟 ∈ ℝ tempered, 𝑟 ∈ 𝑖 ℝ non-tempered); or a character twist.
Finite places carry Satake parameters ( 𝛼 𝑝 , 𝛽 𝑝 ) with 𝛼 𝑝 𝛽 𝑝 = 1 (unitarity) and max(| 𝛼 𝑝 | , | 𝛽 𝑝 |) = 𝑝 𝜃 𝑝 .

Remark 55.2.2 (domain of Deligne 1974: holomorphic sector only). Deligne 1974 establishes the Ramanu-
jan–Petersson bound for the Hecke eigenvalues of a holomorphic weight-𝑘 cusp form via the Riemann
hypothesis for ℓ -adic cohomology of a suitable Kuga–Sato variety. The bound transfers to temperedness
of the associated automorphic representation at every finite prime. Deligne 1974 applies to holomorphic
cuspidal forms; for Maass cusp forms, no algebraic variety whose Frobenius eigenvalues give the Hecke
eigenvalues is available, and the Ramanujan bound in the Maass sector is an open problem. The current
state of the art on the Maass sector is Kim–Sarnak 2003 𝜃 ≤ 7/64; this is a sub-convex Ramanujan
bound, strictly weaker than full temperedness.

Proposition 55.2.4 (what a local parameter bound controls). If | 𝛼 𝑝 | ≤ 𝑝 𝜃 and 𝜎 > 𝜃 , then

A bound on a difference of native pairings further requires their comparison maps. For bounded maps
𝑓 , 𝑔 from a Hilbert space into a common Hilbert space, one has

                       | ℎ ( 𝑓 𝑣, 𝑓 𝑤 ) − ℎ ( 𝑔𝑣, 𝑔𝑤 )| ≤ ∥ 𝑓 − 𝑔 ∥ (∥ 𝑓 ∥ + ∥ 𝑔 ∥) ∥ 𝑣 ∥ ∥ 𝑤 ∥ .

Proof. The reverse triangle inequality gives |1 − 𝛼 𝑝 𝑝 − 𝑠 | ≥ 1 − 𝑝 𝜃 − 𝜎 > 0. For the pairing estimate,
subtract and add ℎ ( 𝑔𝑣, 𝑓 𝑤 ), then apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the two terms. Rescaling a native bilinear
pairing while leaving its Satake parameters fixed shows why a parameter bound alone cannot control
that pairing’s comparison with a given Hermitian norm.

  2 consists of one-dimensional automorphic representations lifted from the determinant character
𝐿res
(Moeglin–Waldspurger 1995 Spectral Decomposition and Eisenstein Series II.2; specifically the trivial
character gives the one-dimensional residual piece, measured by the Fock vacuum |0⟩ ∈ V prim ). CAP

entirely to the Maass case. The theorem (Chapter 55.2.3) conditional on Ramanujan covers the Maass
sector, and the residual spectrum (one-dimensional trivial character) is covered by the vacuum.

of 𝜁 contributing to the Li sum are exactly the zeros of 𝜉ℝ , all of which are discrete; the Eisenstein

Eisenstein-series poles in 𝜉 at 𝑠 = 0, 1 are Tate poles (Chapter 22.3.7), cancelled by the factor 𝑠 ( 𝑠 − 1)/2

Proof. Li’s sum is over non-trivial zeros of 𝜁 , equivalently zeros of 𝜉ℝ . The non-trivial zeros are a count-

55.4    Langlands–Shahidi Normalisation
The Koszul–Petersson identity can be extended to the full V prim , including the Eisenstein continuum,
only after the Koszul pairing on principal-series inductions is identified with the positive Langlands–
Shahidi Plancherel measure. The scalar 𝑁 LS of Chapter 55.4.1 is not by itself such an identification.
The discrete-core reduction of Section 55.3 is the construction used for the Li trace; the present section
records the conditional continuum extension.

Proof. The equality is the direct-sum and adelic assembly of the proved local pairing-map identities, as

Remark 55.6.2 (variance and native maps). Petersson is Hermitian and the Koszul form is bilinear. The
conjugate-linear native map 𝑐 gives the second expression its Hermitian variance. On the represented
model this is 𝐵 𝑞 ( 𝑋 , 𝐽𝑞𝑌 ) = ℎ𝑞 ( 𝑋 , 𝑌 ), with two distinct maps for a native factor and its dual. Inserting
𝐽𝑞 into a Hermitian pairing instead would be bilinear and would fail the scalar test.

55.7    Native and Analytic Comparison Conditions
The first native requirement is the construction of pairing maps, with a compatible adelic domain.
Automorphic bounds then control which representation factors belong to a domain where those maps
have been constructed. They do not establish the maps, their norm discrepancy or their interaction with
phases. The local modular operator is unbounded independently of those bounds, while its Hilbert
pairing is positive by construction.
   Continuous-spectrum pairings require their actual measure and regularization. Excluding that spec-
trum defines a smaller domain but does not construct a native embedding into the remaining discrete
55.8. Bibliography                                                                                      529


spectrum. A proposed scalar normalization extends the pairing identity only after its compatibility with
the native maps and spectral measure has been proved.
    Finally, a Hilbert–Pólya or Li-positivity argument needs a map from the relevant arithmetic test space
to the realized core and a trace or norm identity on that domain. The local GNS normalization and the
radial shell pairing model do not supply this last map. These missing comparisons are independent of
the explicit positivity of a squared 𝐿 2 norm.

Occupation and Modular Spectra in the
Hilbert–Pólya Problem

The prime character uses the nonnegative occupation energies log 𝑚. The modular operator of a state
acts on observables, so its energies are differences of occupation energies. We construct the comparison
between these two operators before asking for a Hilbert–Pólya realization. Their relation involves a closed
creation subspace and a factor of two in the convention 𝑁BC = − 21 log Δ1 . It is not an identification of
the two full Hilbert spaces.

Theorem 56.2.5 (spectrum of the full log-modular operator). . The finite tensor eigenbasis is a
core for 𝑁BC , whose closure is self-adjoint. Its set of eigenvalues is
                                       1
                                         2 log( 𝑎/𝑏 ) : 𝑎, 𝑏 ∈ ℕ ≥1 .

Each eigenvalue has countably infinite multiplicity. The spectrum as a closed subset of ℝ is all of ℝ,
although every spectral measure is atomic. Moreover 𝐽1 𝑁BC 𝐽1 = − 𝑁BC . In particular the full log-modular
operator is not nonnegative.

Proof. The logarithm of a finite product of prime powers is the logarithm of a positive rational number;
conversely every such rational is obtained from finite positive and negative occupation differences. This
gives exactly the stated eigenvalues. Keeping a fixed difference and varying the common diagonal shift of
𝑖, 𝑗 gives infinitely many orthogonal eigenvectors; separability makes the multiplicity countable. The
positive rational numbers are dense in the positive real numbers, and logarithm is continuous, so the
eigenvalue set is dense in ℝ. For a diagonal self-adjoint operator, every limit of eigenvalues lies in the
spectrum: unit eigenvectors at approaching eigenvalues are approximate null vectors for the shifted
operator. A point at positive distance from the eigenvalues has a bounded diagonal resolvent. These two
facts identify the spectrum with their closure. Self-adjointness and the core assertion follow by truncating
the weighted square sum of coefficients. Finally 𝐽1 reverses each occupation difference. Already in a single
prime, 𝐸10 and 𝐸01 have opposite nonzero energies.

can identify the full 𝑁BC with the nonnegative occupation operator, since the former has negative
eigenvalues. Nor is the creation subspace a substitute for the full GNS space when division, modular
conjugation, or genuine arithmetic phases are required.
Deﬁnition 56.3.4 (an oscillator enlargement and its lift). An oscillator enlargement is a specified Hilbert
completion of finite-support number states |n⟩ ⊗ 𝛿𝑚 , with creation and annihilation operators satisfying
the chosen Heisenberg relations, a vacuum and a nonnegative diagonal energy 𝐿0osc . Its zero-mode energy
is 𝑁occ . A GNS lift of this enlargement is an isometry of its number-state core into H1 extending 𝜄0 ,
intertwining the specified operators on their domains and preserving the given inner products. The
            Ar
notation FHeis ,prim denotes such a chosen core when one is supplied.
Lemma 56.3.5 (completion of an oscillator lift). . An oscillator lift extends uniquely to an isometry
of its Hilbert completion onto the closed span of its image. It supplies no identification of that image
with a native arithmetic Hochschild or automorphic carrier.

Proof. An isometry sends Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences and preserves the norm of their limits.
This gives the unique extension and identifies its closed image. The assertion uses only the specified lift
maps, not a classification of additional GNS coordinates as automorphic sectors.

56.4    The Primary-Heisenberg Twist and the Determinant-Trace Opera-
        tor
The occupation operator 𝑁occ has spectrum {log 𝑚 }𝑚 ∈ℕ× . The Hilbert–Pólya condition asks for a
self-adjoint operator 𝐴 together with the determinant condition forcing the divisor of 21 id + 𝑖 𝐴 to
be the zero divisor of 𝜉ℝ . The primary-Heisenberg twist names the data required to compare the first
spectrum with this determinant divisor and its Weil–Connes trace. Its existence with the prescribed
determinant-trace property is H-PAr .

Statement of the Twist

grading operator is

The determinant and trace requirements on 𝐴 are additional hypotheses below.
Proposition 56.4.2 (the literal energy-intertwining obstruction). Suppose the source grading
has a nonzero vacuum 𝑣1 with 𝐺 F 𝑣1 = 0. Requiring 𝐴𝑈 𝑣 = 𝑈 𝐺 F 𝑣 on a core containing 𝑣1 is incom-
patible with the requirement that the eigenvalue divisor of 21 + 𝑖 𝐴 equal the nontrivial zero divisor of
𝜉ℝ .
Proof. The proposed identity would give 𝐴𝑈 𝑣1 = 0, and 𝑈 𝑣1 ≠ 0 because 𝑈 is an isometry. Hence 1/2
would be an eigenvalue of 21 + 𝑖 𝐴 and would have to be a zero of 𝜉ℝ . It is not. Indeed the alternating

and removing the Tate poles multiplies by the nonzero factor 21 𝑠 ( 𝑠 − 1) at 𝑠 = 1/2. Thus 𝜉ℝ (1/2) ≠ 0.

   The grading comparison (56.1) and the literal 𝐴-intertwining condition are therefore different targets.
The former is explicitly constructed once 𝑈 is given. The latter is ruled out on a vacuum-preserving
domain. Neither statement constructs, or excludes in general, a self-adjoint operator with the required
zeta-zero determinant and trace.

Determinant-Trace Requirement: Hadamard Inversion
The condition on 𝐴 is the Hilbert–Pólya determinant-trace condition for 𝜉ℝ . Write a non-trivial zero as
𝜌 = 𝛽 𝜌 + 𝑖 𝛾 𝜌 . The self-adjointness of 𝐴 puts the normal operator Θ𝜉 = 1/2 + 𝑖 𝐴 on the critical line.
H-PAr asks that its regularised determinant divisor be the original zero divisor and that its Weil–Connes
trace be the zero distribution. Equivalently, the determinant identity forces 𝛽 𝜌 = 1/2 for every zero; after
this zero-placement the trace of 𝐴 is supported at the ordinates 𝛾 𝜌 . This is not the spectrum of 𝑁occ ,
which is {log 𝑚 }𝑚 ∈ℕ× . The prime and zero sides are related by the Mellin transform of 𝜉 through its
Hadamard factorisation:

(von Mangoldt 1895). Outside ℜ 𝑠 > 1 the prime series is not silently retained: the continued logarithmic
derivative is a meromorphic function, while the Weil formula uses the compact-test pairing and exponen-
tial weight of Theorem 87.2.8. The twist 𝐴 is the operator-level analogue of inverting this duality: from
the log-prime spectrum of 𝑁occ , construct a normal zero-divisor operator whose determinant is governed
by the Hadamard expansion and whose trace is the Weil–Connes zero distribution. The Hadamard
expansion is a statement about an entire function. The assertion that a self-adjoint operator carries this
determinant divisor and trace distribution is additional data, the content of H-PAr .

The Hilbert–Pólya Hypothesis and Its Determinant-Trace Consequences
Hypothesis 56.4.3 (H-PAr -twist). There exist graded determinant-trace comparison data (H𝜉 , 𝑈 , 𝐴) in
the sense of Chapter 56.4.1 with the additional zero-placement spectral property
                      Spec( 𝐴) = { 𝛾 𝜌 | 𝜌 = 𝛽 𝜌 + 𝑖 𝛾 𝜌 is a non-trivial zero of 𝜉ℝ },
with multiplicities matching zero multiplicities, together with the determinant condition div det∞ ( 𝑠 id −
( 21 id + 𝑖 𝐴)) = div 𝜉ℝ , and the ℤ/2-symmetry 𝛾 𝜌 ↦→ − 𝛾 𝜌 acting on the spectrum as the arithmetic 𝑆 -
modular involution.
Remark 56.4.4 (relation to H-PAr ). Chapter 56.4.3 is the functional-analytic content of Chapter 22.3.2:
an operator 𝐴 with the specified determinant divisor and trace distribution is exactly 𝐻HP of the refor-
mulation chapter, and Θ𝜉 = 1/2 + 𝑖 𝐴 is the arithmetic zero-divisor operator. The arithmetic realization
asks in addition for the specified occupation grading, native maps and arithmetic trace comparison. The
grading intertwiner 𝑈 in Chapter 56.4.1 does not intertwine 𝐴 with 𝑁occ . Imposing the latter identity
on the vacuum contradicts Chapter 56.4.2.

Proposition 56.5.2 (the divisor leaves an exponential ambiguity). For every 𝑐 ∈ ℂ, the function

Both normalizations in (56.2) are necessary.

Proof. The exponential has no zero, has value one at zero, and contributes 𝑐 to the logarithmic derivative.
Multiplication preserves the stated order bound.

   The prescription above uses no complex powers of 𝑠 − Θ 𝑍 . A determinant defined by such powers
requires a spectral cut and meromorphic continuation of its trace. Agreement with Δ 𝑍 requires the
same second logarithmic derivative and the two stated initial conditions. These conditions determine
equality locally near zero by integration, and globally by analytic continuation.

Remark 56.5.4 (comparison with Berry–Keating). Berry–Keating (SIAM Review 41, 1999) propose
𝐻 = 𝑥 𝑝 + 1/2 on 𝐿 2 (ℝ>0 , 𝑑𝑥 / 𝑥 ) as the candidate 𝐻HP . Their proposal reproduces the leading-order

however, requires a self-adjoint extension not supplied by the model. The present twist has the same
logical form: the occupation log-prime spectrum {log 𝑚 }𝑚 ∈ℕ× is classical and self-adjoint, and the lift
to the zero determinant divisor via the Hadamard-dual twist is the content of H-PAr . See Chapter 36.3.17
for the HPAr-converse analysis.

56.7    Operator and Arithmetic Comparison Boundary
The tensor shift state at 𝛽 = 1 has a well-defined GNS space and modular operator. Its full log-modular
spectrum is ℝ, with an atomic spectral resolution on the dense set 21 log ℚ>0 . The occupation operator
has the discrete nonnegative spectrum log ℕ≥1 . The map 𝑊 of Chapter 56.3.1 identifies the latter with
2 𝑁BC on the creation subspace. Division and modular conjugation require the larger GNS carrier.
Genuine arithmetic phases require their own compatible algebra before an adelic comparison can be
made.
Proposition 56.7.1 (the remaining determinant-trace construction). The local GNS and occu-
pation constructions supply neither an operator 𝐴 with the zero-divisor property of Chapter 56.4.3 nor a
native pairing map into its Hilbert space. The requested additional data are that self-adjoint operator and
core, the specified determinant and trace regularizations, and the native realization maps. The separate
grading comparison is (56.1); imposing it on 𝐴 itself is excluded by Chapter 56.4.2.

Proof. The constructions give the displayed diagonal operators and the isometry 𝑊 . Their spectra,
carriers and actions are computed above. The occupation operator retains its vacuum and the full
modular operator has both signs and infinite eigenspace multiplicity. Neither has the asserted zeta-zero
divisor. Transport of the grading only constructs 𝐺𝜉 . It imposes no spectral condition on the separate
56.8. Bibliography and Source List                                                                     539


operator 𝐴. The proposed stronger energy intertwining is the vacuum contradiction already proved.
Thus the additional hypotheses remain the exact unconstructed comparison data, not consequences of
the local state normalization.

Remark 56.7.2 (prime weights and native realization). The weight 𝑘 log 𝑝 is the occupation energy of 𝑝 𝑘 .
It is obtained from 2 𝑁BC only after the stated creation-subspace restriction at 𝛽 = 1; at general inverse
temperature 𝛽 the factor is 2/ 𝛽 . A prescribed scalar partition determines neither the native pairing maps
nor the full algebra of phases. In particular a local KMS normalization cannot establish uniqueness of
an arithmetic Hilbert–Pólya representative.
Remark 56.7.3 (scope of the Hilbert–Pólya implication). If a self-adjoint 𝐴 has the required determinant
divisor and trace, then 21 + 𝑖 𝐴 is supported on the critical line and the assumed divisor comparison
transfers this support to the zeros. Constructing such an 𝐴 remains the Hilbert–Pólya problem in
the specified carrier. The present normalization calculations do not decide that existence problem or
the positivity of a distinct native arithmetic operator. Comparisons with absorption traces or motivic
realizations additionally require maps to those particular carriers.

Weil Pairings and Automorphic Coefficient
Multipliers

The Weil functional acts on compact smooth functions of the logarithmic variable. Its zero formula
evaluates their entire Fourier transforms. Keeping these two spaces distinct fixes the prime weights and
the archimedean sign. It also distinguishes two coefficient multipliers, one of which can produce only
finite Fourier polynomials.

57.2    The Hermitian form and the two polar moments
Define 𝑞𝑊 ( 𝑓 , 𝑔 ) = 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑔 ∗ ), with the first variable linear. The zero multiset is invariant under 𝑧 ↦→ 𝑧¯ ,
by the functional equation and conjugation of 𝜉 . Absolute convergence therefore gives 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ ) = 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ).
Consequently 𝑞𝑊 is Hermitian.

57.6    The arithmetic pairing requirement
Theorem 57.6.1 (the remaining positive comparison). A Hilbert realization of the full Weil form
consists of a positive Hilbert space 𝐾 , a linear map 𝐽 : A → 𝐾 , and the identity
                               ⟨ 𝐽 𝑓 , 𝐽 𝑔 ⟩𝐾 = 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑔 ∗ )    ( 𝑓 , 𝑔 ∈ A ).
Such a realization exists if and only if 𝑞𝑊 is positive semidefinite. When it exists, its minimal realization
is the completion of A /{ 𝑓 : 𝑞𝑊 ( 𝑓 , 𝑓 ) = 0}. Its existence is RH-equivalent. Neither coefficient map
in (57.4) provides the pairing identity.
546                    Chapter 57. Weil Pairings and Automorphic Coefficient Multipliers


Proof. A Hilbert realization implies nonnegativity. Conversely, positivity and polarization give Cauchy–
Schwarz for 𝑞𝑊 . Its nullspace is a linear subspace orthogonal to every vector. Quotienting and completing
therefore gives the asserted Hilbert space and canonical map. Weil’s criterion supplies the equivalence to
RH. The coefficient maps construct holomorphic functions with specified coefficients. Their definitions
contain no equality with the full Weil form, and the finite-prime counterexample excludes the proposed
full-space positive realization of that separate term.

    The arithmetic problem asks for this pairing through a specified native carrier, its operators, and
its realization maps. The compact formula, the exact coefficient calculation, and the two obstruction
theorems retain those separate requirements.
