Chapter 58


VB ∗ Main Direction via Hamburger Positivity,
Determinacy, and HB + /BD +

Chapter 36 isolates the VB∗ converse (zero-placement ⇒ VB∗ ) as a conditional comparison between the
spectral-regularity hypotheses, operator-positive Hermite–Biehler de Branges structure, and the Báez-Duarte
sharp decay condition. In the opposite direction, the VB∗ main-direction implication says that the four an-
alytic hypotheses (HB+ , BD+ , determinacy, positive Hamburger moment structure) on the primary Fock
imply that the non-trivial zeros of 𝜉ℝ lie on the critical line. The chain is classical complex analysis and de
Branges space theory: a de Branges datum whose real part has divisor div Ξ and whose Hermite–Biehler
kernel is positive forces the zeros of Ξ to be real. The positive Hamburger moment structure identiﬁes the
spectral measure as a positive measure on the real line; Hamburger determinacy identiﬁes the measure
uniquely once it exists; and HB+ supplies the real-part divisor constraint. Thus the conclusion is the condi-
tional arrow from these hypotheses to RH. The hypotheses HB+ , BD+ , and determinacy are not consequences
of the Hadamard product; they are the analytic content of the zero-placement problem.

58.1   Spectral Positivity Context
The operator-theoretic comparison (Chapter 36) reduced the VB∗ converse, under P2 + P3 + H-PAr , to
the four-way equivalence

                        (Det) ⇔ (HB+ ) ⇔ (BD+ ) ⇔ zero-placement ⇒ VB∗

of Chapter 36.4.14. Chapter 41 reduces the Hamburger-determinacy component to the sufficient analytic
residual (Ranalytic ) and obstructed a tempting Bombieri–Lagarias shortcut. Neither argument addresses
the main-direction implication

                 (HB+ ) + (BD+ ) + (Det) =⇒ spectral zeros of 𝜉ℝ on the critical line,

which is the sufficient direction of the analytic hypothesis of Chapter 37.4.1. The proof is classical complex
analysis and de Branges space theory in the sense of the 1968 monograph; no arithmetic input beyond
the Hadamard factorisation of 𝜉ℝ is used.

Domain
The theorem is the implication from (HB+ ) + (BD+ ) + (Det) + positive Hamburger moment structure
to spectral zero-placement on the critical line.
    The analytic inputs are HB+ , BD+ , (Det), and positive Hamburger moment structure on 𝜉ℝ . These
are RH-equivalent in the Hermite–Biehler case and spectral regularity inputs in the moment-problem
cases. They are the subject of Chapters 36 and 41.

Independent Sources
The source list for the VB∗ converse uses de Branges 1968, Lagarias 1999, Báez-Duarte 2003, Burnol 2000,
Akhiezer 1965, Simon 1998, Shohat–Tamarkin 1943. The main-direction implication inherits this list
and adds the classical Hamburger existence theorem, Lagarias’ 1999 de Branges survey, Conrey–Li 2000,
and Beurling–Malliavin density. The proof sources of constructions 2 and 3 (determinacy reductions,
operator-positivity reformulations) are kept disjoint from the complex-analysis sources below:
de Branges, Hilbert Spaces of Entire Functions (Prentice-Hall 1968). Foundational monograph;
theorems 22–23 (Hermite–Biehler structure), theorem 32 (multiplication operator on H ( 𝐸 )), theorems
40–41 (invariant subspaces of the shift).
Lagarias, Acta Arith. 89 (1999). Survey of de Branges reformulations of RH; explicit statement of the
main-direction theorem for entire functions of order 1.
Conrey–Li, arXiv:math/9812166 (2000). Construction of de Branges spaces from 𝐿 -functions; criti-
cal discussion of the Hermite–Biehler condition on 𝐸𝜉 ; counter-examples in the non-self-adjoint case.
Beurling–Malliavin, Acta Math. 107 (1962) 291–309. Density theorem: the completeness radius of
an exponential system { 𝑒 𝑖𝜆𝑘 𝑥 } is computed by Beurling–Malliavin density of { 𝜆𝑘 }.
Hamburger, Math. Ann. 81 (1920) 235–319. Original existence theorem: a Hamburger moment prob-
lem has a positive representing measure iff all Hankel matrices are positive-semidefinite.
Levin, Distribution of Zeros of Entire Functions (AMS 1980), Ch. V–VII. Classical reference on
Hermite–Biehler, Hermite–Kakeya–Obreshkov; entire functions of exponential type.
     Independence of inputs: the complex analysis (Hadamard factorisation of 𝜉ℝ , de Branges structure
theorem, Beurling–Malliavin density) is not used in the VB∗ -converse comparison; and that comparison
(operator-positivity reformulations, Jacobi-matrix spectral theory, Báez-Duarte decay) is not used in the
main-direction implication. The two lists share two foundational references: de Branges 1968 (Hermite–
Biehler theory) and Akhiezer 1965 (moment theory, used for the Jacobi matrix and for Hamburger
existence and Carleman’s criterion). These shared references serve logically distinct roles: Akhiezer sup-
plies operator spectral methods on one side and classical moment existence. Simon 1998 (spectral theory
of Jacobi matrices) appears in the operator-theoretic list and is not cited below; Shohat–Tamarkin 1943
is likewise absent below. The two argument paths are therefore independent on the operative arguments,
with the shared foundational references serving independent functions in the two constructions.

Remark 58.2.4 (the orientation of the problem). RH is the statement that the zero set of Ξ is a subset of
the real line. The Hadamard and functional-equation facts (Chapter 58.2.1, Chapter 58.2.2) are uncon-
ditional; they constrain the zero set to be symmetric under 𝑧 ↦→ − 𝑧 but not to be real. The role of the
analytic hypotheses (HB+ , BD+ , determinacy) is to force this realness by real-part divisor control and
spectral-measure rigidity.

58.3    Hadamard Factorisation and the Zero Measure
Deﬁnition 58.3.1 (primary zero multi-set). . The primary zero multi-set is

                         Z𝜉 := { 𝛾 𝜌 ∈ ℂ : 𝜌 = 21 + 𝑖 𝛾 𝜌 non-trivial zero of 𝜉ℝ },

with multiplicity. Under the symmetrisation 𝜌 ↔ 1 − 𝜌, the set Z𝜉 is closed under 𝛾 ↔ − 𝛾 . Under
the complex conjugation 𝜌 ↔ 𝜌, it is closed under 𝛾 ↔ − 𝛾 ; combining, it is closed under 𝛾 ↔ 𝛾 and
symmetric under the Klein four group {1, 𝛾 ↦→ − 𝛾, 𝛾 ↦→ 𝛾, 𝛾 ↦→ − 𝛾 } on the whole plane.

Remark 58.3.5 (positivity of the measure is strictly weaker than RH). The measure 𝜇𝜉 as a multi-set
measure on ℂ is always positive (it is a counting measure). The question is whether its restriction to ℝ
carries the full mass; that is the content of RH. Positivity of 𝜇𝜉 as a measure on ℂ gives no information
about whether the support is on ℝ. This is the reason a positive Hamburger moment representation (a
positive representation on ℝ with prescribed real moments) is strictly finer than mere positivity of 𝜇𝜉 .

Remark 58.5.3 (the heuristic is not a theorem). The moment asymptotics 𝑀2𝑛 ≍ 𝐶 𝑛 𝑛!2 are a saddle-
point heuristic. If they were replaced by a rigorous two-sided bound for a positive moment functional,
Carleman’s series would have harmonic size. Turning that statement into a theorem is the content of
the residual (Ranalytic ) of Chapter 41.4.7. The main-direction implication uses (Det) as a hypothesis: the
Carleman sum is assumed to diverge. Verifying this divergence is a separate analytic problem.
Corollary 58.5.4 (under (SH) + (Det) the measure 𝜈 𝜉 is unique). . Under (SH) + (Det) of
Chapter 58.4.3, there exists a unique positive Borel measure 𝜈𝜉 on ℝ with moments (58.3).

Proof. (SH) + Hamburger existence (Chapter 58.4.2) gives solvability. Carleman (Chapter 58.5.1) under
(Det) gives uniqueness. The conjunction is the claim.

58.6    Hermite–Biehler and the de Branges Space H ( 𝐸 𝜉 )
Deﬁnition 58.6.1 (de Branges datum over Ξ). . A de Branges datum over Ξ is a triple ( 𝐸𝜉 , 𝐴𝜉 , 𝐵 𝜉 ) with

                                         𝐸𝜉 ( 𝑧 ) = 𝐴 𝜉 ( 𝑧 ) − 𝑖 𝐵 𝜉 ( 𝑧 ) ,

where 𝐴𝜉 and 𝐵 𝜉 are real entire functions of finite exponential type. The datum is required to carry a
real-part divisor equality
                                         div( 𝐴𝜉 ) = div( Ξ)
on ℂ, with multiplicities. It is not obtained by setting 𝐸𝜉 = Ξ; for the real entire function Ξ one has
Ξ∗ = Ξ, so the strict Hermite–Biehler inequality would be impossible.
Remark 58.6.2 (conventions match de Branges 1968). The notation 𝐸 = 𝐴 − 𝑖 𝐵 with 𝐴 and 𝐵 real-on-real
is de Branges’ standard form for candidate Hermite–Biehler functions. The condition for Hermite–
Biehler is | 𝐸 ( 𝑧 )| > | 𝐸 ∗ ( 𝑧 )| for Im 𝑧 > 0, where 𝐸 ∗ ( 𝑧 ) = 𝐸 ( 𝑧 ). The divisor equality for 𝐴𝜉 is part of
the arithmetic datum; Hermite–Biehler positivity of an unrelated entire function says nothing about
zeros of Ξ.
Deﬁnition 58.6.3 (de Branges space H ( 𝐸𝜉 )). . Assuming 𝐸𝜉 = 𝐴𝜉 − 𝑖 𝐵 𝜉 is Hermite–Biehler (see (HB+ )
below), the de Branges space H ( 𝐸𝜉 ) is the reproducing-kernel Hilbert space of entire functions 𝑓 with
𝑓 / 𝐸𝜉 , 𝑓 ∗ / 𝐸𝜉 ∈ 𝐻 2 (ℂ+ ), with reproducing kernel

                                                 𝐸𝜉 (𝑤 ) 𝐸𝜉 ( 𝑧 ) − 𝐸𝜉∗ (𝑤 ) 𝐸𝜉∗ ( 𝑧 )
                               𝐾𝐸𝜉 (𝑤, 𝑧 ) =                                             .                   (58.5)
                                                            2𝜋 𝑖 (𝑤 − 𝑧 )
58.7. BD + : Beurling–Malliavin Super-Critical Density                                                          555


Proposition 58.6.4 (Hermite–Biehler kernel positivity). (de Branges 1968 Thm. 22; Lagarias
1999 Acta Arith. 89 §3). For an entire function 𝐸 = 𝐴 − 𝑖 𝐵 of bounded type in ℂ+ , the following are
equivalent:
   (i) 𝐸 is Hermite–Biehler: | 𝐸 ( 𝑧 )| > | 𝐸 ∗ ( 𝑧 )| for Im 𝑧 > 0.
  (ii) The reproducing kernel 𝐾𝐸 ( 𝑤, 𝑧 ) of (58.5) is positive-semidefinite: 𝑗,𝑘 𝑐𝑗 𝑐𝑘 𝐾𝐸 ( 𝑤 𝑘 , 𝑤𝑗 ) ≥ 0
                                                                             P
       for every finite collection ( 𝑤𝑗 , 𝑐𝑗 ).
If these conditions hold, the zeros of the real entire functions 𝐴 = ( 𝐸 + 𝐸 ∗ )/2 and 𝐵 = ( 𝐸 − 𝐸 ∗ )/(2 𝑖 )
are real; if 𝐸 has no real zeros, these zeros are simple and interlace.

Proof. (1) ⇔ (2): de Branges 1968 Thm. 22 proves that 𝐾𝐸 is positive-semidefinite exactly when 𝐸 is
Hermite–Biehler. The forward implication uses the Szegő/Blaschke factorisation of | 𝐸 | 2 − | 𝐸 ∗ | 2 as a
positive harmonic function on ℂ+ ; the converse uses that positive-semidefiniteness of 𝐾𝐸 at the specific
points 𝑤 = 𝑧 implies | 𝐸 ( 𝑧 )| 2 ≥ | 𝐸 ∗ ( 𝑧 )| 2 strictly in the open upper half plane. The last assertion is the
Hermite–Biehler separation theorem.

Theorem 58.6.5 (Hermite–Biehler real-part control forces zero placement). . Under (HB+ ), the
zero multi-set Z𝜉 of Ξ is contained in ℝ.

Proof. By (HB+ ), 𝐸𝜉 = 𝐴𝜉 − 𝑖 𝐵 𝜉 is Hermite–Biehler and div( 𝐴𝜉 ) = div( Ξ). The Hermite–Biehler
separation theorem gives that every zero of 𝐴𝜉 is real. Hence every zero of Ξ is real.

Corollary 58.6.6 (zero multi-set is real under HB + ). . Under (HB+ ), no non-trivial zero of 𝜉ℝ
has Im 𝛾 ≠ 0 in the coordinate 𝜌 = 21 + 𝑖 𝛾 .

Proof. Chapter 58.6.5 gives 𝛾 ∈ ℝ for every zero.

Remark 58.6.7 (HB+ is an RH-strength datum). Chapter 58.6.6 shows that (HB+ ), including real-part
divisor control over Ξ, forces every non-trivial zero 𝛾 of Ξ to be real. Translated back via 𝜌 = 21 + 𝑖 𝛾 , this
is exactly Re 𝜌 = 21 . Thus (HB+ ) is not a soft positivity assumption: it already contains the de Branges
real-part mechanism at RH strength.

Theorem 58.7.2 (Beurling–Malliavin completeness theorem). (Beurling–Malliavin, Acta
Math. 107 (1962); Koosis, The Logarithmic Integral II (Cambridge 1992) Ch. VIII). Let Λ = { 𝜆𝑘 } ⊂ ℝ.
The exponential system { 𝑒 𝑖𝜆𝑘 𝑥 } is complete in 𝐿 2 ((− 𝜋 𝑎, 𝜋 𝑎)) for every 𝑎 < 𝐷BM ( Λ) and incomplete

Proposition 58.7.3 (BD + gives uniqueness sampling). . Under (BD+ ) and (HB+ ) (Chapter 58.4.3),
the evaluation map

                        H ( 𝐸𝜉 ) → ℓ 2 (Z𝜉 ; | 𝐾𝐸𝜉 | −1 ) ,   𝑓 ↦→ ( 𝑓 ( 𝛾 )) 𝛾 ∈ Z𝜉 ,

is injective on the Paley–Wiener realisation of H ( 𝐸𝜉 ). If the stronger sampling inequality is included,
the values on Z𝜉 determine 𝑓 by the corresponding de Branges interpolation formula.

Proof. The exponential type of 𝐸𝜉 is 𝜋 (normalised so that Ξ has exponential type 𝜋 ; Lagarias 1999 §4.2).
Beurling–Malliavin (Chapter 58.7.2) gives completeness for strict density and leaves the endpoint to an
explicit completeness assumption. This is exactly the BD+ clause. Under (HB+ ) the set Z𝜉 is real, so the
exponentials are defined on 𝐿 2 ((− 𝜋, 𝜋 )). The de Branges space H ( 𝐸𝜉 ) is the Paley–Wiener realisation
of this space under the Mellin–Fourier transform associated with 𝐸𝜉 (de Branges 1968 Ch. III; Lagarias
1999 §4). Completeness says that no non-zero vector is orthogonal to all exponentials, which is injectivity
of the sampling map. A reconstruction formula requires the stronger sampling inequality, hence is part
of the strengthened input.

Corollary 58.7.4 (zero set is sampling for H ( 𝐸 𝜉 ) ). . Under (HB+ ) + (BD+ ), the zero multi-set
satisfies Z𝜉 ⊂ ℝ and is a uniqueness family for H ( 𝐸𝜉 ): no non-zero element of H ( 𝐸𝜉 ) vanishes on all
of Z𝜉 . If the strengthened sampling inequality is imposed, the values on Z𝜉 reconstruct the function.

Proof. (HB+ ) and Chapter 58.6.6 give Z𝜉 ⊂ ℝ. (BD+ ) and Chapter 58.7.3 give injectivity of the evalua-
tion map.

58.8   Main Theorem: (HB + ) + (BD + ) + (Det) ⇒ RH
Theorem 58.8.1 (VB ∗ main-direction implication). . Assume the spectral positivity hypothesis
(SH) + (Det) + (HB+ ) + (BD+ ) of Chapter 58.4.3 on the primary Fock. Then all non-trivial zeros of 𝜉ℝ
lie on the critical line Re 𝑠 = 21 . Equivalently, Z𝜉 ⊂ ℝ; equivalently, RH holds.

Proof. By (HB+ ) and Chapter 58.6.5, Z𝜉 ⊂ ℝ. The definition of Z𝜉 then gives 𝜌 = 21 + 𝑖 𝛾 𝜌 with
𝛾 𝜌 ∈ ℝ for every non-trivial zero of 𝜉ℝ . Thus Re 𝜌 = 21 .
Remark 58.8.2 (the logical order of the hypotheses). The zero-placement implication uses the real-part
divisor control in (HB+ ). The clauses (SH), (Det), and (BD+ ) belong to the stronger spectral-measure
hypothesis: they concern positivity, uniqueness, and sampling of the zero measure, not the realness of
the zeros itself.
Corollary 58.8.3 (valid forms of the main-direction implication). . Each of the following
hypotheses suffices for RH:
   (i) (HB+ ), where (HB+ ) includes real-part divisor control over Ξ (reduces to Chapter 58.6.6).
  (ii) The full conjunction (SH) + (Det) + (HB+ ) + (BD+ ).
 (iii) A de Branges formulation in which the real part of the specified Hermite–Biehler function has
       divisor div Ξ.
 (iv) The Conrey–Li 2000 construction: H ( 𝐸𝜉 ) admitting a self-adjoint multiplication operator
       whose spectral measure is the zero-counting measure on Z𝜉 ∩ ℝ.
No assertion is made that (SH) + (Det) + (BD+ ) alone gives zero placement without the Hermite–Biehler
or real-spectrum input. The main theorem proves the sufficient implication stated above.
58.9. Analytic Hypotheses on 𝜉 ℝ                                                                         557


Proof. (1): Chapter 58.6.5. (2): the theorem itself. (3): Lagarias Acta Arith. 89 (1999), with the de Branges
datum specified. (4): Conrey–Li arXiv:math/9812166 Thm. 2, with real spectrum part of the hypothesis.


Theorem 58.8.4 (main direction as a component of Chapter 37.4.2). . The positive Hamburger
and sampling spectral hypothesis stated in Chapter 37.4.1 and used in Chapter 37.4.2 is precisely the
conjunction (SH) + (Det) + (HB+ ) + (BD+ ) of Chapter 58.4.3. Chapter 58.8.1 records the implication
from this conjunction to RH inside the P1, P2, P3 framework of Chapter 37.4.2.

Proof. The spectral hypothesis of Chapter 37.4.1 names ‘‘the positive Hamburger spectral condition:
VB∗ on the primary Fock, equivalently the strengthened HB+ /BD+ forms of Chapter 36.4.14’’; this
unpacks to (SH), (Det), (HB+ ), (BD+ ) by Chapter 36.4.16. The implication is Chapter 58.8.1.

58.9    Analytic Hypotheses on 𝜉 ℝ
Remark 58.9.1 (analytic content). Chapter 58.8.1 proves the main-direction implication from the four
hypotheses. It does not prove RH, because none of HB+ , BD+ , or (Det) is proved for 𝜉ℝ by the Hadamard
product alone. The three analytic assertions have different logical strength:
• (HB+ ) proof is RH (Chapter 36.4.9; de Branges 1994).
• (BD+ ) proof is a quantitative spectral-regularity input with the Petersson constant fixed
  (Chapter 36.4.13).
• (Det) proof is the positive regularised moment functional with 𝑀21/(2

Theorem 58.9.2 (sufficient residual form of RH). . Under P2, P3, H-PAr , the conjunction of the
four conditions (SH), (Det), (HB+ ), (BD+ ) on the primary Fock implies the Riemann Hypothesis. The
converse is not asserted here.

Proof. This is exactly Chapter 58.8.1. The reverse implication would require the spectral-regularity
hypotheses of Chapter 36.4.14, and is not part of this theorem.

Remark 58.9.3 (the analytic arrow). The analytic content is the main-direction arrow

                              (SH) + (Det) + (HB+ ) + (BD+ ) =⇒ RH,

isolating the analytic content as the proof of these four hypotheses on 𝜉ℝ . The main-direction argument
makes the sufficient chain explicit and identifies the exact shape of the required analytic theorem.
Remark 58.9.4 (relation to the structural equivalence). Chapter 36.4.14 gives a conditional comparison
between Reg, HB+ , BD+ , and the VB∗ converse under P2, P3, H-PAr , and the stated Fock-space identifi-
cations. The complementary arrow is (SH) + (Det) + (HB+ ) + (BD+ ) ⇒ RH. Together they say that
regularity is the needed input and that the full spectral hypothesis is sufficient for RH.

   (i) 𝜉ℝ is entire of order 1, Hadamard genus 1, with 𝜉ℝ ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉ℝ (1 − 𝑠 ); hence Ξ ( 𝑧 ) = 𝜉ℝ ( 21 + 𝑖 𝑧 )

Unconditional Bound on 𝑆 (𝑇 )
Theorem 59.2.3 (unconditional Titchmarsh bound on 𝑆 ( 𝑇 ) ). (Titchmarsh §9.4; Selberg 1944).
The quantity 𝑆 (𝑇 ) defined in (59.2) satisfies

                                   | 𝑆 (𝑇 )| ≤ 𝐶 log 𝑇       (𝑇 ≥ 2) ,                             (59.4)

for an absolute constant 𝐶 > 0. The classical unconditional constant is 𝐶 = 1/ 𝜋 plus an
𝑂 (log log 𝑇 /log 𝑇 ) remainder (Titchmarsh §9.4, Selberg 1944); the sharper Korobov–Vinogradov
zero-free region lowers this further.

Proof. The argument is classical Hadamard–Jensen. By Jensen’s formula applied to 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) on discs centred
at 𝑠 = 2 + 𝑖𝑇 of radius 3/2, the number N (𝑇 , ℎ) of zeros with 𝑇 − ℎ < 𝛾 ≤ 𝑇 + ℎ satisfies

                                        N (𝑇 , 1) = 𝑂 (log 𝑇 ) ,                                    (59.5)

by the Hadamard factorisation of 𝜉ℝ ( 𝑠 ) and the usual Stirling–convexity bound for Γ ( 𝑠 /2) 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) in
vertical strips (Titchmarsh §5.1).
   The argument function arg 𝜁 (1/2 + 𝑖𝑇 ) is continuous in 𝑇 except at zeros, where it jumps by 𝜋 per
zero. Between consecutive zeros it varies by a bounded amount; integration of 𝜁 ′ / 𝜁 over a short contour
combined with (59.5) gives

                                | arg 𝜁 (1/2 + 𝑖𝑇 )| ≤ log 𝑇 · (1 + 𝑜 (1))

for 𝑇 large. Dividing by 𝜋 yields | 𝑆 (𝑇 )| ≤ 𝜋 −1 log 𝑇 (1 + 𝑜 (1)). The sharper constant 𝐶 = 1/ 𝜋 with
the error 𝑂 (log log 𝑇 /log 𝑇 ) follows from Selberg 1944.

Corollary 59.2.4 ( 𝑁 ( 𝑇 ) to main term, log 𝑇 precision). . Combining (59.1) and (59.4),

                                              𝑇       𝑇
                                  𝑁 (𝑇 ) =       log      + 𝑂 (log 𝑇 ) ,
                                              2𝜋     2𝜋 𝑒
unconditionally. No RH content is used; only the functional equation, Stirling, and the Jensen-disc
zero count.

Proof. Substitute the 𝑆 (𝑇 ) bound into (59.1) and absorb the 7/8 and 𝑂 (1/𝑇 ) into the 𝑂 (log 𝑇 ) bound.

The Gaussian Test Family

Remark 59.3.3 (on the admissibility of Gaussians for Weil). The classical Weil explicit formula (59.6)
requires compactly supported 𝑓b. The Gaussian 𝑓b𝜆 is not compactly supported, so the literal classical
formula does not apply. However, Burnol 2000 (Sur certains espaces de Hilbert de fonctions entières) and
Meyer R. 2005 (A distributional approach to Selberg’s moments and later work) extend the explicit formula
to a class of Schwartz test functions that includes the Gaussians, via the convergent Dirichlet series on the
prime side; the archimedean term is a convergent integral against Stirling’s digamma expansion. We use
this extension; see Cartier–Voros 1990 (in Grothendieck Festschrift Vol. II) for a self-contained derivation
of the Gaussian-admissible form.

Remark 59.3.12 (the Gaussian identity). Chapter 59.3.11 shows only the balanced explicit-formula identity
on Gaussian convolutions. It does not evaluate the Chapter 57 Weil positivity quadratic form. The latter
is the RH-equivalent object and is not supplied on any test class large enough to detect an off-line zero.
The closed form is the identity (59.12), not a positivity theorem.
Remark 59.3.13 (residual (H) Gaussian identity). Ch 41 Corollary 41.5.2 names residual (H) as the H-P
trace bridge; the Weil-at-Gaussians computation of Chapter 59.3.7 supplies the explicit form of the Weil
distribution against the Gaussian test family, which is the specific admissible test class needed for residual
(H) to be computed cleanly. The computation does not close H-PAr ; it supplies a clean Gaussian-level
reference for the Gaussian specialization of the balanced explicit formula.

59.4    Formal-Noetherian Terms R1.formal.b and R1.formal.c
Ch 32 (Chapter 32.4.4, Chapter 32.4.7) reduced R1.formal.b to (b.1) + (b.2) and R1.formal.c to (c.1) +

Lemma 59.4.2 (Noetherian local structure of Λ ). . Λ  ℤ 𝑝 [[𝑇 ]] is a two-dimensional regular local
Noetherian ring with maximal ideal 𝔪 = ( 𝑝, 𝑇 ) and residue field 𝔽 𝑝 . Its 𝔪-adic topology coincides
with the profinite topology.

Proof. This is Lang, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. VII §5. Regularity follows from the embedding
into ℤ 𝑝 [[𝑇 ]] which is a power-series ring over a regular local ring; dimension is 2; the maximal ideal is
finitely generated by ( 𝑝, 𝑇 ); the topology coincidence follows because both topologies are determined
by 𝔪𝑛 = ( 𝑝, 𝑇 ) 𝑛 ⊃ 𝑝𝑛 Λ + 𝑇 𝑛 Λ.

59.5   Consequences
Proposition 59.5.1 (three exact inputs). . The following assertions hold.
   (i) The sharp Riemann–von Mangoldt identity (59.1) with | 𝑆 (𝑇 )| = 𝑂 (log 𝑇 ) is unconditional
       (Chapter 59.2.1, Chapter 59.2.3, Chapter 59.2.4). This proves the density estimate entering Ranalytic ,
       but not the positivity or linear-growth assertions.
  (ii) The Gaussian specialization of the balanced Weil explicit formula is the closed identity (59.11)
       and (59.12). The convolution identity (59.13) is only the balanced explicit formula and is not a
       Weil-positivity statement (Chapter 59.3.12).
 (iii) The 𝔪-adically-complete pieces of R1.formal.b and R1.formal.c satisfy Artin–Rees over the Iwa-
       sawa algebra (Chapter 59.4.6, Chapter 59.4.7).

Proof. The first assertion is Chapter 59.2.1 together with Chapter 59.2.3. The second assertion is Chap-
ter 59.3.7 and Chapter 59.3.11. The third assertion is Chapter 59.4.6 and Chapter 59.4.7. None of these
assertions is the Weil positivity criterion, the Hilbert–Polya assertion, or the derived-formal comparison
away from the Noetherian sector.

Chapter 55: V prim P3 and Koszul–Petersson Compatibility
The native positivity statements of Chapter 55.2.1 and Chapter 55.2.3 require an injective automorphic
realization and the pairing maps of Chapter 26.1.1. Under these maps the Koszul–Petersson identity
follows from the bilinear Hilbert–Schmidt pairing and modular conjugation. On an actual cuspidal 𝐿 2
space, positivity is the positivity of its integral norm.
    Ramanujan bounds constrain Satake parameters; they do not produce the native maps. Chapter 55.2.4
gives an Euler-factor bound and a separate norm criterion for comparing realization maps. The discrete-
spectrum conclusion of Chapter 55.3.6 also requires the compatible pairing blocks of Chapter 55.3.3: 𝑐
preserves the dual blocks, and 𝐵 vanishes between distinct blocks. The stated adelic assembly is required
on each block. For the continuous spectrum, the native pairing measure and the regularized automorphic
measure must be identified before the Langlands–Shahidi normalization can transfer an identity of forms.
The Li trace needs its own spectral realization.

Chapter 56: The Hilbert–Pólya Operator Skeleton
Chapter 56.2.5 constructs the product GNS operator 𝑁BC = − 21 log Δ1 at inverse temperature one. Its
point eigenvalues are 21 log( 𝑎/𝑏 ), each with infinite multiplicity, and its spectrum is ℝ. The positive
occupation weights belong to 𝑁occ on ℓ 2 (ℕ× ). Chapter 56.3.1 proves 𝑊 𝑁occ = 2 𝑁BC𝑊 onto the
closed creation subspace. The weighted zero-mode embedding is 𝛿𝑚 ↦→ 𝑚 −1/2 [ 𝜇𝑚 ]. An oscillator
extension requires the additional lift of Chapter 56.3.5.
    The product GNS space is an incomplete Hilbert tensor product of local GNS spaces; it is not
identified with global Hilbert–Schmidt operators at 𝛽 = 1. Indeed the occupation Gibbs density has
infinite trace there. Its phases and its comparison with native arithmetic objects are separate from this
tensor construction.
576                                Chapter 60. The Archimedean Tate Positivity Reduction


   The determinant and trace assertions of Chapter 56.5.1 and Chapter 56.6.1 require a zero-divisor
operator and a compatible regularization. Occupation weights supply neither. Literal vacuum-preserving
intertwining with 𝑁occ is excluded by Chapter 56.4.2. The proposed grading and the self-adjoint zero
operator must therefore be specified separately.

Chapter 57: HP–Li Positivity and the Archimedean Residual
For an actual cusp form, Chapter 57.4.1 computes the Rankin–Selberg integral from its own Fourier
coefficients. The finite-prime form on A = 𝐶𝑐∞ (ℝ) has the signed translation representation (57.6).
On the two-dimensional space 𝑉𝑏 , Proposition 57.7.2 constructs explicit positive and negative lines. Its
positive-line isometry is an actual restricted comparison. The negative line excludes an extension as a
positive Hilbert norm on the full test algebra. For the complete arithmetic form, (57.7) gives a signed
zero-evaluation representation, with the finite-prime, polar, and gamma terms unchanged. Positivity on
all tests is equivalent to RH by Chapter 57.7.4. The Rankin–Selberg norm supplies no equality with
these prime weights.

Chapter 58: VB∗ Main Direction
Chapter 58.8.1 () records the conditional implication (SH) + (Det) + (HB+ ) + (BD+ ) ⇒ RH on
the primary Fock space. Chapter 58.9.2 records RH as the four-way conjunction of these analytic hy-
potheses on 𝜉ℝ . Primary sources: de Branges 1968 monograph; Lagarias 1999 Acta Arith. 89; Conrey–Li
arXiv:math/9812166; Beurling–Malliavin 1962 Acta Math. 107; Hamburger 1920 Math. Ann. 81; Car-
leman 1922/1926; Koosis 1992 Log. Integral II; Levin 1980 AMS Monograph. The Hermite–Biehler
positivity assertion is RH-equivalent; the BD+ and (Det) assertions are the additional spectral-regularity
inputs isolated in Chapter 36. Their proof is not attempted in Chapter 58.

Chapter 59: Density of Zeros, Weil at Gaussians, and Formal-Noetherian Closures
Chapter 59.2.1 () establishes the sharp Riemann–von Mangoldt density with the Titchmarsh bound
| 𝑆 (𝑇 )| = 𝑂 (log 𝑇 ) unconditionally. Chapter 59.3.7 () gives the closed-form Weil evaluation on Gaus-
sians. Chapter 74.2.3 determines the exact Gaussian sign range of the gamma form. The complete Weil
value retains the polar and finite-prime terms. Chapter 59.4.6 () closes R1.formal.b on the 𝔪-adically-
complete sector; Chapter 59.4.7 () closes R1.formal.c.2 on the same sector. Primary sources: Riemann
1859 Monatsber. Berlin Akad.; von Mangoldt 1895 J. Reine Angew. Math. 114; Titchmarsh 1986 (2nd
edn); Selberg 1944; Weil 1952; Tate 1950; Burnol 2000; Cartier–Voros 1990; Atiyah–Macdonald 1969;
Bourbaki 1961 (Alg. Comm. III); Lang 1994. The positivity/linear-upper-growth portion of Ranalytic
is RH-adjacent and remains open; R1.formal.c.1 (Arinkin–Gaitsgory derived-formal extension) and
R1.formal.c.3 (Fargues–Scholze flat-locus matching) each require a genuine theorem condition.

      60.4     The Refined Sufficient Path to RH
      The sufficient path of Chapter 22.6.1 took four inputs:
   (P1) arithmetic Positselski: the G-row biconditional 𝜅GAr + ( 𝜅 ! )GAr = 0 ⇔ 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 );
  (KP) Koszul–Petersson compatibility ⟨𝑣, 𝑤 ⟩ Pet = ⟨𝑣, 𝜎 BC ( 𝑤 )⟩ Koszul on V prim ;
  (HP) Hilbert–PólyaAr : a self-adjoint 𝐻HP with det∞ ( 𝑠 id − Θ𝜉 ) = 𝜉ℝ ( 𝑠 ) and Weil–Connes trace distribu-
        tion;
(HPLi) HP–Li positivity: 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓 ∗ ) ≥ 0 on admissible Weil test functions.

      Form of the Four Inputs After Chapters 49–59
         (i) P1 (arithmetic Positselski). Upgraded from Conditional to conditional theorem on the abelian
             Heisenberg sector by Chapter 54.5.3. The remaining condition is the Consani–Marcolli adele-class
             duality used in Chapter 54; the non-abelian Iwahori extension is explicit out-of-domain.
        (ii) KP (Koszul–Petersson compatibility). On the native discrete core the identity requires the
             pairing maps, compatible pairing blocks, injective automorphic realization, and assembly hypothe-
             ses of Chapter 55.3.6. These conditions apply also to holomorphic and residual sectors; Maass
             parameter bounds are additional analytic information.
       (iii) HP (Hilbert–Pólya). The operator 𝑁occ supplies weights log 𝑚, with 𝑊 𝑁occ = 2 𝑁BC𝑊 at
             𝛽 = 1 (Chapter 56.3.1). The determinant-divisor and trace comparison in Chapter 56.4.3 remain
             additional data; literal vacuum-preserving intertwining fails.
       (iv) HPLi (HP–Li positivity). The full compact-test form has the signed representation (57.7). The
             positive line in Proposition 57.7.2 realizes only the finite-prime restriction. Full HP–Li positiv-
             ity is strictly equivalent to archimedean Tate positivity A-TP (Chapter 57.2.4), which is strictly
             equivalent to RH.

Proof. Chapter 57.2.4 proves the biconditional A-TP ⇔ Weil positivity on admissible Weil test functions.

Remark 60.5.2 (Reduction to A-TP). Chapter 60.5.1 is a reduction, not a proof of RH. Its content is
the isolation of an archimedean positive-trace obstruction equivalent to RH. The arithmetic-chiral-
algebra framework relocates the Hilbert–Pólya and Weil-positivity obstructions from their classical form
as an opaque positive-trace inequality on the full Paley–Wiener cone to a specific archimedean Tate
distributional inequality, preserving the logical equivalence with RH. It does not assert that the other
arithmetic comparison problems have disappeared.
Remark 60.5.3 (relation to A-TP, Connes, and VB∗ ). The three RH-strength formulations are:
   (i) A-TP: archimedean Tate positivity on A (Chapter 57.2.3);
  (ii) Connes absorption-trace condition: existence of a self-adjoint operator on a specified arithmetic
       Hilbert space, with a separate comparison to the product GNS carrier, whose normal zero-divisor
       operator has determinant divisor div 𝜉ℝ and Weil–Connes trace equal to the zero distribution
       (Chapter 56.4.3);
 (iii) the de Branges/Hermite–Biehler, Báez–Duarte, and determinant spectral-regularity conditions
       on 𝜉ℝ (Chapter 58.8.3, Chapter 36.4.14).
60.6. Disjoint-Source Comparison                                                                     581


These three are forms of the same zero-placement difficulty, not unconditional theorems. A-TP is the
harmonic-analytic form on the archimedean place; the operator realization additionally requires the
specified carrier and trace maps; the VB∗ condition is the complex-analytic form on the entire character
𝜉ℝ . Chapter 58.8.3 and Chapter 36.4.14 establish their precise logical relationship.

Independence Statement
Proposition 60.6.1 (orthogonal source comparison). . No source appears on both sides of any
single ProvedHere statement’s proof and comparison sources across Chapters 49–59. Cross-chapter
sharing (e.g., Bost–Connes 1995 appears in Chs. 52, 54, 55, 56) occurs only as comparison sources, never
as proof sources for the same mathematical assertion.

Proof. The source lists above give:
• The derivation corpus of the arithmetic branch (the initial construction of Chapters 1–48, the bar–
  cobar calculation of Beilinson–Drinfeld 2004, the Positselski derivation Positselski 2009/2011, the
  Bost–Connes derivation of the 𝐶 ∗ -algebra structure in Bost–Connes 1995 §1.2 used in the Chapters
  1–48 disjointness comparison) does not recur as a comparison source within the same chapter. The
  comparison sources of Chapters 49–59 are always drawn from the disjoint lists above.
• Within Ch. 54, the sub-item closures use four disjoint classical theorems (Pontryagin 1934, Greenlees–
  May 1992, Matlis 1958, Bost–Connes 1995 + Consani–Marcolli 2006) on four disjoint sub-statements.
• Within Ch. 52, the three closures use three disjoint lists: Chenevier 2014 + Bellaiche–Chenevier 2009
  for (Ch1); GKRW 2024 + BFN 2008 + AG 2015 for (AG.det); Lurie HA + Francis–Gaitsgory 2012
  for F2.c.
• Bost–Connes 1995 appears in Chs. 52, 54, 55, 56 but in each case it is used as a primary-source com-
  parison for a distinct structural claim (Koszul-dual description in Ch. 54; tempered cuspidal KMS1
  identification in Ch. 55; operator skeleton in Ch. 56). In each case the proof source for the claim is
  different (bar–cobar in Vol I; comodule–contramodule in Positselski; GNS formalism in Takesaki).
  No single claim uses Bost–Connes 1995 on both sides.
The disjointness holds globally across Chapters 49–59.

60.7    Implication Form
The reductions used in the sufficient path have the following formal content.

Implications
Chapters 49–59 contain the following implications:
• Arithmetic Positselski (Conditional → conditional theorem on abelian Heisenberg sector) via
  Ch. 54.
• G-row biconditional P1 (Conditional → conditional theorem on abelian Heisenberg sector) via
  Ch. 54.
• Koszul–Petersson compatibility on discrete core (conditional on native pairing maps, compatible
  pairing blocks, and injective automorphic realization in every sector) via Ch. 55.
• F1.a.3.C wild-EG compact generation (Conjectured → conditional theorem; wild-prime local model
  remains open) via Ch. 51.
• (Ch1) Chenevier cross-prime pseudocharacter (Conjectured → conditional theorem) via Ch. 52.
60.8. Domain of Chapters 49–59                                                                      583


• F2.c restricted-tensor 𝐸2 transport (Conjectured → conditional theorem on the central idempotent
  pointed-unit 𝐸2 domain) via Ch. 52.
• Signed arithmetic comparison. The complete compact-test identity and explicit positive and negative
  finite-prime lines are equation (57.7) and Proposition 57.7.2.
• VB∗ main direction (Conditional → formal implication (SH) + (Det) + (HB+ ) + (BD+ ) ⇒ RH)
  via Ch. 58.
• 𝑁BC log-modular operator (implicit Conditional → Theorem, unconditional) via Ch. 56.
• Riemann–von Mangoldt density (implicit reference → Theorem, unconditional in sharp form) via
  Ch. 59.
• Weil at Gaussians (Heuristic → Theorem, closed form) via Ch. 59.
• F1.a.3.A block-additivity, generic-block Ext1 , R1.formal.b/c.2 (Conjectured/Conditional → Theo-
  rem on stated domain) via Chs. 50, 59.

Conjectural Conditions
The unresolved conjectural assertions are four:
   (i) A-TP (archimedean Tate positivity): strictly equivalent to RH.
  (ii) Connes absorption trace (twist existence): strictly equivalent to RH.
 (iii) HB+ /BD+ /(Det) on 𝜉ℝ : HB+ is RH-equivalent by Lagarias 1999; BD+ and (Det) are spectral-
       regularity inputs.
 (iv) Maass Ramanujan conjecture: external open problem in the Langlands programme, independent
       of RH.
   The adjacent spectral assertions are:
  (v) (AG.det.transition) 𝐸2 -centre gluing on the codimension-2 transition locus.
 (vi) (BCglue.local) ℓ = 𝑝 local transition theorem for coherent Springer sheaves.
(vii) (BCglue.glue) prismatic-flat cross-prime coherent sheaf descent.
    The Paskunas/F1.a local categorical conditions are (R.A, R.B.1, R.B.2, F1.a.1 non-ordinary, F1.a.2
class-match, R1.formal.c.1/c.3), which are finite theorem conditions outside the RH-equivalent analytic
residual.

60.8    Domain of Chapters 49–59
Chapters 49–59 operate within the following domain boundaries.
   (i) A-TP and RH. Chapter 57.2.4 establishes the strict equivalence A-TP ⇔ RH (Chapter 57.2.3).
       The arithmetic-chiral-algebra framework relocates the Weil positivity obstruction from the full
       Paley–Wiener cone to the archimedean gamma distribution; the obstruction itself is preserved
       with full logical equivalence to RH.
  (ii) LACD on the cuspidal sector. Chapter 49 closes the cuspidal sector. The Eisenstein extension
       requires Langlands–Shahidi intertwining theory in coherent-categorical form, or a Moœglin–
       Waldspurger residual-spectrum categorification; these are open conditions outside the domain of
       Chapter 49.
 (iii) (BCglue.local) and (BCglue.glue). The transition theorem across the ℓ ≠ 𝑝 / ℓ = 𝑝 divide for
       coherent Springer sheaves (BCglue.local) is not in the literature. The prismatic-flat cross-prime
584                                  Chapter 60. The Archimedean Tate Positivity Reduction


      descent lifted to the coherent-sheaf level (BCglue.glue) requires extensions beyond Bhatt–Scholze
      2022 and Bhatt–Lurie 2022. Both are primary-source theorem conditions.
 (iv) Maass Ramanujan. Chapter 55 uses the Kim–Sarnak bound 𝜃 ≤ 7/64 only as a local exponent
      estimate. It gives no Dirichlet-summable Euler error on the Maass sector. Full closure on the
      Maass sector depends on the Ramanujan conjecture, an external open problem in the Langlands
      programme.
  (v) Hilbert–Pólya operator with zeta-zero determinant divisor. Chapter 56 constructs the occu-
      pation operator 𝑁occ with eigenvalues log 𝑚, and identifies it with 2 𝑁BC on the creation subspace
      at 𝛽 = 1. The twist to an operator with determinant divisor div 𝜉ℝ and Weil–Connes zero trace is
      the Connes absorption-trace conjecture, equivalent to the Hilbert–Pólya/RH obstruction.
 (vi) HB+ , BD+ , (Det) on 𝜉ℝ . Chapter 58 proves the implication (SH) + (Det) + (HB+ ) + (BD+ ) ⇒
      RH. The proof of each of the four hypotheses on 𝜉ℝ lies outside the domain of Chapter 58.
(vii) Remaining primary-source conditions. The non-RH categorical hypotheses are
      (AG.det.transition), (BCglue.local), (BCglue.glue), the Eisenstein extension of LACD , the
      Paskunas narrow residuals, the non-ordinary F1.a.1/F1.a.2 extensions, and the R1.formal extensions.
      The analytic hypothesis A-TP is RH-equivalent and is not absorbed by these categorical
      hypotheses.
Remark 60.8.1 (Structure of the obstruction set). Chapters 49–59 separate structural comparison data
from analytic hardness. The obstruction set decomposes into four classes: (i) theorems on their stated
domains; (ii) narrow-domain categorical residuals; (iii) primary-source conditions (AG.det.transition,
BCglue.local, BCglue.glue, Eisenstein extension); (iv) the RH-equivalent residual A-TP. Other compar-
ison residuals remain visible; they are not implied by A-TP.

60.9    Further Obstructions
The remaining obstructions are as follows.

Direct Positivity for A-TP

Langlands–Shahidi Extension of LACD
The Eisenstein/continuous-spectrum extension of LACD can be attempted via Shahidi 2010 (AMS Col-
loquium 58) normalisation theory. The required object is a categorical lift of the intertwining operators
𝑀 ( 𝑠 ) of Moeglin–Waldspurger 1995 §IV, realising LACD on the continuous spectrum compatible with
the Weil-positive extension. The alternative domain-restricted correction (Correction (a) of Ch. 55) suf-
fices only for the discrete trace normalisation of the Li path after the stated H-PAr spectral identification;
the Langlands–Shahidi extension reduces the full V prim identity to the same measure identification.
60.10. Boundary                                                                                       585


Paskunas Wild-Prime Class Match
Residuals (R.A), (R.B.1), (R.B.2) of Ch. 50 remain open. (R.A) is the per-block BH projective-to-closed-
point matching and is block-local over each Bernstein block. (R.B.1) is the very-special Breuil–Mezard
multiplicity. (R.B.2) is the Paskunas block-centraliser structure theorem lifted from 𝑝 ≥ 5 to 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3}.
None is RH-equivalent; each is a finite explicit computation.

(AG.det.transition) Direct Obstruction
(AG.det.transition) is the 𝐸2 -centre compatibility on the transition locus of the determinantal Selmer
cleavage. The theorem condition consists of Arinkin–Gaitsgory 2012 (nilp SSupp on the two strata) +
Galatius–Kupers–Randal-Williams 2024 ( 𝐸2 -centre cellular structure) + Ben-Zvi–Francis–Nadler 2008
( 𝐻 𝐻𝐸•2 of smooth sub-stack). The combination is a primary-source theorem condition. The transition
locus is codimension at most 2 on the determinantal sector; the compatibility is a sheaf-gluing datum.

Connes Absorption-Trace Realisation
The Connes absorption-trace conjecture (Chapter 56.4.3) is the operator-algebraic formulation of the
Hilbert–Pólya obstruction. A direct obstruction requires: (i) a Hilbert space H𝜉 carrying a natural
action of the BC automorphism group; (ii) an identification of the twist data (𝑈 , 𝐴) with the action
of a specific Wilson-line or intertwining operator on the archimedean adelic sector. Consani–Marcolli
2006 supply the adele-class space framework; the realization of a zero-divisor operator with a compatible
arithmetic trace remains an additional construction. It cannot be literal intertwining of the occupation
grading on the vacuum, by Chapter 56.4.2.

Hermite–Biehler Positivity on 𝜉ℝ
Hermite–Biehler positivity for 𝐸𝜉 ( 𝑧 ) = 𝐴𝜉 ( 𝑧 ) − 𝑖 𝐵 𝜉 ( 𝑧 ) is equivalent to RH by Lagarias 1999. An
obstruction requires either: (i) a direct proof that the real part 𝐴𝜉 has only real zeros and div( 𝐴𝜉 ) =
div( Ξ) (de Branges 1968 Thm. 22); (ii) explicit construction of a self-adjoint multiplication operator on
H ( 𝐸𝜉 ) with spectrum Z𝜉 ∩ ℝ (Conrey–Li 2000 Thm 2 negative direction); or (iii) a Conrey–Li-style
positive construction that avoids the Siegel-zero obstruction documented in Conrey–Li 2000 for certain
𝐿 -functions.

60.10    Boundary
   (i) Chapters 49–59 sharpened several residuals from Chapter 48 on the sufficient path of Chapter 22.
  (ii) The arithmetic Positselski equivalence upgrades from Conditional to a conditional theorem on
       the abelian Heisenberg sector (Chapter 54.5.2).
 (iii) The Koszul–Petersson compatibility on the native discrete-spectrum core requires the stated
       pairing and realization maps, preservation of dual blocks by 𝑐 , vanishing of mixed bilinear terms,
       and the adelic assembly (Chapter 55.3.6).
 (iv) The occupation grading is constructed by 𝑁occ , with its precisely normalized GNS comparison
       (Chapter 56.3.1); the zero-divisor operator requires a separate construction.
  (v) The complete Weil form has the signed comparison (57.7). The positive finite-prime line is con-
       structed in Proposition 57.7.2; extending its norm identity to the full test algebra is impossible.
 (vi) RH is equivalent to the archimedean Tate positivity conjecture A-TP (Chapter 57.2.3), on the
       stated path (Chapter 60.5.1).
586                                Chapter 60. The Archimedean Tate Positivity Reduction


 (vii) The reductions of Chapters 49–59 preserve the orthogonality of derivations and comparisons
       (Chapter 60.6.1).
(viii) The reductions leave no additional numerical identity hidden in the comparison chain; the re-
       maining content is analytic positivity or categorical gluing.
  (ix) A-TP locates one RH-equivalent hardness at the archimedean gamma distribution.
   (x) The remaining obstructions are: direct positivity for A-TP; Langlands–Shahidi extension of LACD ;
       Paskunas wild-prime class match; (AG.det.transition) sheaf-gluing; Connes absorption-trace real-
       isation; and the proof of HB+ /BD+ /(Det) on 𝜉ℝ .
   The arithmetic branch contains a mathematically explicit RH-equivalent archimedean statement:
the archimedean Tate positivity conjecture A-TP. It also contains the comparison residuals recorded in
the obstruction decomposition above.

The gamma term in the Weil formula has density 𝑘 ( 𝑢) = log 𝜋 − ℜ𝜓Γ (1/4 + 𝑖𝑢/2). It is positive
near zero and negative at large frequency. This sign is fixed by Fourier inversion, independently of any
positivity conjecture for the complete arithmetic form.

61.3    The complete Weil inequality
Put
                                      𝑅 [ 𝑓 ] = 𝑃 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓 ∗ ) − 𝑊fin ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓 ∗ ) .
The polar form has both signs. The finite-prime form also has both signs by Proposition 57.7.2.
Theorem 61.3.1 (the arithmetic inequality with all terms retained). For each 𝑓 ∈ A , the in-
equality 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓 ∗ ) ≥ 0 is exactly either of the following equivalent inequalities:

              𝐶 [ 𝑓 ] ≤ 𝐷 [ 𝑓 ] + 2𝜋 𝑅 [ 𝑓 ] ,       𝐴 [ 𝑓 ] + 4 𝜋 log 𝜋 ∥ 𝑓 ∥ 22 ≤ 𝐵 [ 𝑓 ] + 2 𝜋 𝑅 [ 𝑓 ] .   (61.4)

Requiring these inequalities for all 𝑓 ∈ A is equivalent to RH. The separate positive gamma cone does
not remove the terms in 𝑅 [ 𝑓 ].

Proof. Insert 𝑊 = 𝑅 − 𝑊∞ and the signed decomposition. The equivalence to RH is Weil’s criterion
on A .

Proposition 61.3.2 (limits of frequency restrictions). No nonzero 𝑓 ∈ A has ℎ 𝑓 supported in a
bounded real frequency interval. Neither compact support of 𝑓 nor nonnegativity of the auxiliary form
implies a fixed sign of the gamma form.

Proof. The Fourier transform ℎ 𝑓 is entire. Vanishing on a real interval forces it to vanish identically, and
Fourier inversion gives 𝑓 = 0. The dilation and modulation examples prove the sign assertions.

Remark 61.3.3 (comparison with the complete arithmetic form). The exact signed representation (57.7)
places the gamma term, both polar moments, and the prime translations on a common test algebra. A
positive realization of that complete form requires the full inequality (61.4).

62.3     Construction II: Weight 𝑘 → ∞ Limit Along Compatible Newforms

𝑘 → ∞; a compatible family of newforms of increasing weight furnishes an exhausting sequence of

Remark 62.3.7 (weight-limit is effectively the Selberg trace on 𝐺 𝐿2 ). Assuming Chapter 62.3.5, the right-

holomorphic-discrete-series contribution to the Selberg trace from its per-weight pieces. Obstruction
(O2) (Maass exclusion) is not lifted by this construction.

that limiting kernel is separately identified with the von Mangoldt distribution.

Remark 62.4.3 (Construction III lifts (H3)). Construction III absorbs the Tate-polar contribution into
the one-dimensional residual sector, eliminating Hypothesis (H3). It contributes nothing to (O1) or
(O2): the residual sector is one vector, not dense in any sector larger than its own span. The value of
Construction III is in removing Hypothesis (H3) as a restriction on the test class.

Proposition 62.5.3 (JPSS strip width remains bounded). . The JPSS convergence cone for 𝜋
cuspidal on GL𝑛 /ℚ gives, in the normalisation used here, a Mellin strip of width ( 𝑛 − 1)/(2𝑛). As
𝑛 → ∞ this tends to 1/2, not to the whole plane.
Proof. JPSS 1983 Prop. 3.1 gives the convergence half-plane for the RS integral as Re( 𝑠 ) > 1 − (2𝑛) −1 ;
the reflected strip on the critical line is |Re( 𝑠 ) − 1/2| < ( 𝑛 − 1)/(2𝑛), approaching 1/2 as 𝑛 → ∞.
Combined with weight-rank lifts, the strip width extends through higher symmetric powers but remains
bounded by 1/2. For holomorphic newforms these lifts are available by Gelbart–Jacquet, Kim–Shahidi,
Kim, and Newton–Thorne; for Maass forms the corresponding functoriality remains conjectural.

Remark 62.5.4 (JPSS construction against Ramanujan). The JPSS construction requires temperedness
of 𝜋 at every prime, which for an arbitrary cuspidal representation of GL𝑛 /ℚ is the generalised Ra-
manujan conjecture. For symmetric-power lifts of holomorphic newforms, functoriality is known by
Gelbart–Jacquet, Kim–Shahidi, Kim, and Newton–Thorne, and temperedness follows from Deligne’s
bound on the original GL2 parameters. For Maass symmetric powers and for general GL𝑛 cusp forms,
Construction IV remains conditional on temperedness.

Remark 62.7.2 (net domain of the extension). The extension of the Weil–Petersson isometry from PWhol      𝐹
to the Schwartz closure of PWext has three effects. (1) The test class widens to a Schwartz-dense subspace of

(3) The extension does not affect 𝑊∞ : each construction’s Petersson inner product uses an archimedean
local factor (holomorphic discrete series, Maass Bessel, residual vacuum, or higher-rank principal-series),
each evaluating to an | Γ | 2 -type archimedean density on the critical line, while 𝑊∞ evaluates to the log-
derivative Re 𝜓 . These two densities are unequal by Chapter 57.5.2; no choice of test class or archimedean
local type within the tempered Langlands spectrum converts one into the other.

62.10    Isometry Boundary
   (i) The Rankin–Selberg kernel comparison baseline (Chapter 57.6.1) closed the Weil–Petersson isom-
       etry on PWhol
                  𝐹
                     for a fixed holomorphic cuspidal eigenform of weight 𝑘 ≥ 12. The domain boundary
       was the Mellin-strip width ( 𝑘 − 1) of hypothesis (H2) and the (H3) Tate-polar vanishing.
  (ii) Four extension constructions address the domain boundary: Construction I (Maass) conditional
       on Ramanujan; Construction II (weight 𝑘 → ∞) unconditional with Petersson normalisation;
       Construction III (residual) absorbs Tate-polar; Construction IV (higher-rank JPSS) unconditional
       for symmetric powers ≤ 4.
 (iii) The union PWext (Chapter 62.6.1) is Schwartz-dense in PW(ℝ) (Chapter 62.6.2).
 (iv) Prime-side Weil positivity closes on PWext available (Chapter 62.6.3), then extends by Schwartz
       continuity to the full PW(ℝ) (Chapter 62.6.4).
  (v) The residual obstruction to full HP–Li positivity is exactly the A-TP archimedean Tate positivity
       (Chapter 62.7.1), strictly equivalent to RH (Chapter 57.2.4). The extension reduces the domain
       obstruction to the archimedean Tate constraint; it does not reduce the archimedean Tate constraint
       itself.

Langlands–Shahidi Normalisation of the
Eisenstein Koszul Density

The bounded-interval reduction, construction C. Chapter 55 (the restricted-class comparison) reduced Koszul–
Petersson compatibility on the discrete-spectrum core by domain restriction: the Eisenstein continuous sector
was placed outside the P3 identity, and the Li trace was separated from it under the H-PAr spectral realisation.
The Langlands–Shahidi alternative was sketched as the second normalisation of §55.4. The exact conditional
normalisation problem is this: multiplication by a Langlands–Shahidi scalar removes the unitary phase
only after a choice of positive Plancherel measure has been ﬁxed; the boundary Euler product on Re( 𝑠 ) = 1/2
is meromorphic, not absolutely convergent. Thus the Langlands–Shahidi normalisation is a conditional
construction, not an unconditional closure of the Eisenstein residual.

Lemma 63.1.1 (unit modulus of 𝜉 (2 𝑠 ) / 𝜉 (2 𝑠 − 1) on the critical line). . For 𝑠 = 1/2 + 𝑖𝑡 , away
from the Tate boundary and common zeros of the two factors,

                                               𝜉 (2 𝑠 )/ 𝜉 (2 𝑠 − 1) = 1.

Proof. For 𝑠 = 1/2 + 𝑖𝑡 , write 2 𝑠 = 1 + 2 𝑖𝑡 and 2 𝑠 − 1 = 2 𝑖𝑡 . The completed zeta 𝜉 satisfies 𝜉 ( 𝑤 ) = 𝜉 (1 −
𝑤 ) (functional equation; Titchmarsh 1986 §2.1), giving 𝜉 (1 + 2 𝑖𝑡 ) = 𝜉 (−2 𝑖𝑡 ). Complex conjugation
gives 𝜉 (1 + 2 𝑖𝑡 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 2 𝑖𝑡 ) (Schwarz reflection: 𝜉 is real on the real axis, hence 𝜉 ( 𝑤 ) = 𝜉 ( 𝑤 )).
Combining, 𝜉 (1 + 2 𝑖𝑡 ) · 𝜉 (1 + 2 𝑖𝑡 ) = 𝜉 (1 + 2 𝑖𝑡 ) 𝜉 (1 − 2 𝑖𝑡 ) = 𝜉 (1 + 2 𝑖𝑡 ) 𝜉 (2 𝑖𝑡 ) by the functional
equation. Similarly 𝜉 (2 𝑖𝑡 ) · 𝜉 (2 𝑖𝑡 ) = 𝜉 (2 𝑖𝑡 ) · 𝜉 (2 𝑖𝑡 ) = 𝜉 (2 𝑖𝑡 ) · 𝜉 (−2 𝑖𝑡 ) = 𝜉 (2 𝑖𝑡 ) · 𝜉 (1 + 2 𝑖𝑡 ) by
FE. Therefore | 𝜉 (2 𝑠 )| 2 = | 𝜉 (2 𝑠 − 1)| 2 , giving (63.1.1).

The ratio 𝜉 (2 𝑠 )/ 𝜉 (2 𝑠 − 1) has modulus one on the critical line, so it is a scattering phase, not a positive
density. Therefore the desired comparison cannot be a consequence of multiplying scalar densities. It is
precisely the conditional assertion that the bar–cobar Eisenstein quadratic form is transported to the
Shahidi positive Plancherel measure. With that transport supplied, (63.1) is the definition of the matched
normalisation.

Remark 63.2.3 (why no scalar square proves the match). The diagonal pairing is only a distributional
Maass–Selberg object before truncation is regularised. Since 𝜉 (2 𝑠 )/ 𝜉 (2 𝑠 − 1) has unit modulus on the
critical line, taking absolute values removes the phase but does not identify the underlying Plancherel
normalisation. The non-formal point is exactly the identification of the bar–cobar Eisenstein quadratic
form with the Shahidi positive Plancherel measure.

Under the LS redefinition Chapter 63.2.1, the Koszul and Petersson normalisations on the Eisenstein
continuous spectrum of 𝐿 2 ( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 ]) coincide after the positive Plancherel-measure identification.

Proof. Chapter 63.2.2 is the stated measure-identification hypothesis written in the LS normalisation.
No Ramanujan input is used on the continuum; the continuum is Eisenstein-induced and tempered on
the unitary axis by construction.

63.3    Compatibility Checks
Three compatibility properties of the LS-corrected pairing are verified: the arithmetic Heisenberg Koszul
self-duality 𝜅 Ar + ( 𝜅 ! ) Ar = 0 on the Eisenstein summand (check (i)); the Tate restricted-tensor factori-
sation of 𝑁 LS across places (check (ii)); and the compatibility with the discrete-core result of Chapter 55
(check (iii)).

Compatibility Check (i): Heisenberg Self-Duality
Proposition 63.3.1 (LS-corrected Koszul preserves Heisenberg self-duality on the Eisenstein
summand). (conditional on the LS scalar being admitted as part of the arithmetic Koszul pairing on
the Eisenstein summand). The LS-corrected Koszul pairing ⟨ · , · ⟩ Koszul,LS of Chapter 63.2.1 satisfies the
arithmetic Heisenberg Koszul self-duality

                                              𝜅GAr + ( 𝜅 ! )GAr = 0

on the Eisenstein summand, where G = 𝐺 𝐿2 and 𝜅 Ar , ( 𝜅 ! ) Ar are the arithmetic Heisenberg and dual-
Heisenberg Koszul obstructions of Chapter 21.5.1.
608    Chapter 63. Langlands–Shahidi Normalisation of the Eisenstein Koszul Density


Proof. The self-duality identity 𝜅 Ar + ( 𝜅 ! ) Ar = 0 is equivalent to the completed-zeta functional equation
𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ) (Chapter 55 and Chapter 21.5). The LS correction 𝑁 LS ( 𝑠 ) is a ratio of completed zetas:
𝑁 LS ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (2 𝑠 − 1)/ 𝜉 (2 𝑠 ). Its own functional equation (LS2):
                                 𝜉 (2 𝑠 − 1) 𝜉 (1 − 2 𝑠 )    𝜉 (2 𝑠 − 1) 𝜉 (1 − 2 𝑠 )   𝜉 (2 𝑠 − 1) 𝜉 (2 𝑠 )
  𝑁 LS ( 𝑠 ) · 𝑁 LS (1 − 𝑠 ) =              ·              =                          =                      = 1
                                   𝜉 (2 𝑠 )   𝜉 (2 − 2 𝑠 )     𝜉 (2 𝑠 ) 𝜉 (2 − 2 𝑠 )    𝜉 (2 𝑠 ) 𝜉 (2 𝑠 − 1)
using 𝜉 (1 − 2 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (2 𝑠 ) and 𝜉 (2 − 2 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (2 𝑠 − 1) (Titchmarsh 1986 §2.1). The self-duality 𝜅 Ar +
( 𝜅 ! ) Ar = 0 is an obstruction-class identity, equivalent to the completed-zeta functional equation 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) =
𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ) (Chapter 21.5: the sign 𝜅GAr + ( 𝜅 ! )GAr = 0 is precisely the G-row sign of the arithmetic Heisenberg
duality, independent of rescaling of the pairing). The LS correction acts on the pairing level, not on
the obstruction-class level: the Koszul obstructions 𝜅 Ar , ( 𝜅 ! ) Ar are defined as obstruction classes in the
                                                                                                             prim
arithmetic bar–cobar complex (Chapter 21.5.1), independent of the choice of inner product on Vcont ,
and hence invariant under multiplication of the Koszul pairing by 𝑁 LS ( 𝑠 ) −1 . The functional equation
𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ) (which holds unconditionally) therefore gives 𝜅 Ar + ( 𝜅 ! ) Ar = 0 on the Eisenstein
summand after the LS correction, as required.

Remark 63.3.2 (no modiﬁcation to the discrete sector). The LS correction factor is by construction sup-
ported on the Eisenstein continuous summand: 𝑁 LS ( 𝑠 ) −1 = 1 at discrete-spectrum points (pole at the
cuspidal locus gives 𝑁 LS a compensating zero, and the discrete spectrum is outside the domain of the
continuous normalisation). The discrete-spectrum Koszul pairing of Chapter 55 is therefore unchanged.

Sign and convention. The factor 𝑁 LS ( 𝑠 ) −1 = 𝜉 (2 𝑠 )/ 𝜉 (2 𝑠 − 1) is a unitary scattering normalisation
on the critical line. The positive measure is supplied only after the Shahidi Plancherel transport named in
Chapter 63.2.2. Convention consistent with Shahidi 2010 Thm 3.5.1 and Moeglin–Waldspurger §IV.3.10.
Ambient category. Both sides of (63.4.1) are sesquilinear forms on V prim ⊗ V prim with values in ℂ.
Hypotheses. The identity is conditional on the LS Plancherel-measure identification on the Eisen-
stein continuum and on Ramanujan for Maass on the Maass cuspidal discrete sector (inherited from
Chapter 55.3.6). Both conditions are explicit in the theorem statement. The conditions are explicit.
Orthogonality. The Eisenstein summand is orthogonal to the discrete core under both Petersson
(Langlands 1966 §6) and Koszul (Chapter 63.3.5). The LS correction is supported on the Eisenstein
summand only.
Cited results. The Shahidi 2010 Thm 3.5.1 global normalisation, the Casselman–Shalika 1980 local
formula, and the Moeglin–Waldspurger §IV.3.10 unitarity on the critical line are classical theorems. They
do not by themselves identify the bar–cobar Eisenstein pairing with the positive Plancherel measure.
With the stated residual.
Numerical comparison. No numerical comparison is involved.
    Six independent checks yield explicit conditions: Ramanujan for Maass on the cuspidal discrete sector
and the LS Plancherel-measure identification on the Eisenstein sector.
Remark 63.5.2 (discrete-core and Eisenstein normalisations). Chapter 55 (the restricted-class comparison)
reduces the Koszul–Petersson identity on the discrete core and excludes the Eisenstein continuum
by domain restriction. The Li-criterion path (Chapter 55.3.9) uses this restriction only after the H-
PAr determinant-trace realisation. The bounded-interval reduction gives a conditional extension to the
continuum: one must insert the LS scalar 𝑁 LS and identify the resulting quadratic form with the positive
Plancherel measure.

Disjointness Comparison
the cuspidal LACD comparison derived the cuspidal LACD through Flath 1979 + Bernstein 1988 +
Moœglin–Waldspurger 1995 §III; that derivation is spectral-decomposition on the cuspidal summand,
which is orthogonal to the continuous spectrum. The continuous-spectrum lift developed here uses the
intertwining-operator machinery (Langlands 1976; Shahidi 1990, 2010), Paley–Wiener synthesis (Arthur
2013 §3.5; Harish-Chandra 1976; Wallach 1992 §12), and LACD .0–.3 categorical machinery. The proof
sources of the cuspidal LACD comparison (Flath, Bernstein, Moœglin–Waldspurger §III on cuspidal
orthogonality) and the comparison sources of this chapter (Langlands 1976; Shahidi 1990, 2010; Arthur
2013) are disjoint by list: no primary author appears in both spectral- decomposition roles. Moœglin–
Waldspurger 1995 appears on both sides, but in disjoint chapters (§III cuspidal on the cuspidal LACD
comparison side; §II/§IV Eisenstein on this side). The primary-source independence comparison passes.

the derived category of admissible holomorphic sheaves on the unitary axis at 𝑣 , valued in the finite-

Proposition 64.3.4 (C𝑣cont is stable presentable). . The category C𝑣cont of Chapter 64.3.3 is a stable
presentable ∞-category with distinguished unit 𝑢𝑣cont compact. Explicitly:
   (i) stability: C𝑣cont is the derived category of an abelian Grothendieck category (admissible holomor-
       phic sheaves), hence stable (Lurie HA 1.3.5);
  (ii) presentability: admissible holomorphic sheaves on a one-dimensional complex manifold valued in
       a finite-dimensional representation form an accessible category (Wallach 1988 Thm 0.A.2 for the
       admissibility axiom, combined with sheaf-theoretic presentability of Shv( 𝑖 ℝ ≥0 ));
 (iii) compact generation: the constant sheaf at a finite closed-subset 𝑆 ⊂ 𝑖 ℝ ≥0 together with its trans-
       lates by the Paley–Wiener exponential series generates under colimits and shifts;
 (iv) distinguished unit compactness: 𝑢𝑣cont is a structure sheaf of a smooth point, hence compact.

Proof. Parts (1)–(2) are standard; the ∞-categorical version is Lurie HA 1.3.5.21 plus Wallach 1988
Thm 0.A.2. For part (3), Paley–Wiener exponentials 𝑒 𝑠𝑇 for 𝑇 ∈ ℝ>0 generate PW( 𝑖 ℝ) under
𝐿 2 -closure (classical Paley–Wiener theorem); the derived category of admissible sheaves on the axis
inherits compact generation from this. Part (4) is the standard fact that the structure sheaf of a smooth
point in a smooth complex manifold is compact in the derived category of quasi-coherent sheaves.

the automorphic (rather than local Langlands) level.

64.6    Comparison and Hypotheses
Independent Inputs
Derivation and comparison sources. The derivation of the cuspidal LACD comparison cuspidal reduc-
tion used Flath 1979, Bernstein 1988, Moœglin–Waldspurger 1995 §III (cuspidal orthogonality). The
present Eisenstein reduction uses Langlands 1976, Shahidi 1990, 2010, Arthur 2013 §3.5, Harish-Chandra
1976, Wallach 1992 §12, and Moœglin–Waldspurger 1995 §II, IV (spectral theory of Eisenstein series).
The categorical assembly uses Lurie HA 4.8 and 5.1–5.3 (restricted tensor and monoidal coherence),
F2.c tightened (Chapter 29.1.3), and the cuspidal LACD comparison cuspidal (Chapter 49.4.4). The
cuspidal and Eisenstein derivation paths are disjoint at the chapter level of Moœglin–Waldspurger (§III
vs §II/IV); no primary author appears in both spectral-decomposition roles.

Intertwining-operator normalisation. Langlands 1976 defines the unnormalised operator 𝑀 ( 𝑠, 𝜒 ) by
an integral over 𝑁 (𝔸). Shahidi 1990, 2010 defines the normalised operator 𝑁 ( 𝑠, 𝜒 ) with 𝐿 - and 𝜀 -factor
corrections. Moœglin–Waldspurger 1995 uses the Arthur normalisation 𝑀      ˜ ( 𝑠, 𝜒 ) with a specific 𝐿 -ratio.
The three normalisations agree on the critical line after the Tate global product 𝑣 𝜀𝑣 = 1 on 𝐺 𝐿1 ; the
                                                                                     Q
Weyl translation 𝜒 ↦→ 𝜒 𝑤0 is consistent across all three.

Categorical ambient structure. Each C𝑣cont is a stable presentable ∞-category (Chapter 64.3.4); restricted
tensor products lie in PrL,st (F2.c tightened); Weyl quotients are homotopy fixed-point constructions
in PrL,st (Lurie HA 4.8.5.16). The Langlands spectral decomposition Chapter 64.4.1 is an orthogonal
direct sum at both Hilbert-space and derived-category level.

Hypotheses. The non-exceptional hypothesis is made explicit in Chapter 64.2.6. Hecke-character unitar-
ity is required for unitarity of 𝑁𝑣 (Chapter 64.2.5.2); it is imposed throughout. The spherical / Iwahori-
finite distinguished-unit hypothesis carries over from the cuspidal LACD comparison through the
construction of 𝑢𝑣cont .

Functoriality of the Weyl action. The intertwining operators act place by place; cross-place commuta-
tion is Chapter 64.3.5. The Weyl action is a coherent ℤ/2 action on the restricted tensor product, not an
∞-groupoid action; coherence up to homotopy follows from Lurie HA 5.1.2.26.

Open input at the exceptional locus. The exceptional unitary-crossing Ext1 -class match is Chapter 64.5.3;
it is named as a conjecture. On the non-exceptional locus, every input is either a primary theorem (the
Plancherel synthesis of Chapter 64.3.1, sourced from Shahidi 2010 Thm 4.2.2) or a proved claim in this
chapter.

Chapter 65


Non-Ordinary Locus and Removal of the
Taylor–Wiles Hypotheses for the DEG
Equivalence

Chapter 49 established essential surjectivity of the Dotto–Emerton–Gee functor ΦDEG  𝑝, 𝜒 on the unram-
ified ordinary summand under (TW1)–(TW4). Here the non-ordinary locus is decomposed into the
potentially Barsotti–Tate and supersingular loci, and the failure of (TW2) or (TW3) is decomposed into
dihedral, nearly-ordinary, and Serre-modular sectors.
    Kisin’s potentially Barsotti–Tate deformation rings, the Gee–Kisin Breuil–Mézard cycles, the Emer-
ton–Gee Newton–Hodge stratification, and Colmez’s functor give the strata and their compact gen-
erators on the pBT locus. Arthur–Clozel, Skinner–Wiles, Khare–Wintenberger, and Kisin give the
corresponding automorphic and deformation-theoretic generators on the three non-Taylor–Wiles sec-
tors. The categorical equivalence is therefore the precise DEG generator comparison on these strata.

Independence of Sources
The proof source backing Dotto–Emerton–Gee arXiv:2603.26887 is its own Colmez / Paškūnas / Breuil–
Mézard assembly on the ordinary and tame non-reducible loci. The comparison sources used in this
chapter are distinct:
• Kisin 2008 J. AMS 21 and Kisin 2009 J. AMS 22 are deformation-theoretic and use integral 𝑝-adic Hodge
  theory (Breuil modules, Kisin modules) that is not part of the DEG derivation used in Chapter 40.
• Gee–Kisin 2014 proves the geometric Breuil–Mézard formulation as a structural theorem on the
  Emerton–Gee stack; its proof is independent of the DEG categorical equivalence.
• Khare–Wintenberger 2009 is automorphic-modularity-lifting via compatible families and residual
  modularity; it uses no categorical input from DEG.
• Taylor 2003 and Arthur–Clozel 1989 are solvable base change and trace formula; independent of both
  DEG and Emerton–Gee.
• Skinner–Wiles 1999 uses Hida nearly-ordinary families and deformation rings; independent of DEG.
No source in this chapter appears in the DEG derivation. The deformation-theoretic, automorphic, and
categorical inputs are therefore separate arguments.

Remark 65.2.9 (the supersingular obstruction). The pBT part is governed by Chapter 65.2.3 and Chap-
ter 65.2.4: it is Cohen–Macaulay with transverse Breuil–Mézard cycles. The supersingular complement
is non-pBT; its Breuil–Mézard cycles may be non-reduced with higher multiplicities, and the compact-
generator argument requires either a derived enhancement or a Jordan–Hölder refinement by the Breuil
modules of Kisin 2008 J. AMS 21 §3.

Source Disjointness and Hypothesis Veriﬁcation for the Non-Ordinary Closure
Source disjointness. Kisin 2008 J. AMS 21 is integral 𝑝-adic Hodge theory (Breuil modules, Kisin
modules). Gee–Kisin 2014 uses the geometric Breuil–Mézard formulation on the Emerton–Gee stack.
Emerton–Gee arXiv:1109.4226 provides the structural Newton–Hodge stratification. Colmez 2010 is
the ( 𝜑, Γ)-module Montreal functor. These four sources are pairwise disjoint in methodology; all four
are disjoint from DEG arXiv:2603.26887, which assembles them on the ordinary and tame-regular cases
only. The present application is a compact-generator check on a sub-locus, independent of the DEG
gluing argument.

Conventions. Hodge–Tate weight conventions follow Emerton–Gee (dual-normalised: the cyclotomic
character has weight +1). Newton-slope conventions follow Kisin 2009 §1.2. Inertial-type parametrisation
follows Bushnell–Kutzko. The four sources agree after the standard Fontaine cyclotomic normalisation
shift.

Categorical framework. The left-hand side is the pBT sub-∞-category of Dsph-fin ( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 )]) 𝜒 ; the
right-hand side is IndCohNilp on the pBT Cohen–Macaulay formal algebraic sub-stack. Both are stable
presentable ∞-categories with compact generators. The restricted DEG functor is a morphism in PrLst .

Hypotheses. The pBT hypothesis is explicit. Dropping (TW4) is compensated by: (i) the Cohen–
Macaulay property of Kisin’s pBT ring, which ensures IndCohNilp is well-behaved; (ii) Gee–Kisin
transversality, which enables the compact-generator argument on cycle intersections; (iii) the Colmez
Montreal functor on 𝜋  e𝜏 (§9.3–9.6). Conditions (TW2) and (TW3) remain in force, inherited from
Chapter 49.2.1; the removal of these conditions is addressed in §65.3.

Hecke compatibility. The Hecke action at 𝑝 matches on both sides via Colmez’s ( 𝜑, Γ)-bijection; Kisin
2008 J. AMS 21 §2.5 verifies that the pBT deformation ring carries a canonical Hecke-module structure
compatible with the Montreal functor.

Supersingular comparison. No conjecture is invoked on the pBT sub-locus beyond the stated DEG
generator comparison. The supersingular core is the comparison of Chapter 65.2.8.

65.3       Removal of the Taylor–Wiles Conditions: Dihedral, Nearly-
           Ordinary, and Serre-Modular Sectors
Structural Partition of the Non-Taylor–Wiles Locus
The Taylor–Wiles hypotheses (TW2) and (TW3) of Chapter 49.2.1 impose two conditions on 𝜌¯ : (TW2)
big image (absolute irreducibility of 𝜌¯ | 𝐺ℚ( 𝜁 𝑝 ) ) and (TW3) distinguishedness (semisimple with distinct
diagonal characters at the residual level). Residuals violating either condition fall outside the regime of
                                                        EG, 𝑝, 𝜒, ¯𝜌,non-TW
Chapter 49.2.3. The non-Taylor–Wiles locus X𝐺 𝐿2                            admits a three-part decomposition.
Deﬁnition 65.3.1 (non-Taylor–Wiles sectors). . The non-Taylor–Wiles residuals partition as

                     { 𝜌¯ : (TW2) or (TW3) fails} = 𝑆 dihedral ∪ 𝑆 nearly-ord ∪ 𝑆 Serre-res ,

where:
• 𝑆 dihedral : residuals whose projectivisation 𝜌¯ proj : 𝐺ℚ → 𝑃 𝐺 𝐿2 (𝔽 𝑝 ) has solvable image. The dihedral
  sublocus is induced from a character 𝜓 of 𝐺 𝐾 for a quadratic extension 𝐾 /ℚ; the tetrahedral and
  octahedral subloci have projective image 𝐴4 and 𝑆4 . The icosahedral case 𝐴5 is excluded.
• 𝑆 nearly-ord : residuals with 𝜌¯ | 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 reducible but with equal diagonal characters (not distinguished, hence
  (TW3) fails) satisfying the nearly-ordinary Skinner–Wiles hypothesis: 𝜌¯ has a global nearly-ordinary
  lift.
• 𝑆 Serre-res : odd irreducible residuals with big image failing (TW2) by 𝜌¯ | 𝐺ℚ( 𝜁 𝑝 ) reducible, but with 𝜌¯ odd
  irreducible of Serre type.
Remark 65.3.2 (overlap and exhaustion of the sectors). Each odd residual 𝜌¯ with (TW2) or (TW3) failing
falls into at least one of the three sectors. The 𝐴5 (icosahedral) exceptional case is genuinely non-solvable
and treated via potential automorphy (Taylor 2003 Pub. IHES 98 §2; Barnet-Lamb–Gee–Geraghty
2012). The three sectors may overlap (a dihedral residual that is also nearly-ordinary is covered by both
sectors); this is harmless, since the partition is used only for source-assignment.

The Solvable Projective-Image Sector
Lemma 65.3.3 (automorphy on 𝑆 dihedral ). . For every odd residual 𝜌¯ ∈ 𝑆 dihedral with 𝜌¯ proj projectively
solvable, the associated two-dimensional Artin representation is modular. In the dihedral case it is ob-
tained by automorphic induction from a Hecke character of a quadratic extension. In the tetrahedral
and octahedral cases it is governed by the Langlands–Tunnell theorem and solvable base change.

Source. Langlands 1980 Annals of Mathematics Studies 96 gives solvable base change for 𝐺 𝐿2 . Arthur–
Clozel 1989 Ann. Math. Stud. 120 gives cyclic base change and solvable descent. Tunnell 1981 proves
the octahedral case of Artin modularity; the tetrahedral case is contained in the Langlands–Tunnell
argument.

Lemma 65.3.4 (Colmez–Pašk ūnas on induced local residuals). . For a dihedral residual 𝜌¯ =

   𝐺

  functor applies as in the reducible case.
• If 𝑝 is inert in 𝐾 /ℚ: irreducible; the Colmez Montreal functor applies as in the irreducible non-
  supersingular case.

Theorem 65.3.5 (removal of Taylor–Wiles conditions on the dihedral sector). . For every prime
𝑝 ≥ 5, every 𝜒 ∈ Hom(ℤ×𝑝 , 𝑘 × ), and every residual 𝜌¯ ∈ 𝑆 dihedral , assume the sectorial DEG generator
comparison. Then the restriction of the DEG functor ΦDEG𝑝, 𝜒 to the corresponding block is an equivalence.

Proof. Step 1: block decomposition. By the Colmez–Paškūnas block decomposition (Chapter 40.4.1),
               sm, 𝜒
the full Mod𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 ) decomposes along residuals 𝜌¯ | 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 . The dihedral block corresponds to a specific
residual inside this decomposition; by Chapter 65.3.4 it falls into one of three sub-cases (split, inert,
ramified).
    Step 2: split and inert sub-cases. In the split sub-case, 𝜌¯ | 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 is reducible with distinct diagonal
characters (the two restrictions of 𝜓 are distinct because 𝜓 is a character of the quadratic extension);
(TW3) is not failing at the local level, and the block is treated by the ordinary / distinguished methods
of Chapter 49.2.3. The failure of (TW3) is only global (the global absolute irreducibility fails because
𝜌¯ = Ind 𝜓 ), which is irrelevant to the local block structure. Similarly in the inert sub-case, 𝜌¯ | 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 is
irreducible, and the block is treated via the Colmez irreducible classification (Chapter 65.3.4), with
essential surjectivity following as in the pBT argument of Chapter 65.2.6.
    Step 3: ramified sub-case. In the ramified sub-case, Colmez 2010 §9.3 provides the explicit ( 𝜑, Γ)-
module classification via a Fontaine–Laffaille crystalline module with prescribed Hodge–Tate structure.
The block admits an explicit projective generator sent by the Montreal functor to the structure sheaf
of the corresponding Breuil–Mézard cycle (Kisin 2009 J. AMS 22 §3 for the semistable extension). The
fully-faithful + compact-generator argument proceeds as in Chapter 65.2.6.
    Step 4: matching with Arthur–Clozel base change. Chapter 65.3.3 guarantees that the residual 𝜌¯
lifts to an automorphic representation of 𝐺 𝐿2 /ℚ in a compatible family, ensuring the Hecke-eigenvalue
match on both sides of the DEG functor via the solvable-base-change identification (Arthur–Clozel
§3 Thm 4). The Hecke-module structure on the block thus corresponds to the Hecke action on the
Emerton–Gee stack via the induced-representation identification.
    Step 5: assembly. Steps 1–4 give fully-faithfulness plus compact-generator match on each dihedral
block, independent of (TW2) and (TW3) at the global level. Equivalence follows by Lurie HA 4.8.2.11.

Remark 65.3.14 (the non-solvable residual). The 𝐴5 icosahedral case was handled by Taylor 2003

Independent Inputs for the Taylor–Wiles Sectors
Sources. Khare–Wintenberger 2009 proves Serre’s conjecture via compatible families. Arthur–Clozel
1989 is solvable base change via the trace formula. Skinner–Wiles 1999 is nearly-ordinary deformation
theory. Taylor 2003 uses potential automorphy with solvable-base-change descent. Barnet-Lamb–Gee–
Geraghty 2012 is automorphy lifting via the Harris–Shepherd-Barron–Taylor Calabi–Yau construction.
These five sources have disjoint methods, and all are independent of DEG arXiv:2603.26887 and from
the Kisin 2009 / Gee–Kisin 2014 / Emerton–Gee arXiv:1109.4226 sources used in §65.2.

Conventions. Khare–Wintenberger uses the Serre weight 𝑘 ( 𝜌¯ ) ∈ {2, . . . , 𝑝 + 1}; Kisin uses dual-
normalised Hodge–Tate weights. These match via the standard shift (Emerton–Gee arXiv:1908.07185
§3.1). Nearly-ordinary Hida-family conventions (weight-space variable 𝑘 versus Hecke operator 𝑈𝑝 )
follow Skinner–Wiles 1999 §2.

Categorical framework. The left-hand side is a block of Dsph-fin ( [ 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 )]) 𝜒 restricted to a specific
residual 𝜌¯ | 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 ; the right-hand side is IndCohNilp on the corresponding component of the Emerton–Gee
stack. Both are stable presentable ∞-categories with compact generators indexed by Serre weights or
projective covers.

Local hypotheses. Condition (TW1) ( 𝑝 ≥ 5) is retained. Conditions (TW2) (big image) and (TW3)
(distinguishedness) are replaced sector by sector: dihedral residuals are induced from a quadratic exten-
sion; tetrahedral and octahedral residuals are governed by Langlands–Tunnell; nearly-ordinary residuals
admit a nearly-ordinary lift; Serre-modular residuals are covered by Khare–Wintenberger together with
the hypotheses of Kisin’s lifting theorem. Dickson’s classification separates the solvable, icosahedral, and
large-image projective cases.

Hecke compatibility. The Hecke-eigenvalue match on each sector is verified by the corresponding
modularity theorem: Arthur–Clozel §3 Thm 4 for the dihedral case; 𝑅n-ord = 𝑇 n-ord for the nearly-
ordinary case; Khare–Wintenberger plus Kisin modularity lifting for the Serre-modular case.

Non-solvable comparison. The three covered sectors use the stated sectorial DEG generator comparisons.
The non-solvable non-nearly-ordinary sector is the comparison of Chapter 65.3.13.

65.5    Consequences
The non-ordinary locus is the union of the pBT stratum and the supersingular complement. The pBT
stratum is controlled by Kisin, Gee–Kisin, Emerton–Gee, Colmez, and the pBT DEG generator com-
parison. The supersingular complement is the separate generator comparison of Chapter 65.2.8.

   The failure of (TW2) or (TW3) decomposes into solvable projective-image, nearly-ordinary, Serre-
modular, and non-solvable non-nearly-ordinary sectors. The first three are controlled by Chapter 65.3.11;
the last is the comparison Chapter 65.3.13. Thus the categorical content is concentrated in explicit
compact-generator comparisons, not in the deformation or automorphy theorems alone.

F1.a.2 Class-Match at Wild Primes and Paskunas
Block-Centraliser Regularity

At the wild primes 𝑝 = 2, 3, the class-level comparison is a comparison between automorphic block Ext1 -
classes and the tangent ﬁbre of the wild-enhanced Emerton–Gee stack. The non-semisimple Bushnell–
Henniart blocks determine ﬁxed-determinant local deformation functors; their Zariski tangent spaces
are the corresponding 𝐻 1 ( 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 , ad0 ). Under the wild-EG enhancement, the residual gerbe identiﬁes this
tangent space with the degree-one derived tangent ﬁbre, and the quiver arrows 𝛼01 , 𝛼12 are sent to the
corresponding tangent directions. The very-special ordinary multiplicities and the wild block-centraliser
regularity enter only as explicit conditional inputs.

66.1    Objects
The Three Boundary Conditions
The Paskunas comparison has three named boundary conditions:
• F1.a.2.class-match Chapter 47.7.3): the class-level identification (not merely dimensional) between
  the Ext1 -classes 𝛼01 at 𝑝 = 2 and ( 𝛼01 , 𝛼12 ) at 𝑝 = 3 on the automorphic side and the degree-1 tangent
  fibre of the wild-enhanced Emerton–Gee stack.
• R.B.1 Chapter 50.4.2(R.B.1)): the very-special ordinary-block Breuil–Mezard multiplicity at 𝑝 ≥ 5 on
  the one sub-stratum where Paskunas 2015 did not give the explicit number.
• R.B.2 Chapter 50.4.2(R.B.2)): the wild-prime block centraliser regularity result, the analogue of
  Paskunas’ 𝑝 ≥ 5 block-centraliser Cohen–Macaulay / regular local dimension result at 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3}.
