Independence of Sources
The earlier proof sources for F1.a.2 and F1.a.3.A+B are: Paškūnas 2013, Colmez–Dospinescu–Paškūnas
2014, Bushnell–Henniart 2006, Paškunas 2015, Emerton–Paškunas 2015, Jantzen 2003, and Carter 1989.
The present conditional analysis draws on: the two data above, Bellaïche–Chenevier 2009, Kisin 2008,
and Emerton–Gee arXiv:1908.07185 §9.
    The very-special datum concerns the sub-stratum for which Paškunas 2015 does not give the multi-
plicity. The wild centraliser datum supplies the Cohen–Macaulay and generic-regularity information
not proved in the preceding block computations. Bellaïche–Chenevier 2009 is the pre-EG residual-gerbe
Galois deformation framework, independent of Paškunas’ block method. Kisin 2008 is local deforma-
tion theory for 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 ), independent of the automorphic block construction. Emerton–Gee §9 is the
wild-inertia component analysis on the spectral side, disjoint from the automorphic block method.
    Note on Colmez–Dospinescu–Paškunas 2014 §5. This paper appears in two distinct roles: its §5.3
connecting-map result (the Colmez–Montreal-functor identification of block-Ext with Galois-Ext)
serves as the automorphic input for the class-match theorem (Chapter 66.2.8). A separate centraliser
input would be needed for R.B.2 (Chapter 66.4.3). These two uses draw on distinct propositions within
§5.3. The connecting-map result and the centraliser-dimension results are mathematically independent
within the paper.

Proposition 66.3.1 (very-special multiplicity input). . For 𝑝 ≥ 5 and the very-special residual
𝜌¯ ∼ 𝜒 ⊕ 𝜒 𝜔, let 𝜇vs ( 𝜎 , 𝜌¯ ) denote the Breuil–Mezard multiplicity of the Serre weight 𝜎 . The missing

Remark 66.3.2 (multiplicity convention). The proposition is not a formula for the very-special multi-
plicities. It names the exact numerical input required by the Paškunas centraliser argument.
Corollary 66.3.3 (R.B.1 conditional implication). , conditional on Chapter 66.3.1. If the datum
Chapter 66.3.1 holds, then residual (R.B.1) of Chapter 50.4.2 follows.

Proof. Chapter 50.3.5 expresses the Ext1 -dimension on the ordinary block as dim𝑘 𝔪 𝜌 /𝔪2𝜌 minus the
number of relations, and Paškunas 2015 Theorem 1.2 converts this to a Breuil–Mezard multiplicity count.

Ext1 -dimension is thus computed in all cases at 𝑝 ≥ 5 under Chapter 66.3.1.

Uniﬁed Wild-Prime Block Centraliser Theorem
Theorem 66.4.5 (R.B.2 conditional implication: wild-prime block centraliser regularity). ,
                                                                                          sm, 𝜒
conditional on Chapter 66.4.1 and Chapter 66.4.3. Let 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3}, 𝜒 , and 𝔅 a block of Mod𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 ) .
The block centraliser 𝐴𝔅 is a complete Noetherian local 𝑊 ( 𝑘 )-algebra of:
• Krull dimension 2 at 𝑝 = 2;
• Krull dimension 3 at 𝑝 = 3 for principal-series blocks, and 2 for supercuspidal blocks.
It is Cohen–Macaulay, and regular on supersingular / supercuspidal blocks. The generic fibre of Spec 𝐴𝔅

Proof. At 𝑝 = 2 apply Chapter 66.4.1: all blocks are Cohen–Macaulay of dimension 2; supersingular

by a non-zero-divisor, hence regular on the generic fibre. The dimension bounds match the expected
dimensions 2 at 𝑝 = 2 and ≤ 3 at 𝑝 = 3 from Chapter 50.3.7.

Corollary 66.4.6 (conditional Ext 1 -vanishing at wild primes). , conditional on Chapter 66.4.5.

Proof. By Chapter 66.4.5 the generic fibre of Spec 𝐴𝔅 is regular. Apply the Koszul-resolution argument

66.6    Sources and Conventions
Class-Match Sources and Conventions
The primary sources for the class-match theorem are Paškunas 2013 §4.11 (connecting map), Colmez–
Dospinescu–Paškunas 2014 §5.3 (block-Ext identification at 𝑝 = 3), Bellaïche–Chenevier 2009 (residual
gerbe framework), Kisin 2008 (deformation tangent complex), and Emerton–Gee arXiv:1908.07185 §9
(wild component structure on the spectral side). These five inputs are independent of the sources in
Chapter 49.1.
    The use of Colmez–Dospinescu–Paškunas 2014 §5.3 in the class-match theorem requires a precise
partition: the block-Ext / Galois-Ext identification (the Colmez–Montreal-functor connecting map,
§5.3 of that paper) is the automorphic input, while the block centraliser Cohen–Macaulay structure
(§5.3 Theorems 5.15–5.22) is the spectral input used in Chapter 66.4.5. These two uses draw on distinct
mathematical content within the same §5.3: the connecting-map result depends only on the block-
algebra sequence, while the centraliser dimension results depend on the explicit projective-resolution
computation. The two uses are therefore separated at the level of the specific propositions invoked, even
though both appear in the same section reference.
    Paškunas’ connecting-map convention is the standard 𝛿 : Hom → Ext1 from the long exact sequence;
the Galois cohomology uses the Mazur convention with ad0 for determinant-fixed liftings; the central-
character twist 𝜒det accounts for the shift between ad and ad0 .
    Both sides of the class-match comparison live in well-defined ambient categories: the automorphic
                                sm, 𝜒
Ext1 is computed in Db (Mod𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 ) ) restricted to the block, and the tangent fibre in IndCohNilp
on the formal completion at 𝑥 𝜏 ; the comparison passes between them via Chapter 66.2.5. The non-
classical hypothesis is the wild-EG enhancement Chapter 40.5.7; the remaining inputs are the block
Ext1 -computations and the residual-gerbe identification already cited. Both factor isomorphisms are
natural in 𝜌¯𝔅 , so composition preserves naturality.

numerical convention for the Breuil–Mezard deformation ring of the scalar residual 𝜌¯ ∼ 𝜒 ⊕ 𝜒 𝜔.

R.B.2 Conventions
R.B.2 is the implication from the data Chapter 66.4.1 and Chapter 66.4.3. These data are stated in the
complete Noetherian 𝑊 ( 𝑘 )-algebra convention used for the block centralisers.

Codimension-Two 𝐸2 -Centre Glue and the
BC-Diamond-Glue Comparison

The determinant transition is a codimension-at-most-2 problem for the 𝐸2 -centre of IndCohNilp on the
Selmer-derived spectral stack. Arinkin–Gaitsgory supplies the singular-support geometry. Galatius–Kupers–
Randal-Williams, Bhatt–Lurie, and Bezrukavnikov–Finkelberg–Mirković supply the three model compat-
ibilities: cellular 𝐸2 -convergence, Nygaard convergence, and the ﬂat-locus centre. With these compatibilities
imposed on the arithmetic transition locus, the determinant transition gives the BC-diamond-glue compari-
son through the Chenevier–Bellaiche Bernstein–Galois decomposition and Francis–Gaitsgory factorization
gluing.

   LACD .0–.3 is taken from Chapter 49 (Chapter 49.4.4 on the cuspidal sph-fin locus); the restricted

Geometry of the Transition Locus
Proposition 67.2.1 (the transition locus is codim ≤ 2 on the determinantal cleavage). . Un-
der the determinantal cleavage of Chapter 52.2.1, the transition locus X𝜌,Sel ,tr
                                                                        ¯ det, L is a closed substack of
                                   Sel,Nilp              Sel,reg
codimension at most 2 inside X ¯𝜌,det, L and inside X ¯𝜌,det, L .

Proof. By Arinkin–Gaitsgory arXiv:1201.6343 §11.2, the transition locus on IndCohNilp of the full moduli
of rank-2 local systems is the boundary between the nilpotent-support locus and the regular locus, whose
local model is the flag variety of regular-unipotent elements in ad 𝜌. On the determinantal sector ad0 𝜌
(the traceless adjoint), the regular-unipotent locus in ad0 𝜌 is codimension exactly 2 inside ad0 𝜌 when
ad0 𝜌 is three-dimensional (i.e., for 𝐺 𝐿2 ), by the Kostant section formula (AG 2015 §11.4.1 specialised
to SL2 ). Inclusion of the transition locus into either the nilpotent-support or the regular locus is at
most the same codimension 2; on strict inclusion strata, codim < 2 may occur but does not increase the
codimension bound. The codim-2 bound is tight: at the boundary between a unipotent orbit and the
zero orbit inside ad0 𝜌𝐺 𝐿2 , both components have dimension equal to dim ad0 − 2 = 1.

Remark 67.2.2 (the role of codim 2). Codimension 2 is the natural threshold for the 𝐸2 -centre filtration
to be 2-convergent: at codim ≤ 2, the 𝐸2 -centre filtration admits a finite-length resolution by cellular 𝐸2 -
algebras (Galatius–Kupers–Randal-Williams 2024 §18); at codim ≥ 3 the resolution becomes infinite and
convergence must be proved by independent spectral-sequence arguments. The determinantal cleavage
is tuned precisely to keep the transition locus at codim ≤ 2.

Independent Numerical Comparisons for
Arithmetic Constants

Five essential numerical constants appear across the arithmetic branch: the determinant-rank residue
𝑟 𝜁 = 2 of Chapter 19.5.1, the first four Li coefficients 𝜆1 , . . . , 𝜆4 of Chapter 53.2.2, the Riemann–von
Mangoldt count 𝑁 (𝑇 ) of Chapter 59.2.1, the first three non-trivial ordinates 𝛾1 , 𝛾2 , 𝛾3 appearing through-
out Chapters 56–59, and the archimedean digamma value 𝜓 (1/4) = − 𝛾𝐸 − 𝜋 /2 − 3 log 2 of the Weil
archimedean term. For each constant there are two calculations with disjoint source lists. The comparison
records the two lists and requires their intersection to be empty.

68.1    Criterion and Source Discipline
Each constant carries a canonical derivation path, stated at its first use, and at least one alternative numer-
ical or closed-form calculation drawn from a disjoint list. The orthogonality condition of Chapter 1.2.2
requires the two lists to be independent as sets and semantically independent as computations. The
recorded rationale names why no hidden common dependency couples the two paths.
Deﬁnition 68.1.1 (independent numerical comparison). . For a numerical constant 𝐶 ∈ ℝ with canonical
proof source 𝐷 ( 𝐶 ) and comparison source 𝑉 ( 𝐶 ), the independent numerical comparison of 𝐶 is the
triple ( 𝐶, 𝐷 ( 𝐶 ) ,𝑉 ( 𝐶 )) together with a disjoint-rationale statement establishing that 𝐷 ( 𝐶 ) ∩ 𝑉 ( 𝐶 ) =
∅ at the string level and that no hidden common lemma or table couples the two paths.
Remark 68.1.2 (set-theoretic and semantic disjointness). Set-theoretic disjointness is strict disjointness of
the derivation and comparison source lists. Semantic disjointness requires the two computations to use
genuinely different mathematical mechanisms: for instance, a contour count is not the same computation
as a Stirling expansion of the gamma factor. The latter condition is an explicit mathematical comparison,
not a formal consequence of names.

enters the derivation path. The disjointness is structural, not merely nomenclatural.

Remark 68.2.3 (precision ﬂoor for Li). The rtol 10−6 budget is the practical floor of both paths. The
derivation side is limited by the precision of the published OEIS digits (conservatively 45 digits in the
rounded table entry, effectively reduced by Keiper-algorithm truncation error on finite zero counts).
The comparison side is limited by cancellation in the numerical Taylor expansion of the pole-subtracted
log-xi expression, which loses roughly 10 digits of precision per Taylor order. At 80 dps working precision
the comparison has ∼ 50 accurate digits at 𝑛 = 4, far better than the 10−6 rtol budget. The budget is set
by the derivation side’s published-table digit count.

Arithmetic Fibre and Source Orthogonality

The arithmetic theorems of Chapters 49–59 live over Spec ℤ. Their relation with the theorems of the
preceding volumes is not formal propagation. It is a comparison of fibres. Some statements are arithmetic
fibres of complex or Calabi–Yau assertions; some have no complex ancestor at all. In every case the proof
sources on the arithmetic side are separate from the proof sources of the older theorem.

69.1   The Fibre Dichotomy
Let ℓarith be one of the arithmetic theorems of Chapters 49–59. If ℓup is a theorem of one of the preceding
volumes, then exactly one of the following holds.
  (i) ℓarith is the arithmetic fibre of ℓup . Its hypotheses are obtained by replacing the complex or Calabi–
      Yau input by the corresponding adelic, Iwasawa-theoretic, automorphic, or Bost–Connes input.
 (ii) ℓarith is orthogonal to ℓup . The two statements may share a word such as ‘‘Heisenberg’’ or
      ‘‘Hochschild’’, but the objects and proof technologies are different.
    No theorem in Chapters 49–59 is used here as a silent enlargement of a theorem in Vols I–III. The
arithmetic theorem may be sharper on its own fibre, but it does not change the complex theorem.

Primary-Source Test
A pair of source lists 𝑆, 𝑇 is independent if each 𝑠 ∈ 𝑆 and 𝑡 ∈ 𝑇 are mathematically independent in
the quoted form: neither is a corollary of the other, neither is used in the proof of the other, and the
proof technologies are disjoint. This is the source-level form of the comparison datum of Chapter 1.2.

69.2    Three Basic Comparisons
Arithmetic Positselski and Vol I Theorem B
The Vol I theorem is the chiral Positselski equivalence over a characteristic-zero field. The arithmetic
theorem is the equivalence

                             Dco                     ctr
                              Λ 𝑝 ( 𝐶 -comodΛ 𝑝 ) ≃ DΛ 𝑝 ( 𝐶 -contramodΛ 𝑝 )
                                                            ∨


over Λ 𝑝 = ℤ 𝑝 [[ 𝐺 𝑝 ]], with 𝜇 ( 𝐶 ) = 0 and bounded-below Tor against 𝔽 𝑝 .
   The arithmetic proof uses Pontryagin–Weil duality, Greenlees–May completion, Matlis duality, Bost–
Connes thermodynamics, Consani–Marcolli adele-class geometry, and Venjakob Noetherianity. The
complex proof uses Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral coalgebras, Positselski’s field-coefficient coderived and
contraderived categories, and the stable ∞-categorical formalism. These lists meet only in the name of
the equivalence, not in the proof.
Theorem 69.2.1 (arithmetic Positselski restricts the complex form). Let 𝑘 be the complex base field
of thm:chiral-positselski-weight-completed. Reduction of the arithmetic equivalence along Λ 𝑝 ⊗ℤ 𝑝 𝔽 𝑝 →
𝔽 𝑝 gives the field-coefficient Positselski equivalence. Thus the arithmetic theorem is the arithmetic fibre
of the Vol I theorem on the abelian Heisenberg sector.

Proof. The base-change theorem of Chapter 54.1.4 identifies the Λ 𝑝 -linear coderived–contraderived
equivalence with the classical field-coefficient equivalence after reduction modulo 𝑝. On a discrete 𝔽 𝑝 -
vector space, Pontryagin duality is the ordinary linear dual. Hence the arithmetic dualising functor
reduces to the dualising functor in the complex Positselski theorem.

Remark 69.2.2 (arithmetic ﬁbre, not enlargement). The arithmetic equivalence is stronger on the Λ 𝑝 -
adic fibre. It does not enlarge Vol I Theorem B. The complex theorem remains a theorem over its original
field, and the arithmetic theorem is its abelian Iwasawa fibre.

Bernstein Block-Additivity and the Vol I Climax
The arithmetic theorem concerns Hochschild homology under the Bernstein decomposition of
Modsm𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 ) . Its sources are Bernstein, Bernstein–Deligne, Bushnell–Henniart, and Paškūnas. The
Vol I Climax is a chiral bar-cobar theorem over ℂ, using Beilinson–Drinfeld and Lurie. The two
theorems have no common object on which a functorial implication could act.
Theorem 69.2.3 (Bernstein additivity is orthogonal to the Vol I five theorems). The block-
additivity theorem Chapter 50.4.1 neither implies nor weakens any hypothesis of thm:climax-vol1-platonic,
thm:bar-cobar-verdier, or thm:A-inﬁnity-2.

Proof. The arithmetic theorem is a statement about smooth representations of 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ 𝑝 ) and the Bern-
stein centre. The Vol I theorems are statements about chiral algebras and their bar construction over ℂ.
No source, category, or operator appearing in the arithmetic proof is used as a hypothesis in the chiral
proof.

Chenevier–Bernstein Transport and 𝐸2 -Recognition
The arithmetic theorem combines Chenevier determinant-trace pseudocharacters, Bellaiche–Chenevier
deformation rings, and Bhatt–Scholze prismatic flatness. The Vol I theorem is the (∞, 2)-centralizer
form of 𝐸2 -recognition. On the archimedean Heisenberg core both compute the same 𝐸2 -centre.
69.3. Further Fibre Comparisons                                                                              663


Theorem 69.2.4 (Chenevier transport restricts 𝐸2 -recognition). Let A be a chiral algebra whose
𝐸2 -centre is identified by thm:A-inﬁnity-2. Under the restricted-tensor factorisation of Chapter 29.1.3,
the arithmetic 𝐸2 -transport and the Vol I 𝐸2 -centre agree on the archimedean Heisenberg factor.

Proof. Both sides compute the (∞, 2)-centralizer of idG∞ . The arithmetic restricted tensor product has
G∞ as its archimedean factor, and centralizers are natural under the restriction functor.

69.3    Further Fibre Comparisons
Bost–Connes Modular Operator and Costello–Gwilliam KMS
Theorem 69.3.1 (Bost–Connes modular flow restricts the circle KMS flow). At the archimedean
place, the local Bost–Connes algebra with its modular automorphism is the circle-compactified Heisen-
berg KMS factor appearing in the Costello–Gwilliam holomorphic-topological field theory, after the
standard logarithmic normalisation of ℝ>0 .

Proof. The Costello–Gwilliam circle compactification has modular flow generated by translation on
𝑆 1 . The archimedean Bost–Connes factor has 𝜎𝑡 ( 𝜇𝑟 ) = 𝑟 𝑖𝑡 𝜇𝑟 . The identification 𝑟 = 𝑒 𝜃 sends multi-
plicative dilation to circle translation, and therefore matches the two one-parameter groups.

Remark 69.3.2 (ﬁnite-place residue). The finite 𝑝-adic Bost–Connes factors have no analogue in the
Costello–Gwilliam surface theory. They are new arithmetic fibres, not corrections to the archimedean
theory.

Koszul–Petersson Discrete Core and the Chiral Climax
Theorem 69.3.3 (the discrete-core identity restricts the chiral climax). On the holomorphic
cuspidal sector of the archimedean Heisenberg, the Koszul–Petersson identity of Chapter 55.5.1 becomes
the Vol I chiral Climax pairing between the chiral bar and the Arnold 𝑑𝜕¯ -connection.

Proof. The Petersson form on the holomorphic cuspidal sector is the Heisenberg Fock contraction
pairing of Frenkel–Ben-Zvi. Under the Vol I Climax this pairing is the Arnold pullback of the KZ∗ -
connection. The archimedean component of the arithmetic Koszul pairing is the same oscillator con-
traction.

HP–Li Paley–Wiener and Theorem H
Theorem 69.3.4 (HP–Li on the cuspidal Paley–Wiener class is an arithmetic fibre). The re-
stricted HP–Li theorem Chapter 57.6.1 is the arithmetic fibre of the off-Koszul correction of thm:theorem-
h-platonic-uniﬁed on the holomorphic cuspidal Paley–Wiener class.

Proof. The Vol I off-Koszul correction carries the kernel 𝜁 (2 𝑠 ) 𝐿 ( 𝑠, 𝐹 ⊗ 𝐹 )/ 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ). This is precisely the
Rankin–Selberg kernel 𝐾𝐹 ( 𝑠 ) of Chapter 57.5. The arithmetic theorem is the Petersson-positive face of
this kernel at the archimedean place.

de Branges Positivity and the Phi Functor
Theorem 69.3.5 (de Branges positivity is orthogonal to the Phi functor). The implication from
Hermite–Biehler divisor control and moment positivity to critical-line zero placement in Chapter 58.8.1
is independent of the Vol III two-stage Phi functor thm:phi-two-stage-factorisation-headline.
664                                       Chapter 69. Arithmetic Fibre and Source Orthogonality


Proof. The de Branges theorem is a statement about entire functions, Hermite–Biehler functions, and
Stieltjes–Hamburger moment determinacy. The Phi functor is a statement about cyclic 𝐴∞ -Calabi–Yau
categories and 𝐸2 -factorization algebras. The shared Heisenberg notation carries different structures in
the two theorems and gives no implication in either direction.

Remark 69.3.6 (signature convention). The Mukai pairing uses signature (1, 1) on its hyperbolic blocks.
The Hermite–Biehler condition uses positivity in the upper half plane. The two conventions are com-
patible because the positive Hermite–Biehler block is one summand of the hyperbolic plane.

Riemann–von Mangoldt Density and BD Acyclicity
Theorem 69.3.7 (zero density is orthogonal to genus-zero chiral acyclicity). The Riemann–von
Mangoldt density formula and the Tate-Gaussian explicit formula do not enter the proof of thm:BD-
genus-zero; conversely BD genus-zero acyclicity does not enter the proof of the zero-density formula.

Proof. The first proof is by contour integration and the Hadamard product of 𝜉 . The second is Beilinson–
Drinfeld chiral homology. The objects and sources are disjoint.

spectral-positivity, and Riemann–von Mangoldt density theorems are orthogonal to their nearest formal

analogues. The adelic descent and wild-prime compact-generation theorems are native arithmetic

Proof. The fibre assertions are proved in Chapter 69.2.1, Chapter 69.2.4, Chapter 69.3.1, Chapter 69.3.3,

two native assertions have no source theorem in the preceding volumes, by their adelic and wild-prime
domains.

Independent Comparison of Chapters 49–59

Chapters 49–59 form eleven constructions toward the G-row biconditional

                             𝜅GAr + ( 𝜅 ! )GAr = 0   ⇐⇒    𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ) .

Their common comparison has seven faces: source disjointness, sign normalisation, ambient category,
hypotheses, functoriality, imported equivalences, and numerical computations. The comparison below
records only mathematical content. It isolates three conditional points and leaves the rest at the strength
stated in the corresponding chapters.

70.1   The Eleven Local Comparisons
Chapter 49: F1.a.1, F1.a.2, and LACD
The Taylor–Wiles ordinary comparison uses Clozel–Harris–Taylor, Kisin, Gee–Kisin, Emerton–Gee,
and Hida on the derivation side, and Dotto–Emerton–Gee together with Fargues–Scholze on the
categorical side. The two source families are disjoint. Berger–Colmez fixes the Hodge–Tate convention,
and the block-diagonal Hecke action preserves compactly generated presentable stable ∞-categories.
The non-ordinary extension, the non-semisimple class comparison, and the Eisenstein extension remain
the named conditional statements Chapter 49.2.9, Chapter 47.7.3, and Chapter 49.4.6.
   The Dotto–Emerton–Gee input is used only in its fixed-central-character 𝑝 ≥ 5 fully faithful form.
No essential-surjectivity theorem and no global variation of the central character is imported.

Chapter 50: F1.a.3 (A+B)
The block-additivity argument is an ∞-categorical statement in Pr 𝑠𝑡𝐿 . Bernstein, Bushnell–Henniart,
Paskunas, Ben-Zvi–Francis–Nadler, and Lurie supply disjoint inputs for the block decomposition and
the tensor formalism. The co-Hochschild convention is the one of HA 5.5.3 and is compatible with
Costello–Gwilliam.
   The ordinary block is controlled only after the stated deformation hypotheses. The wild-prime
centraliser and per-block residuals are not deduced from Paskunas alone; they are precisely the narrower
conjectural pieces named in Chapter 50.

Chapter 51: F1.a.3.C
Emerton–Gee gives the ambient Noetherian formal stack. It does not by itself give a finite nilpotent
stratification, wild-prime quiver local models, or residual-gerbe generators. The compact-generation
theorem is therefore conditional on the local-model input stated in Chapter 51.4.1. Under that input,
recollement and compact-generation are formal consequences of Beilinson–Bernstein–Deligne, Gaits-
gory–Rozenblyum, and Arinkin–Gaitsgory.




                                                     667
668                                   Chapter 70. Independent Comparison of Chapters 49–59


    The equality 2 = 2 in the 𝑝 = 3 block is a tangent-dimension comparison. It is not a class-level identi-
fication of the two gerbe directions. The class-level statement belongs to the Paskunas–wild comparison
and is not smuggled into the compact-generation proof.

Chapter 52: Chenevier and 𝐹 2.𝑐
The determinant-trace comparison is Chenevier’s pseudocharacter formalism. The 𝐹 2.𝑐 closure uses
the elementary structure of finite adelic test categories and does not require perfectoid descent. The
𝐴𝐺.𝑑𝑒𝑡 transition is the sole non-formal point: it requires the arithmetic 𝐸2 -centre gluing input isolated
in Chapter 52. Bhatt–Scholze supplies prismatic and pro-𝑒´tale comparison technology, but no unquoted
theorem is used as a black box for the Emerton–Gee trace comparison.

Chapter 53: The Elementary Closure
The five elementary constructions of Chapter 53 are consequences of the earlier chapters and of the
explicit formula. They do not add a new equivalence to RH. The only RH-equivalent content is the
Weil positivity inequality already isolated as A-TP. The elementary chapter is therefore a normal form
for the implication chain, not an independent proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

Chapter 54: Arithmetic Positselski
Pontryagin duality, Greenlees–May duality, Matlis duality, and the Bost–Connes/Consani–Marcolli
formalism close the four abelian Positselski subitems at the stated domain. The upgrade of the
abelian Heisenberg G-row is conditional on the precise adele-class/cobar-sheaf identification in
Consani–Marcolli. Without that primary-source identification the result is a conditional theorem, not a
theorem in the absolute sense.

Chapter 55: Koszul–Petersson
The Petersson comparison is a discrete-spectrum theorem. The Eisenstein sector is excluded from the
theorem and reappears as the Langlands–Shahidi extension. The Maass part is conditional on the Ra-
manujan input named in Chapter 93. No continuum trace is silently folded into the discrete computa-
tion.

Chapter 56: H-PAr
The GNS construction supplies the Hilbert-space skeleton. It does not construct the Hilbert–Polya
operator. The twist-existence condition is the classical zero-line obstruction in operator form. Thus the
chapter separates construction of the representation from positivity of the spectral measure.

Chapter 57: HP–Li Positivity
The Mellin–Rankin–Selberg isometry reduces the restricted Li positivity statement to the archimedean
Tate distribution. The archimedean Tate positivity statement is equivalent to RH and is not proved there.
The chapter identifies the exact positivity functional and does not replace Weil positivity by positivity
on a smaller test class.

Chapter 58: VB∗
The de Branges, Hamburger, Beurling–Malliavin, determinant, and self-adjointness hypotheses form a
chain of sufficient conditions for the Weil inequality. Each hypothesis is at RH strength or is explicitly
conditional. The chapter proves the implication chain, not the hypotheses at the far end of the chain.
70.2. The Three Conditional Points                                                                      669


Chapter 59: Ranalytic
The sharp Riemann–von Mangoldt term, the Gaussian value of the balanced explicit formula, and the
Iwasawa Artin–Rees residuals are elementary at their stated domain. Gaussian evaluation of the balanced
explicit formula is not Weil positivity. The missing bridge is the full two-sided moment asymptotic strong
enough to remove the (log 𝑛) 4𝑛 loss.

70.2    The Three Conditional Points
   (i) The wild-prime compact-generation theorem of Chapter 51 is conditional on finite nilpotent local
       models and class-level residual-gerbe generators. Emerton–Gee alone supplies the ambient formal
       stack.
  (ii) The 𝐴𝐺.𝑑𝑒𝑡 transition of Chapter 52 is conditional on arithmetic 𝐸2 -centre gluing. The geometric
       centres of Ben-Zvi–Francis–Nadler and Francis–Gaitsgory are not, by themselves, the arithmetic
       gluing theorem.
 (iii) The abelian Heisenberg G-row upgrade of Chapter 54 is conditional on the exact Consani–
       Marcolli adele-class/cobar-sheaf comparison used there.

70.3    Conclusion
With these three qualifications, Chapters 49–59 state precisely what they prove. They give independent
reductions of F1, of LACD , of the abelian Positselski sector, and of the discrete Koszul–Petersson identity.
The RH-equivalent assertion is not hidden in any of these reductions; it remains the archimedean Tate
positivity, equivalently Weil positivity.

the Riemann–Siegel asymptotic.
   Primary-source disjointness: Riemann 1859, Siegel 1932, and Edwards 1974 do not appear as proof

theorem cited in Chapter 61.1 are disjoint from the Riemann–Siegel list used here: the former are classical
complex-analytic identities for the digamma; the latter are classical analytic-number-theory constructions
on the critical line.

Remark 71.2.3 (source and sign conventions for the exact identity). Source separation. The identity
combines Chapter 61.1.1 (Hurwitz list) with Chapter 71.2.1 (Riemann–Siegel list). The two source
classes are structurally disjoint; the identity is a direct differentiation, not a propagation.
Sign convention. We use log Γ on the principal branch along 1/4 + 𝑖𝑡 /2; this branch is uniquely deter-
mined by continuity from 𝑡 = 0, where log Γ (1/4) ∈ ℝ. The imaginary part Im log Γ has the same sign
as the standard arg Γ convention (Edwards 1974, §6.5), fixed by the 𝑡 = 0 normalisation.
Ambient category. The identity lives in real-analytic functions on ℝ; no derived-category or sheaf issue.
Missing hypothesis. Differentiation under Im log Γ requires real-analyticity at 𝑡 , which holds for all
𝑡 ∈ ℝ since Γ is analytic and non-vanishing on the vertical line 1/4 + 𝑖𝑡 /2.
False functoriality. We assert no functorial property of 𝜃 RS beyond real-analyticity.
Unproved equivalence. The identity is an equality, not an equivalence.

Remark 71.6.2 (source and numerical conventions for the residual theorem). Source separation. The
Stirling list (Edwards 1974) is strictly disjoint from the Hurwitz list (Hurwitz 1882) used in Chapter 61.
The two analyses agree on the numerical values of 𝑔 (verified at 50-digit precision); they agree because
they are two expansions of the same entire function.
Sign convention. 𝜃 RS uses the standard Riemann–Siegel convention (Riemann 1859; Siegel 1932; Ed-
wards 1974 §6.5, eq. (2)) with 𝜃 RS (0) = 0.
Ambient category. Real-analytic functions on ℝ.
Missing hypothesis. All Stirling bounds hold uniformly in 𝑡 ∈ ℝ at 𝑧 = 1/4 + 𝑖𝑡 /2; the real part
Re 𝑧 = 1/4 > 0 is uniform.
False functoriality. None asserted. The 𝜃 RS is a specific function, not a functor.
Unproved equivalence. The Z-phase reformulation (Chapter 71.5.1) is an equivalence; its proof is a
direct substitution.
Numerical constant. The constants 𝑇St4 = 0.8729590 . . ., 𝑡∗ = 0.8506623 . . ., 𝜅∗ = 3.0827 . . .,
𝜅∗mean = 1.488 . . ., 𝜅∗ /𝜅∗mean ≈ 2.07 are all verified to 50-digit mpmath precision.

71.7   Non-Elementary Residual Constructions
Remark 71.7.1 (four non-elementary obstruction constructions). The Stirling refinement leaves the SHF-
complement as the irreducible residual. Four non-elementary constructions remain, in parallel with the
three of Chapter 61.3.3 plus one added by the Riemann–Siegel reformulation.
   (i) Sharper Stirling-6 or Stirling-8 closure: the next Bernoulli coefficient 𝐵 6 = 1/42 gives an even
       tighter expansion 𝑔 ( 𝑡 ) = 𝑔St6 ( 𝑡 ) + 𝑂 (| 𝑧 | −6 ). The threshold 𝑇St6 where 𝑔St6 − ( 𝑡 ) > 0 satisfies

       𝑇St6 = 0.9310 . . . > 𝑇St4 = 0.8730 . . .: at the optimal-truncation regime around | 𝑧 | ≈ 𝑘 , the next
       Stirling order is unstable. No further Stirling improvement at | 𝑧 | ≈ 0.43 gains unconditional
       ground. Form: elementary cap reached.
  (ii) Riemann–Siegel asymptotic formula: the full Riemann–Siegel main-sum-plus-corrections                expan-
       sion 𝑍 ( 𝑡 ) = 2 𝑛𝑁=1 𝑛−1/2 cos( 𝜃 RS ( 𝑡 ) − 𝑡 log 𝑛) + 𝑅 ( 𝑡, 𝑁 ) with 𝑁 = ⌊ 𝑡 /2 𝜋 ⌋ offers precise
                         P                                                               √︁

       control for large | 𝑡 | but not for the bounded interval [−𝑡∗ , 𝑡∗ ]. Form: not applicable to the residual.
 (iii) Hermite–Biehler reformulation of the bounded residual: the phase-derivative formulation (71.7)
       admits a reformulation in the de Branges space H ( 𝐸𝜉 ) of Chapter 58. The positivity of the integral
       becomes a Hermite–Biehler inequality for the shifted phase. Form: non-elementary, equivalent in
       strength to HB+ of Chapter 58.8.1.
 (iv) Gaussian Weil test functions via Riemann–Siegel saddle-point: for 𝑓 a Gaussian, the integrals
       𝐴 [ 𝑓 ] and 𝐵 [ 𝑓 ] can be evaluated by saddle-point applied to 𝑒 𝑖𝜃RS ( 𝑡 ) -weighted integrands. The
       positivity question reduces to an explicit finite-dimensional moment problem on the Gaussian
       family (Hardy 1942; Chapter 59). Form: non-elementary, equivalent in strength to the Gaussian
       explicit-formula closure.
   None of (1)–(4) closes A-TP on the full cone; each is a mathematical route equivalent in strength to
de Branges, Connes, Deninger, or Hardy. The Stirling refinement sharpens the elementary ceiling by a
factor ≈ 2 in the sub-class, names the obstruction precisely in Riemann–Siegel language, and exhausts
the elementary constructions.

A-TP via Nyman–Beurling Closure and the
Baez-Duarte Refinement

The Nyman–Beurling comparison. Chapter 61 reduced the archimedean Tate positivity conjecture A-TP to
a bounded-interval question on [−𝑡∗ , 𝑡∗ ] with 𝑡∗ ≈ 0.8507; the irreducible residual is the elementary ceiling.
The same obstruction has a classical 𝐿 2 (0, 1) expression through Nyman 1950 and Beurling 1955, sharpened
by Baez-Duarte 2003. The Nyman–Beurling criterion reformulates RH as a closure statement in 𝐿 2 (0, 1)
generated by the functions 𝜌 𝛼 ( 𝑥 ) = { 𝛼 / 𝑥 } − 𝛼 {1/ 𝑥 } for 𝛼 ∈ (0, 1]; Baez-Duarte shows RH is equivalent
to the asymptotic vanishing of the Möbius-coeﬃcient distance 𝑑 𝑁 = inf 𝑐𝑘 ∥ 𝜒[0,1] − 𝑘𝑁=1 𝑐𝑘 𝜌1/𝑘 ∥ 𝐿2 (0,1) .
                                                                                            P
The results are fourfold. First, an explicit Mellin normal form: the 𝐿 2 (0, 1) norm of 𝜒[0,1] − 𝑐𝑘 𝜌1/𝑘 is an
                                                                                                 P
integral on the critical line against a kernel built from 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ). A-TP and the Baez-Duarte vanishing have the
same RH truth value; the Mellin identity does not identify the ﬁnite-dimensional distance with the Weil
quadratic form. Second, on the bounded-interval reduction HFD sub-class of Chapter 61, the expected Ny-
man–Beurling estimate becomes a weighted approximation problem for 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) −1 on the critical line; neither
the Mellin identity nor PNT proves the 1/log 𝑁 √rate. Third, a Möbius partial-sum control: the conditional
Mertens bound 𝑀 ( 𝑁 ) := 𝑘 ≤ 𝑁 𝜇 ( 𝑘 ) = 𝑂 ( 𝑁 log2 𝑁 ) under RH sharpens the unconditional PNT
                               P
bound 𝑀 ( 𝑁 ) = 𝑜 ( 𝑁 ); the corresponding 𝑀1 ( 𝑁 ) := 𝑘 ≤ 𝑁 𝜇 ( 𝑘 )/𝑘 = 𝑜 (1) (unconditional, PNT)
                                                                  P
is only a scalar shadow of the critical-line 𝐿 2 -approximation. Fourth, the complementary class carries a
compact-core Baez-Duarte shadow of the same bounded-interval residual; this compact shadow is not a
substitute for the global Nyman–Beurling criterion.

The Nyman–Beurling Theorem (Recall)
Theorem 72.2.4 (Nyman–Beurling 1950/1955). . The Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to

                                                𝜒 ∈ 𝐻 2 (0, 1) .

rational sums; the converse uses that 𝜁 −1 extending to the strip Re 𝑠 ≥ 1/2 + 𝜀 controls the closure.

72.3    Mellin Normal Form and RH-Level Comparison
The Mellin–Plancherel identity converts the Nyman–Beurling 𝐿 2 (0, 1) norm into a critical-line integral.
The Weil explicit formula and the Nyman–Beurling criterion both have RH as their zero-placement
content; this is equality of logical strength, not an identity of quadratic forms.

Theorem 72.3.4 (A-TP and Nyman–Beurling have the same RH content). . The archimedean
Tate positivity A-TP of Chapter 57.2.3 is equivalent to the Nyman–Beurling closure 𝜒 ∈ 𝐻 2 (0, 1);
equivalently to the Baez-Duarte vanishing lim 𝑁 →∞ 𝑑 𝑁 = 0.

Proof. Both conditions are equivalent to RH. A-TP ⇔ RH by Chapter 57.2.4. RH ⇔ 𝜒 ∈ 𝐻 2 (0, 1)
by Chapter 72.2.4. RH ⇔ 𝑑 𝑁 → 0 by Chapter 72.2.5. Transitivity closes the reformulation. The two
equivalent RH formulations are related by an explicit Mellin-Plancherel integral identity.

72.4    Restricted-Class Estimate on HFD
The bounded-interval reduction HFD sub-class (Chapter 61.2.3) enters the Nyman–Beurling framework
through the spectral weight on the critical line: the HFD condition concentrates | 𝑓b| 2 on | 𝑡 | > 𝑡∗ . This
concentration gives archimedean 𝑊∞ -positivity in Chapter 61.2.4; it does not, by itself, give a weighted
Baez-Duarte estimate.

there is no ( 𝑠 − 1) −1 polar term in (72.2). The obstruction is the weighted critical-line norm in (72.3),
not a finite-dimensional polar remainder.
688     Chapter 72. A-TP via Nyman–Beurling Closure and the Baez-Duarte Refinement


Remark 72.7.5 (obstruction 5: the cross-reduction identity (72.3) is circular). The identity (72.3) is a Mellin–
Plancherel identity and contains no zero-square residue formula. It is independent of the Weil distri-
bution, but independence of identities is weaker than a bound. The missing step is precisely a uniform
estimate for the displayed integral.
Remark 72.7.6 (obstruction 6: disjoint sources do not prove the missing estimate). The Nyman–Beurling
construction uses Nyman 1950, Beurling 1955, and Baez–Duarte 2003, a line distinct from Rankin–
Selberg. Distinct lineage does not imply (72.4); the required weighted estimate remains an analytic
input.
Remark 72.7.7 (obstruction 7: closing A-TP on HFD𝑐 via Nyman–Beurling). The compact-core norm
(72.5) measures only the archimedean negative interval. Closing A-TP on HFD𝑐 still requires the 𝑅 [ 𝑓 ]-
term in Chapter 61.4; replacing it by the global Nyman–Beurling vanishing is exactly the RH-equivalent
Baez-Duarte criterion.

Remark 72.8.2 (comparison with the bounded-interval residual inequality). The bounded-interval reduc-
tion (Chapter 61) reduced A-TP to a bounded-interval domination 𝐵 [ 𝑓 ] ≤ 𝐴 [ 𝑓 ] + 2 𝜋 𝑅 [ 𝑓 ], with the
high-frequency archimedean tail controlled by the compact core and the residual. The Nyman–Beurling
form gives a compact-core distance for the negative interval and a global distance equivalent to RH.
Neither distance removes the 𝑅 [ 𝑓 ]-term from the bounded-interval inequality. The Nyman–Beurling
construction supplies exactly the following data:
   (i) the exact Mellin normal form for the weighted critical-line estimate and an 𝐿 2 (0, 1) distance;
  (ii) the precise weighted estimate whose proof would be required for HFD closure;
 (iii) a reformulation of the irreducible residual as a concrete Baez-Duarte distance problem.
It adds no closure of A-TP beyond the 𝑅 [ 𝑓 ]-coupled sub-classes. The elementary ceiling is the same
ceiling seen in Mellin coordinates.

Remark 72.9.1 (the Beilinson principle on the Nyman–Beurling comparison). The Nyman–Beurling
comparison proves neither RH nor an independent HFD closure. Its mathematical content is the ir-
reducible residual recast in 𝐿 2 (0, 1) language and the exact weighted estimate which would imply the
missing HFD bound.
Remark 72.9.2 (cross-volume dependency). The inputs are Chapter 57 (Rankin–Selberg kernel obstruc-
tion, A-TP conjecture 57.2.3), Chapter 61 (HFD sub-class, bounded-interval reduction), and PNT
(Hadamard 1896, de la Vallée-Poussin 1896, Landau 1911). They are independent of the de Branges /
Hermite–Biehler analysis of Chapter 58, the Ranalytic density-of-zeros analysis of Chapter 59, or the
Positselski four sub-items of Chapter 54. The Nyman–Beurling construction is orthogonal to these.

Proposition 73.1.4 (sampling weights and operator multiplicities). The sampling model has one

Proof. The complete orthonormal basis determines every eigenspace of the first diagonal operator. Its

instead contain each zero occurrence. Changing a scalar product weight changes the norm of a vector,
but not the dimension of its eigenspace.

Independent Sources
Four classical sources enter the analysis.
Stirling 1730. Stirling, J. Methodus Differentialis. London 1730, Prop. 28. Asymptotic expansion of
log Γ ( 𝑧 ) and its logarithmic derivative 𝜓 ( 𝑧 ), with alternating Bernoulli tail.
Bernoulli numbers (Euler 1755). Euler, L. Institutiones Calculi Differentialis. St. Petersburg 1755, II.
ch. vi. Signs and magnitudes of 𝐵 2𝑘 ; alternation property.
Plancherel 1910. Plancherel, M. Contribution à l’étude de la représentation d’une fonction arbitraire
par des intégrales déﬁnies. Rend. Circ. Mat. Palermo 30 (1910), 289–335. Parseval identity for the Fourier
transform on 𝐿 2 (ℝ).
Slepian–Pollak 1961. Slepian, D.; Pollak, H.O. Prolate spheroidal wave functions, Fourier analysis, and
uncertainty, I. Bell Syst. Tech. J. 40 (1961), 43–63. Prolate eigenvalue structure of the bandpass concentra-
tion operator on 𝐿 2 ( [−𝑇 , 𝑇 ]) → 𝐿 2 ( [−Ω, Ω]).
    Stirling 1730, Euler 1755, Plancherel 1910, and Slepian–Pollak 1961 do not enter Weil 1952, Li 1997,
the Rankin–Selberg integral, or the Hurwitz derivation used in Chapter 61. The Stirling–Bernoulli
tail is a separate elementary complex-analysis classic from the Hurwitz series. The Plancherel identity is
orthogonal to the Paley–Wiener classification, and Slepian–Pollak 1961 is a separate analytic-geometric
theorem about bandpass operators not cited previously.

Remark 75.3.6 (which proﬁle IE captures and HFD misses). The HFD class is constrained by pointwise

in HFD and fail IE. The two conditions are transverse sufficient criteria.

Three Non-Elementary Constructions Revisited
The three non-elementary constructions of Chapter 61.3.3 (zero-density refinement, Gaussian reduction,
Hermite–Biehler/de Branges) remain independent. The IE theorem does not obviate them.
Remark 75.6.2 (construction interactions). (i) Zero-density reﬁnement. The IE class handles tail-heavy
       PW; the Riemann–von Mangoldt asymptotic density 𝑁 (𝑇 ) ∼ (𝑇 /2 𝜋 ) log 𝑇 controls the density
       of zero ordinates, but it does not turn the zero functional into a positive form. For IE-captured 𝑓 ,
       A-TP is obtained before appealing to a zero-side interpretation. For residual 𝑓 , the obstruction is
       precisely the Weil positivity problem; it cannot be removed by calling the zero-side term positive.
                                                                          2     2
  (ii) Gaussian reduction. Gaussian test functions 𝑓 ( 𝑢) = 𝑒 − 𝑢 /(2 𝜎 ) are not compactly supported,
       hence not PW-strict; they are Schwartz of infinite PW type. Their spectral density is Gaussian
                       √         2 2
       with 𝑓b( 𝑡 ) = 𝜎 2 𝜋 𝑒 − 𝜎 𝑡 /2 . For 𝜎 ≪ 1, spectrally wide: 𝛼 small, 𝛽 large, IE condition holds. For
       𝜎 ≫ 1, spectrally narrow: 𝛼 close to 1, IE fails. The Hardy–Littlewood Gaussian-Weil obstruction
       pursues the narrow-Gaussian regime, a model for the IE residual. See Chapter 59.
 (iii) de Branges structure. The prolate-eigenvalue characterization Chapter 75.4.3 is a time-frequency
       estimate in the Paley–Wiener model. The de Branges construction asks for positivity in H ( 𝐸𝜉 ).
       The two structures are compatible, but the prolate estimate is not a substitute for Hermite–Biehler
       positivity.

numerical inequality is verified.

Remark 75.7.1 (far-tail Beilinson principle). The integral-energy reduction obeys the Beilinson principle:
a transverse sufficient criterion is an honest substitute for no inclusion theorem. The estimate is explicit,
elementary, and computable: the constants 𝑀 ≈ 3.083, 𝑡∗ ≈ 0.8507, 𝑡𝐿∗ ≈ 0.8946, and the Stirling lower
bound 𝑔 𝐿 are all closed-form. The residual is precisely the failure of all logarithmic far-tail payments.
Remark 75.7.2 (quantiﬁcation of the bounded step). Relative to the bounded-interval reduction HFD
(sup-bound sub-class), the integral-energy reduction proves 𝑊∞ ≥ 0 on:
• All 𝑓 satisfying a verified two-scale prolate inequality (Chapter 75.4.5).
• All 𝑓 satisfying the integral-energy condition 𝑀 𝛼 ≤ 𝑔 𝐿 (𝑇1 ) 𝛽 for some 𝑇1 .
The uncovered residual is the failure of the weighted far-tail inequality. Bridging this residual requires a
separate positivity mechanism, such as a proved Gaussian reduction or the de Branges Hermite–Biehler
construction. The elementary ceiling reached by integral-energy bounds is the IE sub-class.

The Mellin–Barnes reduction. The archimedean Tate kernel is tested via the Mellin–Barnes contour
representation of the digamma function and the Binet second integral representation. The digamma kernel
 𝑔 ( 𝑡 ) = Re 𝜓 (1/4 + 𝑖𝑡 /2) + log 𝜋 admits two classical integral representations whose insertion into the
archimedean Weil contribution exchanges the pointwise sign problem on [−𝑡∗ , 𝑡∗ ] for a contour residue sum
(Mellin–Barnes) or for an absolutely convergent positive-kernel decomposition (Binet). Three unconditional
consequences follow. First: the Binet representation yields an explicit decomposition 𝑔 = 𝑔log + 𝑔shift −
2 𝑔Binet in which 𝑔Binet is the integral of the Planck weight 1/( 𝑒 2𝜋 𝑢 − 1) against a real-part Cauchy kernel
in 𝑢, isolating
           ∫1     an absolutely convergent positive component. Second: the Hankel integral representation
𝜓 ( 𝑠 ) = 0 (1 − 𝑢 𝑠 −1 )/(1 − 𝑢) 𝑑𝑢 − 𝛾𝐸 inserted into 𝑊∞ yields a Laplace-transform representation of the
archimedean Weil distribution, revealing a decomposition 𝑊∞ ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) = 𝐿 [ 𝑓 ] − Res[ 𝑓 ] with 𝐿 [ 𝑓 ] ≥ 0
transparent. Third: a conditional closure on the sub-class of test functions 𝑓 whose Laplace-kernel integrand
is pointwise non-negative; this sub-class properly contains a subset of PWhol

residue sum at 𝑤 = −𝑛 converges conditionally but each term carries sign (−1) 𝑛 , and the alternation defeats

    Pairing residues: 𝑅2𝑘 ( 𝑡 ) + 𝑅2𝑘+1 ( 𝑡 ) is the sum of two residues whose leading signs differ, and this

factor [(·)2𝑘 − (·)2𝑘+1 ] which vanishes on transitional loci of 𝑡 . A positive decomposition of 𝑔 via this
construction is therefore not available uniformly.

Remark 76.4.4 (Mellin–Barnes obstruction: analytic content). The Mellin–Barnes contour construction
is informative about the analytic structure of 𝑔 (in particular the double poles of Γ ( 𝑤 ) 2 encode the
trivial zeros of 𝜁 at −2𝑛 after identification through the Riemann 𝜉 -function). However the residue
expansion does not isolate a positive-definite kernel. By contrast, the Binet construction (Chapter 76.3.5)
produces a genuine unconditional positive kernel, and the Hankel sub-class closes a non-empty region
missed by the bounded-interval reduction. The structural difference: the Binet representation replaces
the digamma pole at 𝑠 = 0 by an integrable Planck weight, whereas Mellin–Barnes distributes the same
content over an alternating residue sum.

A-TP via the Exact Hadamard Factorisation:
Reflected Resolvents and Tautology Comparison

77.1    Hadamard Factorisation
Setup
The archimedean Tate positivity conjecture A-TP (Chapter 57.2.3) is the statement that the Weil dis-
tribution 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) ≥ 0 for all 𝑓 in the Paley–Wiener space PW(ℝ) (entire functions of exponential
type whose restriction to ℝ is square-integrable; 𝑓e( 𝑥 ) := 𝑓 (− 𝑥 )). Chapters 58 and 61 tested A-TP via
de Branges / Hermite–Biehler spectral theory and via the digamma-kernel elementary decomposition,
respectively; each construction bottomed out at a hypothesis equivalent to RH.
    Hadamard factorisation gives 𝜉ℝ ( 𝑠 ) = 𝑒 𝑎+𝑏𝑠 𝜌 (1 − 𝑠 / 𝜌) 𝑒 𝑠/ 𝜌 of 𝜉ℝ as an entire function of order 1
                                                     Q
and genus 1 (Chapter 58.2.1). Logarithmic differentiation yields 𝜉ℝ′ / 𝜉ℝ as a sum over zeros plus a linear
correction. The reflected-resolvent kernel K 𝜌 ( 𝑡 ) obtained by multiplying opposite critical-line resolvents
is not the Guinand–Weil zero summand; it is nevertheless sign-indefinite even when 𝜌 lies on the critical
line. Thus the Hadamard construction gives no termwise positivity theorem. The positivity statement is
the full Weil distribution, hence RH-level.

Classical Sources
The Hadamard-factorisation obstruction uses four classical sources disjoint from the restricted-class
comparison and the bounded-interval reduction.
Hadamard 1893. Hadamard, J. Étude sur les propriétés des fonctions entières et en particulier d’une fonc-
tion considérée par Riemann. J. Math. Pures Appl. (4) 9 (1893), 171–215. Original Hadamard factorisation
theorem for entire functions of finite order.
Guinand–Weil 1948/1952. Guinand, A.P. A summation formula in the theory of prime numbers.
Proc. London Math. Soc. (2) 50 (1948), 107–119. Weil, A. Sur les formules explicites de la théorie des
nombres premiers (cited above). Pair-pole representation via Hadamard derivative; Parseval between
critical-line Fourier and zero-sum.
de Bruijn 1950. de Bruijn, N.G. The roots of trigonometric integrals and a theorem of Hurwitz. Duke
Math. J. 17 (1950), 197–226. Heat-flow family Ξ𝜆 ; monotone shift of roots towards the real axis.
Newman 1976, Rodgers–Tao 2020. Newman, C.M. Fourier transforms with only real zeros.
Proc. AMS 61 (1976), 245–251. Rodgers, B.; Tao, T. The de Bruijn–Newman constant is non-negative.
Forum Math. Pi 8 (2020), e6. The de Bruijn–Newman constant Λ; RH iff Λ ≤ 0; unconditional lower
bound Λ ≥ 0.

77.4     Tautology Comparison: Where Positivity Becomes Circular
Even under RH, a single pair-pole kernel is sign-indefinite. The following proposition records the failure
of the pointwise construction.
Proposition 77.4.1 (pointwise pair-pole positivity fails). . The statement ‘‘K 𝜌 ( 𝑡 ) ≥ 0 pointwise
for every non-trivial zero 𝜌 ’’ is false for the zeta zero set. Hence any attempt to prove A-TP by term-by-
term pointwise non-negativity of K 𝜌 ( 𝑡 ) is not merely circular; it has no valid on-critical case.

Proof. For an on-critical zero, 𝛼 = 0, and K 𝜌 (0) = − 𝛾 −2 < 0. Thus RH itself does not make the
pair-pole kernel pointwise non-negative.

Remark 77.4.2 (pointwise positivity versus integrated positivity). Proposition 77.4.1 establishes that point-
wise K 𝜌 ( 𝑡 ) ≥ 0 cannot be the mechanism for A-TP. Sum-level non-negativity belongs to the actual
Weil distribution; the reflected-resolvent form R ref is not that distribution. The Hadamard logarithmic
derivative has the same RH ceiling as the de Branges construction (Chapter 58) and the digamma-kernel
construction (Chapter 61).
77.5. de Bruijn–Newman Λ ≤ 0 is RH                                                                    723


Corollary 77.4.3 (the valid reformulations coincide). . The two valid positivity statements
  (i) (Weil) 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) ≥ 0 for all 𝑓 ∈ PW(ℝ);
 (ii) (Hermite–Biehler) the de Branges datum 𝐸𝜉 ( 𝑧 ) = 𝐴𝜉 ( 𝑧 ) − 𝑖 𝐵 𝜉 ( 𝑧 ) (defined in Chapter 58) is
      Hermite–Biehler and satisfies div( 𝐴𝜉 ) = div( Ξ);
are equivalent and each equivalent to RH. The pointwise pair-pole positivity statement is false and is
not a third reformulation.

Proof. (1) ⇔ RH: Chapter 57.2.1. (2) ⇔ RH: Lagarias’ Hermite–Biehler theorem and Chapter 58.6.5.
Chapter 77.4.1 excludes the pointwise pair-pole statement.

77.5   de Bruijn–Newman Λ ≤ 0 is RH
The pair-pole pointwise positivity statement is false. The de Bruijn–Newman bound Λ ≤ 0 is a valid
construction to A-TP only because it is RH itself.

Λ ≤ 0 Implies A-TP via RH
Lemma 77.5.3 (critical-line reformulation of Λ ≤ 0). . The statement Λ ≤ 0 is equivalent to: every
non-trivial zero of 𝜉ℝ lies on the critical line Re 𝑠 = 1/2.

Proof. Λ ≤ 0 ⇔ Ξ0 = Ξ has only real zeros ⇔ 𝜉ℝ (1/2 + 𝑖𝑡 ) = 0 for 𝑡 real only ⇔ every non-trivial
zero 𝜌 of 𝜉ℝ satisfies Re 𝜌 = 1/2. This is RH.

Corollary 77.5.4 ( Λ ≤ 0 implies A-TP). . Under Λ ≤ 0 (equivalent to RH), A-TP holds.

Proof. Lemma 77.5.3 reduces Λ ≤ 0 to RH. Then Chapter 57.2.1 gives A-TP.

Remark 77.5.5 (Λ ≤ 0 is equivalent to RH). Λ ≤ 0 is equivalent to RH, not weaker. The Rodgers–Tao
theorem Λ ≥ 0 places the constant at the Newman barrier. change on Λ is change towards RH, not
a weaker substitute. The Hadamard-factorisation construction is tautological: it reduces A-TP to RH
without passing through any strictly weaker intermediate.
   The candidate ‘‘Λ ≤ 𝜆0 for some 𝜆0 > 0 still implies A-TP’’ is not supplied by the de Bruijn–
Newman theory. The heat flow parameterises the zero-reality problem; the value 𝜆 = 0 is exactly RH.
Proposition 77.5.6 (zero-free regions do not give a pair-pole positivity criterion). . A classical
zero-free region, including the Korobov–Vinogradov region, does not imply A-TP or a partial-support
A-TP statement through the pair-pole kernels. It excludes zeros near the edge of the critical strip; it does
not make the central principal-value kernels positive.

Proof. Chapter 77.3.6 shows that even an on-critical zero gives a sign-indefinite principal-value kernel.
Moving zeros away from the edge of the strip cannot turn these central kernels into positive kernels. A
zero-free region is a zero-location theorem; A-TP is a positivity theorem for the full Weil sum.

Remark 77.5.7 (zero-free region boundary). The Korobov–Vinogradov region is an edge exclusion near
Re 𝑠 = 1, with the reflected exclusion near Re 𝑠 = 0. It is not a central critical-line positivity statement.
No partial-support A-TP closure is recorded here from that input.

77.6    Zero Density and Pair-Pole Convergence
Convergence of the Pair-Pole Sum
Proposition 77.6.1 (reflected pair-pole form converges distributionally after pairing). . For
𝑓 ∈ PW(ℝ), the reflected pair-pole form (77.6) is a paired principal-value distribution. It is not, in
general, an absolutely convergent sum of ordinary integrals. Absolute convergence holds only after
imposing vanishing near the finitely many zero ordinates met by supp 𝑓b, or after keeping the explicit
regularisation.

Proof. Away from 𝑡 = ± 𝛾 , the displayed kernel has the stated | 𝛾 | −2 decay after pairing, and the zero-
counting estimate controls the tail. At 𝑡 = ± 𝛾 , however, the on-critical kernel is PV( 𝑡 2 − 𝛾 2 ) −1 , whose
absolute value is not locally integrable. Thus the reflected-resolvent expression is a principal-value distri-
bution unless the test function kills those poles or a regularisation is retained.

Remark 77.6.2 (sum-level positivity versus pointwise positivity). For 𝜌 = 𝛽 + 𝑖 𝛾 with 𝛼 = 1/2 − 𝛽 , the
functional-equation partner 1 − 𝜌 = (1 − 𝛽 ) − 𝑖 𝛾 has 𝛼 ′ = 1/2 − (1 − 𝛽 ) = − 𝛼 . Since (77.5) depends on
𝛼 2 , K1− 𝜌 ( 𝑡 ) = K 𝜌 ( 𝑡 ); the two kernels are equal. The sum-level non-negativity of the Weil distribution
is equivalent to RH by Chapter 57.2.1. It is not the pointwise positivity of K 𝜌 , and it is not the positivity
of the reflected-resolvent form R ref .

Exact Domain of the Hadamard-Factorisation Construction
Theorem 77.6.3 (Hadamard-factorisation construction: exact domain). . The exact Hadamard-
factorisation obstruction on A-TP has the following outcomes.
   (i) Reﬂected pair-pole diagnostic (Chapter 77.3.5): unconditional; explicit pointwise form (77.5), but
       not the Guinand–Weil zero side.
  (ii) No termwise positivity under RH (Proposition 77.3.6): under RH, K 𝜌 ( 𝑡 ) = PV( 𝑡 2 − 𝛾 2 ) −1 , and
       single pair-pole terms can be negative.
77.7. Conclusion                                                                                               725


 (iii) Valid reformulations coincide (Chapter 77.4.3): Weil positivity and Hermite–Biehler positivity are
       equivalent to RH. Pointwise pair-pole positivity is false (Proposition 77.4.1).
 (iv) de Bruijn–Newman suﬃcient condition (Chapter 77.5.4): Λ ≤ 0 implies A-TP; but Λ ≤ 0 ⇔
       RH, so this is not weaker than RH.
  (v) Zero-free region boundary (Chapter 77.5.6): the Korobov–Vinogradov-style zero-free region does
       not give a pair-pole positivity criterion or a partial-support A-TP closure.
The genuine content of the Hadamard-factorisation construction is the logarithmic-derivative identity
and the reflected-resolvent diagnostic. It does not give a termwise Weil decomposition and does not close
A-TP below the RH threshold.

Proof. Combine the cited results.

Remark 77.6.4 (the tautology map). The three constructions to A-TP considered across the restricted-
class comparison, the bounded-interval reduction, and the analytic refinement are:
the de Branges spectral comparison (de Branges). HB+ + BD+ + Det + SH; tautology level: each
hypothesis is RH-equivalent or strictly finer.
the bounded-interval reduction (digamma). Bounded-interval positivity on [−𝑡∗ , 𝑡∗ ] after elemen-
tary reductions, with the finite-prime and polar functional 𝑅 [ 𝑓 ] retained; tautology level: the full in-
equality is RH-equivalent.
the Hadamard reduction (Hadamard). Logarithmic derivative and reflected pair-pole diagnostic; fail-
ure mode: pointwise positivity is false even on the critical line (Chapter 77.4.1).
All three constructions bottom out at RH. The content each provides is a different local rewriting of the
same positivity question. The Hadamard construction offers the pointwise reflected-resolvent formula
(77.5), which clarifies the sign obstruction but does not give the Weil zero side.

The reflected kernel (77.5) is not the Guinand–Weil zero summand. Pointwise non-negativity of K 𝜌 fails
even under RH (Proposition 77.4.1), so the Hadamard construction cannot prove A-TP by termwise
positivity. The de Bruijn–Newman constant Λ ≤ 0 is likewise equivalent to RH (Lemma 77.5.3). The

of A-TP remain Weil positivity and the Hermite–Biehler condition (Corollary 77.4.3).
Remark 77.7.1 (the non-tautological content of the Hadamard construction). The Hadamard construction
yields the exact logarithmic derivative of 𝜉ℝ and an explicit reflected-resolvent kernel (77.5). Pointwise pair-
pole positivity is false (Proposition 77.4.1), so the construction does not close A-TP via this mechanism.
Classical zero-free regions remain zero-location input, not positivity input.

A-TP as Gram Matrix Positivity: Hermite Basis

integrals of the digamma kernel 𝑔 ( 𝑡 ) = Re 𝜓 (1/4 + 𝑖𝑡 /2) + log 𝜋 against products of angular Weber–

78.1   Hermite Cutoff
Chapters 57 and 61 reduced the Riemann Hypothesis in the Hilbert–Pólya–Li form to the archimedean
Tate positivity conjecture A-TP, then to a bounded-interval positivity inequality on [−𝑡∗ , 𝑡∗ ]. A-TP is
equivalent to a negative quadratic form on the Paley–Wiener test class. The Weber–Hermite functions
span the Schwartz space, not the Paley–Wiener class, so their Gram matrices give a regularized oscillator
model rather than a literal PW basis.

Quadratic Reduction
The Weil quadratic form has regularized Hermite moments. Li-coefficient numerics do not transfer to
negative semidefiniteness of the Hermite blocks without an 𝑁 → ∞ theorem.

78.2     The Quadratic Form and Its Operator Kernel
The Weil distribution 𝑊 is a linear functional on test functions; applied to the convolution 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e it
produces a quadratic form Q [ 𝑓 ] = −𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) whose sign on PW(ℝ) is the content of A-TP.

Weil Distribution as Quadratic Form
Deﬁnition 78.2.1 (Weil quadratic form). . For 𝑓 ∈ PW(ℝ) real even, define the Weil quadratic form

           Q [ 𝑓 ] := −𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) = 𝑊∞ ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) + 𝑊fin ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) − 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e 21𝑖 − 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e − 21𝑖 .

Remark 78.2.4 (domain issue). The operator 𝑄 is not defined on all of 𝐿 2 (ℝ): the integrand | 𝑓b( 𝑡 )| 2 𝑔 ( 𝑡 )

off the real axis). Throughout, 𝑄 is interpreted as a densely defined sesquilinear form on PW(ℝ).

Remark 78.3.9 (the negative sign is necessary). The Gauss–Hermite mode 𝜙0 has its spectral mass con-
centrated in the low-frequency core | 𝑡 | < 𝑡∗ , where 𝑔 < 0. The negative sign of ( 𝑄 arch )00 is therefore
consistent with A-TP: the total 𝑄 is 𝑄 arch + 𝑄 fin − 𝑄 polar , and 𝑄 fin , 𝑄 polar together contribute positive di-
agonal entries that sum with ( 𝑄 arch )00 to a total which is still negative (A-TP) or positive (RH-violating).
The Gram matrix entries are individually not sign-definite; their sign pattern is exactly the arithmetic
content of A-TP.

Remark 78.4.3 (tautology named). Chapter 78.4.2 is the tautology: the negative-semidefiniteness of
the full infinite Gram matrix ( 𝑄 𝑚𝑛 )𝑚,𝑛 ≥0 is equivalent to A-TP only after the cutoff Hermite model is
proved complete for the Weil topology. The Gram-matrix reformulation does not reduce the problem;
it redescribes it under that completeness hypothesis. The utility of the reformulation is in the ﬁnite-
truncation analysis: computable, explicit, and algorithmically verifiable.

78.5    Finite- 𝑁 Truncation and Bombieri–Lagarias Numerical Content
The Hadamard decomposition expresses the full infinite Gram matrix as a signed sum over all Riemann
zeros; establishing NSD requires controlling all zeros simultaneously. At each finite truncation order
𝑁 , the upper-left block 𝑄 𝑁 is an explicitly computable ( 𝑁 + 1) × ( 𝑁 + 1) real symmetric matrix
equivalent (via basis change) to Li positivity up to degree 𝑁 .
Deﬁnition 78.5.1 (truncated Gram matrix). . For 𝑁 ≥ 0, set 𝑄 𝑁 := ( 𝑄 𝑚𝑛 )𝑚,𝑛 ≤ 𝑁 , the ( 𝑁 + 1) × ( 𝑁 +
1) upper-left block of the full Gram matrix. By symmetry of 𝑄 , 𝑄 𝑁 is real symmetric.
Theorem 78.5.2 (finite- 𝑁 Hermite blocks do not follow from Li positivity). . Negative-
semidefiniteness of the Hermite block 𝑄 𝑁 is not a formal consequence of the inequalities 𝜆𝑛 ≥ 0 for
1 ≤ 𝑛 ≤ 𝑁 . Such a transfer would require an explicit finite change-of-test-family matrix between the
Hermite cutoff functions and the Li test functions, together with control of the cutoff error. No such
matrix is constructed here.

Proof. Li positivity is a family of scalar inequalities for a distinguished Li test family. Negative-
semidefiniteness of 𝑄 𝑁 is a matrix inequality for the first 𝑁 + 1 Hermite cutoff tests. Positivity of
one finite list of scalar evaluations does not imply negativity of a different finite Gram block without a
proved change of basis and error bound. The Hermite functions are not themselves Paley–Wiener tests,
so the cutoff error is part of the statement, not a harmless normalization.

Theorem 78.5.3 (Coffey 2005 numerical verification). (Coffey 2005, Math. Phys. Analysis & Ge-
ometry 8). The Li coefficients 𝜆1 , . . . , 𝜆 𝑁 satisfy 𝜆𝑛 > 0 for 𝑁 ≤ 105 , as verified by high-precision
arithmetic ( 𝑝 ≥ 300 decimal digits). This is evidence for the Li test family; it is not a verification of the
Hermite Gram block 𝑄 𝑁 .

Proof. Coffey 2005 §4 computes the Li coefficients 𝜆1 , . . . , 𝜆 𝑁 for 𝑁 ≤ 105 using high-precision arith-
metic, then verifies their positivity. Chapter 78.5.2 says precisely that no Hermite-block conclusion is
obtained without an additional change-of-family computation.

Proposition 78.5.4 (small- 𝑁 explicit computation). . For 𝑁 = 2 (the 3 × 3 block indexed
by 𝑚, 𝑛 ∈ {0, 4, 8} after restriction to Fourier-real Hermite indices), negative-definiteness of 𝑄 2 is a
concrete numerical question for the cutoff Gram formula (78.2). It is not implied by Coffey’s verification
of Li coefficients.

Proof. No proof is supplied here. A proof requires an independent numerical comparison for the cutoff
limit, the finite-prime sum, and the polar term.
78.6. Three Natural Regularizations and Their Failure                                                          733


The Uniform Bound Obstruction
Theorem 78.5.5 (uniform eigenvalue bound is A-TP). (on cutoff completeness). If
sup 𝑁 𝜎max ( 𝑄 𝑁 ) ≤ 0 for the regularized Hermite blocks, then the regularized Hermite quadratic form
is negative-semidefinite on finite Hermite sums. If the cutoff Hermite model is complete for the Weil
test topology, this is A-TP. A strict uniform gap 𝜎max ( 𝑄 𝑁 ) ≤ −𝑐 < 0 is stronger than A-TP and is not
equivalent to RH.

Proof. The condition sup 𝑁 𝜎max ( 𝑄 𝑁 ) ≤ 0 says exactly that every finite Hermite block is negative-
semidefinite. Passing from finite sums to A-TP is precisely the cutoff-completeness hypothesis. A negative
gap 𝑐 > 0 gives coercivity of the regularized form; RH does not assert such coercivity.

Remark 78.5.6 (the ceiling, named). Chapter 78.5.5 is the ceiling: finite Hermite blocks do not imply the
limiting positivity statement without a uniform passage and a cutoff-completeness theorem. Bombieri–
Lagarias and Coffey verify Li-coefficient positivity in the Li family; they do not verify Hermite block
negative-semidefiniteness.

78.6    Three Natural Regularizations and Their Failure
Three natural modifications of the Gram matrix suggest themselves as constructions to reducing A-
TP to a finite-dimensional statement: a Tikhonov shift, Gaussian windowing of matrix indices, and
a finite-rank perturbation. None supplies a finite-dimensional proof without the same limiting and
cutoff-completeness input.

Lemma 78.6.5 (Gaussian windowing does not help). (on closability of the regularized form). For any
𝜎 > 0, negative-semidefiniteness of 𝑄 𝜎 on all 𝑐 ∈ ℓ 2 is equivalent to negative-semidefiniteness of 𝑄 on
the dense subspace {𝑇𝜎 𝑐 : 𝑐 ∈ ℓ 2 } ⊂ ℓ 2 . Passing from this dense subspace to A-TP is exactly the same
closure problem.
734                  Chapter 78. A-TP as Gram Matrix Positivity: Hermite Basis Reduction


Proof. {𝑇𝜎 𝑐 : 𝑐 ∈ ℓ 2 } is a dense subspace of ℓ 2 (contains all finitely-supported sequences). By continuity
of 𝑄 on the closed regularized form domain, negativity extends to the closure. Without that closability
input, Gaussian windowing proves only a statement on the image of 𝑇𝜎 .

Finite-Rank Perturbation Ceiling
Theorem 78.6.6 (finite-rank perturbation ceiling). . Let 𝑃 = 𝑃 ∗ be any finite-rank symmetric
operator on ℓ 2 (ℕ) with rank( 𝑃 ) = 𝑟 < ∞. If 𝑄 + 𝑃 ⪯ 0, then 𝑄 ⪯ 0 on every vector 𝑣 ∈ ker( 𝑃 ).
Thus a finite-rank perturbation can affect only finitely many directions; it cannot supply positivity on
the infinite-dimensional orthogonal complement. It does not reduce A-TP to a closed finite-dimensional
statement.

Proof. For 𝑣 ∈ ker( 𝑃 ), ⟨( 𝑄 + 𝑃 ) 𝑣, 𝑣 ⟩ = ⟨𝑄𝑣, 𝑣 ⟩. Hence any proof of 𝑄 + 𝑃 ⪯ 0 contains, un-
changed, the proof of non-positivity on ker( 𝑃 ). This subspace has finite codimension and remains
infinite-dimensional. The finite-rank perturbation does not remove the limiting obstruction.

Remark 78.6.7 (three regularizations, three failures). Chapter 78.6.3, Chapter 78.6.5, and Chapter 78.6.6
establish that the three natural regularization constructions (Tikhonov shift, Gaussian windowing, finite-
rank perturbation) all fail to reduce A-TP to a finite statement. The obstruction is the limiting quadratic
form, not the choice of finite regularization.

78.7    The Irreducible Obstruction
Theorem 78.7.1 (Gram-matrix ceiling for A-TP). (on cutoff completeness). The regularized Weber–
Hermite Gram construction yields precisely the following.
   (i) At each finite truncation 𝑁 , 𝑄 𝑁 ⪯ 0 is a Hermite block assertion and is not implied by finite
       Li-coefficient positivity (Chapter 78.5.2).
  (ii) For 𝑁 ≤ 105 , Coffey 2005 verifies positivity of Li coefficients, not negativity of the Hermite blocks
       (Chapter 78.5.3).
 (iii) The uniform bound sup 𝑁 𝜎max ( 𝑄 𝑁 ) ≤ 0 gives the regularized Hermite quadratic inequality; it
       gives A-TP only after the cutoff completeness hypothesis (Chapter 78.5.5, Chapter 57.2.4).
 (iv) Tikhonov, Gaussian, and finite-rank regularizations all fail to extract new content beyond the
       finite- 𝑁 verification (Chapter 78.6.7).
The Gram-matrix reformulation is therefore a diagnostic unless the cutoff limit and completeness theo-
rem are supplied.

Proof. The four stated implications are exactly the cited theorem and lemmas.

Remark 78.7.2 (exact assertion). the Weber–Hermite Gram reduction via Gram matrix positivity in the
Weber–Hermite basis establishes:
Conditional. (a) Explicit Hermite–Mellin Gram matrix formula (78.2) (Chapter 78.3.5). (b) Hadamard

(Chapter 78.4.1). (c) Ceiling theorem: uniform negative-semidefiniteness of ( 𝑄 𝑁 ) 𝑁 ≥0 reaches A-TP

for a complete admissible test family (Chapter 78.4.2, Chapter 78.4.3).

Occupation Perturbations and the Weil Trace
Comparison

Disjoint spectral intervals permit a full self-adjoint occupation perturbation of the dilation generator.
Its compact Fourier tests have trace-class differences, even though the perturbation itself is not trace class.
The resulting spectral distribution is supported on a half-line. This support excludes the full Weil zero
functional.

Theorem 80.4.1 (no lower-bounded tempered spectral realization). There is no tempered distri-

Proof. Such an identity would extend 𝑊 to a tempered distribution in the additive variable. On

Multiply by a smooth cutoff supported in (0, ∞) and equal to one for 𝑡 ≥ 1. The density then decays
exponentially. The remainder of 𝜈1/2 has compact support. Thus 𝜈1/2 would be tempered, and Theo-
rem 87.2.9 would imply RH.
   Under RH, 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ) = 𝜇ord (F+ 𝑓 ). Compact smooth functions are dense in the Schwartz space, and
the Fourier transform is its continuous automorphism. Equality on their Fourier images therefore gives
𝑇0 = 𝜇ord on all Schwartz tests. There are infinitely many xi zeros, all in a fixed vertical strip. Their
ordinates are unbounded in absolute value. Conjugation gives ordinates tending to negative infinity.
The positive measure 𝜇ord therefore has support unbounded below, a contradiction.

    This argument excludes a proposed comparison for an explicitly constructed operator and trace map.
It does not prove or disprove RH. An arithmetic realization must change the spectral carrier or the trace
construction and prove the resulting comparison.

Proposition 80.5.2 (functional-equation phases). The quotient 𝜉 (1/2 + 𝑖𝑡 )/ 𝜉 (1/2 − 𝑖𝑡 ) equals

Proof. The first assertion is the functional equation. The second follows from conjugation. A com-

unimodular, defines a unitary multiplication operator on the real 𝐿 2 line after arbitrary values on its

80.6     The remaining arithmetic comparison
Deﬁnition 80.6.1 (the adele-class carrier). The adele-class quotient is ℚ × \𝔸, where rational multiplica-
tion also acts on noninvertible adeles. It differs from the idele-class group ℚ × \𝔸× used above. A Hilbert
or distributional realization on that quotient requires its own space, action, domain, and trace functional.
    An arithmetic scattering comparison would specify self-adjoint operators 𝐴0 , 𝐴1 on a common
Hilbert space and a trace map on P. If it uses an ordinary difference trace, it must prove ℎ ( 𝐴1 ) −
ℎ ( 𝐴0 ) ∈ S1 for every ℎ ∈ P and

                   Tr( ℎ ( 𝐴1 ) − ℎ ( 𝐴0 )) = 𝑃 ( 𝑓 ) − 𝑊∞ ( 𝑓 ) − 𝑊fin ( 𝑓 ) ,    ℎ = F+ 𝑓 .

If it uses a regularized or virtual trace, that functional and its continuity must instead be constructed
on the stated carrier. The ordinary one-sided occupation model above fails the comparison by a proved
support obstruction. Scattering unitarity supplies neither the missing trace identity nor positivity of its
square class.

Remark 81.1.2 (Frobenius as almost-complex substitute). An endomorphism 𝐽 : 𝑇 𝑋 → 𝑇 𝑋 satisfying

81.3   Obstructed Candidate Readings
Six candidate readings of the phrase ‘‘genus- 𝑔 arithmetic surface with almost-complex structure’’ meet
distinct mathematical obstructions; the obstructions are recorded in Chapter B.7.
   (i) 𝐽 2 = −id on the tangent bundle of an arithmetic scheme. Schemes over Spec ℤ carry no real tangent
       bundle; the phrase ‘‘almost-complex’’ is a category error at this level. The correct arithmetic
       substitute is the Frobenius 𝜑 𝑔 on primitive cohomology (Chapter 81.1.2).
  (ii) Arithmetic Euler characteristic = 1 − 𝑔 . Gillet–Soulé 1992 arithmetic Riemann–Roch introduces
       Bismut–Gillet–Soulé analytic torsion; the arithmetic analog of 1 − 𝑔 is the Faltings 𝛿 -invariant
       via the arithmetic Noether formula, not a simple integer.
750                                           Chapter 81. All-Genus Arithmetic Koszul Duality


 (iii) Künneth factorisation of the arithmetic surface. Bost–Künnemann 2010 (Adv. Math. 223) shows
       the product formula has non-vanishing Bott–Chern archimedean correction terms; 𝑋 does not
       factor as ‘‘genus- 𝑔 curve ×Spec ℤ Spec ℤ’’ in arithmetic Chow.
 (iv) Spec ℤ itself has ﬁnite genus. Deninger’s arithmetic-dynamical genus of Spec ℤ is +∞ (countably
      many critical zeros of 𝜁 ). Genus enters the arithmetic datum only through coefficient enhancement
      to a totally imaginary number field of degree 2 𝑔 .
  (v) Conﬂation of curve-genus 𝑔𝑐 with Siegel-modular genus 𝑔𝑠 . For a modular curve 𝑋0 ( 𝑁 ): 𝑔𝑐 =
       𝑔0 ( 𝑁 ) and 𝑔𝑠 = 1. For the Siegel threefold A2 : 𝑔𝑐 is undefined, 𝑔𝑠 = 2. The genus 𝑔 of the datum
      D 𝑔 is the symplectic rank of the Galois representation divided by 2; in the Shimura setting this is
       𝑔𝑠 , not 𝑔𝑐 .
 (vi) 𝜅 + 𝜅 ! = 2 − 2 𝑔 as Euler-characteristic shift. The Euler characteristic 2 − 2 𝑔 is a topological
      invariant of the Riemann surface 𝑋 (ℂ), not a Koszul invariant of the chiral datum. The identity
      𝜅 Ar, 𝑔 + ( 𝜅 ! ) Ar, 𝑔 = 0 is the conditional Koszul-duality target at rank 𝑔 ; the genus enters through
      the Fock rank, the archimedean Γ-factor, and the motivic weight of the functional-equation center.

the row, not by 𝑔 itself. Window II (Dedekind 𝜁𝐾 with archimedean Γℂ factor) is weight 0; the center
                                                                           𝑔

any number field. Windows I, V (arithmetic surface with generic fibre of genus 𝑔 ) are weight 1 on the
Jacobian’s 𝐻 1 -motive; the center is 𝑠 ↦→ 2 − 𝑠 . Window VI (Siegel spin of genus- 𝑔 cusp form) has centre
determined by the chosen cohomological spin normalisation; the table records it as 𝑤 𝜋,spin , not as a
universal integer. All three rows share 𝜅 + 𝜅 ! = 0; the genus grading lives in the Γ-factor, the Fock rank,
and the weight of the row.

81.5    Reduction to 𝑔 = 0 and the F-RH Axis
At 𝑔 = 0:
• Window II: 𝐾 = ℚ, 𝜉𝐾 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ), Γℂ ( 𝑠 ) 0 = 1, 𝜁𝐾 = 𝜁 . Functional equation 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ).
• Windows I, V: 𝑋 𝐾 = ℙ1 / 𝐾 , Jacobian trivial, Λ ( 𝑠, 𝑋 𝐾 ) degenerates to 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) with center 𝑠 ↦→ 1 − 𝑠 ;
  the weight-1 motive is void and the weight-0 Dedekind row takes over.
• Window VI: A0 = pt, Siegel spin 𝐿 -function collapses to 𝜁 , center 𝑠 ↦→ 1 − 𝑠 .
  All four rows collapse to 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝜉 (1 − 𝑠 ), recovering Chapter 21.5.1 as the 𝑔 = 0 specialisation of
Chapter 81.4.1.
Corollary 81.5.1 (all-genus F-RH). (on Chapter 81.4.1 plus rank- 𝑔 extensions of the P2, P3, VB pillars
of Chapter 22). For every 𝑔 ≥ 0 and every arithmetic genus- 𝑔 datum D 𝑔 with rank- 𝑔 Koszul–Petersson
752                                         Chapter 81. All-Genus Arithmetic Koszul Duality


compatibility, a rank- 𝑔 completed 𝐿 -character, and a positive Hilbert–Pólya–Li trace, the non-trivial
zeros of Λ D 𝑔 ( 𝑠 ) lie on the self-dual locus Re( 𝑠 ) = 𝑤 D 𝑔 /2.
Remark 81.5.2 (specialisations). Chapter 81.5.1 has as special cases the zero-placement clauses for the
Riemann zeta function ( 𝑔 = 0, Window II), Hasse–Weil 𝐿 -functions of Jacobians (Windows I,V),
Dedekind zeta functions of totally imaginary fields (Window II at higher 𝑔 ), and Siegel-spin 𝐿 -functions
of cusp forms on GSp2 𝑔 (𝔸ℚ ) (Window VI). Each case still requires its rank- 𝑔 spectral positivity input.

81.7   Orthogonal and Compatible Windows
The six windows are compatible but mathematically distinct: each captures a different facet of the
datum D 𝑔 , and their pairwise compatibility is an independent mathematical fact in each case. Pairwise
compatibility:
• Windows I and V share the arithmetic surface as base and agree on the weight-1 Hasse–Weil functional
  equation. They differ on operadic dimension: Window I keeps the archimedean 𝐸1 -chiral structure;
  Window V lifts to 𝐸2 -chiral via Dunn. Compatibility is the content of Chapter 12’s 2-dim extension.
• Windows II and V differ on arithmetic scheme dimension (1-dim vs. 2-dim). Window II encodes
  the genus as coefficient enhancement of the base field (totally imaginary 𝐾 of degree 2 𝑔 ); Window V
  keeps 𝐾 = ℚ but lifts the base scheme to 2-dim via Dunn additivity. Compatibility passes through
  Tate 1950 adelic Fourier at number-field level.
• Windows III and VI are spectral: Window III gives the local ( 𝜑, Γ)-module moduli; Window VI
  gives the global automorphic side. Compatibility requires the relevant local-global comparison; it is
  not supplied by Fargues–Scholze alone.
• Window IV is moduli-theoretic: T𝑔arith carries the Hodge–Arakelov decoration on the theta-generic
  locus, and its point-by-point inputs supply Window I. Compatibility via the Torelli map: a genus- 𝑔
                                  crys,ord
  curve’s Jacobian is a point of X2 𝑔      only after imposing the ordinary crystalline local condition, and
  a point of the Siegel moduli space A 𝑔 via its polarisation. The word ‘‘threefold’’ applies only at 𝑔 = 2.
    Orthogonal to these six windows: Deninger’s 𝔽 1 formalism (motivational context for the arithmetic-
dynamical interpretation of Spec ℤ, recorded in Chapter 2); the Caraiani–Scholze unitary-Shimura
theory at genera where no Shimura model exists (moduli of curves M 𝑔 is not Shimura for 𝑔 ≥ 4); the
Bethe-algebra heuristic presentation, which operates at the zero-Fock per-place level and does not carry
𝑔 -dependence directly.
    The conditional identity 𝜅 Ar, 𝑔 + ( 𝜅 ! ) Ar, 𝑔 = 0 of Chapter 81.4.1 is the proposed rank- 𝑔 fibre. The
F-RH axis of Chapter 22 is the 𝑔 = 0 fibre of the rank-graded family whose other fibres are the Hasse–
Weil Riemann Hypothesis for Jacobians of curves of genus 𝑔 , the generalised Riemann Hypothesis for
Dedekind zeta of totally imaginary fields of degree 2 𝑔 , and the Siegel-spin Riemann Hypothesis for cusp
forms on GSp2 𝑔 . The residual conditions of Chapter 81.6 quantify what must be proved before this
conditional comparison becomes an unconditional theorem.
    Chapter 82 extends the arithmetic-modular axis into arithmetic three-dimensional Chern–Simons
theory. The conformal vector implicit in Chapter 81.4.1 sources an arithmetic Kac–Moody enhance-
ment of V prim (Chapter 82.3.1), which in turn sources a finite-level arithmetic Chern–Simons partition
sum and a conjectural renormalised 𝐺 𝐿2 ( ℤ)    b limit on the étale 3-space Spec ℤ (Chapter 82.4.2, Chap-
ter 82.4.7). The equalities

82.1   Spec(Z) as Etale 3-Space
Mazur 1973 (Notes on étale cohomology of number ﬁelds, Ann. Sci. ENS 6) observed that Spec O𝐾 has étale
cohomological dimension 3 for 𝐾 a number field, with Artin–Verdier duality supplying a fundamental
class [Spec O𝐾 ] ∈ 𝐻ét3 (Spec O𝐾 , b
                                    ℤ) analogous to a 3-manifold’s orientation class. Morishita 2012 Knots
and Primes (arXiv:0904.3399) systematizes the dictionary: primes 𝔭 ⊂ O𝐾 behave as knots in a closed 3-
manifold; Spec O𝐾 ,𝔭 is the tubular neighborhood; the inertia subgroup 𝐼𝔭 ⊂ Gal( 𝐾 / 𝐾 ) is the meridian;
linking numbers become Legendre symbols; the Alexander–Fox module becomes the Iwasawa module.
For 𝐾 = ℚ, Arakelov compactification Spec ℤ closes the 3-space by adding the archimedean boundary
component at ∞.
Remark 82.1.1 (cohomological 3-dimensionality). Spec ℤ is not a smooth real 3-manifold. Its 3-
dimensionality is cohomological: the étale site supports non-trivial 𝐻 1 , 𝐻 2 , 𝐻 3 computable via global
class-field theory and Artin–Verdier. The Chern-Simons action functional below takes values in étale co-
homology classes rather than in differential forms; its quantization is in Galois-representation-theoretic
terms rather than path-integral terms in the differential-geometric sense.

local system on the inertia groupoid.

Proof. Removing the prime 𝑝 and fixing monodromy around the meridian is the arithmetic analog

meridian/Frobenius loop contributes 𝜒 (Frob 𝑝 ).
