Remark 82.4.8 (ﬁnite vs. proﬁnite ACS: gap between theorem-grade and conjecture-grade). The closed
finite-level state sum is theorem-grade: Chapter 82.4.2 constructs it from étale local systems, the Artin–
Verdier fundamental class, and finite groupoid cardinality. Functorial finite-level TQFT language still
requires a specified arithmetic cobordism category. The larger residual is the renormalised profinite
limit 𝐺 𝑁 → 𝐺 𝐿2 ( b   ℤ), the comparison of its archimedean boundary category with V prim , and the
identification of its renormalised partition function with 𝜉 ( 𝑘 Ar ).
    There is a concrete obstruction to treating the closed finite tower as the zeta partition function. On
the closed base Spec ℤ, finite etale local systems are trivial by Hermite–Minkowski, so the bare finite
state sum for 𝐺 𝑁 = 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℤ/ 𝑁 ℤ) is the groupoid-cardinality scalar | 𝐺 𝑁 | −1 , or 1 after finite-gauge
normalisation. This scalar does not contain prime weights 𝑝 − 𝑠 , the archimedean Γℝ -factor, or the polar
correction. A zeta-valued profinite ACS theory therefore requires extra data: compatible continuous
level classes, a counterterm or measure system on the congruence tower, a profinite boundary category,
a Morita comparison with the local Iwahori trace factors, and a regularised character map.

82.5    The Ordered Incidence Bar
The arithmetic Ran space lacks the finite-place collision and diagonal thickenings that the Beilinson–
Drinfeld/Costello–Gwilliam framework uses to build a factorization homology model. The ordered
incidence bar replaces the Ran space by the simplest category that admits a bar-complex computation
while preserving the factorization structure: it encodes the primes of ℤ via the auxiliary total order
2 < 3 < 5 < 7 < · · · < ∞, with the archimedean place placed last. This order is not geometric structure
on Spec ℤ; the comparison with Beilinson–Drinfeld/Costello–Gwilliam arithmetic chiral homology is
conditional (Chapter 82.5.5).
Deﬁnition 82.5.1 (ordered incidence category). . Put 𝑉 = ℙ ∪ {∞}, with the order 2 < 3 < 5 < · · · < ∞.
Let Inc< (𝑉 ) be the category whose objects are finite ordered block decompositions of finite ordered sub-
sets of 𝑉 . A singleton block is written 𝑣 , and the merge of two adjacent blocks is written by concatenation.
Morphisms are generated by order-preserving adjacent contractions

              {𝑣1 < · · · < 𝑣𝑖 < 𝑣𝑖 +1 < · · · < 𝑣𝑛 } −→ {𝑣1 < · · · < ( 𝑣𝑖 𝑣𝑖 +1 ) < · · · < 𝑣𝑛 },

where 𝑣𝑖 𝑣𝑖 +1 denotes the formal merged block carrying the product operation of the coefficient system,
not a new arithmetic place. The simplicial nerve of Inc< (𝑉 ) is the one-dimensional ordered collision
model for the arithmetic Ran space.

of V prim , with adjacent products

82.7    Arithmetic-Gravity Construction to F-RH
Witten 2007 (Three-Dimensional Gravity Revisited, arXiv:0706.3359) proposed that 3D quantum gravity
admits a Chern-Simons formulation whose partition function’s spectrum controls the zeros of arith-
metically significant 𝐿 -functions. Vol II Part VI states this as the complex-side 3D quantum gravity
climax. The arithmetic base Spec ℤ supplies an analogous conditional formulation via the preceding
ACS construction.
Theorem 82.7.1 (arithmetic-gravity F-RH). (on Chapter 82.4.7, Chapter 82.4.9, Chapter 82.5.5, and
Chapter 22’s three-pillar + VB structure, including a holomorphic complex-level partition function). The
zeros of 𝑍 ACSqu (Spec ℤ; 𝑘 Ar ) as a function of the level 𝑘 Ar ∈ ℂ coincide with the non-trivial zeros of
𝜉 ( 𝑘 Ar ). The zero-placement claim is RH-level: these zeros lie on the self-dual locus Re( 𝑘 Ar ) = 1/2
exactly when the corresponding Riemann-hypothesis zero-placement statement holds. The stronger
F-RH condition still includes the positive Hilbert–Pólya trace inputs of Chapter 22.
Remark 82.7.2 (three-step construction). The construction proceeds in three steps.
  (i) Bulk construction. Finite-level ACS is constructed in Chapter 82.4.2. The open bulk step is the
      renormalised profinite limit limren 𝑍 𝐺Ar     and its zeta partition function, as stated in Chap-
                                     ←− 𝑁     𝑁 ,𝛼𝑁
      ter 82.4.7.
82.8. Genus- 𝑔 Extension                                                                                     765


  (ii) Boundary identiﬁcation and ordered-model computation. Finite-level boundary categories are con-
       structed in Chapter 82.4.4 after choosing the finite arithmetic cobordism category. The compari-
       son with V prim is Chapter 82.4.9. The ordered-bar calculation is theorem-grade for the ordered
       incidence model by Chapter 82.5.4; the remaining comparison to BD/CG arithmetic chiral ho-
       mology is Chapter 82.5.5.
 (iii) Positive trace. Apply the Hilbert–Pólya–Li residual of Chapter 22. The ordered model and the
       completed-zeta character do not by themselves supply positivity; the missing input is the positive
       Hilbert–Pólya trace.

82.10    Ordered-Bar Boundary
Two first-principles results close unconditionally. First, closed finite-level arithmetic Chern–Simons

alone (Chapter 82.4.2). Second, the ordered incidence bar computes the derived colimit of V prim over
the auxiliary ordered place set via the normalized simplicial replacement (Chapter 82.5.4); this gives the
Bost–Connes Euler/log-prime skeleton (Chapter 82.6.3) unconditionally.

Chapter 83


Deninger’s Arithmetic Cohomology as a Chiral
Candidate

Deninger’s conjectural formalism demands a cohomology theory for Spec ℤ whose regularised Fredholm
determinant equals the completed Riemann zeta function and whose closed orbits recover the explicit
formula. The bar–cobar construction does not construct this cohomology. It constructs a candidate: the
ordered-incidence homology of V prim (the Hochschild trace class of the identity on the global arithmetic
Iwahori Hecke category of 𝐺 𝐿2 ), two formal Tate polar lines, and the Bost–Connes Euler-prime-side
character. Whether this candidate realizes Deninger’s axioms depends on the spectral-flow hypothesis of
Chapter 82.6.5. The central result of this chapter is the obstruction theorem: no unconditional triple
identification exists among Deninger’s conjectural cohomology, the ordered-incidence candidate, and
the boundary homology of the arithmetic Chern–Simons bulk.

self-adjoint. For the Riemann zeta function the middle degree should carry the non-trivial zero divisor.

83.2    Surviving Inputs
The bar–cobar construction produces four inputs with theorem-grade form; the remainder of the
Deninger axioms are either conditional or open.
   (i) The finite-level arithmetic Chern–Simons state sum and gluing formula of Chapter 82.4.2. This
       is a closed finite groupoid state-sum statement, not a full profinite TQFT.
  (ii) The ordered-incidence bar Chapter 82.5.3 and its normalized-bar computation Chapter 82.5.4.
       This computes the explicitly defined incidence model, not automatically BD/CG factorization
       homology on Spec ℤ.
 (iii) The Bost–Connes Euler skeleton Chapter 82.6.3. It gives the KMS character 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) and the prime-
       power logarithmic derivative in Re( 𝑠 ) > 1.
 (iv) The Deninger spectral-flow hypothesis Chapter 82.6.5: the zero-side determinant divisor, trace
       distribution, and Hilbert–Pólya self-adjoint determinant-trace operator. This is the single missing
       piece that the bar–cobar construction does not supply.

83.7    Duality and Positivity
Koszul duality for the arithmetic bar complex gives the functional-equation symmetry 𝑠 ↔ 1 − 𝑠 . The
question is whether this duality implies Poincaré duality for the Deninger cohomology, and specifically
whether it forces the middle degree to be positive definite.
Theorem 83.7.1 (duality gives the functional equation, not positivity). (on the relevant Koszul and
ACS comparison hypotheses). The Koszul self-duality framework accounts for the functional-equation
symmetry 𝑠 ↔ 1 − 𝑠 . It does not by itself imply positivity of the Deninger middle pairing or RH.

83.8    Purity as the RH-Level Input
Duality accounts for the functional equation but not for the zero-placement. Purity of the middle
cohomological degree is the assertion that the zero-side operator Θ𝜉 is self-adjoint with spectrum on the
line Re( 𝑠 ) = 1/2, which is RH.

83.12   Residual Conditions
The residue is a single mathematical obstruction: construct the middle operator and prove the trace for-

84.2       Connes’ Trace Formula
The Weil explicit formula is a distributional identity; the question is whether the zero sum on its left side
admits a determinant-trace interpretation, i.e., whether some natural normal operator has determinant
divisor div 𝜉ℝ and Weil–Connes trace supported at the ordinates 𝛾 𝜌 after zero-placement. Connes’
adele-class-space construction provides a partial answer.

distributional trace is not by itself a spectral measure.

84.3    Ordered-Bar Euler Skeleton
The Connes–Meyer trace recovers the full Weil distribution (84.1) as an operator trace. The ordered-
incidence bar complex approaches the same object from the Koszul-duality side: its regularised character
computes the Euler product. The question is whether that character calculation closes the gap left by
Connes.

The Euler-product character of Proposition 84.3.1 yields 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) only after regularisation. Under the regu-

then identifies this with the full Weil distribution. The three trace functionals are conditionally equal.

84.5    The Bar Reorganises, Not Locates
The equivalence of the three trace functionals established conditionally in Section 84.4 raises a sharper
question: does the ordered-bar construction supply an independent mechanism for placing the zero
ordinates 𝛾𝑛 on the critical line, beyond what 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) itself encodes? The bar computation reorganises the
zero data of 𝜉 ; it does not add new data.
Theorem 84.5.1 (bar computation reorganises zero data). . The ordered-incidence bar complex
determines the individual zero ordinates 𝛾𝑛 only through the scalar function 𝜉 : no additional self-adjoint
operator or positivity mechanism is produced by the bar calculation.

Proof. The bar supplies the Euler-product character and, after conditional regularisation, the scalar
function 𝜉 . The zero ordinates are then the zero set of that scalar function. The bar calculation produces
no self-adjoint operator, spectral theorem, or positivity input beyond what 𝜉 already carries.

Remark 84.5.2 (the Hilbert–Pólya obstruction). A self-adjoint operator with spectrum { 𝛾𝑛 } would place
the zeros on the critical line by the spectral theorem. Constructing such an operator is precisely the
spectral-flow obstruction of Chapter 82.6.5.

of an arithmetic Hamiltonian whose primitive periodic orbits are the primes.

84.7    Connes–Meyer and the Gutzwiller Gap
The arithmetic Gutzwiller hypothesis of the previous section requires a smooth symplectic Hamiltonian
system with a chaotic classical limit. The question is whether the Connes–Meyer construction already
supplies this structure, or whether the Gutzwiller construction is genuinely new input.
Theorem 84.7.1 (Connes–Meyer as distributional trace, not Gutzwiller system). . The standard
adele-class-space realization used in the Connes–Meyer trace formula is a noncommutative scaling trace
construction. It is distinct from a smooth symplectic Hamiltonian system of the kind required by the
classical Gutzwiller theorem.
Proof. The adele class space 𝔸/ℚ∗ is modeled by a noncommutative quotient; its 𝐶 ∗ -algebraic descrip-
tion gives an operator-algebraic trace. The Gutzwiller formula requires a smooth symplectic phase space,
a Hamiltonian flow, isolated primitive periodic orbits, and monodromy matrix determinants. None of
these are part of the Connes–Meyer construction as stated.
Remark 84.7.2 (other geometrisations remain open). Other geometrisations of the adele class space may
supply a symplectic structure; the theorem records only that the standard Connes–Meyer trace formula
is not itself a Gutzwiller mechanism. An arithmetic Gutzwiller system, if it exists, is new structure beyond
Connes–Meyer.

84.8    Statistical Upside
The explicit formula (84.1) is a distributional identity; it does not determine the individual zero ordinates
𝛾𝑛 beyond what 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) already encodes. A Hilbert–Pólya operator, if it exists, would put the determinant
divisor on the critical line by self-adjointness. The further statistical prediction, that the local spacing
statistics of the 𝛾𝑛 follow the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE), is not implied by either the explicit
formula or self-adjointness alone. It requires a dynamical mechanism: the Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit
(BGS) principle connecting chaotic classical dynamics to random-matrix statistics. The relevant symme-
try class is GUE because 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) has no anti-unitary time-reversal symmetry; the unitary symmetry class
applies. Let 𝑅2 ( 𝑢) denote the two-point level spacing correlation function.
Theorem 84.8.1 (Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit principle). . Quantum systems whose classical limits
are chaotic are expected, after symmetry class is fixed, to exhibit random matrix local spectral statistics.
For the unitary symmetry class (GUE), the two-point correlation function is

                                                           𝜋𝑢
84.8. Statistical Upside                                                                                  779


Theorem 84.8.2 (conditional statistical upside). (on Chapter 82.6.5, Chapter 84.6.2, arithmetic
quantum chaos, and the BGS universality theorem Chapter 84.8.1). If the ACS Hamiltonian of Chap-
ter 82.6.5 has a chaotic semiclassical limit with prime periodic orbits, then the local statistics of the zero
ordinates are governed by the corresponding random-matrix ensemble; in the expected zeta case by GUE
statistics (84.3).

Proof. Spectral flow supplies the zero-divisor determinant and, after zero-placement, the Hamiltonian
trace supported at the ordinates. Arithmetic Gutzwiller identifies the classical periodic orbits with prime
powers. The BGS principle then transfers chaotic spectral statistics to the zero ordinates. Every substan-
tive step is one of the stated hypotheses.

Remark 84.8.3 (GUE statistics as new content beyond the explicit formula). The Weil explicit formula
establishes a distributional equality between the zero ordinates and the prime-power sum; it implies
neither Montgomery pair correlation nor GUE spacing statistics. A 3D Hamiltonian realization of the
arithmetic ACS theory adds that statistical mechanism, conditional on the semiclassical and spectral-flow
hypotheses of Chapter 82.6.5.
Remark 84.8.4 (open conditions as explicit hypotheses). Chapter 84.8.2 rests on seven open conditions:
(1) the profinite quantum ACS on Spec ℤ; (2) the Bezrukavnikov–Finkelberg and Costello–Gwilliam
comparison with the ordered-incidence model; (3) the regularised character equality 𝑍 = 𝜉 ; (4) the
spectral-flow operator realizing Hilbert–Pólya; (5) the full Weil–Guinand contour shift from the Euler
skeleton; (6) the arithmetic semiclassical phase space and Hamiltonian flow; (7) chaos and random-
matrix universality for that flow. These are the explicit hypotheses of Chapter 84.8.2. The ordered bar
supplies the finite Euler skeleton (84.2); the equality 𝑍 = 𝜉 also requires the archimedean, polar, and
regularised character inputs. Conditions (1), (4), (6), and (7) constitute the spectral-flow problem of
Chapter 82.6.5.
Chapter 85


The Wilson Line–Frobenius Identity on Spec ℤ

The prime knot 𝐾 𝑝 ⊂ Spec ℤ is the codimension-two defect at a rational prime 𝑝; the Wilson loop
𝑊𝜌 ( 𝐾 𝑝 ) is the holonomy of a flat 𝐺 -connection around that defect, evaluated in a representation 𝜌.
The fundamental question of this chapter is whether, for an unramified 𝜌, the Wilson expectation
equals the Frobenius trace: whether ⟨𝑊𝜌 ( 𝐾 𝑝 )⟩ = tr 𝜌 (Frob 𝑝 ). Witten’s 1989 path-integral construction,
transplanted via the Morishita dictionary to the arithmetic 3-space, reduces the Wilson integral to a
character evaluation on the Frobenius conjugacy class in the punctured tubular category. On the closed
base the finite etale torsor is trivial; non-trivial Frobenius data enter after the defect is retained. This
identification is finite-level local and is conditional at the profinite limit (Theorem 85.5.1(2)), with the
single residual being the renormalised inverse limit of Chapter 82.4.7.

85.1   Setup and Conventions
The arithmetic 3-space is 𝑀 = Spec ℤ, the Arakelov compactification of Spec ℤ by the archimedean
place {∞}. By Mazur 1973 and Artin–Verdier, 𝑀 is etale cohomologically 3-dimensional with funda-
mental class [ 𝑀 ] ∈ 𝐻ét3 ( 𝑀 , ℤ)

is Spec ℤ 𝑝 . Its complement is 𝑀 \ 𝐾 𝑝  Spec ℤ[1/ 𝑝] ∪ {∞}. Under the Mazur 1973 / Morishita 2012
(arXiv:0904.3399) dictionary, 𝐾 𝑝 plays the role of a framed knot: the meridian is the inertia subgroup
𝐼 𝑝 ⊂ 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 ; the longitude and Frobenius class carry the decomposition quotient 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 / 𝐼 𝑝 = ℤb · Frob 𝑝 .

Remark 85.1.2 (the arithmetic loop is a Frobenius, not a geometric loop). Spec ℤ is not a smooth 3-manifold;
the loop around 𝐾 𝑝 is not a smooth curve. Following Chapter 82.1.1, loop around the knot 𝐾 𝑝 is a name for
the generator of the etale fundamental group of the tubular neighbourhood Spec ℤ 𝑝 \ 𝐾 𝑝 = Spec ℚ 𝑝 ;
this fundamental group is the absolute Galois group 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 , whose inertia quotient ℤ        b is topologically

evaluate functions on conjugacy classes of 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 , not on free-homotopy classes of a geometric circle.

observable: the classical Wilson insertion 𝜒 ( 𝜌 (Frob 𝑝 )) depends on 𝜌 only through the conjugacy class
[ 𝜌 (Frob 𝑝 )], since 𝜒 is a class function. This is functoriality of the Wilson-character correspondence.

Remark 85.4.2 (meridian and longitude). At a rational prime 𝑝, the local fundamental group 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 fits
in the Morishita dictionary as follows: the meridian is 𝐼 𝑝 (topologically a b
                                                                             ℤ(1) at tame primes); the
longitude is a fixed lift of Frob 𝑝 ∈ 𝐺ℚ 𝑝 / 𝐼 𝑝 . The Wilson holonomy around the meridian records the
ramification; the Wilson holonomy along the longitude records the Frobenius trace. In the unramified
case, 𝜌 factors through the longitude and the Wilson loop reads the Frobenius trace cleanly.

Remark 85.5.2 (what the proof provides and what it does not). Part (1) is a fully unconditional iden-
tity at each finite level 𝑁 coprime to 𝑝, for each unramified 𝜌 𝑁 , with the Frobenius trace appearing
as a class-function insertion in the finite state sum. It upgrades the Wilson-line evaluation from ax-
iom Chapter 82.4.7(3) at the finite level to an arithmetic-geometric theorem. Part (2) is conditional
on the continuous-group renormalised limit of Chapter 82.4.7. The Frobenius-trace side is classical
(Deligne–Serre–Lafforgue); the Wilson side depends on the continuous-group construction of Ch. 82.
The residual is the limit step, not the identity itself.
Remark 85.5.3 (independence of sources and domain of the main theorem). The derivation of Theo-
rem 85.5.1 rests on five independent constructions: Witten 1989 Commun. Math. Phys. 121 (path integral
for Wilson loops in 3D Chern–Simons); Morishita 2012 arXiv:0904.3399 (knots-primes dictionary); Kim
2015 arXiv:1510.05818 and Chern–Dan–Kim–Park 2018 arXiv:1609.03012 (classical arithmetic Chern–
Simons); Borger 2009 arXiv:0906.3146 §8 (𝜓 𝑝 = Frobenius trace in the 𝜆-ring language); Fargues–
Scholze 2021 arXiv:2102.13459 (local geometrisation). These are pairwise independent and disjoint from
the derivation path of Chapter 82.
    The geometric-versus-arithmetic Frobenius distinction is fixed in Convention 85.1.3; the character is
unitary; cohomological and etale conventions are bridged by the Artin–Verdier fundamental class. At
each finite level the ambient category is finite groupoids; the continuous-group step is a lim in nuclear

Remark 85.6.4 (independence of sources and domain of the Langlands compatibility). Theorem 85.6.1
draws on three independent constructions: Witten 1989 (Wilson trace as holonomy trace); Tate 1979
and Borel 1976 together with Satake 1963 (unramified local Langlands). These are independent from
the Chapter 82 construction path. The geometric-versus-arithmetic Frobenius distinction is fixed in
Convention 85.1.3; the motivic-weight analytic shift is recorded in Remark 85.6.3. The ambient category
is finite-dimensional ℚℓ -vector spaces tensored with the category of meromorphic functions in 𝑠 . Un-
ramifiedness at 𝑝 is required; at ramified primes the L-factor carries local epsilon factors (see Section 85.7).
The Satake isomorphism is functorial in 𝜌; the Wilson insertion is functorial via the class-function lift.

from the Kim Chern–Simons state-sum calculations, providing an independent numerical check.

85.7    Residual Obstructions
Theorem 85.5.1 is proved on the unramified locus and for 𝐺 𝐿2 ; four boundary conditions fall outside
this domain.
   (i) Ramiﬁed and wild primes. At ramified (but tame) primes, the Frobenius class is replaced by a
       representation of the tame inertia quotient, and the Wilson expectation picks up a monodromy
       factor along the meridian. At wild primes the arithmetic tubular neighbourhood carries ramifica-
       tion filtration data beyond the tame quotient; the Wilson identity becomes a local epsilon-factor
       equation (Deligne–Laumon; Laumon 1987 Publ. IHES 65). The tame-ramified extension is a
       direct generalisation via the tame-inertia quotient; the wild locus is treated in Chapter 57.
  (ii) Proﬁnite renormalisation. The limren -step in Theorem 85.5.1(2) is exactly Chapter 82.4.7. The
                                        ←−
       Wilson–Frobenius identity is unconditional at each finite level; the continuous-group limit is the
       open problem of Chapter 82, recorded here without modification.
 (iii) Archimedean Wilson-surface realisation. Corollary 85.6.2 requires identification of the
       archimedean Γ-factor with a Wilson-surface expectation at {∞} via the Arakelov area form
       (Chapter 83.5.7). This analytic continuation is treated in Chapter 83.
 (iv) 𝐺 𝐿𝑛 for 𝑛 ≥ 3. Theorem 85.5.1 is stated for 𝐺 𝐿2 , matching the gauge-group choice of Chapter 82.
       Extension to 𝐺 𝐿𝑛 proceeds via Chapter 81’s genus- 𝑔 extension with 𝐺 = 𝐺 𝐿2 𝑔 ( b ℤ); the Morishita
       functor of Theorem 85.4.1 extends directly to 𝐺 = 𝐺 𝐿𝑛 ( ℤ) by replacing tr with the appropriate
                                                                  b
       class function. The profinite-renormalisation obstruction of item (2) is carried over.
Remark 85.7.1 (the abelian case is closed unconditionally). On the closed base, Chapter 85.2.2 gives
the trivial-torsor value. On the punctured unramified local category, the finite abelian Wilson loop
reads 𝜒 (Frob 𝑝 ) unconditionally. Under Chapter 82.4.7, the identity extends to the continuous-group
       ℤ) and produces the finite-prime Frobenius-trace input used by the Deninger skeleton. It does
𝐺 𝐿𝑛 ( b
not construct Deninger’s global Frobenius flow on the middle cohomology. The chapter discharges the
finite-level unramified Wilson calculation and leaves the continuous-group axiom Chapter 82.4.7(3) as
part of the profinite ACS renormalisation datum.

85.8    Wilson–Frobenius Boundary
   (i) The prime knot 𝐾 𝑝 ⊂ Spec ℤ is the Morishita avatar of a codimension-two defect; its meridian is
       𝐼 𝑝 and its longitude is Frob 𝑝 (Chapter 85.1.1, Chapter 85.4.2).
  (ii) Classical Kim ACS Wilson loops on the closed base have only the trivial finite etale torsor.
       Non-trivial unramified Frobenius characters are read in the punctured tubular category 𝑀 𝑝◦ :
       ⟨𝑊𝜒cl ( 𝐾 𝑝 )⟩ = 𝜒 (Frob 𝑝 ) there (Chapter 85.2.2).
 (iii) The Morishita dictionary lifts to a functor ΦMor : KnotAr → Conj( 𝐺 𝑁 ) on the unramified locus;
       this functor intertwines Wilson insertion with Frobenius-class evaluation (Chapter 85.4.1).

 (iv) At each finite level 𝑁 coprime to 𝑝, the finite-level Wilson-loop expectation is a finite state sum,
      with the Frobenius trace appearing as a class-function insertion (Chapter 85.5.1(1)), uncondition-
      ally.

  (v) At the profinite limit, the Wilson-loop identity 𝑊𝜌 ( 𝐾 𝑝 ) = tr 𝜌 (Frob 𝑝 ) holds conditionally on
      Chapter 82.4.7 (the continuous-group renormalisation), but unconditionally once that conjecture

      when the Wilson datum records the full conjugacy class, or equivalently all power traces. The single

Remark 86.3.2 (prime-zeta sum vs. Riemann-zeta residue). The Dirichlet series 𝑐ℙ ( 𝑠 ) uses the prime-

Arithmetic black-hole motivation: primon gas as the ﬁrst determinant
The partition function 𝑍 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝑝 𝑛 ≥1 (1 − 𝑝 − 𝑠𝑛 ) −2 defined in §86.3 is the arithmetic-Chern–Simons

thermal determinant over prime knots before the zero-side trace formula is available. The following
heuristic identifies its origin in the primon-gas thermodynamics of Julia; no black-hole existence theorem
enters the proof of Lemma 86.3.5, and no positivity statement is inferred from the calculation.
    In ordinary three-dimensional gravity written as Chern–Simons theory, a black-hole sector is not
a propagating local graviton. It is a flat connection with non-trivial holonomy around the cycles of a
solid torus. Its one-loop determinant is built from the closed geodesics of the filling. The arithmetic
replacement used throughout Chapters 82–85 is:

Remark 86.5.5 (disjoint derivation and residue sources). The local chiral calculation uses Kac–Raina
Bombay Lectures on Highest Weight Representations of Inﬁnite-Dimensional Lie Algebras (World Scien-
tific 1987), §3.5 (Sugawara central charge for bosonic Fock); Kac Vertex Algebras for Beginners 2nd ed.
(AMS 1998), Chapter 3 (rank-𝑛 Heisenberg vertex algebra and Virasoro central charge formula). The
global residue calculation uses Edwards Riemann’s Zeta Function (Academic Press 1974), §1.6 (Laurent
expansion of 𝜁 at 𝑠 = 1) for the residue-extraction half; Serre Cours d’Arithmétique (PUF 1970) Ch. VI
(Euler product) for the global partition rewriting. The two source sets (Kac/Kac–Raina for the local
central charge, Edwards/Serre for the global residue) are disjoint; the computed scalar (2) matches on
both sides.

The Spectral Flow 𝑁occ ⇝ 𝐻HP : Operator and
Domain Comparisons

The positive occupation spectrum and the zero-ordinate spectrum belong to different operators. Chap-
ter 56.3.1 constructs 𝑁occ 𝑣𝑚 = (log 𝑚) 𝑣𝑚 and its exact embedding in the product GNS space. The
Hilbert–Pólya target is a self-adjoint operator whose shifted determinant has the actual zero divisor of
𝜉ℝ . An intertwining problem must specify its carriers and domains before a Mellin or residue formula
can address it.
    Two elementary obstructions are decisive. A bounded intertwiner from the atomic occupation dy-
namics to the continuous Mellin dynamics is zero. An injective intertwiner to a zero-divisor operator
cannot include the occupation vacuum in its domain. The continuous Mellin, residue and rigged-space
constructions below retain their own carriers; comparison with the atomic arithmetic source is an addi-
tional problem.

them are specified below.

Proposition 87.1.3 (atomic-to-continuous intertwining obstruction). Let 𝑀𝜏 be multiplication
by 𝜏 on 𝐿 2 (ℝ, 𝑑𝜏 ). If a bounded linear map 𝐼 : HBC → 𝐿 2 (ℝ) satisfies 𝐼 𝑒 𝑖𝑡 𝑁occ = 𝑒 𝑖𝑡 𝑀𝜏 𝐼 for every
real 𝑡 , then 𝐼 = 0. The same conclusion holds with any fixed Hilbert space as multiplicity factor on the
target.

Proof. Put 𝑓𝑚 = 𝐼 𝑣𝑚 . For every rational 𝑡 , ( 𝑒 𝑖𝑡 𝜏 − 𝑒 𝑖𝑡 log 𝑚 ) 𝑓𝑚 ( 𝜏 ) = 0 almost everywhere. Discard the

nonzero. Thus 𝑓𝑚 is supported at {log 𝑚 }, a null set, and is zero. Boundedness and density of the finite
span of the 𝑣𝑚 ’s give 𝐼 = 0. The proof applies verbatim to Hilbert-valued functions.

   An embedding into distributions can send 𝑣𝑚 to a Dirac mass at log 𝑚, but a Dirac mass is not an

Remark 87.1.7 (domain of ‘‘canonical’’). ‘‘Canonical’’ means: the spectral resolution of 𝐻HP is deter-
mined by the inherited structure up to a unitary equivalence whose parameters are themselves determined
by that structure. A diagonal construction with eigenvalues labelled by an arbitrary enumeration is not
canonical; a diagonal construction whose eigenvectors are explicit functions of arithmetic data (adelic
characters, automorphic forms, spectral projectors of a globally defined operator) is.

       domain;

  (v) the spectral identity
                                       Spec( 𝐻HP ) = { 𝛾 𝜌 | 𝜌 ∈ Z}
      with multiplicities matching.
A solution is a tuple (H𝜉 , 𝐴, 𝐻HP ) satisfying all five items. The Hilbert–Pólya twist is a solution.
Proposition 87.1.9 (vacuum obstruction to literal spectral flow). The spectral-flow conditions
cannot hold if 𝑣1 ∈ D ( 𝐴) and the intertwining identity applies there, with a target whose shifted
determinant has the actual divisor of 𝜉ℝ .

Proof. Since 𝑁occ 𝑣1 = 0, intertwining gives 𝐻HP 𝐴𝑣1 = 0. Injectivity gives 𝐴𝑣1 ≠ 0. The shifted operator
then has eigenvalue 1/2, so its determinant divisor would contain 1/2. But 𝜉ℝ (1/2) ≠ 0, as proved in
Chapter 56.4.2.

   Any remaining literal spectral-flow variant must specify a domain excluding this test or an altered
comparison. A construction with a separate occupation grading and zero operator, as in Chapter 56.4.1,
does not assert literal intertwining.
Remark 87.1.10 (unitarity of 𝐴). Chapter 87.1.8 does not require 𝐴 to be bounded or unitary. The closed-
operator intertwining (87.1) admits unbounded 𝐴; in the regular case one asks for a polar decomposition
𝐴 = 𝑈 | 𝐴 | with 𝑈 partial isometry and | 𝐴 | self-adjoint non-negative, on which the intertwining reads
𝑈 | 𝐴 | 𝑁occ | 𝐴 | −1𝑈 ∗ = 𝐻HP on its natural domain. It becomes a unitary intertwining of one-parameter
groups only when the polar partial isometry is unitary between the two Hilbert closures, the domains are
invariant under the two Stone groups, and the closed-operator identity holds on a common core. Then
𝑈 exp( 𝑖𝑡 𝑁occ ) 𝑈 ∗ = exp( 𝑖𝑡 𝐻HP ). We use the closed-operator form throughout; when the literature
writes ‘‘ 𝐴 is a unitary twist’’ it is the polar 𝑈 in this restricted sense.

87.2     Prime-Zero Mangoldt-Hadamard Duality Recap

pairings and do not construct a Hilbert-space operator.

Corollary∫87.2.10 (the ordinate shadow on the full test class). Equality ℨ𝜉 ( ℎ) = 𝜇ord ( ℎ) for
every ℎ ( 𝑧 ) = 𝑓 ( 𝑡 ) 𝑒 𝑖 𝑧𝑡 𝑑𝑡 , 𝑓 ∈ 𝐶𝑐∞ (ℝ), is equivalent to RH.

Proof. Under RH the equality is termwise. Conversely the equality makes the zero functional on compact
Fourier tests the restriction of a tempered Fourier transform. The cutoff argument in Theorem 87.2.9
then proves 𝜈1/2 ∈ S ′ . That theorem implies RH.

   The uncentered critical measure remains non-tempered even under RH. Centering subtracts its
exponentially growing main density; a statement about this difference does not change the carrier of the
original prime measure. These distinctions are required before any Fourier, Mellin, or spectral comparison
can be made.

The candidate spectral-flow operator exists at the symbolic level as the composite of Mellin transform
and Hadamard residue extraction; the two obstructions that prevent its promotion to a Hilbert-space
operator are named below.

Remark 87.3.2 (domains of the residue map). On 𝐶𝑐∞ (ℝ>0 ) the displayed formula is a linear map to

requires a target norm, convergence of the full residue sequence, and a source domain. Closedness must
be checked in those two norms. Theorem 87.12.9 and Theorem 87.12.14 construct evaluation completions
and compute their graphs explicitly.

Remark 87.4.6 (operator comparison between the completions). The atomic and continuous Hilbert
spaces are separable and have infinite dimension, so they admit abstract unitary isomorphisms. The
specified dynamics impose a stronger condition: an occupation eigenvector cannot map to a nonzero
continuous Mellin eigenvector. Chapter 87.1.3 proves the bounded group-intertwiner obstruction. The
explicit distribution map preserves logarithmic multiplication, while normalized dilation induces the
full residue-jet operator of Proposition 87.12.7. Their compositions are distinct.

The Hadamard inversion step is the bottleneck.

87.6    Connes 1999 Partial Approach and Its Limitation
Connes’ adele class space construction gives an explicit Hilbert space and scaling generator together with
the trace formula. The Hilbert–Pólya input is the further assertion that its absorption trace distribution
is the non-trivial zero distribution, with critical-line support.

The Connes Construction
Deﬁnition 87.6.1 (Connes adele class data). (Connes 1999 arXiv:math/9811068 §IV). The Connes adele class
Hilbert space is HConnes = 𝐿 2 ( 𝑋ℚ , 𝑑𝑥 ) with 𝑋ℚ = 𝔸/ℚ × the adele class space and 𝑑𝑥 the Haar measure
inherited from 𝔸 modulo ℚ × ; the quotient is non-Hausdorff, and the 𝐿 2 -structure is realised via the
crossed product 𝐶 ∗ (𝔸/ℚ × ) = 𝐶0 (𝔸) ⋊ ℚ × . The Connes scaling generator is 𝐷Connes = − 𝑖𝜕log 𝜆𝑈 ( 𝜆)
at 𝜆 = 1, where 𝑈 ( 𝜆) 𝑓 ( 𝑥 ) = | 𝜆 | −1/2 𝑓 ( 𝜆 −1 𝑥 ). On the cuspidal subspace E ⊂ HConnes (orthogonal
to the Tate-regularised constants), 𝐷Connes is conjectured to have absorption trace equal to the zero
distribution of 𝜉ℝ . Under zero-placement this trace is supported at the ordinate multiset { 𝛾 𝜌 }.

Remark 87.6.4 (the source of an absorption comparison). An operator on an adelic Hilbert space has

Remark 87.6.6 (the role of the adelic construction). An independently constructed adelic carrier specifies

87.7    Meyer 2005 Partial Approach and Its Limitation
Meyer’s global representation supplies a character formula and spectral multiplicities on a nuclear
bornological carrier. Continuous Mellin scaling supplies a separate Hilbert-space calculation. The com-
parison below specifies the maps needed to relate their operators.

The Meyer Construction
Deﬁnition 87.7.1 (continuous norm test space). . In the product Hilbert space of Chapter 87.4.5, take

this Hilbert space requires an additional map.

Remark 87.7.3 (the local quotient map). At a zero 𝜌 of order 𝑟 , the map O 𝜌 /( 𝜉ℝ ) → ℂ𝑟 taking full

directly from the invertible Taylor-to-residue matrix in Equation (87.9). The trace on this block equals
the trace on 𝑟 scalar copies of 𝜌, although their nilpotent actions differ when 𝑟 > 1. Thus a character
identity alone does not identify the full representations or their positive pairings.

Remark 87.7.5 (the positive Hilbert comparison). The local quotient map preserves the full zero multi-
plicity. Theorem 87.12.14 completes these local data in an explicit positive norm. The resulting dilation
is symmetric exactly for simple zeros on the chosen line. The construction chooses its norm from the
divisor and interpolation data. An arithmetic realization additionally requires the actual global pairing
and character maps, with their domains and continuity. Meyer’s character theorem and the continuous
Mellin unitary do not construct the occupation map in the preceding proposition.

Hilbert comparisons with speciﬁed domains
The continuous Mellin unitary and the global arithmetic character act on different spaces. A comparison
begins with the inner products and densely defined maps between these spaces. All Hilbert spaces below
are complex, with inner products linear in the first variable.
Proposition 87.7.6 (extension of a core isometry). Let 𝑇𝑗 be densely defined operators on Hilbert
spaces H𝑗 , with domains C𝑗 , for 𝑗 = 1, 2. Suppose a complex-linear bijection 𝑈0 : C1 → C2 satisfies

                              ⟨𝑈0 𝑣, 𝑈0 𝑤 ⟩2 = ⟨𝑣, 𝑤 ⟩1 ,   𝑈0𝑇1 𝑣 = 𝑇2𝑈0 𝑣,

where 𝑇1 C1 ⊆ C1 and 𝑇2 C2 ⊆ C2 . Then 𝑈0 extends uniquely to a unitary 𝑈 : H1 → H2 . It identifies the
closures of the graphs and the adjoint domains:

                              𝑈 Dom 𝑇1∗ = Dom 𝑇2∗ ,           𝑈 𝑇1∗ = 𝑇2∗𝑈 .

If the operators are closable, then 𝑈 𝑇 1 = 𝑇 2𝑈 , with equality of the transported domains. In particular,
essential self-adjointness and deficiency spaces are preserved.

Proof. For 𝑣 ∈ H1 , choose 𝑣𝑛 ∈ C1 with 𝑣𝑛 → 𝑣 and define 𝑈 𝑣 = lim 𝑈0 𝑣𝑛 . The isometry identity
proves existence and independence of the sequence. The range is closed and contains the dense space C2 ,
so 𝑈 is onto. The unitary 𝑈 ⊕ 𝑈 maps the graph of 𝑇1 onto that of 𝑇2 . It therefore maps their graph
closures onto one another. For 𝑦 ∈ H1 , the functional 𝑣 ↦→ ⟨𝑇1 𝑣, 𝑦 ⟩1 is bounded in the Hilbert norm
exactly when 𝑈0 𝑣 ↦→ ⟨𝑇2𝑈0 𝑣, 𝑈 𝑦 ⟩2 is bounded. This gives the adjoint-domain identity and the adjoint
action. Hence 𝑈 ker(𝑇1∗ ∓ 𝑖 ) = ker(𝑇2∗ ∓ 𝑖 ).

   The same proof applies without invariance of the cores when a unitary 𝑈 is already given and 𝑈 𝑇1 =
𝑇2𝑈 on the exact domains. In particular, if 𝐻𝑗 are self-adjoint, C𝑗 are their graph cores, and the preceding
hypotheses hold for their restrictions, then 𝑈 Dom 𝐻1 = Dom 𝐻2 and 𝑈 𝐻1 = 𝐻2𝑈 .

Proposition 87.9.3 (scattering and arithmetic comparisons). . Suppose a scaling realization

    Separately, let Ω± : K0 → K𝑎 be the isometric wave maps of a specified scattering pair. Their

Proof. The first assertions are Proposition 87.7.7 and Corollary 87.7.8. Proposition 87.7.11 proves the

Spectral Flow as 3D ACS Bulk-Boundary Correspondence
Proposition 87.9.5 (bulk and occupation operator types). . Suppose a positive bulk Hilbert space

Proof. The transport assertions follow from the explicit formula and Proposition 87.7.7. For the deriva-

and zero. Thus evaluation of the section derivative does not factor through the value in the fiber. A

Remark 87.9.6 (partition functions and bulk comparisons). An identity between a bulk partition function
and 𝜉ℝ is a scalar identity. The bulk Hilbert pairing, scaling generator, occupation map, and ordinary
or regularized character require their own constructions. The arithmetic object V prim is a Hochschild
trace class; its Hilbert realization is additional data. Under the unitary and trace hypotheses above, the
complete operator realization transfers by the proved maps.

Proof. Complete the core isometries by Proposition 87.7.6. Their graph identities give equality on the
self-adjoint domains. Proposition 87.7.7 applied to 𝑈𝑗−1 proves the first three claims and the formula for
𝐴𝑗 . Corollary 87.7.8 proves the fourth. For the positivity description, the map [ 𝑓 ] ↦→ 𝐶 𝑓 extends to
the unitary in Proposition 87.7.10. The explicitly required operator and character identities then permit
the same transport argument.

Remark 87.9.8 (critical-line placement and the comparison problem). If one self-adjoint 𝐻𝑗 has shifted
spectral divisor equal to the entire zero divisor of 𝜉ℝ , every such zero has real part 1/2. This follows
because the eigenvalues of 𝐻𝑗 are real. It proves the Riemann Hypothesis from that realization. The
converse does not supply the core isometries, the arithmetic pairing, or a closed occupation map. In
particular, a positive cyclic form alone does not recover ordinary trace multiplicities, as the finite example
after Proposition 87.7.10 shows. Proposition 87.12.17 excludes an injective literal occupation map on
any domain containing 𝑣1 . These are additional construction conditions in the original spectral-flow
question.

87.10    Polyakov–Dirac Normal Form for the Residual
Under the stated primary Heisenberg hypotheses, the Polyakov rank-residue calculation fixes the scalar
𝑟 𝜁 = 2. For a specified symmetric core, the Dirac double tests essential self-adjointness of that same oper-
ator. The arithmetic determinant, positive Hilbert pairing, occupation map, and character comparison
remain independent hypotheses. The following construction keeps these data separate and proves the
fixed-core equivalence.

Polyakov Rigidity of the Rank Residue
Proposition 87.10.1 (Polyakov rank-residue rigidity). . In the primary Heisenberg domain of
Chapters 14 and 86, any spectral-flow closure compatible with
   (i) the rank-2 per-prime Sugawara Heisenberg stress tensor,
  (ii) the global Fock partition 𝑍 ( 𝑠 ) = 𝑝 𝑛 ≥1 (1 − 𝑝 − 𝑠𝑛 ) −2 , and
                                          Q Q

 (iii) the archimedean Polyakov anomaly of the rank-2 free-field completion,
has determinant rank residue
                                                  𝑟 𝜁 = 2.
This determines the scalar under the stated primary Heisenberg hypotheses. The Hilbert pairing, operator
domains, and arithmetic trace comparisons remain the separate data of Theorem 87.9.7.

Proof. Chapter 86.6.1 proves that the unrenormalised conformal scalar 𝑝 𝑐 ( 𝑝 ) diverges, that the nega-
                                                                       P
tive global modes do not act on the restricted vacuum, and that the global Fock-partition residue gives
𝑟 𝜁 = 2. The same chapter proves the Polyakov rank comparison Chapter 86.5.3, identifying this finite-
prime residue with the rank-2 archimedean conformal anomaly. These inputs leave no determinant
scalar parameter: changing 𝑟 𝜁 would either abandon the Euler-product partition, abandon the Sugawara
rank, or abandon the archimedean anomaly match. None of those changes is a spectral-flow closure
inside the stated primary Heisenberg domain. This scalar argument contains no Hilbert isometry, graph-
core theorem, or arithmetic character map. Those comparisons retain the independent hypotheses of
Theorem 87.9.7.

Remark 87.10.2 (what Polyakov does and does not buy). Polyakov regularisation is decisive for the de-
terminant rank, not for RH. It supplies the finite scalar 𝑟 𝜁 = 2 and rules out the divergent prime-zeta
prescription; it does not produce the Hilbert space on which the zero ordinates are a self-adjoint spec-
trum.

Proof. The fixed unitary matrix 2−1/2 ( 11 −11 ) conjugates the Dirac double on its exact product domain

Boundary Form and Deﬁciency Kernels
Under the stated primary Heisenberg hypotheses, scalar rigidity fixes 𝑟 𝜁 = 2. For the specified symmetric
operator, the boundary quotient Qres tests essential self-adjointness. The arithmetic determinant, pairing,
and occupation map are not determined by this quotient.

Proposition 87.10.11 (the boundary quotient of a fixed symmetric operator). . For the specified
densely defined symmetric operator 𝑇0 , essential self-adjointness is equivalent to
                                                    Qres = 0.
The induced boundary form is nondegenerate on this quotient. Consequently, a bijection from a speci-
fied BV–BFV boundary space to Qres preserving the complete boundary pairing would identify vanishing
of that pairing with essential self-adjointness. Cancellation of a variation merely on the original core
proves only its isotropy. Neither conclusion identifies the arithmetic determinant or constructs an occu-
pation map.

Proof. Since 𝑇0 is symmetric, it is closable and 𝑇 0 ⊆ 𝑇0∗ . The quotient vanishes exactly when their
domains agree; their actions then agree, so 𝑇 0 = (𝑇 0 ) ∗ . If the class of 𝑢 ∈ Dom 𝑇0∗ pairs to zero
with every class, then ⟨𝑇0∗ 𝑢, 𝑣 ⟩ = ⟨𝑢, 𝑇0∗ 𝑣 ⟩ for every 𝑣 ∈ Dom 𝑇0∗ . The adjoint definition gives 𝑢 ∈
Dom(𝑇0∗ ) ∗ = Dom 𝑇 0 . Thus the quotient form is nondegenerate. A bijection preserving the pairing
transfers its vanishing; isotropy of the original core alone says nothing about the remaining adjoint-
domain classes.
    For the missing arithmetic implication, take 𝑇0 = 0 on ℂ. Its boundary quotient is zero, while its
shifted operator has eigenvalue 1/2. Proposition 87.12.17 proves 𝜉ℝ (1/2) > 1/4, so this operator has the
wrong zero divisor. Scalar normalization cannot change that divisor. The occupation and arithmetic
character comparisons require the maps and hypotheses of Proposition 87.7.7.

Lemma 87.10.19 (point conditions are graph-invisible). . Let Γ ⊂ ℝ be locally finite. Then 𝐶𝑐∞ (ℝ \
Γ) is graph-dense in D ( 𝑀𝑡 ). In particular, a boundary condition that is only pointwise at the zero

Proof. The graph norm of 𝑀𝑡 is the 𝐿 2 -norm for the measure (1 + 𝑡 2 ) 𝑑𝑡 . Locally finite sets have zero
measure for this weight. Given 𝑓 ∈ D ( 𝑀𝑡 ), truncate 𝑓 to a compact interval, remove intervals of

The approximants lie in 𝐶𝑐∞ (ℝ \ Γ) and converge in the graph norm.

Corollary 87.10.22 (Hadamard residue data is graph-invisible). . In the ordinary Mellin graph
topology, 𝛽Had does not exist as a non-zero graph-dual boundary functional. Therefore a boundary

Remark 87.10.23 (surviving branches after the graph-dual no-go). The preceding corollary is not an
exhaustive boundary-state classification. It eliminates only the ordinary point-supported graph-dual
path. Assuming the closed Tate-polar quotient and specified Mellin chart have been constructed, a
surviving operator obstruction must take a different form. The known nonexclusive presentations are:
   (i) the exact Hadamard residue or finite-jet trace lives in a stronger rigged, Paley–Wiener, de Branges,
       or reproducing-kernel topology Φ𝜉 ⊂ D ( 𝑀𝑡 )graph , where point evaluation is continuous;
  (ii) the ordinary graph obstruction is nonlocal, represented under the resolvent chart by an 𝐿 2 -vector
       or closed 𝐿 2 -subspace as in Chapter 87.10.18, and is therefore not point-residue data;
87.10. Polyakov–Dirac Normal Form for the Residual                                                         831


 (iii) a physical Ward/BV–BFV argument supplies extra boundary phase space not yet identified with
       Qres ; this is a physics residual, not an operator-theoretic graph-dual boundary functional.
These alternatives use different topologies and boundary spaces. Identifying any one with a specified arith-
metic Tate-positivity or Burnol–de Branges construction requires a pairing isometry, an exact operator-
domain comparison, and the arithmetic trace identity. No such identification follows from the list of
alternatives. The stronger-topology construction requires, at minimum, a continuous Hadamard trace-
and-jet map Φ𝜉 → ℓ 2 ( Γ𝜉crit , 𝑤 ), compatibility with the post-Tate quotient and adjoint domains, and a
proof that the resulting closed condition is not a tautological insertion of the zero divisor.
Remark 87.10.24 (answer of the calculation). The maximal multiplication operator on ordinary 𝐿 2 is
self-adjoint. For a restriction transported by the specified quotient chart, essential self-adjointness asks
exactly for graph density:

in the quotient graph norm. A genuine boundary state must therefore come from a graph-dual functional

Graph Norm and Arithmetic Determinant
The continuous Mellin operator has absolutely continuous spectrum ℝ. A positive atomic model takes
its zero divisor and weights as input. A quotient constructed from arithmetic data would require its own
positive pairing, graph domain, and trace comparison. The following calculations distinguish the first
two constructions and the conditions required to compare either with the third.
Lemma 87.10.25 (continuous Mellin-line graph closure). . Let

                𝑀𝑡0 : 𝐶𝑐∞ (ℝ) ⊂ 𝐿 2 (ℝ, 𝑑𝑡 ) −→ 𝐿 2 (ℝ, 𝑑𝑡 ) ,             ( 𝑀𝑡0 𝑓 ) ( 𝑡 ) = 𝑡 𝑓 ( 𝑡 ) .

Then 𝑀𝑡0 is essentially self-adjoint. Its graph-norm closure is multiplication by 𝑡 on

                         D ( 𝑀𝑡 ) = { 𝑓 ∈ 𝐿 2 (ℝ, 𝑑𝑡 ) | 𝑡 𝑓 ( 𝑡 ) ∈ 𝐿 2 (ℝ, 𝑑𝑡 ) } .

The spectrum is the absolutely continuous spectrum Spec( 𝑀𝑡 ) = ℝ.

Proof. The operator 𝑀𝑡 with the displayed maximal domain is self-adjoint by the spectral theorem
for multiplication operators. The core 𝐶𝑐∞ (ℝ) is dense in the graph norm: truncate 𝑓 by compactly
supported cutoffs and then mollify; both 𝑓 and 𝑡 𝑓 converge in 𝐿 2 . Hence the closure of 𝑀𝑡0 is 𝑀𝑡 . Since
𝑀𝑡 is multiplication by the coordinate on 𝐿 2 (ℝ, 𝑑𝑡 ), its spectrum is the essential range of 𝑡 , namely ℝ,
with absolutely continuous spectral measure.

Proposition 87.10.26 (why the classical closure is insufficient). . The closure of Chapter 87.10.25
does not solve the spectral-flow problem. Its graph norm is complete and its operator is self-adjoint, but
its spectrum is continuous ℝ, not a divisor with zero multiplicities of 𝜉ℝ . Consequently it cannot satisfy

                                  det∞ 𝑠 · id − ( 21 id + 𝑖 𝑀𝑡 ) = 𝜉ℝ ( 𝑠 )

as a zero-eigenvalue determinant.

Proof. The determinant identity in Chapter 87.4 has divisor div 𝜉ℝ . The multiplication operator 𝑀𝑡
on 𝐿 2 (ℝ, 𝑑𝑡 ) has Lebesgue spectral measure on the line, not this determinant divisor. Thus the clo-
sure obtained by ordinary Mellin-line graph completion has continuous spectral type and no point
eigenvalues. This statement concerns the continuous Hilbert space. Meyer’s global nuclear bornological
representation has the separate character and multiplicity theorem recorded in Theorem 87.7.2; it is not
identified with this Hilbert closure.

Theorem 87.10.28 (the Dirac criterion on the fixed quotient). . Suppose the positive quotient
Hilbert space and densely defined symmetric operator 𝑇0 = 𝐻0◦ have been constructed as above. Fix the
determinant convention of Theorem 87.10.6. Then the following statements are equivalent:
   (i) 𝑇0 is essentially self-adjoint and its closure satisfies (87.4);
  (ii) ker(𝑇0∗ − 𝑖 ) = 0 = ker(𝑇0∗ + 𝑖 ), and the self-adjoint closure has the same determinant identity;
 (iii) the Dirac double of this same 𝑇0 has the Dirac closure of Definition 87.10.4.
Under a specified unitary graph-core comparison with an arithmetic Hilbert–Pólya operator, these
conditions transfer to that operator. They do not construct this comparison or an arithmetic trace map.

Proof. The equivalence of the first two statements is the deficiency-index criterion for a densely defined
symmetric operator. The equivalence with the third is the fixed-domain Dirac conjugacy proved in
Theorem 87.10.6. The additional unitary transports closures, adjoints, and the determinant under the
hypotheses of Proposition 87.7.6 and Corollary 87.7.8.

Remark 87.10.29 (the arithmetic signiﬁcance of the divisor). A self-adjoint realization with the complete
xi zero divisor implies critical-line placement, because its shifted eigenvalues have real part 1/2. A graph
closure on the ordinary Mellin line has continuous spectral type. A Hilbert space built by prescribing
the zeros requires an additional arithmetic pairing and trace comparison. The preceding fixed-core
equivalence distinguishes these constructions and preserves the original arithmetic question.

log 𝑚.

distribution 𝑇 𝑣𝑚 is localized at 𝑡 = − log 𝑚. Its Mellin transform is a plane wave multiplied by 𝑚 − 𝑐 on
the line Re 𝑠 = 𝑐 ; it is not a frequency point mass. This distinction accounts for both actions in (87.6).

Evaluation norms and operator closure
A residue value is a linear functional on compact smooth tests. Completing those tests in the squared
sum of their residue values changes the Hilbert space. The change can be measured exactly for finitely
many zeros, without any estimate on the global zero set.
Finite evaluation and its graph

Proposition 87.12.12 (bounded spectral transfer). A bounded map intertwining the unitary
groups of 𝑃𝑐 on H𝑐 and 𝐾 on ℓ 2 ( 𝜇) is zero, in either direction.

Proof. In the direction from the atomic space, the image of 𝑒𝑗 would be an eigenvector of 𝑃𝑐 with

set. Thus it is zero, and density of the finite-coordinate vectors finishes the argument. Taking the adjoint
gives the opposite direction, since both groups are unitary.

    The maximal block operator is closed: convergence in its graph implies convergence in every finite

scalars. If it is symmetric, its restriction to every finite block is symmetric. Theorem 87.12.10 forces every
block to be a real scalar.

    The theorem requires no bound on the multiplicities. The norm depends on the Laurent coefficients
and the chosen interpolation functions. Making a weight smaller preserves every estimate and every
graph approximation in the proof. For a divisor invariant under 𝜌 ↦→ 2𝑐 − 𝜌, one may therefore replace
the two weights on each orbit by their minimum. The resulting residue involution is antiunitary. This
does not make a nontrivial Jordan block symmetric.

Critical-line symmetry and the arithmetic target
An involution can preserve residue data without making the dilation operator symmetric. This distinc-
tion is visible in the signs of full principal parts.

Inversion and conjugation
For real 𝑐 , define on H𝑐
                                          ( 𝐽𝑐 𝑓 ) ( 𝑥 ) = 𝑥 −2𝑐 𝑓 ( 𝑥 −1 ) .

on compact smooth tests, and then on the closed operator domain. For the domain assertion, logarithmic

    Suppose now that the entire function satisfies

invariant under this map.
Proposition 87.12.16 (the residue involution). On full jet coordinates, inversion acts by

                                          ( 𝐽𝑍 𝑎) 𝜌,𝑘 = (−1) 𝑘+1 𝑎 𝜌# ,𝑘 .

Thus R 𝑍 𝐽𝑐 = 𝐽𝑍 R 𝑍 , and 𝐽𝑍 is an antiunitary involution for the Euclidean jet norm. It commutes with
𝐾𝑐 . At a simple critical-line zero, the residue action is minus complex conjugation.
Proof. Put 𝑠 = 𝜌 + 𝑧 . Equations (87.18) and (87.19) identify the quotient for 𝐽𝑐 𝑓 with the conjugate
of the quotient for 𝑓 at 𝜌# − 𝑧 . A coefficient of order −( 𝑘 + 1) therefore acquires the factor (−1) 𝑘+1 .
This proves the formula. The norm and involution assertions follow by permuting coordinates and
conjugating them. For commutation, note that 𝑧 𝜌# ,𝑐 = 𝑧 𝜌,𝑐 and that consecutive signs in the formula
are opposite. Substitution into (87.13) gives 𝐽𝑍 𝐾𝑐 = 𝐾𝑐 𝐽𝑍 .

   The same assertion holds for positive diagonal jet weights invariant under 𝜌 ↦→ 𝜌# . Commutation
with this antiunitary does not remove a Jordan block. The symmetry criterion of Theorem 87.12.10 still
requires simple zeros on the line.

                                              𝐽𝑐 𝑇 𝑣𝑚 = 𝑚1−2𝑐 𝛿𝑚 .

    If the selected zeros are simple and on the critical line, their weighted evaluation completion from

through the selected zero data and weights. This conditional construction does not produce an indepen-
dently defined arithmetic positive pairing or establish critical-line placement. With full multiple-zero
jets, Theorem 87.12.10 gives an additional obstruction to a positive symmetric realization.
Local quotient representations and traces
Let O 𝜌 be the algebra of holomorphic germs at 𝜌. If Ξ has a zero of order 𝑟 there, the linear map
                              O 𝜌 /( Ξ) −→ ℂ𝑟 ,        [ 𝐹 ] ↦−→ ( 𝑅 𝜌,𝑘 𝐹 )0≤ 𝑘 <𝑟
is an isomorphism. Indeed 𝐹 /Ξ has no principal part exactly when 𝐹 is divisible by Ξ as a germ. Taylor
reduction modulo ( 𝑠 − 𝜌) 𝑟 and (87.9) prove surjectivity. Multiplication by 𝑠 becomes 𝜌𝐼 + 𝑆 , where
( 𝑆 𝑎) 𝑘 = 𝑎𝑘+1 . Thus the affine operator 𝑐 + 𝑖 𝐾𝑐 is exactly the local multiplication operator. This com-
parison preserves multiplicity and its nilpotent action.
     This local quotient is the algebraic form of zero multiplicity. Meyer constructs a global virtual repre-
sentation of the idele class group on nuclear bornological spaces. Its character is the Weil distribution, and
its spectral multiplicities are the pole orders of the completed 𝐿 -function (Meyer, arXiv:math/0311468v3,
Theorems 5.8 and 5.11, pp. 43 and 47). Zeros contribute through the negative representation. That result
does not specify the positive evaluation weights constructed here. An identification with these Hilbert
spaces requires maps from the global representation, continuity in both norms, and compatibility with
the scaling action and the chosen pairing.
     For finite blocks the distinction between trace and representation is explicit. The trace tr 𝑝 ( 𝜌𝐼 + 𝑆 ) =
𝑟 𝑝 ( 𝜌) equals the trace on 𝑟 scalar copies of 𝜌. When 𝑟 > 1 these representations are not isomorphic: the
first has a nonzero nilpotent part, while the second has none. For infinite blocks an ordinary operator
trace additionally requires trace-class convergence. In the simple critical-line case,
                               Tr 𝜑 ( 𝐾𝑤 ) =     𝜑 ( 𝛾𝑗 ) if
                                             ∑︁               ∑︁
                                                                  | 𝜑 ( 𝛾𝑗 )| < ∞.
                                            𝑗                   𝑗

To prove this formula, use the orthonormal basis 𝑤𝑗−1/2 𝑒𝑗 and the diagonal trace-class criterion. In
particular the weights disappear from the trace. Hence this trace cannot recover the positive form chosen
on the test functions.

      The occupation operator has a different trace. For real 𝛽 > 1,

                                      Tr 𝑒 − 𝛽𝑁 =

The positive diagonal sum converges by integral comparison and diverges for 𝛽 ≤ 1. A trace over zero
ordinates involves a different index set and requires a proved comparison of the operators and trace
functionals. Mellin evaluation and equality of local multiplicities do not supply that comparison.
The occupation realization that remains
An occupation-to-zero realization would require a Hilbert space H𝜉 , an independently specified positive
inner product, and a self-adjoint operator 𝐻 there. It would also require an injective linear map 𝐴 on a
dense 𝑁 -invariant domain D 𝑁 ⊂ Dom 𝑁 , with dense range in H𝜉 , such that

                              𝐴D 𝑁 ⊂ Dom 𝐻 ,              𝐴𝑁 = 𝐻 𝐴 on D 𝑁 .

Closedness and domain compatibility are part of this operator problem. Matching the arithmetic zero
divisor further requires the eigenvalues of 1/2 + 𝑖 𝐻 , with their multiplicities, to give the actual zeros
of 𝜉ℝ . Any determinant or trace comparison requires its own definition, convergence domain, and
normalization.
    The explicit map 𝑇 constructs the occupation-to-distribution edge on every finite sequence. Its
residue composition fails the required energy identity by Proposition 87.12.3, including multiple zeros. A
domain containing the finite occupation core cannot fix that algebraic failure by completion. Domains
excluding that core are different operator problems and require new maps. Proposition 87.12.17 also
excludes every injective map with the actual zero-divisor target when its domain contains 𝑣1 . The normal-
ized dilation operator instead has the exact jet comparison Proposition 87.12.7; it acts on a continuous
spectral carrier. Its evaluation map is not a closable transfer from the original Hilbert space in the settings
proved above.
    The physical distinction is between logarithmic position and its conjugate momentum. Integer oc-
cupation selects discrete position values. Mellin dilation measures continuous momentum. Residue
evaluation samples a function of that momentum at a chosen divisor; a positive sampling norm changes
the state space. The displayed maps and obstructions specify these operations. They supply no identifi-
cation of their thermal traces or of an arithmetic trace with the sampled norm.

Composition is place-wise; identities are place-wise identities. The resulting category is ArChAlg.
Proposition 88.1.4 ( ArChAlg is a well-defined category). . Composition of morphisms satisfies
the axioms of Chapter 88.1.3: axioms (1)–(5) are place-wise, and axiom (6) follows from place-wise
axioms by the almost-every-place triviality of the units. Identity morphisms are identities in every axiom.
Associativity and unitality are inherited from the underlying categories of 𝐸1 -chiral factorisation algebras
at ∞ and 𝐸0 -coefficient categories at finite places.

using the stacked naturality diagrams. Axiom (5) uses the linear action of the boundary. Associativity
and unitality are automatic at each place. Axiom (6) follows from the almost-every-place compatibility of
the Tate restricted tensor (Chapter 21.3): the set of places at which 𝑢 ( 𝑣 ) fails to be a strict unit is bounded,
and composition preserves this bound.

exactly one of them; hence the functoriality statements below have independent derivations on the finite

Remark 88.2.5 (source disjointness of the three functors). The Deninger functor is derived from Deninger

on its conditional domain, not a restatement of any single derivation.

Independence and domain of the chain-level identiﬁcation
Independence. The ordered-incidence bar rests on Francis 2013 (geometric 𝐸1 -nerve); the Platonic bar
rests on Beilinson–Drinfeld 2004 and arithmetic Positselski (Chapter 37.3.1). The two constructions
come from disjoint source families; Ξ is therefore a genuine Vol IV verification of the identification, not
a tautology.
    Signs. The ordered-incidence differential uses alternating contraction signs on simplicial nerves;
the Platonic differential (37.2) uses Koszul signs on tensor factors. These match under Ξ because the
simplicial normalisation formula turns alternating contraction signs into Koszul tensor signs (standard
Dold–Kan).
    Ambient category. Both bars take values in chain complexes over ℂ with restricted-tensor refinement
to the adelic factorisation structure; the ambient category is identical.
    Conditional hypothesis. The quasi-isomorphism Ξ ( 𝑝 ) on finite-prime factors uses arithmetic Posit-
selski Chapter 24.1.5, conditional on the non-abelian Iwasawa extension. This is the only inherited
conditional; all other steps are unconditional within the primary Heisenberg domain.
856                       Chapter 88. Functoriality of the Triple Identification in A and 𝑔


   Naturality. Axioms (3), (4), (5) of Chapter 88.1.3 supply precisely the intertwining needed at each layer
(units, adjacent products, Parshin–Gersten boundary); no additional functoriality input is required.
   Unconditional domain. The equivalence between ordered-bar and Platonic-bar homology on the
primary Heisenberg domain is the content of Chapter 37.3.4, which holds unconditionally within that
domain. No numerical comparison backs this identification.

Independence and domain of naturality in A
Independence. Beilinson–Drinfeld 2004 supplies the 𝐸1 -chiral functoriality at the archimedean factor;
Kim 2015 and the quantum ACS supply the bulk interface defect functoriality at the 3D side. These
derivation paths are disjoint; the natural isomorphism 𝜂ch,𝜕 verified against both is a genuine independent
check.
   Signs. The bar-differential Koszul signs agree on both sides by construction of Chapter 37.3.1; the
ordered-incidence alternating signs match under Ξ by the simplicial normalisation formula.
   Ambient category. Both sides land in graded ℂ-vector spaces with Frobenius and Poincaré duality; no
compatibility issue.
   Frobenius hypothesis. The naturality of 𝐹∞ under 𝜙 (∞) requires that 𝜙 (∞) preserves the conformal
vector; this is axiom (1) of Chapter 88.1.3, which is part of the definition of a morphism and imposes no
hidden constraint.
   Axiom independence. Axioms (2) and (4) are logically independent: axiom (4) applied at 𝑣 = 𝑝, 𝑤 =
∞ implies axiom (2) only on the unit line (the spherical vacuum at ∞ is fixed by 𝜓 𝑝 up to normalised
Frobenius weight); the full 𝜓 𝑝 -equivariance on all of A ( 𝑝 ) is an additional local constraint not automatic
from (4). Both axioms are needed and neither is redundant.
   Spectral content. The identification of the 𝐹 -spectrum on 𝐻 1 with the nontrivial zeros of 𝜉 ( 𝑠 ) remains
conditional on H-PAr (Chapter 22.3.2), inherited from Chapter 83.6.1. The naturality of 𝐹 established
here requires only its commutation with 𝐻 • ( 𝜙), not a description of its spectrum.

88.6    Master Theorem and Explicit Example
Functoriality in A and genus-filtered functoriality hold independently; the master theorem records
that both hold simultaneously, with a specific chain-level quasi-isomorphism Ξ as canonical witness.
The diagonal morphism HAr → HAr ⊕ HAr tests the non-conformal additive structure; the conformal
diagonal is excluded by the central-charge obstruction.

Proof. A rank-2 Heisenberg conformal vector has central charge 2; the coproduct of two such Heisenberg
factors has conformal vector 𝑇 ⊕ 𝑇 and central charge 4. If the diagonal were conformal, the OPE of the
image of 𝑇 with itself would have to preserve the central term. It instead doubles it. Hence no conformal
ArChAlg-morphism has the displayed diagonal as its underlying map.
    After forgetting the conformal vector, Δ ( 𝑝 ) commutes with 𝜓 𝑝 because 𝜓 𝑝 ( 𝑥, 𝑥 ) = ( 𝜓 𝑝 ( 𝑥 ) , 𝜓 𝑝 ( 𝑥 )).
The spherical unit is preserved: Δ ( 𝑣 ) ( 𝑢 ( 𝑣 ) ) = ( 𝑢 ( 𝑣 ) , 𝑢 ( 𝑣 ) ). The adjacent product on the coproduct is
the diagonal of the adjacent product on each summand; Δ commutes with this by construction. The
tame-symbol boundary 𝜕 PG is linear, so 𝜕 PG ( 𝑥, 𝑥 ) = ( 𝜕 PG ( 𝑥 ) , 𝜕 PG ( 𝑥 )). Tate compatibility is preserved
because the spherical units are preserved and the restricted tensor factors through each summand.
    Claim (1). The Deninger cohomology of the coproduct HAr ⊕ HAr is 𝐻Δ• ( HAr ) ⊕ 𝐻Δ• ( HAr ) because
arithmetic bar commutes with direct sums on the primary domain (the bar is additive in its argument, a
consequence of Chapter 37.3.1 and of the additivity of the tame-symbol boundary). The induced map is
the diagonal. In each degree: 𝐻 0 = ℂ0 → ℂ0 ⊕ ℂ0 , 𝑥 ↦→ ( 𝑥, 𝑥 ); 𝐻 2 = ℂ1 → ℂ1 ⊕ ℂ1 , 𝑥 ↦→ ( 𝑥, 𝑥 );
𝐻 1 -eigenvectors at ordinate 𝛾 𝜌 go to the pair of two copies.
    Claim (2). The Platonic bar is natural in A by Chapter 88.2.2; after forgetting the conformal vector,
applying naturality to Δ gives the chain map on bars. Bar differential compatibility is the Parshin–Gersten
boundary compatibility proved above.
    Claim (3). The bulk-boundary assignment BdryACS( Δ) is by Chapter 88.2.3 the non-conformal 3D
bulk interface whose archimedean boundary restriction is Δ (∞) (the diagonal map of archimedean 𝐸1 -
chiral algebras) and whose finite-place Wilson-line restriction is {Δ ( 𝑝 ) }. The boundary chiral homology
𝜕 of this interface is the induced map on boundary chiral homology. By the additivity of boundary chiral
homology for coproducts in 3DACSSpec ℤ (the disjoint union of two bulk theories has as boundary the
coproduct of the two boundary chiral algebras), the boundary map is the diagonal on the rank-2 chiral
homology.
    Compatibility with 𝜂 . By construction each of the three maps agrees with the others under the natural
isomorphisms: they are all the diagonal of the same underlying primary Heisenberg cohomology object,
related by the chain-level quasi-isomorphism Ξ of Chapter 88.3.2 on each direct summand and the
identity on the direct-sum structure.

Remark 88.6.4 (what the diagonal example witnesses). The diagonal Δ is the simplest non-trivial mor-
phism after the conformal vector is forgotten: it is not an isomorphism, not a projection, not a single-
factor inclusion. It tests additivity of the three comparison functors, but it does not test the conformal
axiom of ArChAlg. Because the coproduct HAr ⊕ HAr sits in ArChAlg 𝑔 =2 (rank-4 archimedean Heisenberg)
while HAr sits in ArChAlg 𝑔 =1 , the example also shows why genus stabilization is not an arbitrary diagonal
embedding: the conformal central charge records the added rank.

Independence and domain of the master theorem
Independence. The master theorem combines three source families: Beilinson–Drinfeld 2004
(archimedean 𝐸1 -chiral structure), Fargues–Scholze arXiv:2102.13459 (finite-prime perfectoid charts),
862                       Chapter 88. Functoriality of the Triple Identification in A and 𝑔


and Kim 2015 arXiv:1510.05818 plus the quantum ACS (3D bulk theory). These families are pairwise
disjoint in the Vol IV orthogonal sense.
    Sign consistency. The Koszul signs in the Platonic bar differential, the alternating signs in the ordered-
incidence bar, and the 3D framed-cobordism signs in the boundary-chiral-homology pairing are mutually
consistent under the chain-level identification Ξ of Chapter 88.3.2.
    Inherited conditional hypotheses. The well-definedness of 𝜕 ◦ BdryACS as a functor (rather than a mere
correspondence) requires a well-defined bulk interface defect category, conditional on Chapter 82.4.4
and the renormalised profinite limit of Chapter 82.4.7. Both conditionals are inherited from Chapter 82.
    Spectral domain. The master theorem claims the functoriality of the triple identification, not the
spectral content. The three spectral statements (Deninger purity, Riemann Hypothesis, 𝐹 -RH) remain
conditional on H-PAr and the archimedean A-TP hypothesis; neither is asserted here.

88.7    Domain of the Master Theorem
Functoriality residuals of Chapter 83
The following implications hold on the conditional domain of the master theorem:
  (i) Chapter 83.12(5): triple-identification functoriality under pullback along number-field extensions
      𝐾 /ℚ. Any such pullback is a morphism in ArChAlg (it preserves spherical units, adjacent products,
      and Parshin–Gersten boundaries by classical number-field theory), and functoriality follows from
      Chapter 88.4.2.
 (ii) Chapter 83.12(6): genus- 𝑔 Wilson-line Frobenius identification. On the residual domain of Chap-
      ter 88.5.3, the genus- 𝑔 restriction of 𝜕 ◦ BdryACS is functorially identified with the genus- 𝑔
                                                                                                     ( 𝑔)
      Deninger cohomology; the rank-2 𝑔 Wilson-loop observables then identify with the rank-2 𝑔 𝜓 𝑝
      by naturality in the direct summand structure.

Inherited conditional hypotheses of the master theorem
The master functoriality theorem Chapter 88.6.1 is conditional on the following inherited hypotheses:
   (i) Arithmetic Positselski (Ch. 54) for the finite-prime factor quasi-isomorphism Ξ ( 𝑝 ) .
  (ii) 3D quantum ACS existence (Chapter 82.4.7) for the well-definedness of BdryACS as a functor.
 (iii) Local-trace comparison (Chapter 82.4.9) for the boundary identification at ∞.
 (iv) H-PAr (Chapter 22.3.2) for the spectrum identification on 𝐻 1 ; not used in functoriality but used
       in spectral content.
  (v) Rank- 𝑔 Künneth compatibility on the Platonic bar, which is standard by rank- 𝑔 Positselski
       (Ch. 81.6(2)).
No new residuals are introduced.

The master theorem and what it forces
On the conditional domain, the triple comparison 𝐻Δ• = 𝐻ch       • = 𝜕 ◦ BdryACS, previously isolated

object-wise for H at genus 𝑔 = 0, is a natural isomorphism of genus-filtered functors on the stated
subcategory of ArChAlg: every morphism of arithmetic chiral algebras induces a commuting triple-square
of cohomology maps, Frobenius-equivariant and Poincaré-dual-compatible; every genus-inclusion and
retraction is intertwined by Künneth natural transformations 𝜗 ★𝑔 . The chain-level quasi-isomorphism Ξ

89.4     Archimedean Wilson-Surface at Genus 𝑔
At the archimedean place, a three-dimensional ACS boundary is a real surface. For the curve row, the
3-space B 𝑔(3) has a closed-surface boundary Σ∞ = B 𝑔(3) | ∞ of real dimension 2, with genus 𝑔 entering
through 𝐻 1 ( Σ∞ ) of rank 2 𝑔 , rather than through the dimension of the boundary. A defect operator
on Σ∞ must integrate an area form rather than a holonomy along a loop: the Faltings 1984 arithmetic
Kähler form 𝜇Ar, 𝑔 on the archimedean fibre is the natural input, since it encodes the metric data of D 𝑔
at the archimedean place and degenerates to zero at 𝑔 = 0, matching the trivial archimedean boundary
of the Riemann 𝜉 -function framework.

89.6     Uniform 𝑔 = 0 Compatibility
At 𝑔 = 0, the constructions of Sections 89.2–89.5 degenerate to the rank-zero skeleton inside the Rie-
mann framework of Chs. 82 and 83. The non-trivial rank-two Wilson sectors are compared, not derived,

Chapter 90


Continuous Scaling and the Arithmetic Zero
Operator

Continuous Mellin scaling has no eigenvectors. Occupation energy has a complete eigenbasis. This spec-
tral distinction prevents their unitary intertwining. A separate diagonal operator on the zero occurrences
gives an exact arithmetic exponential and its purity criterion, with no identification of these different
carriers.

90.1    Continuous Mellin scaling
Deﬁnition 90.1.1 (scaling and its domain). Set 𝐻𝑐 = 𝐿 2 (ℝ>0 , 𝑑𝑥 / 𝑥 ) and (𝑈𝑎 𝑓 ) ( 𝑥 ) = 𝑓 ( 𝑒 − 𝑎 𝑥 ) for
𝑎 ∈ ℝ. In the coordinate 𝑡 = log 𝑥 , define

                        𝐷 𝑐 = − 𝑖𝜕𝑡 ,      Dom 𝐷 𝑐 = { 𝑓 : 𝑓 ( 𝑒 𝑡 ) ∈ 𝐻 1 (ℝ, 𝑑𝑡 )} .

Then 𝑈𝑎 = 𝑒 − 𝑖 𝑎𝐷𝑐 . The derivative convention is 𝐷 𝑐 = 𝑖 𝜕𝑎𝑈𝑎 | 𝑎=0 .
Theorem 90.1.2 (Mellin unitarity). The transform

                                           1

extends to a unitary 𝐻𝑐 → 𝐿 2 (ℝ, 𝑑𝑢) and sends 𝐷 𝑐 to multiplication by 𝑢 on its maximal domain. It
has no eigenvectors. The normal operator Θ𝑐 = 1/2 + 𝑖𝐷 𝑐 has continuous spectrum 1/2 + 𝑖 ℝ.

Proof. The logarithmic coordinate is unitary from 𝐻𝑐 to 𝐿 2 ( 𝑑𝑡 ). Plancherel and integration by parts give
the transform and generator. The weak 𝐻 1 domain maps exactly to {𝑣 : 𝑢𝑣 ∈ 𝐿 2 ( 𝑑𝑢)}. An eigenvector
of multiplication by 𝑢 would be supported on a singleton, which has Lebesgue measure zero. The same

90.2    The occupation and primary-sector comparisons

equality of domains. In particular, the ordinary Fock energy and the integer occupation operator cannot

90.3    The zero exponential and its actual spectrum
Deﬁnition 90.3.1 (arithmetic zero exponential). For the diagonal operator Θ 𝑍 of Theorem 56.5.1, put

Proposition 90.3.2 (spectral measure and failure of local finiteness). For a Borel set 𝐵 ⊂ ℂ,
the spectral projection of 𝐹𝑍 is
                                           ( 𝑃𝑍 ( 𝐵 ) 𝑢) 𝜌 = 1 𝐵 ( 𝑒 − 𝜌 ) 𝑢 𝜌 .

ℂ. Thus it is not an entire-function zero divisor. For any fixed 𝑠 , the product 𝜌 (1 − 𝑒 − 𝑠 𝑒 − 𝜌 ) fails the

necessary factor-to-one condition for an ordinary convergent nonzero product.

Proof. Coordinate functional calculus gives the spectral projection. The spectrum of a bounded diagonal

Theorem 90.3.3 (arithmetic purity and Weil positivity). The following are equivalent:

        | 𝐹𝑍 | = 𝑒 −1/2 1,   ℜ 𝜌 = 1/2 for every zero 𝜌,         𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓 ∗ ) ≥ 0 for every 𝑓 ∈ A .

second is Weil’s positivity criterion on the exact compact convolution test algebra.

Five Source Families and the Archimedean Tate
Positivity Residual

The reduction of Chapter 60 places the Riemann hypothesis in the form of archimedean Tate positivity, A-TP
(Chapter 57.2.3). Five source families meet this same Weil inequality from different sides: Arthur–Selberg
scattering, geometric Langlands, Iwasawa–Kato, arithmetic quantum chaos, and Arakelov–Faltings–
Hriljac. None of them removes the Weil positivity problem. Pair-correlation controls statistics after the
zero-line input; it does not supply the zero-line input. Iwasawa theory controls ﬁnite-prime symmetry; it
does not supply the archimedean sign. Arakelov height positivity gives useful sub-class inequalities only after
the Bott–Chern and vertical terms are controlled.

of Chapter 84.1.2:

A-TP asserts 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓˜ ) ≥ 0 for all 𝑓 ∈ PW(ℝ), equivalent to RH via Weil 1952 (Bull. Soc. Math. France

91.2   Five Source Families
Theorem 91.2.1 (five source-family boundary for A-TP). . The five source families below do not
give an independent proof of A-TP. Each lands on one of three mathematical forms: the Weil inequality
itself, a conditional sub-class diagnostic, or an auxiliary structure which has no archimedean positivity
content without an additional RH-strength input.

             Arakelov–Faltings–Hriljac     The arithmetic Hodge index gives negative definite-

                                   𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) ≥ 0,         𝑓 ∈ PW(ℝ) ,
with polar, finite-prime, and archimedean terms all present. The archimedean digamma kernel is one
summand of this residual, not a replacement for it. Denote the full residual by RA-TP .
Remark 91.2.3 (one obstruction, several shadows). The source families give shadows of the same Weil
inequality. A shadow is not an equivalent coordinate chart unless it retains the polar terms, the von
Mangoldt sum, the archimedean gamma term, and the full Paley–Wiener cone.
