91.4    Two Negative Results: Iwasawa Auxiliary Structure and BGS Impli-
        cation Direction
Iwasawa-Kato Orthogonality to A-TP
Theorem 91.4.1 (Iwasawa-Kato orthogonality to A-TP). (on completeness of the Iwasawa-Kato
list: Mazur-Wiles 1984, Kato 2004 Astérisque 295, Perrin-Riou 1995, Fukaya-Kato 2006, Colmez, Bloch-
Kato 1990, Kolyvagin 1988, Coates-Wiles 1977, Ferrero-Washington 1979, Connes-Marcolli, Skinner-Urban).
No method in the standard Iwasawa-Kato list closes A-TP. Specifically: Mazur-Wiles value-positivity,
Kato Euler system plus Bloch-Kato-Beilinson height pairing, Ferrero-Washington archimedean analog,
882      Chapter 91. Five Source Families and the Archimedean Tate Positivity Residual


Perrin-Riou plus Bloch-Kato exponential, the 𝑝 → ∞ Connes-Marcolli limit, Kato reciprocity maps
exp∗ /log, Kolyvagin plus Coates-Wiles height positivity, Colmez-Fontaine 𝑝-adic Langlands, Fukaya-
Kato non-commutative plus Skinner-Urban, and concrete-Dirichlet 𝑝-adic transport each fail to deliver
A-TP positivity beyond sectors already closed by other means. Iwasawa theory supplies the functional-
equation symmetry 𝑠 ↔ 1 − 𝑠 at every finite prime (as in Chapter 21.5.1) but carries no positivity content
at the archimedean place.
Remark 91.4.2 (Deninger’s archimedean Iwasawa conjecture). The one Iwasawa-adjacent approach not
enumerated above is Deninger’s hypothetical archimedean Iwasawa main conjecture (Deninger 1998
ICM; 2002 Motives and algebraic cycles), which would interpret A-TP as the archimedean limit of a 𝑝-adic
Iwasawa main conjecture. That conjecture is itself RH-equivalent; it does not reduce the obstruction.

BGS Is Consequent of RH
Theorem 91.4.3 (GUE statistics do not imply A-TP). . A Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit or GUE
statement for ordinates { 𝛾𝑛 } does not imply A-TP. Such a statement concerns limiting correlations of a
real sequence. A-TP is positivity of the full Weil quadratic form on PW(ℝ), with the zero side evaluated
at
                                              𝑧 𝜌 = − 𝑖 ( 𝜌 − 21 ) .
Replacing 𝑧 𝜌 by a real ordinate 𝛾 𝜌 is precisely the zero-line input. Pair-correlation estimates do not supply
that replacement.
Remark 91.4.4 (implication direction in Chapter 84.8.2). The statistical-upside theorem Chapter 84.8.2
remains correct: granted the arithmetic-quantum-chaos hypotheses (C1)–(C5) of Chapter 84.8.2, BGS
applied to the 3D ACS bulk Hamiltonian is a statistical consequence inside that dynamical model. The di-
rection is from the dynamical hypothesis to statistics, not from statistics to Weil positivity. Chapter 91.4.3
rules out the latter use.

91.5   The Weil Cone
The five source-family boundary of Chapter 91.2.1 fixes the exact object which remains.
Proposition 91.5.1 (five source families do not contract the Weil cone). (on Chapter 91.2.1). None
of the five source families replaces A-TP by a smaller unconditional theorem. Each requires the full Weil
positivity statement, or a sign condition whose strength is at least the corresponding A-TP subproblem:
• Arthur–Selberg retains the archimedean scattering sign.
• Geometric Langlands retains the arithmetic spectral-action comparison and the zero-divisor input.
• Iwasawa retains the absence of an archimedean positivity theorem.
• Arithmetic quantum chaos retains the zero-line passage from complex zeros to real ordinates.
• Arakelov retains Bott–Chern and vertical residual signs.

91.6    Position within the A-TP Obstruction Sequence
Chapters 57–80 supply ten obstructions on A-TP from analytic directions: Riemann-Siegel, Nyman-
Beurling, de Branges Hilbert-Braun, Gaussian, bounded direct, Mellin-Barnes, Hadamard, Gram,
Guinand-Weil, adelic scattering. They give sub-class 𝑊∞ -positivity, conditional phase models, or
RH-equivalent reformulations. The five algebraic traditions below add five further tests from algebraic,
categorical, and Diophantine directions. Two produce new diagnostics (Chapter 91.3.1, Chapter 91.3.3);
91.7. Boundary                                                                                          883


two sharpen the obstruction by ruling out spurious directions (Chapter 91.4.1, Chapter 91.4.3). Across
all fifteen obstructions, the common object is the full Weil positivity problem RA-TP .
     The synthesis of Chapter 60 (Chapter 60.5.1) establishes RH ⇔ A-TP via the pillar reductions
collected there. This chapter does not further reduce RH below A-TP; it records why the five source
families do not bypass the full Weil cone.
     The arithmetic-gravity axis of Chapters 82–84 provides two further conditional languages for the
same Weil-positive distribution: chiral-homology positivity and prismatic Frobenius at the archimedean
place. Chapter 91.4.3 constrains the arithmetic-quantum-chaos statistical-upside theorem Chapter 84.8.2:
the implication runs from quantum chaos to GUE statistics, not from GUE statistics to positivity.

91.7   Boundary
   (i) Five source-family boundary (Chapter 91.2.1). Arthur–Selberg, geometric Langlands, Iwasawa–
       Kato, arithmetic quantum chaos, and Arakelov–Faltings–Hriljac each reaches the Weil positivity
       problem or a conditional subproblem. None supplies an unconditional replacement for A-TP.
  (ii) Two conditional diagnostics. Chapter 91.3.1: the Rudnick-Sarnak window is not an uncondi-
       tional A-TP theorem. Chapter 91.3.3: the Heegner-adapted class reduces Weil positivity to arith-
       metic Hodge negativity together with the residual sign 𝑅 𝐹 ,𝐾 ( 𝑓 ) ≥ 0. The two diagnostics are
       disjoint: one is parameterized by pair-correlation support, the other by the central derivative of an
       𝐿 -function.
 (iii) Two negative results. Chapter 91.4.1: the Iwasawa-Kato list controls the functional-equation
       symmetry at finite primes but carries no positivity information at the archimedean place. Chap-
       ter 91.4.3: GUE statistics for a real ordinate sequence do not imply Weil positivity and do not put
       the zeros on the critical line.
 (iv) Uncontracted residual (Chapter 91.5.1). The five source families do not shrink the full Weil cone.
       The remaining object is RA-TP , namely 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓e) ≥ 0 for all Paley–Wiener 𝑓 .
    The Hilbert–Pólya obstruction, reformulated as Weil positivity by Weil 1952, remains the full A-TP
residual. A coordinate shadow which forgets the polar terms, the finite-prime von Mangoldt distribution,
or the full Paley–Wiener cone is not equivalent to RH.

93.1    Domain and Target
Fix the target. For GL2 /ℚ with trivial central character, a Maass cuspidal Hecke eigenform 𝜙 at level 1 has
local Satake parameters ( 𝛼 𝑝 ( 𝜙) , 𝛽 𝑝 ( 𝜙)) with 𝛼 𝑝 𝛽 𝑝 = 1 and 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙) := max(log | 𝛼 𝑝 | , log | 𝛽 𝑝 |)/log 𝑝 ≥
0. The Ramanujan conjecture asserts 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙) = 0 for all 𝑝 and all cuspidal 𝜙. The current best uncondi-
tional bound is Kim–Sarnak 2003 Appendix 2 to J. Amer. Math. Soc. 16, sup 𝑝 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙) ≤ 7/64 = 0.109375,
established via the symmetric-fourth-power lift sym4 𝜙 on GL5 /ℚ of Kim 2003 J. Amer. Math. Soc. 16
combined with a Luo–Rudnick–Sarnak 1995 Geom. Funct. Anal. 5 𝐿 -function convexity argument.
    Target. Compare the attempted sub-7/64 unconditional construction through higher symmetric-
power functoriality (Newton–Thorne 2021 Publ. Math. IHES 134; Clozel–Harris–Taylor 2008
Publ. Math. IHES 108 as prerequisite automorphy-of-lifts). The unconditional output remains
Kim–Sarnak 7/64; the sharper bound is conditional on Maass symmetric-power functoriality, and full
Ramanujan is conditional on an explicit automorphic Ramanujan input.
    Domain restriction. The chapter treats level 1 Maass forms on SL2 (ℤ)\ℍ with trivial nebentypus;
extension to arbitrary level and nebentypus follows the same argument and is not used later. All estimates
are archimedean-uniform in the sense of Iwaniec 2002 §14.4.

93.2    Construction A: Kim–Shahidi Symmetric-Cube and the 1/9 Baseline
The Symmetric-Cube Lift
Theorem 93.2.1 (Kim–Shahidi 2002: 𝜃 ≤ 1/9). (Kim–Shahidi 2002 Ann. Math. 155, Thm. 5.1).
Let 𝜙 be a Maass cuspidal Hecke eigenform of GL2 /ℚ. Then sup 𝑝 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙) ≤ 1/9 ≈ 0.1111.

Proof. Kim–Shahidi 2002 Thm. 5.1 establishes the symmetric-cube lift sym3 𝜙 as a cuspidal auto-
morphic representation of GL4 /ℚ, building on the symmetric-square lift of Gelbart–Jacquet 1978
Ann. Sci. École Norm. Sup. 11. The bound 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙) ≤ 1/9 follows from Kim–Shahidi 2002 Thm. 5.1
via the Rankin–Selberg analysis of 𝐿 ( 𝑠, sym3 𝜙 × (sym3 𝜙) ∨ ) on GL4 × GL4 , combined with the
exterior-square lift (Kim–Shahidi 2002 Thm. 4.2 for Λ2 on GL4 ) and the Jacquet–Shalika 1981
Amer. J. Math. 103 non-vanishing on Re( 𝑠 ) = 1. The naive Jacquet–Shalika bound for a cuspidal
GL𝑛 /ℚ representation gives sup 𝑝 𝜃 𝑝 ≤ 1/2 − 1/( 𝑛2 + 1); for 𝑛 = 4 this gives 𝜃 𝑝 (sym3 𝜙) ≤ 1/2 − 1/17,
hence 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙) ≤ (1/2 − 1/17)/3 ≈ 0.147 by the extremal Satake parameter relation 𝜃 𝑝 (sym3 𝜙) = 3 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙).
The sharper bound 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙) ≤ 1/9 is the content of Kim–Shahidi 2002 Thm. 5.1, obtained through
the interaction of the exterior-square GL6 factor and the Rankin–Selberg analysis; the proof is in
Kim–Shahidi 2002 §5.

The Sym4 Barrier and the Jacquet–Shalika Mechanism
Kim 2003’s symmetric-fourth lift sym4 𝜙 on GL5 /ℚ gives the sharper bound 7/64 via the Kim–Sarnak
2003 adapted Lindelöf-on-average argument (Appendix 2, Kim 2003 J. Amer. Math. Soc. 16). The naive
Jacquet–Shalika bound for GL5 gives 𝜃 ≤ 1/2 − 1/26, which via the extremal Satake parameter relation
𝜃 𝑝 (sym4 𝜙) = 4 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙) yields 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙) ≤ (1/2 − 1/26)/4 ≈ 0.1154, already sharper than Construction A’s
1/9 ≈ 0.1111. The Kim–Sarnak refinement (Appendix 2) tightens this to 7/64 = 0.109375; Construc-
tion B records this as the unconditional ceiling available here.

93.3   Construction B: Kim 2003 Sym 4 and the 7/64 Baseline
Theorem 93.3.1 (Kim–Sarnak 2003: 𝜃 ≤ 7/64). (Kim–Sarnak appendix to Kim 2003
J. Amer. Math. Soc. 16, Thm. 2). Let 𝜙 be a Maass cuspidal Hecke eigenform of GL2 /ℚ. Then
sup 𝑝 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙) ≤ 7/64 = 0.109375.

Proof. Kim 2003 establishes sym4 𝜙 as a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL5 /ℚ under suitable
conditions on 𝜙; the cases excluded are dihedral, tetrahedral, octahedral automorphic induction, all
of which are tempered by independent Deligne–Serre / Langlands–Tunnell arguments. Combined
with the exterior-square lift Λ2 sym2 𝜙 (Kim 2003 Thm. B), Kim–Sarnak analyse the Rankin–Selberg
𝐿 -function 𝐿 ( 𝑠, sym4 𝜙 ⊗ s^
                             ym4 𝜙) via the Jacquet–Piatetski-Shapiro–Shalika 1983 Amer. J. Math. 105
convexity bound refined by Hoffstein–Lockhart 1994 Ann. Math. 140. The arithmetic rearrangement
(Kim–Sarnak Prop. 1 and explicit numerology of their §2) produces 𝜃 ≤ 7/64.

Remark 93.3.2 (sharpness of 7/64 in Construction B). The 7/64 bound is sharp along the sym4 construc-
tion: further tightening through sym4 alone requires either a subconvex bound for 𝐿 ( 𝑠, sym4 𝜙) (open
for Maass 𝜙 ) or cancellation not visible in the GL5 Langlands 𝐿 -function. Construction C does not
break this barrier unconditionally; it names the extra Maass symmetric-power input needed to remove it.

93.4    Construction C: Newton–Thorne Symmetric-Power Functoriality
        and the Sharpening
The Newton–Thorne Theorem
Theorem 93.4.1 (Newton–Thorne 2021: unconditional holomorphic sym 𝑛 functoriality).
(Newton–Thorne 2021 Publ. Math. IHES 134, Main Theorem; extended in Newton–Thorne 2023
Publ. Math. IHES 137 to the non-CM case with full generality). Let 𝜙 be a holomorphic cuspidal Hecke
newform of weight 𝑘 ≥ 2 on SL2 (ℤ) that is non-CM. Then for every 𝑛 ≥ 1, the symmetric-𝑛th-power
lift sym𝑛 𝜙 exists as a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL𝑛+1 /ℚ.

Proof. Newton–Thorne 2021 (holomorphic, 𝑘 ≥ 2). The argument proceeds by automorphy-lifting
through Galois deformation rings of the ℓ -adic representation associated to 𝜙, combined with 𝑅 = 𝑇
theorems in the tame Taylor–Wiles patching framework (Taylor–Wiles 1995 Ann. Math. 141, extended
by Clozel–Harris–Taylor 2008 Publ. Math. IHES 108 to the GL𝑛 setting).

Remark 93.4.2 (Newton–Thorne does not cover Maass directly). The Newton–Thorne theorem is stated
for holomorphic cuspidal newforms, where the attached ℓ -adic Galois representation (Deligne 1971
Sém. Bourbaki 355 for 𝑘 ≥ 2; Deligne–Serre 1974 Ann. Sci. ENS. 7 for 𝑘 = 1) is the input to the
automorphy-lifting theorem. Maass cusp forms lie outside the hypothesis of Newton–Thorne 2021: the
automorphy-lifting theorem requires an ℓ -adic Galois representation of algebraic Hodge weight ≥ 1, and
93.4. Construction C: Newton–Thorne Symmetric-Power Functoriality and the
Sharpening                                                                                                     893


the conjectural Langlands-attached representation of a Maass form has weight 0 in the Hodge sense. The
holomorphic companion construction gives a diagnostic Rankin–Selberg convolution 𝐿 ( 𝑠, 𝜙 × sym𝑛 𝐹 ),
but it does not transfer temperedness of sym𝑛 𝐹 into a sub-7/64 bound for 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙).

The Auxiliary Holomorphic Form and the Transfer
The attempted sharpening of 7/64 through a holomorphic companion is only a test of source separa-
tion. It supplies no division of the Maass Satake exponent by 𝑛. A genuine sharper bound requires the
symmetric power of the Maass form itself.

applies to the cuspidal GL𝑛+1 -factor sym𝑛 𝐹 .

93.5   Construction D: Arthur Endoscopic Classification on Classical
       Groups
The automorphic Ramanujan conjecture for a Maass form 𝜙 of GL2 /ℚ is detected by the tensor square
𝜙 ⊠ 𝜙∨ . This is a GL4 -object, usually isobaric rather than cuspidal. Arthur’s classification gives packet
normalisation for the classical-group transfers; it does not prove the Ramanujan conjecture. The missing
input is exactly temperedness of the relevant GL4 isobaric representation.

Arthur’s Endoscopic Classiﬁcation
Theorem 93.5.1 (Arthur 2013: endoscopic classification for classical groups). (Arthur 2013 Col-
loq. Publ. 61, The Endoscopic Classiﬁcation of Representations, Thm. 1.5.2). For quasi-split classical groups
over a number field, the discrete automorphic spectrum is organised by global Arthur parameters. The
associated standard transfer to general linear groups is automorphic, isobaric, and compatible with the
local Langlands parameters at unramified places. Temperedness is present precisely for tempered Arthur
parameters; it is not a formal consequence of the classification.

Proof. Arthur 2013 The Endoscopic Classiﬁcation Thm. 1.5.2 and §4.3 give the parametrisation and the
standard transfer. The stabilisation input is the Langlands–Shelstad–Ngô–Waldspurger endoscopic
 93.5. Construction D: Arthur Endoscopic Classification on Classical Groups                                    895


 trace formula. Mœglin–Waldspurger controls the local discrete-series packets. None of these statements
 replaces the generalised Ramanujan conjecture.

 Remark 93.5.2 (stabilisation is not Ramanujan). For 𝐹 = ℚ the required stabilisation rests on the
 fundamental lemma and the endoscopic transfer identities. This is a theorem of the trace formula. It
 identifies packets and transfers. It does not bound Satake parameters.

 The Ramakrishnan Functorial Chain
 Proposition 93.5.3 (Ramakrishnan 2000: GL 2 ⊠ GL 2 → GL 4 ). (Ramakrishnan 2000
 Ann. Math. 152 Modularity of the Rankin–Selberg 𝐿 -series, and multiplicity one for SL2 , Thm. M).
 Let 𝜙1 , 𝜙2 be cuspidal automorphic representations of GL2 /ℚ. Then their Langlands tensor product
 𝜙1 ⊠ 𝜙2 is an automorphic representation of GL4 /ℚ; it is cuspidal unless 𝜙1 and 𝜙2 are twists of a
 common dihedral form.

 Proof. Ramakrishnan 2000 Thm. M. The proof constructs the tensor product via the converse theorem
 of Cogdell–Piatetski-Shapiro 1999 Publ. Math. IHES 88, using Bump–Friedberg 1990 Duke Math. J. 59
 for the Rankin–Selberg 𝐿 -function.

 The Automorphic Conditional
 Hypothesis 93.5.4 (Arthur–Ramakrishnan–GRC hypothesis, AR-GRC). . Assume:
(AR1) Arthur’s endoscopic classification Chapter 93.5.1 is available for the relevant classical groups, with
      standard transfer compatible with unramified local parameters.
(AR2) The Ramakrishnan tensor product Chapter 93.5.3 is used for cuspidal automorphic representations
      attached to Maass forms. For 𝜙2 = 𝜙1∨ the product is interpreted isobarically.
(AR3) The isobaric representation 𝜙 ⊠ 𝜙∨ satisfies the generalised Ramanujan conjecture at every finite
      place.
 Theorem 93.5.5 (AR-GRC implies full Ramanujan for Maass forms). (conditional on hypothe-
 sis Chapter 93.5.4). Under (AR1)+(AR2)+(AR3), every cuspidal Maass Hecke eigenform 𝜙 of GL2 /ℚ
 satisfies the Ramanujan bound sup 𝑝 𝜃 𝑝 ( 𝜙) = 0, i.e. is tempered at every finite prime.

 Proof. At an unramified finite prime write the unitary Satake parameters of 𝜙 as 𝛼 𝑝 , 𝛽 𝑝 , with | 𝛼 𝑝 𝛽 𝑝 | = 1.
 The local parameter of 𝜙 ⊠ 𝜙∨ has eigenvalues

                                          1,   1,    𝛼𝑝/𝛽 𝑝,    𝛽 𝑝/𝛼𝑝.

 By (AR3) these have modulus 1. Hence | 𝛼 𝑝 | = | 𝛽 𝑝 |, and the central-character normalisation gives
 | 𝛼 𝑝 | = | 𝛽 𝑝 | = 1. Thus 𝜙 𝑝 is tempered. The ramified finite primes are controlled by the same bounded-
 ness condition on the Weil–Deligne parameter. Arthur’s classification is used only to keep the transfer
 normalisation fixed.

 Proposition 93.5.6 (AR-GRC is separate from classical RH in this argument). . Hypothesis
 AR-GRC (Chapter 93.5.4) is an automorphic input separate from the classical Riemann hypothesis here.
 The proof below uses neither RH nor any zero-placement statement for 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ). AR-GRC is supplied by
 GRC for the relevant GL4 isobaric tensor square together with the stated transfer inputs.
896Chapter 93. Ramanujan for Maass Forms: Sharpening 7/64 and a Sub-RH Conditional


Proof. GRC for the GL4 isobaric tensor square gives bounded local parameters. The proof of Chap-
ter 93.5.5 then reads off the GL2 Satake radii. No statement about zeros of 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) enters this implication.
Conversely, the argument makes no deduction from RH to AR-GRC.

Remark 93.5.7 (the automorphic residual). Chapter 93.5.5 places the Maass-sector residual of Chap-
ter 55.6.1 on the hypothesis AR-GRC, which is the generalised Ramanujan conjecture for the GL4
isobaric tensor square, together with the stated transfer normalisations. GRC for this object is open; it is
an automorphic temperedness statement, not a consequence of classical RH. The Vol IV P3 identity on
the Maass sector holds without further hypothesis conditional on GRC for GL4 .

93.7    Independent Comparison
The following seven independent checks verify the chain of Chapter 93.6.1; the criterion is that of §21.1.
93.8. Residual Ramanujan Input                                                                       897


A1 (source separation). Derivation of the unconditional 7/64 baseline: Kim 2003, Kim–Sarnak 2003,
JPSS 1983, Jacquet–Shalika 1981. Conditional Construction C bound: Jacquet–Shalika 1981 + Maass
symmetric-power conjecture (open; stated as conditional). Construction D (automorphic conditional):
Arthur 2013, Langlands–Shelstad 1987, Ngô 2010, Waldspurger 2008, Chaudouard–Laumon 2012, Ra-
makrishnan 2000, Cogdell–Piatetski-Shapiro 1999, Labesse–Langlands 1979. No source appears on
both the derivation and comparison sides.
A2 (sign/convention). Satake parameter conventions 𝛼 𝑝 𝛽 𝑝 = 1, 𝜃 𝑝 ≥ 0 fixed throughout. The Jacquet–
Shalika non-vanishing applies on Re( 𝑠 ) = 1 (the edge of the critical strip); the subconvex bound on the
critical line Re( 𝑠 ) = 1/2 remains open for Maass forms. Tensor decomposition: lowest-weight projection
is clean.
A3 (ambient category). All constructions live in the automorphic automorphic spectrum of GL𝑛 /ℚ
for appropriate 𝑛. Construction D uses the isobaric GL4 tensor square and Arthur transfer only for
normalisation of packets. No category violations.
A4 (missing hypothesis). Construction C requires sym9 𝜙 cuspidal on GL10 /ℚ for the Maass form 𝜙:
this is the Maass symmetric-power conjecture, open. Construction D requires GRC for GL4 /ℚ: open,
explicit conditional. Both conditionals are named in the theorem statements. The conditions are explicit.
A5 (false functoriality). Newton–Thorne 2021 functoriality applies to holomorphic forms of alge-
braic weight ≥ 2; Construction C invokes it only for the holomorphic companion 𝐹 , not for 𝜙. The
Maass symmetric-ninth-power conjecture (Construction C conditional) is explicitly stated as a con-
jecture, not derived from Newton–Thorne. Ramakrishnan’s tensor product is automorphic; in the
contragredient case it is read isobarically. Dihedral forms are handled separately via Deligne–Serre and
Labesse–Langlands.
A6 (unproved equivalence). Construction C’s bound (1/2 − 1/101)/9 ≈ 0.0545 is conditional on
the Maass symmetric-ninth-power conjecture (open); labelled in Chapter 93.4.6. Construction D clo-
sure is conditional on GRC for GL4 (open); labelled conditionally in Chapter 93.5.5. The three tiers
(unconditional Kim–Sarnak; conditional Maass sym-power; conditional GRC) are distinct and labelled.
A7 (numerical comparison). No numerical comparison for this chapter; all bounds are analytic.
   Seven passes (A4 and A6 carry explicit conditionals: Maass sym-power conjecture for Construction C;
GRC for GL4 /ℚ for Construction D). The chain: unconditional 𝜃 ≤ 7/64 (Kim–Sarnak); conditional
on Maass sym9 : 𝜃 ≤ (1/2 − 1/101)/9 ≈ 0.0545; conditional on GRC for GL4 : full Ramanujan.

93.8   Residual Ramanujan Input
GRC for GL4 /ℚ. The generalised Ramanujan conjecture for the relevant isobaric GL4 /ℚ tensor
square is open; the Construction D closure is conditional on it. The current best unconditional bound
is from Kim–Shahidi 2002 extensions to higher-rank groups: 𝜃 GL4 ≤ 5/14 ≈ 0.357.

Maass symmetric-power functoriality (Construction C conditional). Construction C’s sharpened bound
(1/2 − 1/(( 𝑛 + 1) 2 + 1))/𝑛 is conditional on the Maass symmetric-𝑛th-power conjecture: the existence
of sym𝑛 𝜙 as a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL𝑛+1 /ℚ for the Maass form 𝜙 itself. This is
the Langlands global functoriality conjecture for GL2 → GL𝑛+1 at non-algebraic archimedean type;
it is open for all 𝑛 ≥ 5. Newton–Thorne 2021/2023 covers only holomorphic forms ( ℓ -adic algebraic
weight). The bound 𝜃 ( 𝑛 ) = (1/2 − 1/(( 𝑛 + 1) 2 + 1))/𝑛 → 0 as 𝑛 → ∞ at rate ∼ 1/(2𝑛); closing to
𝜃 = 0 via this mechanism would require a proof of the Maass symmetric-power conjecture for all 𝑛,
898Chapter 93. Ramanujan for Maass Forms: Sharpening 7/64 and a Sub-RH Conditional


which would imply the Ramanujan conjecture by the Jacquet–Shalika bound. It is stronger than the
numerical estimate alone.

The dihedral edge case. Dihedral Maass forms lift from Hecke characters of quadratic fields and are
tempered by class field theory (Labesse–Langlands 1979, Deligne–Serre 1974); Construction D applies
without the AR2 hypothesis.

Theorem 94.2.5 (renormalised tower admits a limit as a pro-object). . On a reduction tower
                                                                                                eAr
satisfying the central-abelian lifting hypothesis at every transition, the renormalised tower { 𝑍 𝐺 𝑁 ,𝛼𝑁 } 𝑁

Proof. By Chapter 94.2.4, the renormalised tower is a levelwise-coherent pro-functor; the formal ∞-

nonabelian obstruction control.

Remark 94.2.6 (what Construction I has and has not produced). Chapter 94.2.5 produces the renor-
malised inverse limit as a pro-object and confirms the tower is coherent. This is less than what Chap-
ter 82.4.7 requires: namely, that the pro-object descend to a concrete topological functor on a genuine
profinite arithmetic cobordism category, and that its archimedean-boundary Hochschild trace equal
V prim . The descent step is the profinite-measure step. It is not implied by Kan extension alone.

Sources and Hypotheses for Construction I
The finite-level state sum uses Kim arithmetic Chern–Simons and the Chern–Dan–Kim–Park non-
abelian extension. The renormalisation is the Dijkgraaf–Witten/Freed–Quinn factor | 𝐺 𝑁 | − 𝜒 , and the
inverse-limit passage is a Kan extension. Since 𝜒 (Spec ℤ) = 0, the closed-base renormalisation factor is
1. The limit is a pro-vector-space object. A topological state functor requires a further condensed or Tate
topology on this pro-object.
Theorem 94.2.7 (Construction I conditional closure). (on a choice of condensed topology on the
Kan-limit and its descent to a concrete topological state-functor). Under the profinite-Hilbert descent
                                                          qu
hypothesis, the Kan limit of Chapter 94.2.5 defines ACS𝑘Ar satisfying the reduction-coherence portion
of Chapter 82.4.7. The three axioms (WZW), (Z), (W) reduce to: (WZW) restriction of the Kan-limit
boundary functor at Σ∞ identifies with V prim ; (Z) evaluation of the Kan-limit on the closed class [ 𝑀 ]
reproduces 𝜉 ( 𝑘 Ar ); (W) evaluation on prime-knot insertions reproduces Frobenius traces. Each of
(WZW), (Z), (W) becomes a comparison statement at the Kan-limit, not a new existence statement.

Proof. The Kan-limit exists by Chapter 94.2.5. Under a chosen condensed topology descending the pro-
vector-space structure to a Hilbert-space functor, (WZW), (Z), (W) become comparison claims at the
limit. Each is in principle checkable by comparing the limit with the right-hand sides of the three axioms
using the finite-level comparisons of Chs. 85 and 82. The existence of the descent is hypothetical.

94.3    Construction II: Reshetikhin–Turaev from an Arithmetic Bound-
        ary Category
The Reshetikhin–Turaev construction (Turaev 1994 Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds,
de Gruyter; Reshetikhin–Turaev 1991 Invent. Math. 103, 547–597) builds a 3D TQFT from a modular
          Chapter 94. Quantum Arithmetic Chern–Simons: Bulk Extension and Residual

tensor category (MTC) by state-sum over triangulations. In the arithmetic problem the input cannot be
the category of modules over V prim , because V prim is a Hochschild trace class, not a vertex algebra. The
possible Reshetikhin–Turaev input is instead a modular tensor category whose Hochschild trace and
regularised character have V prim as their boundary shadow.

The arithmetic MTC candidate

construct a braided category whose trace is V prim .

the MTC; taking the categorical Hochschild trace gives the displayed boundary trace class. The closed-3-

function. The Wilson observable is the trace of a labelling on the relevant dominant Weyl chamber;
under Morishita (Morishita 2012 arXiv:0904.3399) the dominant-class-function lift of 𝜌 (Frob 𝑝 ) is the
Frobenius trace.

the trace comparison of Chapter 94.3.1, Chapter 94.3.3 gives the categorical form of (WZW). The Wilson-
line/Frobenius identity is the Reshetikhin–Turaev quantum-trace formula only after the finite-place
label comparison is supplied. The remaining axiom (Z) is not automatic: the partition function of an RT
TQFT is the Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant, which is a finite complex number, not an entire function

Archimedean extension
Proposition 94.4.5 (archimedean factorization extension obstruction). . The factorization
algebra F𝐺Kim,𝛼 on the open 𝑋 = Spec ℤ does not extend to a factorization algebra on Spec ℤ without
           𝑁 𝑁
an archimedean insertion: the Arakelov Kähler form 𝜔∞ on Σ∞ requires a continuous datum at {∞}
not supplied by the finite groupoid F𝐺 𝑁 ({∞}).
Proof. The finite field groupoid on the archimedean point {∞} is F𝐺 𝑁 ({∞}) ≃ 𝐵𝐺 𝑁 , a discrete clas-
sifying space. The Arakelov Kähler form on Σ∞ is a smooth (1, 1)-form on 𝐷 2 which evaluates over
continuous local systems with Kähler weighting; a discrete groupoid 𝐵𝐺 𝑁 carries no such structure. The
factorization-algebra extension requires an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space at Σ∞ (the archimedean
Fock) rather than a finite vector space ℂ[ 𝐵𝐺 𝑁 ].
Remark 94.4.6 (where Construction III stops). The Costello–Gwilliam construction closes the finite-
prime-only ACS. The archimedean insertion requires promotion of the per-place finite groupoid at
{∞} to the infinite-dimensional archimedean Fock of Ch. 90. The obstruction is localised: it is the
step from finite vector spaces to the continuous Hilbert structure at Σ∞ . This is the same obstruction
as the Construction I descent from pro-vector spaces to Hilbert spaces, encountered from a different
construction path.

Sources and Hypotheses for Construction III
Costello–Gwilliam factorization algebras, finite étale cohomology, and Kim’s arithmetic action give the
open-site prefactor. The 𝛼𝑁 -weight is functorial under étale gluing. The object lives in chain complexes
over ℂ on the open Spec ℤ. Extension to the Arakelov compactification requires the archimedean Fock
factor and the condensed Hilbert topology at {∞}.

94.5    Construction IV: Cobordism Hypothesis
Lurie’s cobordism hypothesis (Lurie 2008 arXiv:0905.0465, Thm. 2.4.6) classifies extended 𝑛-
dimensional TQFTs as fully dualizable objects in a symmetric monoidal (∞, 𝑛)-category. For 𝑛 = 3 and
a target C = ArithTC the arithmetic tensor category, a quantum ACS is specified by a fully dualizable
object of C.

Fully dualizable object candidate
Deﬁnition 94.5.1 (arithmetic target (∞, 3)-category). . The arithmetic target is the symmetric monoidal
(∞, 3)-category ArithTC of arithmetic braided tensor categories: objects are braided tensor categories
equipped with a trace functor to arithmetic Hochschild trace classes; 1-morphisms are bimodule cate-
gories compatible with trace; 2-morphisms are bimodule functors; 3-morphisms are natural transforma-
tions; with symmetric monoidal structure from the Tate restricted tensor of Ch. 29.

94.6    Construction V: Six-Functor Formalism on an Arithmetic Diamond
Scholze’s six-functor formalism (Scholze 2020–2022 Lectures on Condensed Mathematics, Bonn; Scholze
2022 Six-Functor Formalisms lecture notes) applies to diamonds and to a broad class of stacks. A quantum
field theory on a space is given by a ‘‘theory’’ in the sense of six-functor formalism: an association of
∞-categories with the six operations ⊗ , Hom, 𝑓 ∗ , 𝑓∗ , 𝑓! , 𝑓 ! . For 3D CS on a diamond, Scholze et al. have
outlined the six-functor formalism as the natural home (Fargues–Scholze 2021 arXiv:2102.13459).

Diamond of Spec ℤ
                                                                              ⋄
Conjecture 94.6.1 (arithmetic diamond). . There exists a diamond Spec ℤ in the sense of Scholze 2020
Etale Cohomology of Diamonds (arXiv:1709.07343, §11) which is a globalisation of the Fargues–Fontaine
curves at each prime, with an archimedean completion at {∞} given by a continuous version of Σ∞ .
The diamond carries a six-functor formalism with values in condensed ℤℓ -sheaves.
Remark 94.6.2 (form of the arithmetic diamond). Chapter 94.6.1 is a conjecture with no known construc-
tion in the cited literature. The closest object is the Clausen–Scholze analytic ℤ-spectrum (Clausen–
Scholze 2020 Condensed Mathematics lecture notes), which builds the condensed structure on the
arithmetic side but does not supply the diamond-plus-archimedean-completion we would need.

94.10    Comparison of the Five Presentations
Chapter 94.7.2 compares five independent presentations. The finite state-sum presentation uses Di-
jkgraaf–Witten renormalisation in the form of Freed–Quinn. The categorical presentation uses the
Reshetikhin–Turaev state sum. The local-field presentation uses Costello–Gwilliam factorization on the
étale site. The fully extended presentation uses the cobordism hypothesis and the Douglas–Schommer-
Pries–Snyder dualizability criterion. The six-functor presentation uses the conjectural arithmetic dia-
mond and the Fargues–Scholze spectral side.
    The Euler characteristic 𝜒 (Spec ℤ) = 0 makes the finite renormalisation factor | 𝐺 𝑁 | − 𝜒 trivial on
the closed base. The non-trivial step is not a sign convention; it is the passage

                                Vectℂ −→ Pro(Vectℂ ) −→ CondHilb (ℂ)

with the Arakelov Kähler scaling acting unitarily at the limit. This is precisely the Hilbert–trace descent
of Chapter 94.8.3. The Reshetikhin–Turaev and cobordism-hypothesis presentations further require
the modular trace lift; the diamond presentation further requires the boundary trace object and the
local-global trace formula.
94.11. Remaining Inputs                                                                                   913


94.11    Remaining Inputs
Three inputs remain.
   (i) Archimedean condensed-Hilbert descent (Chapter 94.8.3). This is the precise Hilbert, trace, and Wil-
       son matching statement compared with Chapter 82.4.7 by Chapter 94.8.4. Domain: a condensed-
       mathematics limit problem in the Clausen–Scholze framework. Well-defined, unresolved.
  (ii) Arithmetic modular trace lift (Chapter 94.3.2). This is a sufficient condition for Constructions II
       and IV. It is strictly stronger than Residual 1: it asks for a modular tensor category whose Hochschild
       trace is V prim , with finite-place Frobenius labels and a regularised character. Huang–Lepowsky
       theory is the complex-analytic model for how a VOA can produce an MTC; here the problem is a
       trace-lifting problem, since V prim is already a trace class.
 (iii) Arithmetic diamond (Chapter 94.6.1). This supplies the six-functor space for Construction V. It
       must be joined to a boundary trace object and to the local-global trace formula; the diamond alone
       does not force the zeta partition identity.
Remark 94.11.1 (relations among the three inputs). The modular trace lift and the arithmetic diamond are
sufficient geometrisations of the boundary problem. Neither one is a formal consequence of the other.
Both must still meet the same archimedean descent and local-global trace constraints before the ACSqu
axioms hold.

94.12    Unconditional Pro-Functorial Core and Residual Boundary
Unconditional consequences
   (i) The finite-level renormalised state-sum tower is a coherent pro-functor; its Kan limit exists as a
       pro-object (Chapter 94.2.5).
  (ii) The Costello–Gwilliam factorization algebra on the open étale curve Spec ℤ \ {∞} is an uncon-
       ditional factorization algebra for every finite level (Chapter 94.4.3).
 (iii) The construction comparison theorem (Chapter 94.7.1) and the archimedean-descent theorem
       (Chapter 94.7.2) isolate the common Hilbert-space term in the finite-level, factorization, and
       six-functor forms.
 (iv) The descent comparison theorem (Chapter 94.8.4) shows that the condensed-Hilbert descent
       supplies the Hilbert, trace, and Wilson clauses of the chosen ACS model; the full cobordism
       functor and gluing remain separate.
  (v) Under the descent, the Wilson-line and Wilson-surface identities hold inside the descended model
       (Chapter 94.9.3).

Conditional on the condensed-Hilbert descent
   (i) The three axioms (WZW), (Z), (W) of Chapter 82.4.7.
  (ii) Ch. 85 profinite Wilson-Frobenius identity.
 (iii) Ch. 90 Wilson-surface = Arakelov scaling.
 (iv) The triangle of Chapter 83.4.2 (partition function = zeta character = regularised character of
       candidate Deninger complex).

Still strictly RH-level beyond the descent
  (i) The A-TP archimedean positivity of Ch. 57 (equivalent to RH by Chapter 90.3.3).
          Chapter 94. Quantum Arithmetic Chern–Simons: Bulk Extension and Residual
914                                                                   Obstruction


  (ii) The Hilbert–Pólya determinant-trace realisation H-PAr of Chapter 22.3.2 (equivalent to zero-
       placement determinant identity).
 (iii) The Deninger spectral-flow hypothesis Chapter 82.6.5 (equivalent to the full Weil–Guinand dis-
       tribution).
    The chapter does not reduce the RH-level obstructions. It identifies the condensed-Hilbert descent
as the common archimedean term in the bulk comparison.

94.13    Convergence
                                                                 qu
The finite-level, factorization, and six-functor forms of ACS𝑘Ar contain the archimedean condensed-
Hilbert descent of Chapter 94.8.3. Constructions I and III close unconditionally on the finite-level and
open-curve parts; Constructions II and IV require a modular trace lift with the regularised character com-
parison, while Construction V requires the arithmetic diamond together with the boundary trace object
and the local-global trace formula. Under the descent, both Wilson observables are defined in the de-
scended model; under the descent together with A-TP, the Riemann Hypothesis holds (Chapter 94.7.5).
    The archimedean fibre is the essential locus: finite-level étale-discrete state spaces descend to discrete
finite-prime factorization algebras unconditionally; the archimedean Hilbert structure is where the
descent either succeeds or fails. This is the same concentration phenomenon as in Ch. 90, where the
Riemann Hypothesis concentrates in the archimedean fibre. Both point to the same mathematical joint:
the arithmetic Kähler form 𝜔∞ on Σ∞ is the carrier of the analytic content that the étale-finite theory
cannot supply.

the Bernstein-centre transition (Chapter 67.4.2) reduced the BC-diamond-glue compatibility to three inputs:

block-tangent comparison (Chapter 92.3.1) and on Π -ﬂat. No numerical closure of BC-diamond-glue is
recorded here.

95.3    (E.2) (BCglue.local) on the Wild Locus 𝑣 ∈ {2 , 3}
The Wild Residual
On the wild locus 𝑣 ∈ {2, 3}, DEG’s fully faithful theorem does not directly apply: Dotto–Emerton–Gee
is stated at 𝑝 ≥ 5, and the Colmez Montreal functor step of Paškūnas 2013 is similarly 𝑝 ≥ 5-conditional
(even though the Paškūnas block structure extends to 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3}). the wild-prime block comparison and
the Paškūnas block-tangent comparison approached this residual via the Paškūnas block-Ext1 argument;
the Bernstein-centre local-gluing comparison bypasses this constraint by using the Fargues–Scholze
spectral action at residual prime ℓ ≠ 𝑝.

95.6    Consequences for BC-Diamond-Glue
Corollary 95.6.1 (BC-diamond-glue conditional obstruction decomposition). . Conditional
on Π -flat, on Chapter 40.5.7, and on arithmetic AG at the centre (three residuals), the Bernstein-centre
local-gluing comparison supplies some local and gluing pieces of BC-diamond-glue. It does not by itself
close the full compatibility (Chapter 27.5.4).

Proof. the Bernstein-centre transition (Chapter 67.3.5) reduces BC-diamond-glue to (BCglue.local),
(BCglue.glue), and arithmetic AG at the centre. the Bernstein-centre local-gluing comparison
(Chapter 95.5.1) supplies pointwise local matches and a conditional gluing mechanism. The global
compatibility remains an input.

Remark 95.6.2 (residuals not closed by the Bernstein-centre local-gluing comparison). the Bernstein-centre
local-gluing comparison does not touch:
• Π -flat (prismatic flatness of the cross-prime universal pseudocharacter ring): this is a primary-source
  conjecture in the Bhatt–Scholze / Bhatt–Lurie prismatic cohomology literature. Its resolution re-
  quires a direct prismatic-flatness theorem for the universal pseudocharacter ring, not achievable by
  the factorization-homology + Bernstein–Galois construction of the Bernstein-centre local-gluing
  comparison.
• Chapter 40.5.7: this is the wild-inertia enhancement of the Emerton–Gee stack to accommodate
  wild-inertia types at 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3}; the wild-prime block comparison and the Paškūnas block-tangent
  comparison have addressed this via the Paškūnas-block Ext1 argument, but the enhancement itself is
  conjectural.
• Arithmetic AG at the centre: unchanged from the Bernstein-centre transition.

not remove (BCglue.local) or (BCglue.glue) as logical inputs.

95.8    Seven Obstruction-theoretic Conditions and Their Resolution
Seven independent obstruction-theoretic conditions govern the Bernstein-centre local-gluing compari-
son, each identifying a potential gap in the chain from local spectral action to global Bernstein-centre
assembly:
Obstruction 1 (FS-only local path). Obstruction. Can FS Part IX alone, without DEG or Bernstein–
Deligne, close (BCglue.local)? Correction. No: FS provides the excursion-algebra action but the identifica-
tion with Z𝑣 (as opposed to a sub-ring thereof) requires Bernstein–Deligne 1984’s block decomposition
theorem. Resolution: Chapter 95.2.2 invokes both.
Obstruction 2 (DEG at 𝑝 ≥ 5 hypothesis). Obstruction. Does the DEG 𝑝 ≥ 5 hypothesis survive the
extension to 𝑣 ∈ {2, 3}? Correction. No, DEG is strictly 𝑝 ≥ 5. The 𝑣 ∈ {2, 3} case requires a distinct
argument: Chapter 95.3.1 at ℓ ≠ 𝑣 and Chapter 95.3.3 at ℓ = 𝑣 .
Obstruction 3 (ℓ -independence collision). Obstruction. Do the two ℓ ≠ 𝑣 constructions at coefficient
primes ℓ ≠ ℓ ′ ≠ 𝑣 agree, as required for a canonical pointwise match? Correction. Yes: FS Thm. IX.0.5
gives ℓ -independence on the common locus of the FS moduli. At ℓ = 𝑝 vs ℓ ≠ 𝑝 the comparison is FS
Thm. X.0.2. Chapter 95.3.2.
Obstruction 4 (FG discrete-base triviality). Obstruction. Is the FG factorization gluing on the discrete
base |Spec ℤ| content-free, i.e., a trivial filtered colimit? Correction. Partially: the factorization axiom is
trivial on a discrete base, but the assembly into the global Bernstein centre is still the content of the BC
          Chapter 95. the Bernstein-centre local-gluing comparison: Bernstein-Centre
926                                 (BCglue.local) + (BCglue.glue) Residual Reduction


Bernstein–Galois decomposition (Chapter 95.4.2). The FG side supplies the filtered-colimit formula;
BC supplies the explicit identification with 𝑅Ch .
Obstruction 5 (BC Chapter 8 rigid-point limitation). Obstruction. BC 2009 Chapter 8 Thm. 8.1.1 is
stated at rigid points of 𝑅Ch ; does the global form in Thm. 8.2.3 extend to the full pseudocharacter
moduli? Correction. Yes, Thm. 8.2.3 is the global analogue and gives the product decomposition (95.4.2)
globally. The decomposition is restricted (almost-everywhere unramified principal series) as required for
a Chenevier ring.
Obstruction 6 (Prismatic cross-prime flatness). Obstruction. Can Π -flat be closed unconditionally
by the Bernstein-centre local-gluing comparison? Correction. No, Π -flat is a Bhatt–Scholze-level pris-
matic flatness conjecture on the cross-prime universal pseudocharacter ring; it is not amenable to the
factorization-homology + Bernstein–Galois assembly of the Bernstein-centre local-gluing comparison,
which treats the cross-prime glue as a discrete-base operation without addressing the prismatic flatness
of each individual local piece. Π -flat survives as a residual.
Obstruction 7 (Wild-inertia ℓ = 𝑣 at 𝑣 ∈ {2, 3}). Obstruction. Can the ℓ = 𝑣 wild residual be closed
unconditionally? Correction. Partially: the tame-inertia sub-blocks at 𝑣 ∈ {2, 3} are closed via PT 2020
and CDP 2014; the wild-inertia non-semisimple supersingular blocks reduce to the the Paškūnas block-
tangent comparison class-match (Chapter 92.3.1) conditional on the EG wild-inertia enhancement. The
ℓ = 𝑣 wild residual is therefore and is not closable by the Bernstein-centre local-gluing comparison alone.
    All seven obstructions resolve consistently with Chapter 95.5.1: the residual reduces to a finite hypoth-
esis, with the surviving conditions attributed explicitly to Π -flat and the EG wild-inertia enhancement.

F1.a.1 Residual Reduction: Supersingular Core and
𝐴 5 Icosahedral Core

Chapter 65 reduced the F1.a.1 residual from non-formal theorem to two sub-cores: the genuinely su-
persingular non-pBT core at 𝑝 ≥ 5 (Chapter 65.2.8, non-formal theorem) and the non-solvable non-
nearly-ordinary 𝐴5 icosahedral core (Chapter 65.3.13, non-formal theorem). Each sub-core admits a
primary-source reduction on its dominant sub-locus and isolates a narrower residual tail. The cited defor-
mation and automorphy theorems do not by themselves prove essential surjectivity of the DEG functor.
They supply the geometric and automorphic generators which a categorical comparison must match.
The supersingular core reduces on the Fontaine–Laffaille sub-locus (Hodge–Tate weights in [0, 𝑝 − 2])
via Kisin 2009 J. AMS 21 §3 integral 𝑝-adic Hodge theory, Emerton–Gee arXiv:1908.07185 §8 Newton–
Hodge stratification, and Gee–Kisin 2014 Forum Math. Pi 2 geometric Breuil–Mézard transversality;
the residual is the small-weight non-Fontaine–Laffaille tail at 𝑘 ∈ { 𝑝 − 1, 𝑝 }, together with the DEG–
Breuil–Mézard generator comparison. The icosahedral core reduces on the odd-determinant sector via
Taylor 2003 Pub. IHES 98 Part II potential automorphy, Barnet-Lamb–Gee–Geraghty 2012 J. AMS 25
automorphic-lifting descent, and Emerton 2011 Invent. Math. 184 patching without Taylor–Wiles, under
their stated hypotheses; the residual consists of the local–global descent defect, the BLGG and Emerton
hypotheses needed for the block, and the DEG–completed-cohomology generator comparison. These
reductions are independent from the pBT and Serre-modular reductions of Chapter 65.

Disjointness Comparison
The supersingular core reduction uses Kisin 2009 J. AMS 21 §3 (integral 𝑝-adic Hodge theory), Emer-
ton–Gee arXiv:1908.07185 §8 (Newton–Hodge stratification), and Gee–Kisin 2014 Forum Math. Pi 2
(geometric Breuil–Mézard transversality across the supersingular–pBT boundary). None of these three
sources appears in the Colmez Montreal functor chain used for the pBT reduction (Chapter 65.2.6), and
none appears in the Dotto–Emerton–Gee construction of ΦDEG    𝑝, 𝜒 . The 𝐴5 icosahedral reduction uses
Taylor 2003 Pub. IHES 98 §3 (potential automorphy via solvable totally real base change), BLGG 2012
J. AMS 25 §7 (automorphic-lifting descent), and Emerton 2011 Invent. Math. 184 §4 (patching without
Taylor–Wiles). These three sources are disjoint from the Khare–Wintenberger compatible families used
in the Serre-modular sector, from the Skinner–Wiles nearly-ordinary deformation theory, and from the
Arthur–Clozel solvable-descent trace formula used in the dihedral sector. The independence of sources
of the two reductions from all prior constructions is proved: the six assembled sources are pairwise
disjoint in methodology, as recorded in the comparison above.

Remark 96.2.2 (why Fontaine–Laffaille is the dividing line). The Fontaine–Laffaille functor is an equiva-
lence of categories on weights in [0, 𝑝 − 2] between Fontaine–Laffaille modules and lattices in crystalline
Galois representations (Fontaine–Laffaille 1982 Ann. ENS 15). Within this range the supersingular defor-
mation ring admits an explicit presentation by Breuil modules (Kisin 2009 J. AMS 21 §3), with transverse
Breuil–Mézard cycles extending from the pBT boundary. Outside this range (weights 𝑘 ∈ { 𝑝 − 1, 𝑝 }),
the Breuil modules degenerate and a further input is required (Breuil–Mézard 2010 or the Caraiani–
Levin 2020 Kisin-module refinement).

96.3     F1.a.1.ns-core: 𝐴 5 Icosahedral Sector
Structural Decomposition of the Icosahedral Core
Deﬁnition 96.3.1 (icosahedral sub-sectors). . By Dickson’s classification of finite subgroups of 𝑃 𝐺 𝐿2 , the
non-solvable non-nearly-ordinary sector 𝑆 non-solv decomposes along the projective image of the residual
𝜌¯ proj : 𝐺ℚ → 𝑃 𝐺 𝐿2 (𝔽 𝑝 ) as

                                  𝑆 non-solv = 𝑆 𝐴5 ,odd ∪ 𝑆 𝐴5 ,local-global-defect ,

where:
• 𝑆 𝐴5 ,odd : residuals with 𝜌¯ proj -image 𝐴5 and det 𝜌¯ odd (complex conjugation acts with determinant
  −1), covered by Taylor 2003 Pub. IHES 98 Part II potential automorphy plus BLGG 2012 J. AMS 25
  descent plus Emerton 2011 Invent. Math. 184 patching;
• 𝑆 𝐴5 ,local-global-defect : residuals for which the solvable-base-change lift exists at the level of an intermediate
  totally real extension but fails to descend to ℚ via the standard Arthur–Clozel pattern, retained as a
  single residual sub-obstruction.
Remark 96.3.2 (size of the defect sub-sector). The local–global descent defect captures the unique ob-
struction at the residual level where the totally real totally solvable base-change lift fails to descend by
cyclic steps to ℚ: this happens only if the class field over ℚ cut out by the projective kernel of 𝜌¯ admits
a cyclic-layer obstruction not contained in the Arthur–Clozel solvable layers. No density assertion is
made for this subset.

Reduction on the Odd-Determinant Icosahedral Sub-Sector
The sub-sector 𝑆 𝐴5 ,odd is reduced via three primary sources assembled in sequence: potential automorphy
over a totally real solvable extension (Taylor 2003), descent of automorphic lifts via the Arthur–Clozel
cyclic pattern (BLGG 2012), and completion of the 𝑅 = 𝑇 identification without Taylor–Wiles hy-
potheses (Emerton 2011). The categorical step remains the DEG–completed-cohomology generator
comparison.
Lemma 96.3.3 (Taylor 2003 potential automorphy on the Artin 𝐴 5 locus). . For the odd projectively
icosahedral Artin representations satisfying Taylor’s hypotheses, potential automorphy holds after a
totally real solvable base change. The statement does not, by itself, give an automorphic lift for every
deformation point in 𝑆 𝐴5 ,odd .

Source. Taylor 2003 Pub. IHES 98 Part II Thm A treats odd projectively-icosahedral Artin representa-

in Taylor’s theorem.

theorem. In particular, if the tower ℚ ⊂ 𝐹1 ⊂ 𝐹2 ⊂ . . . ⊂ 𝐹 is a solvable chain where each step is cyclic
of degree dividing a prime ℓ ≠ 𝑝, the automorphic representation 𝜋 over 𝐹 descends to automorphic
representations 𝜋𝑖 over 𝐹𝑖 by successive Arthur–Clozel solvable descent.

Skinner–Wiles nearly-ordinary deformation theory, and from Arthur–Clozel solvable base change
used directly for the dihedral sector. Potential automorphy via Calabi–Yau descent is methodologically
distinct from Serre’s conjecture via compatible families.

Sign and convention consistency. Automorphic weight: parallel weight 2 on 𝐹 corresponds to weight 2
on ℚ after descent (Gee 2006 Compositio Math. 142 §2). 𝐿 -parameter normalisation follows Taylor 2003
§1.1 (local parameters at the archimedean places of 𝐹 of the prescribed Hodge–Tate type). Completed-
cohomology normalisation follows Emerton 2011 §1.2. All three sources agree after the standard weight /
𝐿 -parameter correspondences.

The Langlands–Shahidi normalised intertwining operator 𝑁 ( 𝑠, 𝜒 ) of Chapter 64.2.3 has a ﬁrst-order
pole at 𝑠 = 1, while its functional-equation dual has the corresponding ﬁrst-order pole at 𝑠 = 0. Chapter 64
reduced the LACD comparison on the non-exceptional sph-ﬁnite locus Σnonexc = 𝑖 ℝ \ {0} and stated the
two remaining points as Conjecture 64.5.3. This chapter treats the exceptional class in that comparison under
the Emerton–Gee wild-cyclotomic enhancement (Conjecture 40.5.7, the same hypothesis sustaining the F1.a.2
class-match of Chapter 66.2.9 at 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3}), and on the restricted-product Paley–Wiener Ext comparison
for the automorphic Ext1 side. The argument proceeds through four modules. Module (X0) records the two-
point residue data: at 𝑠 = 1 the residual spectrum is the one-dimensional trivial representation (Moœglin–
Waldspurger II.2.4); at 𝑠 = 0 the functional-equation dual is a reducible spherical induction with Steinberg
subquotient (Shahidi 2010 §3.5). Module (X1) computes the local Ext1 -extension class at each crossing from the
ﬁrst-order residue of 𝑁𝑣 ( 𝑠, 𝜒 ) (Shahidi 2010 Thm 3.4.1) and assembles the adelic class via Tate factorisation.
Module (X2) identiﬁes the spectral Ext1 -class on the Emerton–Gee stack via Arthur 2013 §1 endoscopic
classiﬁcation: the residual summand at 𝑠 = 1 lies in the trivial Arthur packet and at 𝑠 = 0 in the Steinberg
Arthur packet; in both cases the Arthur SL2 -factor determines a deformation-theoretic tangent direction
matching the Ext1 of (X1). Module (X3) establishes the class-level match via the arithmetic Koszul–Petersson
compatibility of Chapter 63: the LS-corrected Koszul pairing transports the appropriate leading LS coeﬃcient
onto the tangent direction at the Arthur stratum. The Bushnell–Henniart block of Chapter 47 handles
the 𝑝-adic component; the archimedean component uses Harish-Chandra 1976 Thm 1. Under these two
hypotheses, the exceptional Ext1 -class is matched; the global LACD comparison still depends on the standing
local-global and Bernstein-centre gluing inputs.

Proof. Differentiate the cocycle relation 𝑁𝑣 (− 𝑠, 𝜒 𝑤0 ) ◦ 𝑁𝑣 ( 𝑠, 𝜒 ) = id at a first-order pole. Write

tion, and the 𝑤0−1 from the Weyl translation. This is the local statement; the global statement follows by
taking the adelic product, which preserves the relation factor by factor.

Proposition 97.3.2 (existence and non-triviality of 𝛼𝑣𝑠 =1 ). . The residue R 1,𝑣 :=
Res 𝑠=1 𝑁𝑣 ( 𝑠, 𝜒triv ) is a non-zero intertwining operator R 1,𝑣 : St𝑣 → 1𝑣 with kernel the Steinberg

is non-trivial. Equivalently, dimℂ Ext1𝐺 𝐿2 (ℚ𝑣 ) (St𝑣 , 1𝑣 ) = 1, with 𝛼𝑣𝑠=1 the canonical non-zero class.

Proof. Shahidi 2010 Thm 3.4.1 establishes that the residue of a normalised intertwining operator at a
first-order pole is a non-zero intertwining operator between the Langlands subquotients of the induced
representation at the pole; the cocycle relation (Chapter 64.2.5.1) guarantees this residue is an isomor-
phism on its image. For 𝐺 𝐿2 at 𝑠 = 1 the Langlands subquotients are 1𝑣 and St𝑣 (Chapter 97.2.2 applied
with 𝑠 ↦→ 1 − 𝑠 , exchanging 𝑠 = 0 and 𝑠 = 1 via the cocycle). The extension class is non-trivial because
𝐼𝑣 (1, 𝜒triv ) does not split: if it split, the residual spectrum at 𝑠 = 1 would have two summands, not one
(Moœglin–Waldspurger II.2.4). The dimension of Ext1 (St𝑣 , 1𝑣 ) is 1 at each place: at non-archimedean 𝑣
this is Bernstein–Zelevinsky 1977 Thm 2.9 (the principal series has no higher Ext between composition
factors); at archimedean 𝑣 this is Wallach 1988 Ch. 5.4 (the Harish-Chandra module Ext1 between the
trivial and Steinberg at 𝐺 𝐿2 (ℝ) is one-dimensional).

Proposition 97.3.4 (adelic Ext 1 is a line). . Assume the restricted-product Paley–Wiener Ext com-
parison at the exceptional crossing. Then the global Ext1 at the exceptional crossing is one-dimensional:

Remark 97.4.2 (Arthur parameter for 𝐺 𝐿𝑛 ). For 𝐺 𝐿𝑛 /ℚ, the Arthur classification of Moœglin–
Waldspurger 1989 (for residual spectrum) is a theorem, not a conjecture; Arthur 2013 Ch. 1 §1.4 treats
classical groups and specialises cleanly to 𝐺 𝐿𝑛 . The SL2 -factor 𝜈2 is the Saito–Kurokawa-type correction
of the cuspidal parameter to the residual parameter; for 𝐺 𝐿2 residual = trivial representation, this is the
unique non-cuspidal parameter.

97.6    Compatibilities for Theorem 97.5.4
Seven Compatibilities
Sources. The Eisenstein construction uses Langlands 1976, Shahidi 1990/2010, Arthur 2013 §3.5, Harish-
Chandra 1976, Wallach 1992, and Moœglin–Waldspurger IV. The exceptional class comparison uses
Moœglin–Waldspurger II.2, Shahidi 2010 Thm 3.4.1, Arthur 2013 §1.4–1.5, Emerton–Gee §6.2–6.3, Bel-
laïche–Chenevier, Schlessinger, and Mazur. The common authors occur in different theorems: residual
spectrum, first residue, and endoscopic parameter.

Sign. The residue at a simple pole is fixed by the complex orientation. The functional-equation identity
Res 𝑠=0 = −𝑤0−1 Res 𝑠=1 is Chapter 97.2.3. Multiplying a generator of a one-dimensional Ext1 -line by a
non-zero scalar does not change the line.

Categories. The automorphic class lies in the admissible adelic category over ℂ. The spectral class lies in
IndCohNilp (X𝐺EG𝐿,2wild ). The comparison is made on the common exceptional Galois line 𝐻exc 1 ( 𝐺 , 𝜔 ),
                                                                                                    ℚ
after the chosen scalar extension.

Hypotheses. The wild-EG enhancement and the restricted-product Paley–Wiener Ext1 comparison are
explicit hypotheses. The trivial Hecke character is the only character for which the LS normalising factor
has the exceptional simple pole/zero pair at 𝑠 = 1, 0.

Functoriality. The Koszul residue is natural in 𝜒 . The gerbe tangent line is natural in the residual
Galois representation. The composition preserves the one-dimensional exceptional line and asserts no
higher functoriality.
948                Chapter 97. L ACD Exceptional-Crossing Ext 1 -Class Match at Σ exc = {0 , 1}


Theorems Used. Moœglin–Waldspurger gives the residual representation, Shahidi gives the residue,
Arthur gives the packet, and Emerton–Gee–Schlessinger–Mazur give the deformation tangent. The
derived spectral lift is exactly the wild-EG hypothesis.

No Arithmetic Computation. The statement is a comparison of residue, deformation, and gerbe tangent
lines.
    Thus the exceptional crossing is a conditional class match under the wild-EG enhancement, parallel
to the F1.a.2 class match of Chapter 66.

Conditional Inputs
The automorphic Ext1 -class side (Chapter 97.3.2, Chapter 97.3.4) is unconditional: Shahidi 2010
Thm 3.4.1, Moœglin–Waldspurger II.2.4, Bernstein–Zelevinsky 1977, and Wallach 1988 suffice.
    The spectral Ext1 -class side (Chapter 97.4.5, Chapter 97.4.6) is conditional on the wild-EG enhance-
ment Chapter 40.5.7: the derived degree-1 structure on X𝐺EG𝐿,2wild at the cyclotomic closed point is a
hypothesis. The tangent-space identification is the Emerton–Gee–Schlessinger–Mazur deformation
calculation; the lift of the exceptional line to the derived spectral category is the conditional input.
    The class-match isomorphism Chapter 97.5.4 therefore has the same wild-EG hypothesis as the
spectral side. The residue formula (Chapter 97.5.3) is unconditional (Shahidi 2010 Thm 3.4.1, Tate 1950
adelic factorisation).

   (i) F1.a.1.non-ord: essential surjectivity of DEG at 𝑝 ≥ 5 on the non-ordinary locus.
  (ii) F1.a.1.TW-removal: extension beyond Taylor–Wiles hypotheses.
 (iii) F1.a.2.class-match at 𝑝 ∈ {2, 3}: follows from Chapter 66.2.9 under wild-EG enhancement.

  (v) BC-diamond-glue: Bernstein-centre diamond-gluing.

97.8    Consequences
   (i) Two-point residue data (Chapter 97.2.1, Chapter 97.2.2): at 𝑠 = 1 the residual spectrum is the
       one-dimensional trivial representation (Moœglin–Waldspurger II.2.4); at 𝑠 = 0 the dual spherical
       induction is reducible with Steinberg subquotient. Functional-equation duality (Chapter 97.2.3)
       exchanges the two crossings.
  (ii) Local and adelic Ext1 -classes from residues (Chapter 97.3.2, Chapter 97.3.4): the residue of
       the Langlands–Shahidi normalised intertwining operator at each first-order pole is a non-zero
       intertwining operator defining a non-trivial Ext1 -class 𝛼 𝑠=𝑠0 ; the adelic Ext1 is one-dimensional
       and generated by 𝛼 𝑠=𝑠0 for 𝑠0 ∈ {0, 1}.
 (iii) Spectral Ext1 -class via Arthur endoscopy (Chapter 97.4.5, Chapter 97.4.6): the Arthur parameter
       𝜓1 = [triv ⊠ 𝜈2 ] at 𝑠 = 1 and its functional-equation dual 𝜓0 = [idSL2 ] at 𝑠 = 0 correspond to
       closed points 𝑥cyc and 𝑥triv of the Emerton–Gee stack; the degree-1 tangent fibres at these points
       are one-dimensional with canonical generators 𝑒cyc and 𝑒triv .
 (iv) Class-level match at Σexc (Chapter 97.5.4): under the wild-EG enhancement conjecture, the
       automorphic class 𝛼 𝑠=𝑠0 is sent to the spectral class 𝑒cyc𝑠0 by the composition Koszul-residue ◦
       residual-gerbe tangent. The match is natural in 𝜒 and compatible with F1.a.2.class-match at the
       shared wild primes.
  (v) LACD exceptional Eisenstein reduction (Chapter 97.5.5): the restricted tensor product equiva-
       lence extends from the non-exceptional locus Σnonexc to the exceptional crossings only under the
       same local-global comparison inputs and the restricted-product Paley–Wiener Ext1 comparison.
       The composite LACD statement is a reduction, not an LACD theorem.
 (vi) F1 conditions (Chapter 97.7.1): the LACD exceptional Ext1 -class is matched under wild-EG. The
       global descent problem still contains the standing local-global comparison and Bernstein-centre
       gluing inputs.
(vii) Compatibility of sources (Section 97.6): the residue, Arthur-packet, and gerbe-tangent maps
       have compatible signs, coefficient fields, and one-dimensional exceptional lines.
   Conjecture 64.5.3 is reduced to the wild-EG class match. The Bost–Connes Bernstein-centre
diamond-gluing input remains, and the LACD local-global comparison inputs remain part of the global
descent problem.

Chapter 98


Residual Boundary of the Arithmetic Branch

After the Koszul, chiral-homology, and arithmetic Chern–Simons constructions have reached their
natural boundary, the arithmetic branch has named obstructions. One of them is equivalent to the
Riemann Hypothesis. The others are comparison, descent, regularity, and small-prime hypotheses. The
realization formalism of Chapter 1 is orthogonal to these arithmetic conditions.

98.1   Condensed-Hilbert Descent and Archimedean Tate Positivity
The complete Weil form is defined on the compact convolution algebra A . A geometric Hilbert-space
construction and a comparison with this arithmetic form are separate data.
Theorem 98.1.1 (Weil positivity and an additional descent). For A = 𝐶𝑐∞ (ℝ), positivity 𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗
𝑓 ∗ ) ≥ 0 for every 𝑓 ∈ A is equivalent to RH. The same positivity together with a condensed-Hilbert
descent therefore implies RH. The descent is not needed for this analytic equivalence.
Proof. The explicit signed comparison (57.7) identifies the complete arithmetic form, with its two polar
moments. Weil’s criterion proves the equivalence. Adding a further hypothesis preserves the implication
to RH.
Remark 98.1.2 (continuous and arithmetic purity). Continuous scaling satisfies | 𝐹∞ | = 𝑒 −1/2 1 without
RH. The arithmetic zero operator satisfies | 𝐹𝑍 | = 𝑒 −1/2 1 exactly under RH, by Theorem 90.3.3. A descent
to the continuous carrier does not supply an intertwiner with 𝐹𝑍 . That comparison must be specified
and proved separately.

98.2    The RH-Equivalent Obstruction
The archimedean Tate positivity statement (Chapter 57.2.3) asserts:
                               𝑊 ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓 ∗) ≥ 0       ( 𝑓 ∈ A = 𝐶𝑐∞ (ℝ)) .                            (98.1)
Here 𝑓 ∗ ( 𝑡 ) = 𝑓 (−𝑡 ) and multiplication in A is additive convolution. Equivalently, on P = F+ A , the
inequality is W ( ℎℎ♯ ) ≥ 0, where W ( ℎ) = 𝑊 (F+−1 ℎ) and ℎ♯ ( 𝑧 ) = ℎ ( 𝑧¯ ). Fubini gives F+ ( 𝑓 ∗ 𝑓 ∗ ) =
ℎℎ♯ , so this is an exact change of test algebra. The functional includes its two polar moments, the signed
                                           √
gamma density, and the weights Λ ( 𝑛)/ 𝑛. equation (57.7) constructs its signed pairing. Weil’s criterion
makes positivity for every test equivalent to RH. It is denoted A-TP throughout.
Proposition 98.2.1 (A-TP is an RH-equivalent obstruction). . A-TP (98.1) is an RH-equivalent
obstruction in the arithmetic branch. No other residual in this chapter is used as an RH-equivalent
statement.
Proof. The Fourier map is an algebra isomorphism from convolution on A to multiplication on P
and respects the stated involutions. Thus the displayed inequality is exactly Weil’s compact-test criterion.
The additional comparison inputs do not enter that equivalence.

Theorem 98.3.2 (visible non-RH residuals). . Each input in Chapter 98.3.1 is a non-RH residual
named elsewhere in the arithmetic branch. The statement does not assert exhaustion of all possible
residuals.

Proof. Wild-EG (the Emerton–Gee wild-inertia enhancement) carries F1.a.2 by Chapter 92.3.1, the LACD
exceptional Eisenstein crossing by Chapter 97.5.4, and the wild-inertia component of BC-diamond-glue
by Chapter 95.6.1. Π -flat (pro-étale Π -flatness for the prismatic site) is the cross-prime prismatic flatness
of Chapter 35.5.2, unchanged by Chapter 95. Arithmetic AG (arithmetic Arinkin–Gaitsgory singular
support) is the global singular-support conjecture Chapter 20.1.1, required at the centre of BC-diamond-
glue by Chapter 95.6.1. Clausen–Scholze condensed-Hilbert descent supplies the Hilbert, trace, and
Wilson clauses of the chosen quantum ACS bulk model by Chapter 94.8.4. The other rows are the
named conditional inputs constructed in Chapters 54, 52, 35, 31, 33, 62, and 12. Each is non-RH in form
and is not implied by A-TP.

Remark 98.3.3 (Wild-EG concentration). Wild-EG is the only source conjecture carrying three distinct
class-match conditions. Its proof would simultaneously prove F1.a.2, the exceptional LACD Eisenstein
Ext1 crossing at {0, 1}, and the wild-inertia component of BC-diamond-glue.

98.4      The Generalised Ramanujan Conjecture for GL 4
The Rankin–Selberg square of a Maass form on GL2 /ℚ comes from an isobaric automorphic object on
GL4 /ℚ. Full temperedness of that GL4 object at every finite place, equivalently GRC for its cuspidal
98.5. 𝐹1 .a.1 Small Residuals                                                                           955


factors, closes the Maass sector of the V prim Hochschild-trace identity. This conjecture is separated from
A-TP in the proof: it concerns Satake eigenvalues, not zero placement.
Hypothesis 98.4.1 (GRC for GL4 /ℚ in the Selberg class). . The isobaric automorphic representations of
GL4 /ℚ arising from the Rankin–Selberg square of a Maass form have tempered cuspidal factors at every
finite place.
Proposition 98.4.2 (GRC-GL 4 closes the Maass sector). . Conditional on Chapter 98.4.1, full
Ramanujan holds for the Maass forms entering the V prim Hochschild-trace 𝑃3 identity of Chapter 93.6.1.
This closes the Maass sector. The hypothesis is not equivalent to RH; no implication between this
hypothesis and A-TP is used.

Proof. Chapter 93 proves that the Arthur–Ramakrishnan–GRC hypothesis implies full Ramanujan
for Maass forms (Chapter 93.5.5) and reduces that hypothesis to Chapter 98.4.1 (Chapter 93.5.6). The
𝑃3 identity is the exact conditional statement of Chapter 93.6.1. A-TP concerns the zeros of 𝜁 through
Weil positivity; GRC-GL4 concerns Satake parameters. The argument uses the two residuals as separate
inputs.

98.5    𝐹1 .a.1 Small Residuals
Two small residuals occur in the 𝐹1 .a.1 table of Chapter 96. They are not a count of all small residuals in
the arithmetic branch.
Proposition 98.5.1 (small residuals). . Besides the generator-comparison inputs and the automor-
phy/patching hypotheses isolated in Chapter 96.3.4 and Chapter 96.3.5, the 𝐹1 .a.1 table has the following
two small residual tails:
   (i) Supersingular small-weight tail (Chapter 96.2.8): Fontaine–Laffaille representations with
       Hodge–Tate weights 𝑘 ∈ { 𝑝 − 1, 𝑝 }, requires a non-formal theorem.
  (ii) 𝐴5 non-solvable descent defect (Chapter 96.3.8): local-global descent defect in the icosahedral
       sector, requires a non-formal theorem.

Proof. The two listed residual tails are read from Chapter 96.4.2. The Fontaine–Laffaille supersingu-
lar core is reduced to the generator comparison of Chapter 96.2.6. The odd-determinant icosahedral
core is reduced to the conditional theorem of Chapter 96.3.6. The two tails listed above are additional
obstructions in that decomposition.

98.6    Separation from the Realization Formalism
The obstructions above are internal to the arithmetic branch. The realization formalism of Chapter 1
concerns independent verification data for Vols I–III; the arithmetic branch does not supply those data.
Proposition 98.6.1 (realization formalism is orthogonal to the arithmetic branch). . The
arithmetic branch does not construct independent comparison data for the source Vols I–III Proved-
Here claims. Its obstructions concern arithmetic comparison, descent, temperedness, and small-prime
regularity.

Proof. The preceding sections use only the arithmetic conditions A-TP, comparison and descent, GRC
for GL4 , and the two 𝐹1 .a.1 residuals. None of these data is a independent comparison pair for a source
theorem of Vols I–III.
956                              Chapter 98. Residual Boundary of the Arithmetic Branch


98.7    Residual Boundary
Theorem 98.7.1 (arithmetic branch obstruction decomposition). . The arithmetic branch has, at
least, the following obstructions:
   (i) one statement equivalent to RH: archimedean Tate positivity;
  (ii) the comparison and descent inputs of Chapter 98.3.1;
 (iii) one Ramanujan-type hypothesis separated from A-TP: GRC for GL4 /ℚ;
 (iv) the two 𝐹1 .a.1 small residuals of Chapter 98.5.1.
The Vol IV realization formalism for Vols I–III is orthogonal to the arithmetic branch.

Proof. Item (1) is Chapter 98.2.1. Item (2) is Chapter 98.3.2. Item (3) is Chapter 98.4.2. Item (4) is
Chapter 98.5.1. The separation from the realization formalism is Chapter 98.6.1. No implication from
the table to RH is asserted except through A-TP.

Remark 98.7.2 (domain of the boundary). The theorem isolates the displayed RH-equivalent content
into A-TP and places the visible non-RH obstructions in named inputs. It does not prove RH and it
does not claim that the arithmetic comparison is complete.

B.2    Obstructions Across Source Families
The following nine structural assertions about V prim are obstructed at specific algebraic or geometric
joints, identified independently across the fifteen source comparisons:
    (i) V prim is not a vertex operator algebra. The Polyakov obstruction is the central charge: 𝑐 = 𝑝 2 =
                                                                                                    P
        ∞, and 𝜁ℙ (0) has a natural boundary.
   (ii) !𝑝 H ( 𝑝 ) is not defined over a single field. Different ℚ 𝑝 cannot be glued into one ground field.
        N

 (iii) Beilinson–Drinfeld factorization on Spec ℤ is obstructed at the diagonal. The completed tensor
        product ℤ 𝑝 b ⊗ℤ ℤ 𝑝 = ℤ 𝑝 admits no 𝑝-adic diagonal thickening.
  (iv) 𝑇𝑛 does not lift Adams operations to 𝐺 𝐿2 Hecke operators. The explicit Kazhdan–Beilinson
                                   ( 𝑝)             ( 𝑝)            ( 𝑝)
        computation gives 𝑇𝑝2 ( 𝑎−1 |0⟩) − 𝑝 · 𝑎−1 |0⟩ ≠ 𝑇𝑝2 ( 𝑎−1 |0⟩).
   (v) V prim is not a Borger Λ-ring on the Fock ℤ-lattice. The Wilkerson congruence fails there; after
       extension to ℂ the condition loses arithmetic content.
  (vi) Arithmetic Yangian RTT relations have no global spectral parameter. The Yang-Baxter spectral
       parameter 𝑢 − 𝑣 has no analogue across distinct primes; there is no meromorphic 1-form on Spec ℤ.
 (vii) A 4D class-S gauge boundary does not transplant to Spec ℤ. The Hitchin base 𝑖 𝐻 0 ( Σ, 𝐾Σ𝑑𝑖 )
                                                                                        L

       uses a holomorphic canonical bundle on a complex curve. The Arakelov dualizing line on Spec ℤ
       is not such an object.
(viii) The curve-theoretic category of D-modules on Bun𝐺 𝐿2 does not arise from Spec ℤ itself. The
       moduli stack Bun𝐺 𝐿2 (Spec ℤ) is 𝐵𝐺 𝐿2 (ℤ): one coarse point with arithmetic stabilizer. This
       stack has representation theory of the stabilizer, not the geometric Hecke correspondence of the
       curve case.
  (ix) The integral 𝐸2 -chiral-centre enhancement is not obtained by replacing the chain operad
       𝐶• ( 𝐸2 ; ℤ) with Gerℤ . The arity-two permutation action obstructs this comparison by
       Theorem 17.2.1. Integral 𝐸2 -algebras can exist. For an individual DGA, formality has a separate
       obstruction: Theorem 17.7.2 computes it for the explicit relative derived centre 𝐶𝑆,𝑟 .

B.3    Common Structural Constraints
Five structural constraints remain, each identified independently across multiple source comparisons:
   (i) The arithmetic curve is Arakelov-compactified Spec ℤ, not Spec ℤ (across source families).
  (ii) Each finite place carries only 𝐸0 (locally-constant) factorization structure; the 𝐸1 -chiral OPE lives
       at the archimedean place (Drinfeld+Kapranov, Costello+Gwilliam, Kontsevich+Soibelman).
 (iii) The Arnold relation lifts to the Steinberg relation { 𝑝, 1 − 𝑝 } = 0; chiral bar is built on Parshin–
       Gersten (Beilinson–solo).
B.4. Three-Way Gluing of Presentations                                                                   971


 (iv) The Hecke structure is carried by the Iwahori-equivariant affine Hecke category, not the spherical
      category (Bezrukavnikov+Bernstein, Kazhdan+Beilinson).
  (v) The Iwahori Hecke Hochschild trace is the local Bezrukavnikov–Bernstein model. Its global
      identification with V prim is the arithmetic BZN input F3. Kim arithmetic Chern–Simons (Kim
      arXiv:1510.05818) provides the classical boundary torsor construction, and the adelic factorization
      algebra lives on ℂ∞ (Costello+Gwilliam).

B.5    Independence
The fifteen source families are disjoint at the level of primary citations. Each family detects a structural
obstruction in the initial construction. The common object is the intersection of the remaining trace-
theoretic structures.

B.6    Convergence Theorem
Theorem B.6.1 (convergence of the fifteen constructions). The obstructed structures above dis-
appear at disjoint structural joints. The remaining constraints are independent of the source class de-
tecting them. The fifteen independent constructions converge on a common trace object with the
six-conditional-window synthesis of Chapter 19.1.1 and the three boundary conjectures F1–F3 of Chap-
ter 20.1, Chapter 20.2, Chapter 20.3.
    This convergence is the mathematical content of the arithmetic branch: the object V prim is not
the outcome of any single source comparison but the intersection of trace-theoretic structures across
fifteen independent comparisons. This isolates the Hochschild-trace-class construction as the common
remnant.

Obstructions
The six source families jointly obstruct six readings of the initial ansatz (Chapter 81.3 indexes the full
list): the category-error reading of ‘‘almost complex structure on an arithmetic scheme’’ (no real tangent
bundle on Spec ℤ; Newlander–Nirenberg automatic on real 2-manifolds); ‘‘arithmetic Euler character-
istic = 1 − 𝑔 ’’ (Gillet–Soulé analytic torsion term); Künneth factorisation in arithmetic Chow (Bost–
Künnemann Bott–Chern term); finite genus of Spec ℤ in the Deninger frame (Deninger-genus = +∞);
B.7. Six Source Families in Genus 𝑔                                                                   973


conflation of curve-genus with Siegel-genus (distinct integers); and the 𝜅 + 𝜅 ! = 2 − 2 𝑔 Euler-shift
(Koszul sum preserved at 0; genus enters via rank, not shift).

Converged Surviving Object
The arithmetic genus- 𝑔 datum D 𝑔 = (B 𝑔 , E 𝑔 , 𝜑 𝑔 ) (Chapter 81.1.1), with the essential conditional

Source Disjointness
The six genus- 𝑔 source families are disjoint at the level of primary citations. The common arithmetic-
modular datum is their common structural remnant.

C.6    Chain of Implications
The arithmetic branch has the following implication form:
   (i) The G-row conjecture (Chapter C.5.1) would identify the Riemann functional equation as an
       arithmetic Koszul-duality consequence.
  (ii) F3 conditional on F1 and F2 unifies the three presentations of V prim .
 (iii) F1 is the global arithmetic Arinkin–Gaitsgory input.
 (iv) F2 is the perfectoid 𝐸2 -enhancement input.
  (v) F1, F2, and the conditional F3 comparison imply the six-window structural statement.

C.7    Connection to Vol III
Vol III’s B-row 𝜅 + 𝜅 ! = 8 (Mukai-enhanced K3 Heisenberg via Bruinier Heegner Chern-class reciprocity)
has an arithmetic avatar (F4, Chapter 20 §3). Together the arithmetic G-row and the arithmetic B-row
would give two of the five Vol I derived-centre-ceiling values as consequences of automorphic and Galois-
deformation theorems. The chiral centre is then constrained by arithmetic comparison data.

and whose other clauses are the positive Hermitian, Koszul, and Zhu structures on V prim . The arrows

    The two branches are logically independent. The F1–F3 structural branch constructs the trace object.
The four-input RH branch controls zero placement. A theorem on one branch is not a theorem on the
other.

C.11   Dependency Boundary
Three hierarchically ordered conjectures (F1 → F2 → F3) and one independent conjecture (G-row)
govern the synthesis branch. On the RH branch: P1 (functional equation), P2 (Tate adelic), P3 (restricted
Koszul unitarity), H-PAr (Hilbert–Pólya determinant-divisor matching), and VB∗ (arithmetic Virasoro–
Bogomolov zero-mode positivity, RH-equivalent). The restricted pointed central-unit theorem gives
the proved part of F2.c, and the strict abelian primary arithmetic Positselski bar supplies the P1 forward
direction. The arithmetic branch as stated (Chapter 21, Chapter 22) reduces the RH-strength condition
to H-PAr determinant-trace realisation and the positive Hamburger VB∗ condition.
